Name: VidPrevtyn Beta®
Indication: Immunisation to prevent severe disease and death caused by COVID-19
Mechanism of action: VAT00008 uses the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein combined with GSK’s AS03 adjuvant to stimulate immunity. It induces neutralizing antibodies to block the virus from entering cells and activates T-cells for long-term protection, providing robust defense against COVID-19.
Key features and challenges:
Vx Schedule: Day 0 + 21

VAT00008 is an adjuvanted recombinant protein-based COVID-19 vaccine developed by Sanofi and GSK. It uses the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein (S-protein) as its antigen, combined with GSK’s proprietary AS03 adjuvant to enhance immune responses. This vaccine leverages recombinant protein technology, a well-established platform known for safety and scalability. The AS03 adjuvant boosts immunogenicity, enabling a strong and long-lasting immune response even with a smaller dose of antigen. VAT00008 is stable at standard refrigeration temperatures, making it easier to distribute globally, especially in low-resource settings. Clinical trials have evaluated both monovalent and bivalent formulations, targeting emerging SARS-CoV-2 variants. However, the vaccine faces several challenges. Despite its promising safety and immunogenicity profile, it competes in a crowded market dominated by mRNA vaccines, which are faster to adapt to new variants. Additionally, adjuvanted vaccines may raise concerns about reactogenicity, requiring comprehensive safety monitoring. Regulatory approvals, including WHO Emergency Use Listing (EUL), depend on strong efficacy data from ongoing Phase III trials. Another challenge is ensuring equitable global distribution amid logistical hurdles and high demand for COVID-19 vaccines worldwide. Despite these obstacles, VAT00008 remains a promising candidate for broad and durable protection against COVID-19.
Recent updates:
Dec 2024: It received approval for medical use in the European Union in November 2022 under the brand name VidPrevtyn Beta. Clinical trials have demonstrated its efficacy as a booster vaccine, showing significant increases in antibody titers against various SARS-CoV-2 variants, including the Beta strain. 

The vaccine is currently authorized for use in the EU, with ongoing evaluations to determine its efficacy against emerging variants and its potential for broader global distribution.

Name: "Test-it" PrCr urinalysis dipstick test
Indication: Diagnosis of preeclampsia
Target: Protein to creatinine ratio in urine
Mechanism of action: Synthetic antimicrobial peptide that permeabilizes bacterial membranes to induce rapid bactericidal activity against Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
Key features and challenges:
Proteinuria is elevated in women with preeclampsia and a primary clinical indicator for identifying the risk of developing PE/E in pregnant women. PATH and LifeAssays Diagnostics have collaborated on the development of a protein-to-creatinine ratio rapid test as an improvement from protein-only measurement and a quicker diagnosis than standard proteinuria determination (results in 60 seconds versus a 24-hour urine collection test). Test-it™ is a urinary dipstick test that measures the ratio of protein and creatinine concentrations in mg/dL in urine samples at point-of-care. A threshold of 0.30 is applied to classify results as abnormal or normal for proteinuria. 
 
A prospective cross-sectional diagnostic accuracy study was conducted in Ghana in 2018. The test demonstrated improved clinical performance for detection of proteinuria over the current standard-of-care tests widely used in Ghana. Test-it™ showed a sensitivity of 50.7% and specificity of 69.2% when run at the point of care. In contrast, the standard-of-care Accu-Tell® protein dipstick test was found to have a sensitivity of 32.4% and a specificity of 82.2% 
(https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2210778922000733). The test is CE approved 
PATH documentation: (https://media.path.org/documents/FINAL_DFID-DAWN-PrCr-fs-June_2019.pdf).​

Name: 24-hour urine protein excretion test (UPET)
Indication: Diagnosis of preeclampsia
Mechanism of action: Inhibits matrix metalloproteinase activity to prevent cervical extracellular matrix degradation and delay cervical remodeling and contractions.
Key features and challenges:
PE is characterised by reduced renal perfusion and damage to glomerular basement membrane resulting in leakage of proteins in the urine. Normally, pregnant women excrete minimal amounts of proteins in the urine (up to 150 mg/day) because of renal changes that occur during pregnancy; however, proteinuria >300 mg/day is considered abnormal for pregnant women. 
The estimation of 24-hour urine proteins has been considered the gold standard for quantitation of proteinuria and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends measuring proteinuria with either a 24-hour value or a protein to creatinine ratio in a single voided urine for the diagnosis of preeclampsia. (https://journals.lww.com/greenjournal/citation/2013/11000/hypertension_in_pregnancy__executive_summary.36.aspx) 
 
Proteinuria is not mandatory for a diagnosis of preeclampsia but is present in about 75% of cases. Rather, PE is diagnosed by the presence of de novo hypertension after 20 weeks of gestation accompanied by proteinuria and/or evidence of maternal acute kidney injury, liver dysfunction, neurological features, haemolysis or thrombocytopenia, and/or fetal growth restriction. 
(https://www.mdpi.com/1660-4601/17/12/4195)​

Name: 2GARD
Indication:
Prevention and control of malaria in children and adults living in areas with ongoing malaria transmission.
WHO policy: strong recommendation, low certainty evidence
Mechanism of action: Sodium channel modulator and nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) competitive modulators
Key features and challenges:
2GARD® is a next-generation indoor residual spray (IRS) that combines clothianidin, a neonicotinoid, with a complementary active ingredient to provide a dual-action solution for malaria vector control. This innovative formulation offers both immediate knockdown of adult mosquitoes and long-lasting residual efficacy, making it highly effective against insecticide-resistant mosquito populations.  

Designed for versatility, 2GARD® adheres well to various indoor surfaces and maintains its effectiveness for extended periods, reducing the need for frequent applications. By introducing multiple modes of action, it supports resistance management strategies and enhances its role in integrated vector control programs.  

Despite its advanced features, 2GARD® faces challenges, including higher costs compared to traditional single-action IRS products, limited awareness about its benefits in some regions, and the need for trained personnel to ensure proper application. Additionally, ongoing monitoring is essential to prevent resistance to its active ingredients.  

2GARD® represents a significant step forward in vector control, addressing critical challenges of resistance and sustainability. Its dual-action formulation offers a powerful tool for reducing malaria transmission, particularly in high-burden regions. Overcoming barriers to cost and implementation will be vital to maximizing its impact.

Name: 3D power doppler (3DPD) - IUGR
Developers: Benha University; University of Maryland, Baltimore (including CVD)
Indication: Prediction and diagnosis of IUGR
Target: Placental and fetal blood flow indices
Key features and challenges:
​Three-dimensional power doppler is a 3D imaging technique that associates anatomical images (grayscale) with power doppler signal. Power doppler, compared to colour doppler, has the advantage of being based on the study of the amplitude of the US signal and therefore being less dependent on the insonation angle, less sensitive to the distraction or aliasing phenomena, and therefore more sensitive to detect very low velocity flows and smaller vessels. Combined with volume of interest (VOI) analysis, it should in theory be possible with the 3DPD technique to quantify the vascularisation directly within the utero-placental unit. 
 
A study in the USA sought to determine whether fetuses with fetal growth restriction (FGR) are more likely to have abnormal cerebral vascular flow patterns compared to fetuses who are appropriate for gestational age (AGA) when quantified by using 3-dimensional (3D) power doppler ultrasound. Results demonstrated that three-dimensional power doppler measurement of cerebral blood flow, but not the vascularisation pattern, is significantly altered in FGR. The study asserted that this measurement may play a future role in distinguishing pathologic FGR from constitutionally small growth (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28708246/).​

Name: ACAM2000
Indication: Prevention of Mpox disease
Mechanism of action: Immunostimulant
Key features and challenges:
Emergent Biosolutions (formerly Sanofi Pasteur Biologics) has developed a single-dose vaccine against smallpox and monkeypox, ACAM 2000, under a contract with the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), in order to provide the US Government with a modern smallpox vaccine derived from Wyeth Pharmaceuticals' Dryvax® smallpox vaccine. The vaccine has received approval from the US FDA for the treatment of Mpox. ACAM2000® is launched in the USA and Australia, and registered in Singapore, Canada.

ACAM 2000, which is administered by percutaneous scarification using a bifurcated needle, was produced using modern cell culture methods. Preclinical data indicated that the vaccine is free from contaminating bacteria and viruses and could be less neurovirulent than Dryvax®, which was the first-generation vaccine registered in the US and used during the worldwide smallpox eradication programme. As Dryvax® was found to contain multiple subpopulations of vaccinia virus, Acambis derived ACAM 2000™ from Dryvax® through a cloning process. Acambis isolated a clone that closely resembles the first-generation vaccine's profile but also has an acceptable or improved safety profile. A vaccine candidate was subsequently selected, which was consistently less virulent and provided equivalent protection

Key features and challenges:
The Aptima® HIV-1 Quant Dx Assay, developed by Hologic, is a dual-claim diagnostic tool used to confirm HIV-1 infection and measure viral load in HIV-positive patients. Name: ASAQ Winthrop®
Developers: Sanofi; Drugs for Neglected Diseases initiative (DNDi)
Indication: Treatment of uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria in adults, children and infants >5kg (except pregnant women in their first trimester)
Mechanism of action: Free radical stimulant
Key features and challenges: 3-day cure, artemisinin-based combination therapy (artesunate-amodiaquine) (TPP-1). A once-daily tablet of fixed-dose combination of artesunate 200mg and amodiaquine 270mg was developed by Sanofi (formerly sanofi-aventis) and Drugs for Neglected Diseases Initiative (DNDi) Foundation, for the treatment of uncomplicated Plasmodium spp malaria. This product was developed in an effort to provide an easier to use, less expensive, single tablet therapy for patients with malaria. It was launched in sub-Saharan Africa. Treatment failure after amodiaquine monotherapy was more frequent among children who were underweight for their age. Therefore, their response to artesunate + amodiaquine treatment should be closely monitored. Artesunate + amodiaquine is associated with severe neutropenia, particularly in patients co-infected with HIV and especially in those on zidovudine and/or cotrimoxazole. Concomitant use of efavirenz increases exposure to amodiaquine and hepatotoxicity. Thus, concomitant use of artesunate + amodiaquine by patients taking zidovudine, efavirenz and cotrimoxazole should be avoided, unless this is the only ACT promptly available. No significant changes in the pharmacokinetics of amodiaquine or its metabolite desethylamodiaquine have been observed during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy; therefore, no dosage adjustments are recommended. No effect of age has been observed on the plasma concentrations of amodiaquine and desethylamodiaquine, so no dose adjustment by age is indicated. Few data are available on the pharmacokinetics of amodiaquine in the first year of life. Lower price compared to other prequalified artemisinin-based combination therapies (public-sector tenders). Three-year shelf life. Amodiaquine resistance in some countries. Currently being withdrawn from countries where SPAQ is deployed for seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC) following WHO recommendation. Approved in 33 countries. 537 million treatments distributed since 2007
Recent updates: 540 million treatments distributed since 2007. Approved in 33 countries

Name: Abdominal circumference (AC)
Indication: Diagnosis and prediction of IUGR
Mechanism of action: Quantifies INSL5 levels to assess altered metabolic and gut–endocrine signaling associated with insulin resistance in PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
​Abdominal circumference (AC) is one of the basic biometric parameters used to assess fetal size. AC together with biparietal diameter (BPD), head circumference (HC), and femur length (FL) are computed to produce an estimate of fetal weight. In the second trimester, this may be extrapolated to an estimate of gestational age and an estimated due date (EDD). AC is measured with a transverse section through the upper abdomen, which measures the fetal stomach, umbilical vein, and portal sinus. Abdominal circumference measurement should not be taken on a foreshortened abdomen and the callipers should be on the skin surface (skin surface should be visible). The kidneys and cord insertion should not be visible. The umbilical vein should not be seen up to the skin line, considering a true transverse view (portal sinus, fetal stomach, symmetrical fetal ribs, and the level of the junction of umbilical vein) without maternal abdominal compression (https://radiopaedia.org/articles/fetal-abdominal-circumference?lang=gb). 
 
A fetus is considered SGA when its size (biometric evaluation) falls below a predefined threshold for its gestational age. The most common definition of SGA is EFW or AC below the 10th percentile of given reference ranges. While SGA and IUGR are not the same, a fetus with birth weight below the 10th percentile is at increased risk of stillbirth and perinatal mortality, with those with birth weight below the 3rd percentile being at the highest risk. For this reason, fetal size at the lower extreme of the growth charts, for example AC or EFW below the 3rd percentile for given growth charts, can be used as an isolated criterion to define FGR at any gestational epoch.

Name: Actim Partus rapid test
Indication: Prediciton of PTL
Mechanism of action: A commercially available one-step immuno-enzymatic dipstick test (Actim Partus) for detection of the presence of phIGFBP1 in cervical secretions
Key features and challenges:
Actim® Partus is a commercially available, one-step dipstick test designed to detect phosphorylated insulin-like growth factor binding protein-1 (phIGFBP-1) in cervical secretions. The test can be used from 22 weeks of gestation onward in women presenting with symptoms suggestive of preterm labour. Sampling is completed within seconds, and results are available in approximately five minutes. Reported performance characteristics indicate that results are not affected by urine, semen, intercourse, vaginal medications, lubricants, bathing products, or common infections.
PhIGFBP-1 is released into cervical secretions during disruption of the chorio-decidual interface, which is associated with the onset of preterm labour. Detection of this biomarker supports risk stratification in symptomatic women.
In a 2002 study involving 36 pregnant women between 28 and 37 weeks’ gestation with singleton pregnancies, intact membranes, and abdominal pain, the diagnostic accuracy of the Actim Partus test was reported as 66.6%. Sensitivity was higher in women with gestational age below 34 weeks compared with overall sensitivity.
(https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1471-0528.10_17178)
The test has been reported to have a high negative predictive value (approximately 98%), indicating that a negative result effectively rules out imminent preterm delivery in symptomatic women.
Overall, Actim® Partus is positioned as a rapid point-of-care screening tool for threatened preterm labour, particularly useful for ruling out imminent delivery and potentially reducing unnecessary hospital admissions and interventions. Further large-scale validation studies are important to confirm diagnostic performance across diverse populations.

Name: Allplex STI Essential assay - Gonorrhea
Indication: Detection of gonorrhoeae
Mechanism of action: multiplex PCR
Key features and challenges:
Allplex™ STI Essential assay is a multiplex real-time PCR diagnostic platform developed by Seegene for simultaneous detection of sexually transmitted pathogens, including Neisseria gonorrhoeae. The assay is designed to enable high-throughput, etiological diagnosis of STIs from multiple specimen types.
A 2023 study evaluating STI etiologies among men who have sex with men (MSM) in Taiwan assessed the performance of the Allplex™ STI Essential assay in comparison with the BD MAX CT/GC/TV assay (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1684118222001384?via%3Dihub). 
Using nucleic acids extracted by the BD MAX system, the study confirmed effective detection of Chlamydia trachomatis, N. gonorrhoeae, and Trichomonas vaginalis. High STI prevalence was observed, particularly in rectal swabs compared with urine samples, underscoring the importance of sensitive multiplex molecular diagnostics in high-risk populations.
Key challenges include dependence on laboratory infrastructure and specialized instrumentation, cost considerations relative to single-target assays, and the need for validation across diverse geographic and epidemiological settings. Implementation in decentralized or low-resource environments may be limited.
Overall, the Allplex™ STI Essential assay represents a comprehensive multiplex molecular diagnostic platform for gonorrhea and other STIs. Broader implementation studies are required to assess scalability and real-world clinical impact.

A 2023 study investigating STI etiologies among men who have sex with men (MSM) in Taiwan evaluated the performance of the Allplex™ STI Essential assay in comparison with the BD MAX CT/GC/TV assay (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1684118222001384?via%3Dihub). Using nucleic acids extracted via the BD MAX system, the study confirmed effective multiplex detection of STI pathogens. High rates of STI-associated infections were observed, particularly in rectal swabs compared with urine specimens, highlighting the importance of sensitive molecular diagnostics in high-risk populations.
Key challenges include reliance on laboratory-based PCR infrastructure, cost considerations relative to single-target assays, and the need for performance evaluation in diverse clinical and geographic contexts. Resistance detection capabilities are not inherently included and may require complementary assays.
Overall, the Allplex™ STI Essential assay provides a comprehensive multiplex molecular diagnostic approach for M. genitalium and other STIs. Further implementation research is needed to assess scalability and impact in routine clinical practice.

Developers: Shengjing Hospital of China Medical University; Fudan University; Organon & Co.
Indication: Prevention of preterm labour/birth
Mechanism of action: Progesterone receptor agonist
Key features and challenges:
Allylestrenol is a synthetic steroid with progestational activity that has historically been used for threatened miscarriage, recurrent miscarriage, threatened preterm labour, and intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR). It has been marketed widely in parts of Europe and Asia, although it has not been approved in the United States or Canada and has been discontinued in several countries. Current clinical recommendations advise against its routine use in obstetric indications except in cases of confirmed progesterone deficiency.
A 2017 clinical review described allylestrenol as having pregnancy-maintaining and fetal weight-promoting properties, with minimal androgenic activity. The review noted its long-standing use in threatened abortion and threatened preterm labour, typically at doses of 30–40 mg/day when used without additional tocolytics. However, the same source acknowledged that contemporary recommendations limit its use in the absence of documented progesterone deficiency.
(http://dx.doi.org/10.5005/jp-journals-10006-1517)
A 2020 study reported that allylestrenol may exert selective β-adrenergic effects mediated through β₂ receptors on myometrial smooth muscle, reducing uterine activity and promoting relaxation of hypertonic myometrium. The study also discussed investigation of allylestrenol in combination with other tocolytics such as ritodrine.
(Source: 2020 – https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32010251/)
In 2021, a clinical trial was initiated in China to evaluate the efficacy and safety of allylestrenol tablets (Dolim) compared with progesterone soft capsules (Utrogestan) in preventing late miscarriage and preterm birth; results have not yet been reported.
Overall, allylestrenol has a historical role as a progestational agent for threatened preterm labour and related obstetric complications. However, contemporary guidance limits its use to cases of proven progesterone deficiency, and current evidence supporting its routine use in PTL/PTB prevention remains limited.

Name: Amino acid chelated iron
Developers: Cairo University; Ain Shams University; Assiut University; South Valley University
Indication: Indicated for the treatment and prevention of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Immunochromatographic lateral flow assay detecting Trichomonas vaginalis antigens in vaginal specimens.
Key features and challenges:
Amino acid chelated iron is designed to enhance iron bioavailability and avoid interactions with food ingredients. When the iron is chelated, amino acids are bonded to the iron to form a new molecule. This allows the chelated iron to remain intact in the gastrointestinal tract prior to absorption. Therefore, chelated iron is reported to have a more rapid effect with less gastrointestinal tract  side effects. Ferrotron is an amino acid chelated iron that is marketed in Egypt, also containing other multivitamins and essential trace elements. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11688075/ and https://ebwhj.journals.ekb.eg/article_73816.html). 

Amino acid chelated iron has been studied for its use in the prevention and treatment of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy. A study conducted by Ain-Shams University in Cairo, Egypt aimed to find out whether there is a difference between amino acid chelated iron and iron salts (ferrous fumarate) in effect, safety, adverse effects and outcomes in treatment of iron deficiency anemia during pregnancy. Results demonstrated that amino acid chelated iron achieves a faster cure rate than ferrous fumarate in women with iron deficiency anemia in pregnancy (regarding Hb and serum ferritin level) and is also associated with fewer side effects. (https://ebwhj.journals.ekb.eg/article_73816.html) 

Another study by Assiut University (NCT02858505) looked at the impact of one versus two amino acid chelated iron capsules on the prevention of iron deficiency anaemia in non-anemic women with twin gestations. Women were given 27mg or 54mg of elemental iron from 12 to 36 weeks gestation. Haemoglobin was the primary outcome. Results demonstrated that the single dose was comparable to the double dose. Furthermore, the double dose was associated with more side effects. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27894198/)

Developers: Drugs for Neglected Diseases initiative (DNDi); Gilead; Grupo Biotoscana; Sumitomo Pharma Co. Ltd.

Key features and challenges:
The liposomal amphotericin B (AmB) formulation still represents the best therapeutic option for cutaneous and visceral leishmaniasis. However, its clinical efficacy depends on the patient’s immunological status, the clinical manifestation and the endemic region. Moreover, the need for parenteral administration, its side effects, high cost and poor thermostability above 25 oC significantly limit its use in developing countries. 

The most prominent mechanism of action of AmB involves its binding to ergosterol, the main component of fungal or parasitic cell membranes, resulting in transmembrane pores which lead to cell death.

Besides being toxic to fungal and Leishmania cells, AmB can be toxic to human tissues. AmB toxicity is related to its binding to cholesterol, oxidation of cell membranes and production of ROS. Nephrotoxicity represents an AmB major side effect, with AmB supramolecular organization influencing this effect.

(https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9864876/)

Single dose Amphotericin has proven to be highly efficient in VL in Asia in DNDi led clinical trials and is now considered in many national guidelines as first line therapy. Anaphylaxis possible - Toxic renal effects, however in single dose administration rather negligible.

Name: Androstenedione
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS via hyperandrogenism detection
Mechanism of action: Elevated levels of androstenedione can be indicative of hyperandrogenism. High levels are often associated with ovarian dysfunction, adrenal hyperplasia, or other endocrine disorders. It reflects gonadal or adrenal androgen excess, which can disrupt normal menstrual cycles, ovulation, and lead to symptoms like hirsutism.
Key features and challenges:
Androstenedione is a steroid hormone that plays a key role in the production of both testosterone and estrogen. In the context of diagnosing polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), androstenedione is useful for assessing hyperandrogenism, which is a central feature of PCOS. Elevated levels of androstenedione, alongside other androgens like testosterone and DHEA-S, are often found in women with PCOS, helping clinicians diagnose the condition.

Recommendations from Monash University (2023) for PCOS management suggest measuring androstenedione and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS) when total or free testosterone levels are not elevated, acknowledging their lower specificity and age-related decline in DHEAS. Accurate assessment requires validated tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) for total testosterone, androstenedione, and DHEAS. (https://academic.oup.com/jcem/article/108/10/2447/7242360)
​
Measurement of androstenedione is useful not only in diagnosing PCOS but also in assessing the severity of the disease, particularly its metabolic and reproductive features. Recent studies also indicate that this hormone can help distinguish between different PCOS subtypes and monitor the effectiveness of treatments aimed at reducing androgen excess​.

The current PCOS Phenotype in Unselected Populations Study (P-PUP) aims to define diagnostic cut-offs for key PCOS features, including androstenedione, anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), menstrual cycle length, ovarian follicle count, and other androgen levels. By analyzing individual participant data from global studies, the research seeks to clarify the distinction between PCOS and non-PCOS populations and support updates to international diagnostic guidelines. (https://www.mdpi.com/2075-4418/11/11/1953)

Indication: Detection of T vaginalis
Mechanism of action: single real-time PCR
Key features and challenges:
AnyPlex™ II STI-7e panel assay is a multiplex real-time PCR diagnostic platform designed for simultaneous detection of seven major sexually transmitted pathogens, including Trichomonas vaginalis. The assay utilizes Seegene’s proprietary Dual Priming Oligonucleotide (DPO) and Tagging Oligonucleotide Cleavage and Extension (TOCE) technologies to enable pathogen-specific amplification and detection within approximately 3.2 hours following DNA extraction.
A 2022 study compared the performance of the AnyPlex™ II STI-7e assay with standard-of-care diagnostic methods using cervical, vaginal, and urine samples from 1,330 women (https://academic.oup.com/lambio/article/76/1/ovac002/6887826#435213644). 
While the assay demonstrated strong performance for detection of Mycoplasma genitalium and Chlamydia trachomatis, evaluation of T. vaginalis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae was limited due to low prevalence in the study population. Only 0.9% of participants tested positive for T. vaginalis by wet mount microscopy, restricting definitive performance assessment for this pathogen.
Key challenges include limited data for T. vaginalis in low-prevalence populations, dependence on laboratory infrastructure, and cost considerations for multiplex molecular testing. Broader validation in higher-prevalence settings is required to establish diagnostic accuracy for trichomoniasis.
Overall, the AnyPlex™ II STI-7e panel assay provides a comprehensive multiplex molecular diagnostic approach for trichomoniasis and other STIs. Further evaluation in diverse epidemiological settings is needed to confirm its performance and clinical utility.

Aptima Combo 2 Assay is a target amplification nucleic acid probe test designed for the qualitative detection and differentiation of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) from Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. By targeting rRNA rather than DNA, the assay enhances analytical sensitivity due to the higher copy number of rRNA molecules within bacterial cells. It is widely implemented in clinical laboratories for urogenital gonorrhea and chlamydia diagnosis.
Key challenges include reliance on centralized laboratory infrastructure, equipment costs, and inability to provide antimicrobial resistance information. Test-of-cure interpretation may also require careful clinical correlation due to persistent nucleic acid detection after treatment.
Overall, the Aptima Combo 2 Assay is an established, FDA-approved molecular diagnostic for gonorrhea detection with high sensitivity and specificity. Its primary limitation is the absence of resistance profiling capability.

Name: Arterial occlusion balloons
Developers: University of Tokyo (including the Graduate School of Agricultural and Life Sciences); University of Bergen
Indication: Indicated for the prevention and control of postpartum haemorrhage, particularly in the setting of abnormal placentation.
Mechanism of action: Placement of an endovascular balloon to occlude blood flow to the uterus, thereby preventing and controlling postpartum haemorrhage.
Key features and challenges:
Intra-arterial balloons may be placed in the aorta, internal iliac arteries or uterine arteries to prevent or treat postpartum haemorrhage. Most commonly, they are placed prophylactically prior to planned surgical management for abnormal placentation to minimise blood loss during delivery. Less commonly, they are placed to treat life-threatening postpartum haemorrhage. The balloon catheter is inserted via the common femoral artery in the groin. Once inflated, the balloon prevents blood from passing to the uterus, stopping the bleeding and allowing time for definitive management. 
Resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta (REBOA) is one procedure where the balloon is placed in the abdominal aorta. This is a safe procedure for up to 1 hour of inflation. In a nationwide observational study in Japan, 143 patients with PPH underwent REBOA between April 2012 to March 2020. The most common cause of PPH was atonic postpartum hemorrhage (52.4%), followed by disseminated intravascular coagulation (29.4%) and amniotic fluid embolism documented (11.2%). Among patients who delivered at hospitals in which REBOA was performed (n = 55), 38.2% of patients experienced preterm births, and 70.9% delivered via cesarean delivery. The proportion of patients who underwent transcatheter arterial embolization and hysterectomy was 53.8% and 16.1%, respectively. In-hospital mortality was 7.0% (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35444149/).

Name: Aspirin - PE/E
Indication: Prevention of preeclampsia in high risk women
Mechanism of action: Inhibiting COX-1, therefore inhibiting platelet aggregation via TXA2, which slows down progression of placental diseases
Key features and challenges:
Aspirin is classified as a non-selective cyclooxygenase (COX) inhibitor and is available in many doses and forms, including chewable tablets, suppositories, extended release formulations, and others. Acetylsalicylic acid has both anti-inflammatory and antipyretic effects. It also inhibits platelet aggregation and is used in the prevention of blood clots stroke, and myocardial infarction. 
Aspirin is thought to help ameliorate impaired blood flow to the uterine arteries in women at risk of developing preeclampsia. While aspirin, and all non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDS), are contraindicated in the third trimester of pregnancy at standard doses, regular low dose aspirin (LDASA) at around 75mg-150mg (commonly 81mg) is safe for pregnancy. Several clinical trials have investigated the role of aspirin or LDASA in the prevention of preeclampsia in at risk women. A 2007 Cochrane Review found that antiplatelet agents during pregnancy are associated with moderate but consistent reductions in the relative risk of preeclampsia, of birth before 34 weeks' gestation, and of having a pregnancy with a serious adverse outcome (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17512048/). Other trials are ongoing.
A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of aspirin prophylaxis during pregnancy (35 trials) has also shown aspirin prophylaxis substantially lowered the risk of preeclampsia, preterm birth, perinatal mortality, and intrauterine growth restriction without elevated bleeding risks. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33795180/)
Although not approved for this indication, professional associations such as WHO, NICE, ACOG and RANZCOG currently recommend the prophylactic use of low-dose aspirin (75-81mg/day) in women who are considered to be at high risk for preeclampsia.
Recent updates:
The below is still valid.

In 2011, WHO guidelines were published that recommended that low-dose aspirin (75 mg/day) be initiated before 20 weeks of gestation for women at high risk of preeclampsia.

Name: Atosiban - PTL/PTB
Indication: Prolonging gestation in threatened preterm labour/birth through tocolytic/relaxant effects on myometrial contraction
Mechanism of action: Reducing uterine contraction by inhibiting oxytocin receptors
Key features and challenges:
Atosiban is an oxytocin receptor (OTR) antagonist that inhibits uterine contractions by competitively binding to oxytocin receptors in the myometrium. It also binds to vasopressin (AVP) receptors, suppressing vasopressin-mediated uterine activity. By directly targeting oxytocin-mediated contractility, atosiban functions as a tocolytic agent in the management of spontaneous preterm labour.
Clinical development began in Europe in the 1990s. Phase II trials demonstrated that atosiban prolonged uterine quiescence following successful treatment of an acute episode of preterm labour and was generally well tolerated. Comparative trials showed that atosiban was at least as effective as β-agonists in delaying delivery, with a substantially improved maternal side-effect profile. An application for approval was filed with the US FDA in 1997 but was rejected due to concerns regarding a higher incidence of fetal or neonatal death compared with placebo. The sponsor did not reapply. Atosiban was subsequently launched in 2000 in the European Union under the brand name Tractocile and is approved in several European countries for management of preterm labour.
In 2005, a Cochrane review evaluating atosiban versus placebo (two trials; 651 women) found no significant reduction in preterm delivery rates (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16034931/).
A 2014 meta-analysis of randomized trials comparing oxytocin receptor antagonists (including atosiban and barusiban) with placebo reported no reduction in PTL/PTB within 48 hours, before 28 weeks, or before 37 weeks’ gestation. Neonatal morbidity and mortality outcomes were similar between groups. However, atosiban was found to be as effective as betamimetics in delaying delivery within 48 hours, with significantly fewer maternal adverse effects (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24903678/).
In 2021, two multicenter randomized double-blind trials evaluated retosiban (a related oxytocin receptor antagonist) versus placebo and versus atosiban in women with singleton pregnancies and spontaneous PTL between 24 and 33+6 weeks’ gestation. Both trials were terminated prematurely due to recruitment challenges, limiting conclusions. In the same year, an additional clinical trial was completed to evaluate the optimal dosing of atosiban for twin preterm birth; results have not yet been published (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05061641).
Key challenges include limited evidence of impact on long-term neonatal outcomes despite short-term tocolytic efficacy, regulatory concerns regarding neonatal safety in earlier trials, and inconsistent demonstration of reduction in overall preterm birth rates. While atosiban remains widely used in Europe due to its favorable maternal safety profile compared with β-agonists, evidence supporting meaningful improvement in neonatal outcomes remains limited.
Recent updates:
2014: Meta-analysis of randomised trials comparing oxytocin receptor antagonists found that atosiban was as effective as betamimetics for reducing PTB within 48 hours of treatment, with a significantly lower risk of maternal side effects. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24903678/).

July 2005: A Cochrane review was published studied the role of atosiban in preventing preterm labour. It identified two trials comparing atosiban with placebo, involving 651 women. No benefit was found in reducing the preterm delivery rate in either study
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16034931/).

Name: Azithromycin - Gonorrhea
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhea
Mechanism of action: Azithromycin stops bacterial protein synthesis by inhibiting the transpeptidation/translocation step of protein synthesis and by inhibiting the assembly of the 50S ribosomal subunit.
Key features and challenges:
Azithromycin is a broad-spectrum macrolide antibiotic characterized by a long half-life and high tissue penetration. It has historically been used in combination regimens for the treatment of uncomplicated gonorrhoea.
A 2019 Phase III trial compared the efficacy and safety of gepotidacin with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin for the treatment of uncomplicated urogenital gonorrhoea (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04010539). 
The study demonstrated non-inferiority of gepotidacin to intramuscular ceftriaxone (500 mg) plus oral azithromycin (1,000 mg), based on microbiological response (success or failure) at the test-of-cure visit conducted 3–7 days after treatment.
In 2021, a Phase IV trial assessed the non-inferiority of cefixime plus doxycycline compared with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin for the treatment of uncomplicated urogenital, rectal, or pharyngeal gonorrhoea (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06090565). 
The study aimed to evaluate alternative regimens in light of evolving treatment recommendations and antimicrobial resistance patterns.
According to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, the 2020 update to treatment guidelines issued by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends a single 500 mg intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone for uncomplicated gonococcal infection and no longer recommends combination therapy with azithromycin. This change was driven in part by increasing Neisseria gonorrhoeae resistance to azithromycin, observed in both gonococcal and nongonococcal infections (https://www.fda.gov/drugs/development-resources/rationale-fdas-position-azithromycin-susceptible-only-breakpoint-neisseria-gonorrhoeae).
Key challenges associated with azithromycin use in gonorrhoea include rising antimicrobial resistance, reduced guideline support for combination therapy, and concerns regarding its continued role in first-line treatment regimens. Ongoing surveillance and updated clinical evidence are required to clarify its position within evolving gonorrhoea treatment strategies.

Name: Azithromycin - Mycoplasma genitalium
Developers: Cystic Fibrosis Foundation; Pfizer; University of Oxford (including Oxford University Clinical Research Unit Vietnam (OUCRU), Nuffield Department of Women's and Reproductive Health (NDWRH)); University of Wisconsin-Madison
Indication: Treatment of Mycoplasma genitalium
Target: Inhibition of the assembly of the 50S ribosomal subunit
Mechanism of action: Protein 50S ribosomal subunit inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Azithromycin is a macrolide antimicrobial used in the treatment of a range of bacterial infections, including sexually transmitted infections such as Mycoplasma genitalium. It has historically been administered as a single 1 g oral dose for uncomplicated infections. Common adverse effects include nausea, diarrhoea, vomiting, loss of appetite, headache, and alterations in taste perception.
Recent clinical evidence indicates declining efficacy of azithromycin for the treatment of M. genitalium, largely due to increasing macrolide resistance. Widespread use of the 1 g single-dose regimen has been associated with the selection of resistant strains, resulting in reduced cure rates internationally. Reports suggest that treatment failure following azithromycin therapy is increasingly linked to underlying macrolide resistance (https://adisinsight.springer.com/drugs/800017077).
In settings where resistance testing is not routinely available, persistent infection after azithromycin treatment is considered suggestive of macrolide-resistant M. genitalium. High resistance prevalence has been documented among men who have sex with men in several urban settings, including reports of macrolide resistance exceeding 80% in parts of Australia.
Key challenges include high and rising levels of macrolide resistance, reduced effectiveness of single-dose regimens, and limited access to resistance-guided therapy in many clinical settings. These factors have led to reconsideration of azithromycin’s role in first-line management and highlight the need for antimicrobial stewardship and alternative therapeutic strategies.

Name: BD MAX CT/GC/TV assay - Gonorrhea
Indication: Detection of gonorrhoeae
Mechanism of action: NAAT
Key features and challenges:
The BD MAX CT/GC/TV assay is a multiplex nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) designed to detect three of the most prevalent non-viral sexually transmitted infections—Chlamydia trachomatis (CT), Neisseria gonorrhoeae (GC), and Trichomonas vaginalis (TV)—in a single automated platform (https://moleculardiagnostics.bd.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/BD-MAX-CTGCTV-1-223841.pdf). The assay is intended to support comprehensive molecular diagnosis from a single specimen, improving workflow efficiency and syndromic management.
A multicenter study published in 2021 compared commercially available NAAT platforms for the diagnosis of rectal and oropharyngeal CT and NG infections, including the Abbott m2000 RealTime CT/NG assay, BD MAX CT/GC/TV, and the Roche cobas 6800/8800 CT/NG assay (https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jcm.01363-21). 
The study aimed to generate evidence to support regulatory review and clearance for the use of oropharyngeal and anorectal swab specimens in diagnosing CT and NG infections. The cobas assay demonstrated excellent performance for detection of both CT and NG in anorectal and oropharyngeal specimens. The BD MAX assay showed comparable or slightly lower sensitivity, while achieving essentially equivalent specificity for both organisms across sample types. The Abbott m2000 assay demonstrated comparatively lower performance.
Key challenges for the BD MAX CT/GC/TV assay include reliance on centralized laboratory infrastructure, potential cost considerations relative to single-target assays, and the need for continued evaluation in diverse clinical settings. While the assay offers multiplex efficiency and high specificity, sensitivity differences across platforms may influence assay selection in certain high-prevalence or extragenital screening contexts.

Name: BD MAX CT/GC/TV assay - Trichomoniasis
Indication: Detection of T vaginalis
Mechanism of action: NAAT
Key features and challenges:
The BD MAX CT/GC/TV assay is a multiplex nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) designed to detect three of the most prevalent non-viral sexually transmitted infections—Chlamydia trachomatis (CT), Neisseria gonorrhoeae (GC), and Trichomonas vaginalis (TV)—in a single automated platform (https://moleculardiagnostics.bd.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/BD-MAX-CTGCTV-1-223841.pdf). The assay enables simultaneous molecular detection from a single specimen, supporting streamlined laboratory workflows and syndromic STI management.
A multicenter study published in 2021 compared commercially available NAAT platforms for the diagnosis of rectal and oropharyngeal CT and NG infections, including the Abbott m2000 RealTime CT/NG assay, BD MAX CT/GC/TV, and the Roche cobas 6800/8800 CT/NG assay (https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jcm.01363-21). 
The study aimed to generate evidence to support regulatory review and clearance for the use of extragenital swab specimens. The cobas assay demonstrated excellent sensitivity for CT and NG detection in anorectal and oropharyngeal specimens. The BD MAX assay showed comparable or slightly lower sensitivity, while maintaining essentially equivalent specificity across sample types. The Abbott m2000 assay demonstrated comparatively lower performance.

For trichomoniasis, the assay offers the advantage of molecular detection, which is generally more sensitive than traditional microscopy-based methods.
Key challenges include reliance on centralized laboratory infrastructure, cost considerations relative to single-target assays, and the need for continued performance evaluation across diverse specimen types and populations, particularly for T. vaginalis. Implementation feasibility in resource-limited settings may also influence uptake.

The assay is performed on the fully automated BD MAX™ System and enables direct detection and differentiation of pathogen DNA from a single vaginal swab specimen collected from symptomatic women.

Indication: Indicated for the temporary control or reduction of postpartum uterine bleeding when conservative management of uterine bleeding is warranted.
Mechanism of action: Provides direct intrauterine pressure/tamponade to promote haemostasis.
Key features and challenges:
BT-Cath is a soft silicone balloon tamponade catheter specifically developed for the management of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH). The device has an inverted pear-shaped balloon (maximum recommended fill volume 500 mL) designed to conform to the uterine cavity. It features a dual-lumen system: one lumen enables intrauterine saline infusion for balloon inflation, while the second allows continuous intrauterine blood drainage to facilitate timely assessment of tamponade effectiveness. Unlike the Bakri balloon, the BT-Cath drainage port is flush with the top of the inflated balloon, with no protruding tubing, enabling placement closer to the uterine fundus and potentially improving tamponade efficiency.
A 2014 study evaluated the use of BT-Cath in women with uncontrolled haemorrhage secondary to placenta praevia (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25171267/). Among 53 women treated with BT-Cath, haemostasis was achieved in 45 cases (85%). Hysterectomy was required in six women (11%), and two required repeat laparotomy. The mean duration of balloon tamponade was 9.8 hours (standard deviation 6.4 hours). The findings suggested that BT-Cath may be an effective treatment option for PPH associated with placenta praevia when medical management is unsuccessful.
Key challenges include limited large-scale comparative studies versus other balloon tamponade devices, particularly in diverse PPH etiologies. Evidence is primarily derived from single-centre or observational studies, limiting generalizability. Further randomized controlled trials are needed to clarify comparative effectiveness, safety, and optimal positioning within PPH management pathways.

Name: Bakri Balloon
Indication: Indicated for the temporary control or reduction of postpartum uterine bleeding when conservative management of uterine bleeding is warranted.
Mechanism of action: Provides direct intrauterine pressure/tamponade to promote haemostasis.
Key features and challenges:
The Bakri balloon tamponade catheter is a uterine balloon system specifically designed for the management of obstetric hemorrhage. It consists of a silicone balloon (maximum recommended fill volume 500 mL) attached to a 24 French, 54 cm silicone catheter. The collapsed balloon is inserted into the uterine cavity and inflated with fluid, conforming to the uterine shape to exert tamponade pressure on bleeding vessels. A central lumen allows drainage and monitoring of ongoing bleeding above the balloon. The device is intended for single use and is constructed of 100% silicone.
In 2012, a retrospective case series evaluated the use of the Bakri balloon in 50 women with massive postpartum hemorrhage (blood loss >1000 mL) or high anticipated risk of PPH. The overall success rate was 86%. Seven patients required additional interventions; among these, four underwent supravaginal uterine amputation or hysterectomy and three required uterine artery embolization.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22913383/)
A second-generation device, BakriOne, has been developed to expand functionality. BakriOne is a multisize, multimaterial, multiport system with varying catheter and balloon sizes to accommodate patient-specific needs. The device may include clear silicone or polyvinyl chloride (PVC) shafts for improved visualization and incorporates a separate medication port for intrauterine administration of agents such as uterotonics, antibiotics, or tranexamic acid.
(https://innovations.bmj.com/content/6/1/1)
In 2025, a retrospective cohort study compared maternal postpartum hemorrhage outcomes between uterine balloon tamponade and vacuum-induced hemorrhage control devices, contributing comparative data on device-based management strategies.
(https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14767058.2025.2537225#abstract)
Overall, the Bakri balloon remains a widely used device for uterine tamponade in postpartum hemorrhage. Evidence supports high rates of bleeding control, though a subset of patients may require additional surgical or interventional procedures. Continued comparative studies are evaluating its role relative to newer vacuum-induced hemorrhage control systems.

Name: Bicalutimide
Indication: PCOS hyperandrogenism and hirsutism
Mechanism of action: Androgen receptor antagonists
Key features and challenges:
Bicalutamide is an orally active, non-steroidal androgen receptor (AR) antagonist originally developed for the treatment of prostate cancer, where it is used either in combination with luteinizing hormone–releasing hormone (LHRH) agonists or as monotherapy in selected settings. First launched in 1995, it is available in 50 mg, 150 mg, and 80 mg (Japan-only) formulations, although the 150 mg strength has been withdrawn from several markets. Generic versions are widely available.
https://adisinsight.springer.com/drugs/800000790
Given the central role of androgen excess in PCOS pathophysiology, particularly in hirsutism, acne, and androgenic alopecia, bicalutamide has been explored off-label as a therapeutic option for hyperandrogenism. The 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of PCOS acknowledges that anti-androgens, including bicalutamide, may be considered for hirsutism in women who have had a suboptimal response after at least six months of combined oral contraceptives (COCP) and/or cosmetic therapy. However, its use must be accompanied by effective contraception due to teratogenic risk, and clinicians must consider its association with potentially severe hepatotoxicity.
https://academic.oup.com/humrep/article/38/9/1655/7241786
A 2018 clinical trial referenced in a 2023 review reported that bicalutamide (Casodex), when combined with oral contraceptives, was more effective than oral contraceptives plus placebo in reducing hirsutism in women with PCOS. This supports the rationale that selective peripheral AR blockade may provide additional benefit beyond estrogen–progestin therapy alone in managing androgen-driven symptoms.
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1471489222001722?via%3Dihub
Despite evidence of efficacy for hirsutism, bicalutamide remains off-label for PCOS and is not approved for this indication by regulatory authorities. Its risk profile, particularly hepatotoxicity and teratogenic potential, restricts its use to carefully selected patients under close monitoring. Furthermore, it does not address underlying metabolic dysfunction, ovulatory irregularity, or long-term cardiometabolic risk associated with PCOS. Long-term safety data in reproductive-age women are limited, and routine liver function monitoring is required during treatment.

Name: Bioavailable testosterone
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS via detection of hyperandrogenism i
Mechanism of action: Measures testosterone not bound to SHBG to estimate biologically available androgen levels associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
Bioavailable testosterone is the portion of total testosterone in the bloodstream that is available to tissues, including free testosterone and testosterone bound to albumin, unlike the inactive SHBG-bound form. It plays a key role in diagnosing hyperandrogenism, a hallmark of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). 

The Rotterdam criteria mention hyperandrogenism as a diagnostic feature but do not specifically include bioavailable testosterone. Free or total testosterone is commonly measured for hyperandrogenism, with bioavailable testosterone serving as an alternative or supplementary marker for active testosterone. In clinical practice, bioavailable testosterone may complement the Rotterdam criteria in assessing androgen levels in suspected PCOS cases, but it is not a required component of the criteria.

The International Evidence-based Guideline for PCOS (2023) emphasises the importance of bioavailable testosterone, along with free testosterone, for assessing hyperandrogenism. 
(https://www.monash.edu/__data/assets/pdf_file/0003/3379521/Evidence-Based-Guidelines-2023.pdf)

Name: Biparietal diameter (BPD)
Developers: Karolinska Institute, Karolinska Institutet; Universidade de São Paulo
Indication: Diagnosis and prediction of IUGR
Mechanism of action: Measures unbound testosterone fraction to detect biologically active hyperandrogenism associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
Biparietal diameter (BPD) is one of the basic biometric parameters used to assess fetal size. BPD together with head circumference (HC), abdominal circumference (AC), and femur length (FL) are computed to produce an estimate of fetal weight.  In the second trimester this may be extrapolated to an estimate of gestational age and an estimated due date (EDD). The BPD should be measured on an axial plane that traverses the thalami, and cavum septum pellucidum. The transducer must be perpendicular to the central axis of the head, and thus the hemispheres and calvaria should appear symmetric. The callipers should be placed at the outer edge of the near calvarial wall and the inner edge of the far calvarial wall. The cerebellar hemispheres should not be in the plane of the image (https://radiopaedia.org/articles/biparietal-diameter?lang=gb). 
 
Discrepancy in biparietal diameter (BPD) growth between the first and second trimester ultrasound scans may indicate IUGR. Previous studies have shown that discrepancies in early fetal growth, based on ultrasound scan, is associated with adverse outcomes such as IUGR. When considering early fetal growth restriction, it is preferable to use repeated ultrasound measurements with estimation of change over specified time intervals, rather than comparing the discrepancy between expected and estimated fetal size, using the estimated gestational age based on last menstrual period (LMP) and ultrasound scans. 
 
A study by the Karolinska Institute evaluated whether slow growth between the first and early second trimester based on ultrasound measurements of BPD is associated with increased risks of overall SGA birth, preterm, and term SGA birth. Since the study was designed to focus on intrauterine growth restriction, researchers defined severe SGA infants as those with a birth weight of less than the 3rd percentile, excluded infants with malformations and adjusted the analysis for maternal stature and BMI. The study found that parietal growth less than 2.5 percentile between first and second trimester ultrasound examination was associated with elevated risk of being born severe SGA (OR 1.67; 95% Confidence Interval 1.28–2.18). The risks of preterm severe SGA (birth before 37 weeks) and term severe SGA (birth 37 weeks or later) were at similar levels, and the risk of severe SGA was also elevated in the absence of preeclampsia, hypertensive diseases, or gestational diabetes (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0184853). 
 
A 2021 study using magnetic resonance imaging of skull and brain also found significant differences between normal and IUGR pregnancies, particularly skull and brain BPDs (https://www.scielo.br/j/rb/a/dNrhkHv6zKYNyd7NRYw5Z8m/?lang=en&format=html).

Name: Buserelin
Indication: Treatment of endometriosis related pain and infertility, management of lesions
Mechanism of action: LHRH receptor agonist, stimulates the pituitary gland's gonadotrophin-releasing hormone receptor (GnRHR)
Key features and challenges:
Buserelin is a synthetic peptide analog of luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone (LHRH), designed to mimic the natural gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH). This oligopeptide works by binding to the GnRH receptors in the pituitary gland, initially stimulating the release of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH). However, with prolonged administration, Buserelin causes receptor desensitization, leading to sustained suppression of gonadotropin production. This suppression results in the reduced synthesis of gonadal steroids, which is beneficial in the treatment of hormone-dependent conditions. Buserelin is utilized primarily for the palliative management of advanced prostate cancer in males, and for treating endometriosis and other hormone-related gynecological disorders in females. It is available under the brand name Suprefact and in various formulations, including intramuscular injections and nasal sprays. 
(https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB06719)
(https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/50225)
Buserelin has been a significant advancement in the treatment of hormone-dependent cancers and gynecological disorders. One of the notable milestones was the 2003 approval and launch of Buserelin-depo in Russia, a sustained-release intramuscular formulation. This formulation provides long-term suppression of hormone production, making it suitable for managing prostate cancer, breast cancer, endometriosis, and related conditions. Additionally, the nasal spray formulation, Buserelin acetate, received approval in 1998 in Russia for treating endometriosis, womb myoma, hyperplastic endometrium, and infertility. These developments have cemented Buserelin's role as a versatile therapeutic agent in reproductive and oncology medicine, particularly in markets like Russia where it serves as a key treatment option.
(https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800043601)

Name: CFX96 RT-PCR detection system - Gonorrhea
Developers: Bio-Rad Laboratories (including Bio-Rad AbD Serotec GmbH)
Indication: Detection of gonorrhoeae
Mechanism of action: RT-PCR detection system
Key features and challenges:
The CFX96 Real-Time PCR Detection System is a laboratory-based quantitative PCR platform designed to support multiplex molecular testing. The system offers multiple configuration options, can be operated in stand-alone mode without a connected computer, and is suitable for bench-top laboratory use (https://www.gene-quantification.de/bio-rad-CFX96-bulletin-5589.pdf). 
It is commonly used for nucleic acid amplification and detection in research and diagnostic laboratory settings.
A 2023 study conducted in Mbeya, Tanzania evaluated the performance of point-of-care STI testing using self-collected cytobrush and urine samples from young adult females (https://bmcproc.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12919-023-00273-y#Sec245). 
In the study, specimens were tested using the GeneXpert system as the reference standard and compared with results obtained from a multiplex assay run on the CFX96 platform. Findings demonstrated high performance of point-of-care STI testing using self-collected cytobrush samples, followed by urine specimens. The results highlighted the potential role of molecular diagnostics in improving detection of sexually transmitted infections that may be missed by conventional testing methods.
Key challenges associated with the CFX96 system include its reliance on laboratory infrastructure, trained personnel, and controlled operating environments. While it offers flexibility and multiplex capability, its use as a diagnostic platform in resource-limited or decentralized settings may be constrained compared to fully integrated cartridge-based point-of-care systems.

Despite no recent research, this drug is nonetheless used in clinical practice in postpartum women with severe preeclampsia or chronic hypertension exacerbated by pregnancy for control of hypertensive crisis and keeping pressure levels. 
Captopril continues to be used off-label for this indication, although it should be noted that it is not recommended for use in pregnancy.
Recent updates: The use of captopril during pregnancy is limited because of reported fetal and neonatal side effects.

Name: Carbetocin
Indication: Prevention of uterine atony and excessive bleeding following delivery by emergency caesarean section or vaginal delivery
Mechanism of action: Carbetocin binds to oxytocin receptors present on the smooth musculature of the uterus, resulting in rhythmic contractions of the uterus, increased frequency of existing contractions, and increased uterine tone therefore ameliorating bleeding
Key features and challenges:
Carbetocin, is a long-acting synthetic analogue of oxytocin that was developed for the prevention of labour disorders like uterine atony and excessive postpartum haemorrhage following caesarean section. Its indication has since been extended to use with vaginal delivery. 
Carbetocin was first launched in the United Kingdom in 1997. Subsequently, it has been launched in Canada, Australia and in many countries in Europe, Asia and Africa. It has been available in New Zealand since early 2006, and is marketed by Pharmaco (NZ) Ltd., a division of Ferring. It is not however approved for use in the United States. It has also been trialled and approved in an intramuscular version. 
Carbetocin is administered as a single 100 µg/mL intravenous injection (and also intramuscularly) before or after placental delivery which is sufficient to maintain adequate uterine contraction. It is proposed to have advantages over oxytocin in the management of third-stage labour. Like oxytocin, carbetocin selectively binds to oxytocin receptors in the smooth muscle of the uterus; this stimulates rhythmic contractions of the uterus, increases the frequency of existing contractions, and raises the tone of the uterus musculature. Carbetocin can increase the rate and force of spontaneous contractions of the postpartum uterus. Onset of action is rapid with a firm contraction achieved within 2 minutes. 
A downside is that it requires refrigeration and cold-chain storage. However, a new room-temperature-stable formulation of carbetocin is approved in the EU in April 2015, with a large-scale trial completed in 2018 through a collaboration between Ferring, MSD for Mothers and WHO HRP for scale-up globally (see separate entry 'Carbetocin (heat stable)'. 
Carbetocin has the potential to be a near ideal drug for routine PPH prophylaxis, offered in all hospital vaginal deliveries, because it is suitable for both intramuscular injection and intravenous administration, offering convenience and simple implementation; it has quick onset of action; is long-acting, especially compared to oxytocin (carbetocin has a half-life of 85-100 minutes with a more prolonged uterotonic effect compared with endogenous or synthetic oxytocin’s half-life of 3.5min); is rarely associated with adverse drug reactions; and has excellent tolerability. Numerous trials have been conducted on its effectiveness, including in combination with other uterotonics including oxytocin.

Name: Carboprost
Indication: Treatment of postpartum hemorrhage due to uterine atony which has not responded to conventional methods of management.
Mechanism of action: Prostaglandin F2 alpha receptor agonist, with the resultant myometrial contractions providing haemostasis
Key features and challenges:
Carboprost is a synthetic analogue of prostaglandin F2 alpha (PGF2α), specifically the (15S)-15-methyl derivative, with potent uterotonic activity. It exerts its effect by activating prostaglandin F receptors on smooth muscle cells, leading to sustained uterine contractions. Carboprost is administered intramuscularly for the control of postpartum or postabortion haemorrhage, particularly when conventional treatments such as oxytocin and ergot derivatives have failed. It is frequently referenced in postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) management protocols.
The World Health Organization includes carboprost as a second- or third-line treatment option for PPH; however, injectable prostaglandins (including carboprost and sulprostone) are not recommended for routine prevention of PPH. Carboprost remains under active clinical investigation. The Phase IV COPE trial in the United Kingdom is currently recruiting participants to compare the effectiveness of oxytocin versus carboprost as first-line treatments for PPH (ISRCTN16416766: https://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN16416766; study website: https://copestudy.uk/).
Carboprost is contraindicated in patients with severe cardiovascular, renal, or hepatic disease, asthma, and acute pelvic inflammatory disease due to its side-effect profile, which includes hypertension, bronchospasm, vomiting, and diarrhoea. Its stimulation of smooth muscle extends to the gastrointestinal tract, frequently resulting in gastrointestinal adverse effects. Owing to the risk of serious adverse events, carboprost is most appropriately administered in settings with continuous monitoring capability. The product requires refrigeration at 2–8°C. In addition to its use in PPH, carboprost is used for pregnancy termination and is therefore contraindicated during ongoing pregnancy outside of approved indications.
Key challenges include its significant adverse effect profile, contraindications in common comorbid conditions such as asthma and hypertensive disorders, and cold-chain storage requirements. Its positioning as a second- or third-line agent reflects safety considerations rather than lack of uterotonic efficacy. Ongoing trials may further clarify its comparative effectiveness and optimal placement within PPH treatment algorithms.
Recent updates: 2019: Trial currently recruiting, expected to end in December 2022, comparing the effectiveness of carboprost or oxytocin in postpartum haemorrhage treatment (https://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN16416766).

Name: Cefixime
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhea
Mechanism of action: cell wall inhibitor
Key features and challenges:
Cefixime is a third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic used to treat susceptible Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial infections. As a beta-lactam agent, it inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases), thereby disrupting peptidoglycan cross-linking and leading to bacterial lysis, particularly in rapidly dividing organisms (https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB00671#).
A Phase II study completed in 2022 evaluated the effectiveness of cefixime plus doxycycline (CFM + DOX) compared with ceftriaxone plus doxycycline (CRO + DOX) for the treatment of Neisseria gonorrhoeae–Chlamydia trachomatis co-infection (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05216744). Results indicated that CRO + DOX was superior to CFM + DOX. However, the cefixime-based regimen may be considered in patients with ceftriaxone allergy or in settings where ceftriaxone is unavailable.
In 2022, a Phase IV study was initiated to compare cefixime 800 mg plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days with ceftriaxone 1 g plus azithromycin 2 g for the treatment of urogenital, rectal, and pharyngeal gonorrhoea (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06090565). No results are currently available.
Although third-generation cephalosporins are often first-line therapies for several bacterial infections, cefixime is not recommended as a first-line treatment for uncomplicated urogenital, anorectal, or pharyngeal gonorrhoea, as it does not achieve the same bactericidal efficacy as ceftriaxone.
Key challenges include comparatively lower efficacy relative to ceftriaxone, concerns regarding antimicrobial resistance, and limited guideline support for first-line use. Cefixime may retain a role as an alternative therapy in specific clinical scenarios where preferred regimens are contraindicated or inaccessible.

Name: Ceftriaxone - Gonorrhea
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Ceftriaxone works by inhibiting the mucopeptide synthesis in the bacterial cell wall. The beta-lactam moiety of ceftriaxone binds to carboxypeptidases, endopeptidases, and transpeptidases in the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane. These enzymes are involved in cell-wall synthesis and cell division. Binding of ceftriaxone to these enzymes causes the enzyme to lose activity; therefore, the bacteria produce defective cell walls, causing cell death.
Key features and challenges:
Ceftriaxone is a broad-spectrum third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic used to treat a wide range of bacterial infections, including those affecting the respiratory tract, skin, soft tissue, and urinary tract. It is administered parenterally and is considered the cornerstone of therapy for Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection.
In the United States, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends a single 500 mg intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone for the treatment of uncomplicated urogenital, rectal, or pharyngeal gonorrhoea. 
(https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/69/wr/mm6950a6.htm). 
Previous guidance recommended dual therapy with ceftriaxone and azithromycin to mitigate the emergence of reduced ceftriaxone susceptibility. However, concerns regarding potential harm to the microbiome and the impact on antimicrobial resistance in other pathogens led to the removal of routine dual therapy from U.S. recommendations, with ceftriaxone now recommended as monotherapy.
In contrast, Australian STI guidelines from the Australian Sexual Health Alliance recommend ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly in combination with azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose for uncomplicated genital, anorectal, and pharyngeal gonorrhoea. 
(https://sti.guidelines.org.au/sexually-transmissible-infections/gonorrhoea/). 
Azithromycin was added in 2014 with the aim of reducing the emergence and transmission of ceftriaxone-resistant strains; however, ceftriaxone remains the primary active agent in the regimen.
The World Health Organization has identified gonococcal resistance to ceftriaxone as a major public health concern, given its status as the last remaining widely effective empiric first-line therapy. Surveillance through the WHO Enhanced Gonococcal Antimicrobial Surveillance Programme (EGASP) has documented the emergence and spread of ceftriaxone-resistant strains across multiple phylogenetic lineages. 
(https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/multi-drug-resistant-gonorrhoea).
Key challenges include the growing threat of antimicrobial resistance, limited alternative first-line treatment options, and the need for strengthened global surveillance and stewardship efforts. Continued monitoring and development of new therapeutic strategies are critical to preserving ceftriaxone efficacy in gonorrhoea management.

Name: Celox gauze
Indication: Indicated for the temporary control or reduction of postpartum uterine bleeding when conservative management of uterine bleeding is warranted.
Mechanism of action: Celox gauze works to control PPH through mechanical compression, adhesion of the gauze and improved local primary haemostasis. The chitosan activates tissue factor and interacts directly with erythrocytes and thrombocytes to form a cross-linked barrier clot independent of native factors.
Key features and challenges:
Celox gauze is a CE-marked, class III medical device in the EU, and it is approved by the Federal Drug Administration in the US for bleeding control. It was developed initially to stop severe hemorrhage in the military context. Celox gauze is covered with chitosan, a hydrophilic biopolymer obtained through the deacetylation of chitin, a major component of crustacean shells, such as crab or shrimp. The effect of Celox gauze in PPH is based on three principles: mechanical compression, adhesion of the gauze and improved local primary hemostasis. Regarding the latter, chitosan activates tissue factor and interacts directly with erythrocytes and thrombocytes to form a cross-linked barrier clot independent of native factors.
A databased retrospective case–control study of all women with PPH who delivered at the Department of Obstetrics, Charité University Hospital, between May 2016 and May 2019 (https://www.degruyter.com/document/doi/10.1515/jpm-2021-0533/html?lang=en) compared chitosan/Celox tamponade to balloon tamponade. It demonstrated that there were no significant differences in the need for surgical therapy, but a significantly lower number of hysterectomies in the chitosan tamponade group than in the balloon tamponade group. There were no relevant differences in secondary outcomes and no adverse events related to the chitosan tamponade. Since the introduction of chitosan tamponade, the number of PPH related hysterectomies dropped significantly by 77.8%.
In March 2022 Medtrade Products received MDR certification for the entire CELOX CE range of devices for life-threatening bleeding in pre-hospital emergency situations (https://www.celoxmedical.com/medtrade-receives-eu-mdr-certification-for-the-celox-ce-range/). MedTrade have developed a PPH-specific Celox gauze, CELOX PPH Uterine Hemostatic Tamponade. In November 2022 it received CE certification in Europe (https://www.celoxmedical.com/postpartum-haemorrhage/). In February 2023 Medtrade Products Ltd entered into an exclusive agreement with Dahlhausen Medizintechnik to distribute the  CELOX PPH Uterine Haemostatic Tamponade throughout Austria and Germany. 
Celox gauze is currently being studied in a post-market prospective, single arm clinical investigation to assess its safety, performance and effectiveness as a uterine haemostatic tamponade treatment for uterine postpartum haemorrhage (PPH). The study is expected to be completed in 2025. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06033170)
