Indication: Detection of gonorrhoeae
Mechanism of action: in vitro real-time PCR
Key features and challenges:
The Xpert® CT/NG assay, performed on the GeneXpert® Instrument Systems, is a qualitative in vitro real-time PCR test for the automated detection and differentiation of genomic DNA from Chlamydia trachomatis (CT) and Neisseria gonorrhoeae (NG). The assay supports the diagnosis of urogenital chlamydial and gonococcal infections in both symptomatic and asymptomatic individuals. It is validated for use with female and male urine specimens, endocervical swabs, and clinician- or patient-collected vaginal swabs obtained in clinical settings. Time to result is approximately 90 minutes (https://www.cepheid.com/content/dam/www-cepheid-com/documents/package-insert-files/Xpert-CTNG-US-ENGLISH-Package-Insert-301-0234--Rev-K.pdf).
A prospective interventional study initiated in 2023 in Zimbabwe is evaluating a strategy of point-of-care testing for sexually transmitted infections, including chlamydia, gonorrhoea, trichomoniasis, syphilis, and hepatitis B, in antenatal care settings (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05541081). 
The study incorporates comprehensive case management and partner notification and aims to assess the impact of integrated STI point-of-care testing on maternal and reproductive health outcomes. Results are pending.
In 2024, a clinical trial initiated in Nepal proposed combining molecular testing for CT and NG using the Xpert® CT/NG assay with low-cost testing for Trichomonas vaginalis and bacterial vaginosis in women presenting with abnormal vaginal discharge (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05977491). The study seeks to evaluate whether implementation of point-of-care STI testing reduces overtreatment with antibiotics in low-income settings. Results are not yet available.
Key challenges include dependence on GeneXpert instrument infrastructure, cartridge costs, and sustained supply chain requirements. While the assay offers high sensitivity and specificity with near-patient testing capability, scalability in resource-limited settings may depend on integration with existing diagnostic platforms and funding mechanisms.

Name: Cerebroplacental ratio (CPR)
Indication: Diagnosis of IUGR
Target: Doppler indices of the middle cerebral artery (MCA) and the umbilical artery (UA)
Mechanism of action: Ratio of middle cerebral to umbilical artery Doppler indices to detect fetal blood flow redistribution secondary to placental insufficiency.
Key features and challenges:
​The cerebroplacental ratio (CPR) is calculated by dividing the doppler indices of the middle cerebral artery (MCA) by the umbilical artery (UA). It is emerging as an important predictor of adverse pregnancy outcome, and this has implications for the assessment of well-being in fetuses diagnosed as small for gestational age (SGA) and those appropriate for gestational age (AGA) close to term (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26113227/). 
 
The cerebroplacental ratio (CPR) has been proposed for the routine surveillance of pregnancies with suspected fetal growth restriction (FGR), but the predictive performance of this test is unclear. A review study aimed to determine the accuracy of CPR for predicting adverse perinatal and neurodevelopmental outcomes in suspected FGR. It concluded that CPR is useful in predicting perinatal death in pregnancies with suspected FGR, however stated that before incorporating CPR into the routine clinical management of suspected FGR, randomised controlled trials should assess whether the use of CPR reduces perinatal death or other adverse perinatal outcomes (https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/uog.19117). 
 
Another review study found that fetuses with an abnormal CPR that are appropriate for gestational age or have late-onset SGA (>34 weeks of gestation) have a higher incidence of fetal distress in labour requiring emergency caesarean delivery, a lower cord pH, and an increased admission rate to the newborn intensive care unit when compared with fetuses with a normal CPR. Fetuses with early-onset SGA (<34 weeks of gestation) with an abnormal CPR have a higher incidence of the following when compared with fetuses with a normal CPR: (1) lower gestational age at birth, (2) lower mean birthweight, (3) lower birthweight centile, (4) birthweight less than the 10th centile, (5) higher rate of caesarean delivery for fetal distress in labor, (6) higher rate of Apgar scores less than 7 at 5 minutes, (7) an increased rate of neonatal acidosis, (8) an increased rate of newborn intensive care unit admissions, (9) higher rate of adverse neonatal outcome, and (10) a greater incidence of perinatal death (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26113227/).​

Name: Cervical length
Developers: University of Cincinnati; Kandang Kerbau Women's and Children's Hospital
Indication: Prediction & diagnosis of PTL
Mechanism of action: Ultrasound measurement of cervical length to identify premature shortening associated with cervical insufficiency and preterm birth.
Key features and challenges:
The cervical length is defined as the distance between the internal cervical os and the external cervical os. The cervical length is most accurately assessed on a transvaginal scan with an empty bladder, as the presence of a full bladder can increase the cervical length, particularly on a trans-abdominal scan. In a normal gravid situation, the cervical length is considered to be at least 30mm (https://radiopaedia.org/articles/cervical-length). 

Cervical length measured via transvaginal ultrasound is one of the mainstays of PTL prediction and diagnosis. There is a consensus among guidelines that the diagnosis of PTL is based on measurement of cervical length with transvaginal ultrasound, clinical criteria, physical examination, and use of biomarkers, although there is disagreement on the first-line diagnostic test. The NICE and the EAPM are in favour of TVUS CL measurement, whereas the New South Wales Government mentions that fetal fibronectin testing is the mainstay for PTL diagnosis. The NICE guidelines, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the EAPM also highlight the significance of screening for PTL by TVUS CL measurement between 16 and 24 weeks of gestation. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35522432/). 

A study focusing on pregnancies complicated by twin–twin transfusion syndrome compared cervical length measurements with MRI and TVUS, and concluded that while measurement of CL on MRI correlated well with that on TVS overall, it performed poorly at accurately detecting a short cervix. TVS outperformed MRI in evaluation of the cervix and thus remains the optimal modality for CL measurement in pregnancies at risk for preterm birth.
(https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/uog.26184)

Name: Cetrorelix
Developers: Aeterna Zentaris; Merck (also known as Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany), including Sigma-Aldrich, MilliporeSigma and EMD Serono; Shionogi & Co., Ltd.; Benha University
Indication: Treatment of PCOS associated infertility
Mechanism of action: Gonadotropin releasing hormone inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Cetrorelix is a gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) antagonist routinely used in controlled ovarian stimulation protocols for women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) undergoing in vitro fertilization (IVF) or intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI). By competitively blocking GnRH receptors in the anterior pituitary, it rapidly suppresses luteinizing hormone (LH) (and to a lesser extent follicle-stimulating hormone [FSH]) secretion, thereby preventing a premature LH surge and untimely ovulation. This provides tighter cycle control and is particularly valuable in PCOS, where high follicle counts and exaggerated gonadotropin responses increase the risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS).
A 2022 clinical trial assessed whether different GnRH-based pituitary suppression approaches influence oocyte morphology and, by implication, oocyte developmental competence in PCOS patients undergoing IVF/ICSI. The study compared a GnRH agonist long protocol with a GnRH antagonist flexible protocol (where cetrorelix is a commonly used antagonist option), reflecting ongoing efforts to optimize ovarian stimulation strategies while balancing oocyte quality and safety outcomes in PCOS.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04727684
In 2023, a further randomized study commenced comparing a dydrogesterone-primed ovarian stimulation (PPOS) strategy with a GnRH antagonist protocol (including regimens using cetrorelix) in PCOS patients undergoing ICSI. This work is designed to clarify which suppression method produces better cycle outcomes and fewer complications, including OHSS, and to inform best-practice protocol selection in PCOS-related infertility care.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05751681
Although GnRH antagonist protocols using cetrorelix are widely integrated into modern IVF practice, PCOS-specific questions remain regarding the optimal dosing strategy, timing (fixed vs flexible initiation), and comparative effectiveness against emerging alternatives such as progestin-primed ovarian stimulation protocols. In addition, many outcomes of interest—particularly live birth rates, cumulative pregnancy outcomes, and OHSS reduction in high-risk PCOS phenotypes—require consistent reporting across trials to better define cetrorelix’s relative advantage versus other suppression approaches.

Name: Ciprofloxacin
Developers: University of California San Diego School of Medicine
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Target: Bacterial topoisomerase II (DNA gyrase); Topoisomerase IV
Mechanism of action: Ciprofloxacin acts on bacterial topoisomerase II (DNA gyrase) and topoisomerase IV. Ciprofloxacin's targeting of the alpha subunits of DNA gyrase prevents it from supercoiling the bacterial DNA which prevents DNA replication.
Key features and challenges:
Ciprofloxacin is a second-generation fluoroquinolone antibiotic with activity against a broad range of Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria. It has been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of gonorrhoea; however, widespread resistance in Neisseria gonorrhoeae has significantly limited its role in empiric therapy (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK535454/).
In the late 1990s and early 2000s, ciprofloxacin-resistant gonorrhoea was first detected in Hawaii and the U.S. West Coast. By 2004, resistance had increased substantially among men who have sex with men, leading to discontinuation of its use in this population. By 2006, approximately 14% of gonorrhoea isolates were resistant, and in 2007 the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention stopped recommending fluoroquinolones for empiric treatment of gonorrhoea (https://www.cdc.gov/gonorrhea/hcp/drug-resistant/index.html).
A 2021 prospective clinical study evaluated the efficacy of single-dose oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg in patients with culture-positive gonorrhoea whose isolates possessed the wild-type gyrA serine 91 genotype (https://academic.oup.com/cid/article/73/2/298/5882191). 
Among 106 participants in the per-protocol population, microbiological cure at 5–10 days post-treatment was 100%. These findings support the potential role of resistance-guided therapy using molecular assays that predict ciprofloxacin susceptibility. Although such assays are available, they have not been systematically implemented in routine clinical practice.
Key challenges include historically high and geographically variable resistance rates, the need for molecular susceptibility testing to guide appropriate use, and limited availability of rapid genotyping in many settings. Ciprofloxacin may have renewed utility in contexts where resistance-guided strategies can be reliably deployed and where local susceptibility patterns remain favorable.

Name: Clofazimine
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Leprosy.
Target:
Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma
Potassium voltage-gated channel subfamily A member 3
Mechanism of action: Although the precise mechanism(s) of action of clofazimine have not been elucidated, its antimicrobial activity appears to be membrane-directed. It was previously thought that, due to its lipophilicity, clofazimine participated in the generation of intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) via redox cycling, specifically H2O2 and superoxide, which then exerted an antimicrobial effect. A more recent and compelling theory involves clofazimine interacting with bacterial membrane phospholipids to generate antimicrobial lysophospholipids - bactericidal efficacy may, then, arise from the combined membrane-destabilizing effects of both clofazimine and lysophospholipids, which interfere with K+ uptake and, ultimately, ATP production.
Key features and challenges: Clofazimine is indicated for the treatment of lepromatous leprosy, including dapsone-resistant lepromatous leprosy and lepromatous leprosy complicated by erythema nodosum leprosum. To prevent the development of drug resistance, it should be used only in combination with other antimycobacterial leprosy treatments.  It was originally described in 1957 and was the prototypical riminophenazine dye - a bright-red dye that, in its clinical use, results in long-lasting discoloration of the skin and bodily fluids (https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB00845).

Key features and challenges:
Clofazimine is a riminophenazine compound, developed by Novartis, for the treatment of leprosy, multi-drug resistant tuberculosis and nontuberculous mycobacterium infections. The drug was originally synthesized at the University College of Ireland. Clofazimine inhibits ATPase, P-glycoprotein, and phospholipase A2. The antileprotic activity of clofazimine is thought to be due to preferential binding to mycobacterial DNA, which helps in inhibiting DNA replication and cell growth. It is launched for the treatment of leprosy in Australia, Ireland, Japan, New Zealand, South Africa, Switzerland and the UK. Clinical development is ongoing for nontuberculous mycobacterium infections in the US.

WHO suggests the use of a 6-month treatment regimen composed of bedaquiline, delamanid, linezolid (600 mg), levofloxacin, and clofazimine (BDLLfxC) in MDR/RR-TB patients with or without fluoroquinolone resistance(conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). The 6-month BDLLfxC regimen showed high treatment success and is composed of medicines that have been recommended and used widely in all patient groups. The trial's evidence suggests that this regimen may be effectively and safely used in eligible patients with MDR/RR-TB and pre-XDR-TB regardless of their HIV status. 
WHO also suggests using the 9-month all-oral regimens including BLLfxCZ over currently recommended longer (>18 months) regimens in patients with MDR/RR-TB and in whom resistance to fluoroquinolones has been excluded.

Name: Clomiphene citrate - PCOS
Developers: Serono Pharmaceutical Research Institute ; Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS); Teva Pharmaceutical Industries; Mylan Laboratories Ltd (previously Matrix Laboratories)
Indication: Treatment of PCOS-related infertility
Mechanism of action: Estrogen receptor antagonist
Key features and challenges:
Clomiphene citrate is a nonsteroidal selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) with both estrogenic and anti-estrogenic activity. It competitively binds estrogen receptors in the hypothalamus, disrupting negative feedback and stimulating the release of pituitary gonadotropins (follicle-stimulating hormone [FSH] and luteinizing hormone [LH]), thereby inducing ovulation.
https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/Clomiphene%20Citrate
Clomiphene was approved by the U.S. FDA in 1967 for the treatment of ovulatory dysfunction and infertility, including in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). It has since been widely adopted globally as a first-line ovulation induction therapy.
A 2021 study reported no significant difference in infertility outcomes when clomiphene citrate was combined with pioglitazone compared with clomiphene alone in women with PCOS.
https://bmcwomenshealth.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12905-021-01448-5
Another 2021 study comparing stair-step protocols demonstrated higher ovulation, clinical pregnancy, and live birth rates with letrozole compared to clomiphene citrate, along with a shorter time to ovulation.
https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jog.14936
A 2022 study reported that letrozole resulted in higher pregnancy and live birth rates than clomiphene in women with PCOS, although letrozole was associated with increased risk of multiple gestation and certain adverse neonatal outcomes.
https://academic.oup.com/humrep/article/37/4/793/6511990
A 2023 review concluded that clomiphene induces ovulation effectively in women with PCOS but is generally less effective than letrozole in achieving live birth and pregnancy outcomes.
https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/24/8/7454
A 2024 study found that women with higher serum anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) levels required higher doses of clomiphene for ovulation induction, and those with ultra-high AMH may require adjunctive therapies.
https://www.fertstert.org/article/S0015-0282(22)01140-2/fulltext
Combination regimens have also been extensively evaluated. Trials have investigated clomiphene in combination with metformin, pentoxifylline (PTX), alpha-lipoic acid (ALA), gonadotropins, human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), and medroxyprogesterone.
https://adis.springer.com/trials/700004665
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05231980
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04157725
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02436226
https://adis.springer.com/trials/700225541
Comparative trials between letrozole and clomiphene continue to evaluate ovulation rates and endometrial development.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04887402
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05075863
https://adis.springer.com/trials/700036166
http://www.ctri.nic.in/Clinicaltrials/pmaindet2.php?trialid=25010
Evidence regarding clomiphene plus metformin is mixed. A 2021 study found clomiphene + metformin superior to clomiphene + N-acetylcysteine for follicle development and conception rates.
https://impactfactor.org/PDF/IJTPR/11/IJTPR,Vol11,Issue2,Article5.pdf
A 2023 review and guideline summary suggested that clomiphene combined with metformin may improve pregnancy rates, particularly in overweight individuals or those with glucose intolerance.
https://academic.oup.com/humrep/article/38/Supplement_1/dead093.113/7202629
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13669-023-00360-z
However, a 2023 study reported that metformin pre-treatment did not significantly improve ovulation, pregnancy, or live birth rates when added to clomiphene in women with insulin resistance.
https://jfrh.tums.ac.ir/index.php/jfrh/article/view/2145
A 2024 study found that clomiphene combined with metformin improved ovulation, menstrual regularity, and pregnancy rates compared with clomiphene alone.
https://impactfactor.org/PDF/IJPCR/16/IJPCR,Vol16,Issue3,Article82.pdf
Clomiphene remains a first-line ovulation induction agent in PCOS, particularly in resource-limited settings due to its oral administration and low cost. However, it is associated with several limitations. Ovulation rates are lower in women with obesity or high AMH levels, and clomiphene resistance occurs in a significant proportion of patients. Compared with letrozole, clomiphene is generally associated with lower live birth rates and higher risk of anti-estrogenic effects on the endometrium and cervical mucus.

Name: Clonidine
Developers: Novavax; Onxeo (including Topo Target); Curatek Pharmaceuticals LLC; Monopar Therapeutics; Sollis Therapeutics; Therakind; Tris Pharma Inc
Indication: Treatment of postpartum hypertension in women who had hypertensive disorders of pregnancywomen who have hypertensive disorders of pregnancy
Target: α2 receptors in the vasomotor center (CNS)
Mechanism of action: Inducing peripheral vasodilation via sympatholytic mechanism
Key features and challenges:
Clonidine is a centrally acting alpha-2 adrenergic agonist with systemic antihypertensive, sedative, and anxiolytic effects. It was approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in 1974 and is indicated for hypertension, with additional uses in pain management and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. In obstetric practice, clonidine has been used off-label as an alternative antihypertensive agent in pregnant or postpartum women who have contraindications to angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors such as captopril.
The CLONCAP trial (2012–2013; NCT01761916) compared oral clonidine (0.1 mg) with oral captopril (25 mg) in postpartum women with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy experiencing severe blood pressure elevations. The study found that clonidine achieved similar reductions in systolic and diastolic blood pressure compared with captopril. Additionally, the clonidine group demonstrated lower mean systolic blood pressure on the third postpartum day and fewer reported adverse reactions (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28125624/).
Although limited recent research has specifically examined clonidine in preeclampsia, it continues to be used in clinical practice for blood pressure control in late pregnancy and the postpartum period, particularly in cases of severe preeclampsia or chronic hypertension exacerbated by pregnancy. Its use remains off-label for these indications.
Key challenges include the lack of large contemporary randomized controlled trials in pregnant populations, potential central nervous system side effects such as sedation and rebound hypertension upon abrupt withdrawal, and limited data on long-term maternal and neonatal outcomes. Further studies would be required to define optimal positioning relative to other established antihypertensive agents used in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.

An ongoing interventional study initiated in 2024 is evaluating the comparative clinical utility of the cobas® Liat® CT/NG/MG assay as a point-of-care test versus current standard diagnostic practices for urogenital infections caused by CT, NG, and MG (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06369220). 
The study aims to assess whether near-patient molecular testing can improve diagnosis and treatment decisions in routine clinical settings. Results have not yet been published.
Key challenges include the investigational status of the CT/NG/MG assay, pending clinical outcome data, and considerations related to implementation in diverse healthcare settings. While the platform offers rapid, automated molecular detection with potential point-of-care application, evidence on real-world clinical impact and cost-effectiveness will be critical to inform broader adoption.

The cobas® Liat® CT/NG/MG assay is an investigational, automated, qualitative nucleic acid amplification test designed for use on the cobas® Liat® System. The assay utilizes real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) technology for the direct detection of Chlamydia trachomatis (CT), Neisseria gonorrhoeae (NG), and Mycoplasma genitalium (MG) nucleic acid in male and female urine specimens, as well as clinician- and self-collected vaginal swabs collected in cobas® PCR Media.
A 2024 block-randomized, controlled, two-arm prospective study is underway to evaluate the clinical utility of the cobas® Liat® CT/NG/MG assay in individuals at increased risk of sexually transmitted infections (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06369220). 
The study aims to enroll approximately 348 participants, including individuals with known contact with CT/NG/MG or those presenting with symptoms suggestive of STI. Participants provide demographic information and urogenital specimens for testing using the cobas® Liat® system and external laboratory PCR (EL-PCR) testing.
Participants are randomized in a 1:1 ratio to either a Standard of Care (SOC) arm or a Point of Care (POC) arm. In both arms, clinicians evaluate participants and complete a standardized patient management plan. In the POC arm, clinicians receive rapid test results from the cobas® Liat® system to inform clinical decision-making, whereas in the SOC arm, management decisions are made without access to point-of-care results. The study is ongoing and results have not yet been published.
Key challenges include the investigational status of the assay for MG detection, pending clinical outcome data, and considerations regarding cost and implementation in routine care settings. While the platform offers the potential for rapid, integrated molecular diagnosis of M. genitalium alongside CT and NG, evidence on real-world impact and cost-effectiveness will be essential to support broader adoption.

Name: Combined oral contraceptives - Uterine fibroids
Indication: Prevention of uterine fibroids and management of bleeding
Target: Hormones; ovulation; endometrial lining; androgens; insulin; lipids
Mechanism of action: Hormone regulation; ovulation inhibition; endometrial lining thinning; reduced androgen production; improved insulin sensitivity; lipid regulation
Key features and challenges:
Combined oral contraceptives (COCs) are hormonal medications containing estrogen and progestin, primarily indicated for contraception and menstrual cycle regulation. They are frequently prescribed for management of gynecologic conditions, including uterine fibroids, where they may improve heavy menstrual bleeding and dysmenorrhoea. Clinical guidance from the American Academy of Family Physicians and the European Menopause and Andropause Society supports the use of COCs for symptomatic management of heavy menstrual bleeding associated with fibroids (https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2017/0115/p100.html).
https://www.emas-online.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/fibroids.pdf). 
The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists also list COCs as a treatment option, noting that fibroid size may increase slightly in some individuals 
(https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/uterine-fibroids).
A 2021 case–control study involving 346 women reported that 37.8% of hormonal contraceptive users were diagnosed with uterine fibroids compared with 59.6% of non-users, suggesting a protective association (odds ratio 0.4; p = 0.007). 
(https://www.mdpi.com/1648-9144/57/7/717). 
A 2024 prospective observational study of 1,308 African American women reported an inverse association between ever use of COCs and cumulative fibroid incidence over 40 months (adjusted risk ratio 0.76; 95% CI 0.60–0.98), supporting a potential protective effect in a high-burden population. (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0303823).
Key challenges include the fact that COCs do not reduce fibroid size and primarily address symptoms rather than underlying pathology. Additionally, potential slight increases in fibroid growth have been reported, and long-term risk–benefit considerations must be individualized. While COCs remain an accessible and guideline-supported option for symptom control, their role is primarily supportive rather than disease-modifying in uterine fibroid management.

Target: Actin; Capillary permeability; Estrogen receptor; Testosterone congener

Key features and challenges:
Danazol is a synthetic steroid with antigonadotropic and anti-estrogenic properties, primarily used to treat endometriosis and benign breast disorders. It works by suppressing the pituitary-ovarian axis, inhibiting the release of gonadotropins, and reducing ovarian estrogen production. This suppression leads to the inactivation and atrophy of both normal and ectopic endometrial tissue, resulting in anovulation and amenorrhea. While danazol was initially the first FDA-approved treatment for endometriosis, its use has been largely replaced by GnRH agonists. Additionally, danazol may directly inhibit ovarian steroidogenesis and bind to various hormone receptors. It also helps manage hereditary angioedema by increasing C1 esterase inhibitor levels. (https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB01406)
Danazol is approved for the treatment of endometriosis, fibrocystic breast disease, and hereditary angioedema by the FDA, EMA, and MHRA, and is also approved by other national regulatory agencies such as Health Canada and the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) in Australia. However, its use has been restricted or limited in some regions due to safety concerns, particularly liver toxicity, with varying availability depending on local regulations.
In 2023, a Phase 3 clinical trial was initiated to examine women who have endometriosis, to compare the efficacy of dienogest vs danazol treatment; this was assessed based on symptoms severity, CA125 examination, and sonographic examination at baseline, 4 weeks and 16 weeks after treatment. Key features and challenges:
Dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS) is the sulfated form of dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), a steroid hormone produced mainly by the adrenal glands, with minor contributions from the ovaries and testes. DHEAS serves as a precursor for sex hormones like estrogen and testosterone and is more stable in circulation than DHEA, making it the preferred form for measurement in clinical tests. Elevated DHEAS levels can indicate excess androgen production from the adrenal glands.

The 2023 PCOS guideline suggests that if testosterone or free testosterone is normal, healthcare professionals may test for androstenedione and DHEAS, though these have lower specificity and DHEAS declines with age, affecting their accuracy for diagnosis. (https://academic.oup.com/jcem/article/108/10/2447/7242360)

A 2021 study found that DHEAS levels were higher in women with PCOS, especially in lean-PCOS compared to obese-PCOS and non-PCOS. However, DHEAS was a weaker diagnostic marker for PCOS than the free androgen index (FAI) and modified Ferriman-Gallwey (FG) score. DHEAS levels also showed inverse relationships with age, body measurements, glycemia, and reproductive hormones. 
(https://jcpsp.pk/article-detail/dehydroepiandrosterone-sulfate-(dheas)-levels-in-polycystic-ovarian-syndrome-(pcos))

Name: Desogestrel
Indication: Indicated for the prevention and treatment of endometriosis associated pain and abnormal tissue growth
Mechanism of action: Progesterone receptor agonists
Key features and challenges:
Desogestrel, a third-generation progestogen in the gonane family, was initially used in Europe before gaining approval in the U.S. and Canada. It is used in birth control pills, sometimes in combination with an estrogen, and for the treatment of menopausal symptoms in women. 
In the U.S., it is only available in combination with ethinyl estradiol. The first drug containing desogestrel was developed by Organon USA Inc. in 1972 and received FDA approval in 1992. (https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB00304)
The use of combined oral contraceptives and progestogens for the treatment of endometriosis-related pain is recommended by the European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists.
(https://www.eshre.eu/guideline/endometriosis; https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2011/0101/p84.html)
A recent randomized controlled trial at Rajvithi Hospital completed in 2022, examined the efficacy of oral desogestrel versus placebo for preoperative treatment of endometrioma in patients scheduled for surgery within three months. Patients were randomized into two groups and assessed after one and three months of treatment. The study evaluates changes in cyst diameter, pain levels, and side effects. The aim was to determine whether desogestrel reduces cyst size and associated pain more effectively than placebo, providing valuable information for managing endometrioma preoperatively. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04941833; https://adis.springer.com/trials/700339172)

Name: Determine HIV Early Detect
Indication: To screen for or to aid in the diagnosis of HIV infection: adults, adolescents, children and infants > 18 months of age
Target: HIV-1 and HIV-2 antibodies, as well as free HIV-1 p24 antigen
Mechanism of action: The test uses an immunochromatographic assay where the specimen interacts with biotinylated anti-p24 antibodies and selenium colloid-conjugates, producing a red line at the antibody or antigen window to indicate the presence of HIV antibodies or HIV-1 p24 antigen.
Key features and challenges:
Determine HIV Early Detect is a qualitative in vitro immunoassay for detecting HIV-1 and HIV-2 antibodies, as well as free HIV-1 p24 antigen, in human whole blood, plasma, or serum (venous or capillary). The test uses an immunochromatographic method where the specimen interacts with biotinylated anti-p24 antibodies and selenium colloid-conjugates coated with HIV antigens. A red bar at the antibody window indicates the presence of antibodies, while a red bar at the antigen window indicates the presence of HIV-1 p24 antigen. Reactivity at either or both windows suggests potential HIV infection. It is for professional use only, aiding in the diagnosis of HIV infection in individuals aged 18 months and older.

Name: Dexamethasone - PTL/PTB
Developers: University of Auckland (including Auckland UniServices Limited); University of Adelaide
Indication: Foetal lung maturation as an adjuvant treatment in preterm labour/birth
Mechanism of action: Increases surfactant production to improve foetal lung maturation
Key features and challenges:
Dexamethasone is a glucocorticoid medication used to treat rheumatic problems, a number of skin diseases, severe allergies, asthma, chronic obstructive lung disease, croup, brain swelling, eye pain following eye surgery, and along with antibiotics in tuberculosis.
During the final prenatal period of fetal lung development in humans, important maturational processes occur, including the production of surfactant necessary to decrease surface tension at the air-liquid interface of the alveoli. During early gestation, the glucocorticoid receptor is expressed in the fetal lung, and glucocorticoids stimulate the production of surfactant-associated proteins and increase phospholipid synthesis by enhancing the activity of phosphatidylcholine. 
Dexamethasone has potent glucocorticoid activity. It stimulates the synthesis and release of surfactant, which lubricates the lungs, allowing the air sacs to slide against one another without sticking when the infant breathes. As such, administration of dexamethasone is widely used (off-label) - alongside tocolytics to delay labour - as the standard of care in improving foetal lung maturation in case of preterm labour/birth.
Given corticosteroids are regarded as teratogenic, dexamathasone is still being investigated clinically. Dexamethasone accelerates maturation of fetal lungs, decrease number of neonates with respiratory distress syndrome and improves survival in preterm delivered neonates. A single course of corticosteroids is recommended for pregnant women between 24 0/7 weeks and 33 6/7 weeks of gestation who are at risk of preterm delivery within 7 days, including for those with ruptured membranes and multiple gestations. For dexamethasone phosphate, the recommended dosing regimen is four 6 mg i.m. injections at 12 hourly intervals. 
A 2019 study demonstrated the efficacy of either dexamethasone or betamethasone given to women before preterm birth to improve infant and child health. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31523039/)

Name: Dienogest - Endometriosis
Developers: Bayer Healthcare; Mochida Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd.
Indication: Indicated for treatment of endometriosis pain
Mechanism of action: Progesterone receptor agonists
Key features and challenges:
Dienogest is a progestogen with selective progesterone receptor binding, high progestational and anti-androgenic activity, and moderate anti-gonadotrophic effects. It inhibits ovulation, transforms the endometrium, and has anti-proliferative effects. Developed by Bayer HealthCare Pharmaceuticals and originally by Jenapharm (Schering AG), dienogest is used for contraception, menopausal syndrome, dysmenorrhea, and endometriosis. It is approved in many countries for endometriosis treatment and is currently under clinical development for adenomyosis and endometriosis in various regions. (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800008297)
Dienogest was approved by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) on December 21, 2009, and by the Japanese Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) on January 22, 2008. It received approval from the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) in Australia on September 1, 2010, and from Health Canada on November 25, 2011. In China, dienogest was approved on December 17, 2018. While specific approval dates for several other countries and regions are not readily available, dienogest is also approved in India (before March 2021) and launched in various other countries including Argentina, Malaysia, Hong Kong, Switzerland, Norway, and several Middle Eastern nations.(https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB09123; https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800008297)
Despite already being marketed for endometriosis, clinical trials and studies continue to examine the efficacy and effects of Dienogest. Examples include:
A study initiated in 2017 aimed to evaluate the efficacy of dienogest versus GnRH-a in improving ongoing pregnancy rates in women undergoing IVF for endometriosis, using a non-blinded randomized controlled trial. Participants are assigned to receive either dienogest, GnRH-a, or no medical intervention before IVF/ICSI, with ongoing pregnancy rates and secondary outcomes compared across groups. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03142035)
An ongoing study to compare the effectiveness of Dienogest versus medroxyprogesterone acetate in treating pelvic pain and endometriosis recurrence after laparoscopic surgery. It will involve 130 women randomly assigned to either treatment group, with assessments of pain and side effects conducted at three and six months post-intervention. (https://irct.behdasht.gov.ir/trial/52134)
Another study evaluates the effect of Dienogest and GnRH agonist on pelvic pain after laparoscopic surgery for deep infiltrating endometriosis. It involves 104 patients who are randomly assigned to either Dienogest or GnRH agonist treatment, with pelvic pain and fertility outcomes assessed afterward. (https://irct.behdasht.gov.ir/trial/61994)
A Japanese based CT is examining the Efficacy and Safety of Long-Term Dose Dienogest in Patients With Dysmenorrhea Caused by Endometriosis (https://jrct.niph.go.jp/latest-detail/jRCTs041210016)
Recent updates:
NCT07164183 is a prospective open-label randomized parallel groups study to compare efficacy and safety of Indinol Forto® 200 mg capsules and Visanne 2 mg tablets in treatment of endometriosis. This is phase 3 study, based on hypothesis of non-inferiority.
The study population consists of females from 18 to 45 years old inclusively at the moment of screening who have been surgically (laparoscopy or laparotomy) diagnosed with endometriosis within not more than 60 months and not less than 2 weeks of study entry, and reported at least moderate pelvic pain within minimum 2 months of study entry.
Study participants are observed during 1 menstrual cycle during screening period (Screening Cycle). Participants who meet inclusion criteria and don't meet exclusion criteria will be randomly assigned to one of two treatment arms (Group 1: Indinol Forto® 200 mg capsules two times per day or Group 2: Visanne 2 mg tablets once per day). After observation on treatment during 24 weeks (monthly Visits 1-7) the study subjects enter post-treatment period and are observed for one more month (Post-Treatment Period, Visit 8).
Visual Analog Scale (VAS) is used in the study as the main tool for assessment of daily pelvic pain. Cyclic and non-cyclic pain, as well as intensity of vaginal bleeding are assessed daily during the study.
The study primary efficacy endpoint is the change in average daily pelvic pain score (cyclic and non-cyclic, combined) during the 6th treatment period (interval between Visit 6 and Visit 7) in comparison to the Screening period.
Status: Recruiting.
Est. completion date: 2026-11.
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07164183)

Name: Dinoprost
Indication: Control of severe postpartum haemorrhage caused by uterine atony that is not responsive to oxytocin, ergometrine or uterine massage
Mechanism of action: Prostaglandin F2 alpha receptor agonist, with the resultant myometrial contractions providing haemostasis
Key features and challenges:
Dinoprost is a synthetic analogue of the naturally occurring prostaglandin F2 alpha. Prostaglandin F2 alpha stimulates myometrial activity, relaxes the cervix, inhibits corpus luteal steroidogenesis, and induces luteolysis by direct action on the corpus luteum. It is primarily indicated to induce first trimester abortion (https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB01160). 

Dinoprost is an established second line treatment (after carboprost) used to control severe postpartum haemorrhage caused by uterine atony that is not responsive to oxytocin, ergometrine or uterine massage. Prostaglandin F2α (PGF2α) is a potent smooth muscle contractor which is 90% metabolised on first passage through the lungs. A large bolus of PGF2α can overload the lung metabolic pathways and allow unmetabolised PGF2α into the systemic arterial system, with resultant cardiovascular, respiratory and gastrointestinal effects.

Dinoprost has been discontinued worldwide, but limited supply may be available, for example in Australia via a Special Access Scheme. (https://www.tga.gov.au/prostin-f2-alpha-dinoprost-trometamol-discontinuation-supply-medicine). It was also discontinued in the US.
Recent updates: 31 March 2015: Prostin F2 Alpha (dinoprost trometamol) was discontinued from the Australian market by the sponsor, Pfizer. It was also discontinued in the US.

Name: Dinoprostone
Indication: Treatment of postpartum haemorrhage
Mechanism of action: Prostaglandin E receptor agonists
Key features and challenges:
Dinoprostone is a naturally occurring prostaglandin E2 (PGE2). As a prescription drug it is used primarily as a vaginal suppository, to prepare the cervix for labour and to induce labour and as an abortifacient. It is also indicated for treatment of postpartum haemorrhage, and used in the management of nonmetastatic gestational trophoblastic disease (benign hydatidiform mole). (https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB00917)
In spite of its vasodilatory properties, prostaglandin E2 (dinoprostone) causes smooth muscle contraction in the pregnant uterus, thus making it a potentially suitable uterotonic agent. Its principal indication is in induction of labour, but intrauterine placement of dinoprostone has been successfully employed as a treatment for uterine atony (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2316571/). 
According to the 2012 “WHO recommendations for the prevention and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage” the use of prostaglandin E2 alpha (dinoprostone or sulprostone) for the management of retained placenta, a common cause of PPH, is not recommended due very-low-quality evidence (https://www.who.int/reproductivehealth/publications/maternal_perinatal_health/9789241548502/en/). Further, a 2018 update to the guidelines notes that "when used for PPH prevention, injectable prostaglandins…are not beneficial for substantive priority outcomes” and “injectable prostaglandins are currently not available in all settings and where they are available, the unit cost is high”. The guidelines recommend alternative prostaglandin treatment, specifically misoprostol, for the treatment of PPH.
The vasodilatory effect of dinoprostone renders it unsuitable for use in the hypotensive or hypovolemic patient. It may, however, be of use in women with cardiorespiratory disease in whom carboprost is contraindicated.
Recent updates: 2018: Who guidelines recommend against the use of dinoprostone for the treatment of PPH (https://www.who.int/reproductivehealth/publications/maternal_perinatal_health/9789241548502/en/)

Name: Dip.io - Smartphone-enabled home urinalysis
Indication: For early detection of preeclampsia
Mechanism of action: This test is a smartphone-enabled home urinalysis combined with home blood pressure measurement.
Key features and challenges:
Dip.io (Healthy.io) is a smartphone-enabled automated urinalysis system built around a standard 10-parameter dipstick, integrated with a home self-testing kit and mobile application. The device uses a proprietary image-analysis algorithm and cloud-based platform to interpret dipstick results and transmit data to clinicians in real time. Dip.io received CE accreditation in 2016 and U.S. FDA clearance in 2018. It enables lay users to perform urine testing at home, including detection of proteinuria, a key clinical marker in preeclampsia.
In 2019, Healthy.io received UKRI funding to evaluate smartphone-based home urinalysis integrated into antenatal care at the Royal United Hospitals Bath NHS Foundation Trust (https://gtr.ukri.org/projects?ref=105336). The 12-month study recruited 100 women (70 with uncomplicated pregnancies and 30 with hypertensive pregnancies). Participants were provided with a “maternity care box” containing Dip.io test kits and a home blood pressure monitor. Women conducted urine testing and blood pressure measurements prior to antenatal visits, and hypertensive participants were supplied with additional kits for interim monitoring. The study aimed to assess feasibility, acceptability, and potential health system impact, including earlier detection of proteinuria and reduction in face-to-face visits. No peer-reviewed results have been published from this evaluation.
A 2019 feasibility study conducted by Johns Hopkins School of Medicine evaluated Dip.io in prenatal care settings and reported positive findings regarding usability and patient acceptability (https://www.ajog.org/article/S0002-9378(19)30779-3/fulltext). While Dip.io has not been specifically validated as a diagnostic test for preeclampsia, it relies on gold-standard dipstick measurement of proteinuria, integrated with remote clinician oversight. According to Healthy.io, Dip.io is available to pregnant women in the UK and USA and through several health maintenance organizations in Israel, including use in gestational diabetes and preeclampsia monitoring (https://blog.healthy.io/prenatal/how-at-home-prenatal-care-minimizes-risk-for-pregnant-women/).
Key challenges include limited published outcome data demonstrating clinical impact on preeclampsia detection or maternal outcomes, reliance on user adherence and correct test performance, and potential variability in smartphone hardware. Further controlled studies are needed to evaluate diagnostic accuracy, health system efficiency, and cost-effectiveness in diverse antenatal populations.

Name: Doxycycline - Gonorrhea
Developers: Aqua Pharmaceuticals; University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA)
Indication: Treatment and prevention of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Protein 30S ribosomal subunit inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Doxycycline is a second-generation tetracycline antibiotic used to treat a wide range of bacterial infections. It inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 30S prokaryotic ribosomal subunit, thereby interfering with the elongation phase of protein translation and preventing the production of proteins essential for bacterial survival. Compared with first-generation tetracyclines, doxycycline is associated with reduced toxicity. It is approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration as an alternative treatment for uncomplicated gonorrhoea when penicillin is contraindicated (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2022/050641Orig1s032lbl.pdf).
Although not currently recommended as first-line therapy for gonorrhoea due to elevated antimicrobial resistance, doxycycline retains activity against many Neisseria gonorrhoeae strains in the United States. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has issued recommendations supporting doxycycline as post-exposure prophylaxis (doxy-PEP) for the prevention of certain sexually transmitted infections, including syphilis and chlamydia, and in specific populations, gonorrhoea (https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/73/rr/rr7302a1.htm). 
This strategy involves patient-managed administration shortly after sexual exposure.
Several Phase IV and related clinical trials are ongoing or recently initiated. A 2022 Phase IV study is evaluating cefixime plus doxycycline compared with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin for the treatment of urogenital, rectal, and pharyngeal gonorrhoea (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06090565). Additional studies initiated between 2022 and 2024 are assessing doxycycline as post-exposure or on-demand prophylaxis to reduce sexually transmitted infections among men who have sex with men and women using HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis in various settings, including Kenya (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03980223
; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04050540
; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06188442
; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06468462).
Key challenges include variable gonococcal resistance patterns, uncertainty regarding long-term impact on antimicrobial resistance with widespread prophylactic use, and the need for careful stewardship. While doxycycline continues to play a role in combination therapy and emerging prophylactic strategies, its position in gonorrhoea management remains influenced by evolving resistance trends and guideline recommendations.

Name: Doxycycline - Mycoplasma genitalium
Indication: Indicated for Mycoplasma genitalium treatment and prevention
Mechanism of action: Protein 30S ribosomal subunit inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Doxycycline is a broad-spectrum, bacteriostatic tetracycline antibiotic derived from oxytetracycline produced by Streptomyces species. It inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit. Doxycycline is widely used for the treatment of respiratory and skin infections and for malaria prophylaxis. Common adverse effects include diarrhoea, pruritus, and photosensitivity. Hypersensitivity reactions are rare but may include urticaria, respiratory symptoms, and angioedema.
Doxycycline has been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for the prevention or treatment of multiple conditions, including rickettsial infections, sexually transmitted infections, respiratory tract infections, Lyme disease, anthrax, traveler’s diarrhoea, and severe acne. It has also been investigated in oncology research due to potential anti-proliferative and pro-apoptotic effects observed in preclinical studies.
In the management of Mycoplasma genitalium infection, doxycycline is commonly used as part of resistance-guided treatment strategies. It is recommended in cases of known or suspected macrolide-susceptible and macrolide-resistant infection, typically as initial therapy to reduce bacterial load before administration of second-line agents such as macrolides or fluoroquinolones. However, doxycycline monotherapy is associated with relatively modest microbiological cure rates compared to resistance-guided sequential regimens.
Key challenges include lower standalone efficacy against M. genitalium, increasing antimicrobial resistance, and the need for access to resistance testing to optimize treatment sequencing. Despite these limitations, doxycycline remains an important component of current treatment algorithms for M. genitalium infection.

Name: Drospirenone
Indication: Treatment of PCOS - Metabolism; Hyperandrogenism
Target: Progesterone receptors, mineralocorticoid and androgen receptors
Mechanism of action:
Drospirenone is a synthetic analogue of spironolactone with high progestogenic potency and antiandrogenic and antimineralocorticoid properties. It binds progesterone receptors to inhibit ovulation and stabilise the endometrium, functionally blocks androgen receptors to reduce androgenic symptoms, and antagonises aldosterone at mineralocorticoid receptors to promote natriuresis and counteract estrogen-induced fluid retention.
In PCOS, combined ethinylestradiol–drospirenone COCs suppress ovarian androgen production, regularise menstrual cycles, and improve clinical hyperandrogenism, while drospirenone-only regimens have shown direct antiandrogenic benefits.
Key features and challenges:
Drospirenone is a fourth-generation synthetic progestin structurally related to spironolactone, with antiandrogenic and antimineralocorticoid properties. It is widely marketed globally in combined oral contraceptives (COCs), typically in combination with ethinylestradiol (e.g., 30 µg ethinylestradiol + 3 mg drospirenone), as well as in a 4 mg progestin-only formulation for contraception. Drospirenone has an established pharmacokinetic and safety profile 
(https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB01395). 
In polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), COCs are recognised as first-line pharmacological therapy for menstrual irregularity and hyperandrogenism in international guidelines, with drospirenone-containing formulations frequently used due to their antiandrogenic effects (https://www.asrm.org/practice-guidance/practice-committee-documents/recommendations-from-the-2023-international-evidence-based-guideline-for-the-assessment-and-management-of-polycystic-ovary-syndrome/).
Earlier clinical studies demonstrated that ethinylestradiol–drospirenone COCs reduce circulating androgen levels, improve hirsutism and acne, and restore menstrual cyclicity in women with PCOS, with some evidence of favourable effects on selected metabolic markers (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2504056/). 
Phase IV trials such as NCT00593294 and NCT00640224 evaluated cardiovascular and metabolic risk markers in PCOS populations, including comparisons with insulin-sensitising agents. Findings suggest that drospirenone-containing COCs do not significantly worsen surrogate cardiovascular markers in selected patients, although insulin-sensitising therapies may provide superior cardiometabolic benefit while COCs remain more effective for hyperandrogenism 
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00593294
; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00640224
; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19913778/). 
A 2023 pharmacological review highlighted drospirenone’s antimineralocorticoid action, which may mitigate estrogen-related fluid retention and blood pressure increases (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9905034/).
More recent investigations have expanded potential applications. In 2024, a Phase I trial (NCT06608186) was initiated to evaluate drospirenone for prevention of premature luteinising hormone (LH) surge during controlled ovarian stimulation in women with PCOS undergoing assisted reproductive technology (ART), comparing drospirenone with the GnRH antagonist cetrorelix (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06608186). 
In 2025, a study of a drospirenone-only pill in women with PCOS reported improvements in acne and hirsutism, along with reductions in 17-hydroxyprogesterone over six months (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40928522/).
Key challenges include the class-associated risks of estrogen-containing COCs, particularly venous thromboembolism and cardiovascular events, which are relevant given the higher prevalence of obesity and metabolic risk factors in PCOS populations 
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23449010/). 
Potential impacts on insulin resistance and lipid parameters necessitate individualized cardiometabolic risk assessment prior to initiation. Hyperkalaemia is a theoretical concern due to antimineralocorticoid activity, although clinically significant events are uncommon in individuals without renal impairment or interacting medications 
(https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB01395).
Overall, drospirenone is a well-established hormonal option with strong evidence for improving menstrual irregularity and hyperandrogenism in PCOS. Emerging research suggests potential utility beyond chronic COC use, including short-term LH suppression during ART, although careful management of cardiometabolic and thromboembolic risk remains essential.
Recent updates:
2023: Pharmacological review summarised drospirenone’s antiandrogenic and antimineralocorticoid profile and its clinical use in contraception and gynaecology.
2024: Phase 1 trial NCT06608186 registered to test oral drospirenone for LH surge prevention during controlled ovarian stimulation in PCOS ART cycles vs cetrorelix. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06608186)
2025: New clinical data on drospirenone-only therapy in PCOS demonstrating reductions in acne, hirsutism and 17-OH-progesterone after 6 months. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40928522/)

Name: Dukoral
Indication: Active immunisation against Vibrio cholerae serogroup O1 in adults and children from 2 years of age who will be visiting endemic/epidemic areas. The use of Dukoral should be determined on the basis of official recommendations taking into consideration the variability of epidemiology and the risk of contracting disease in different geographical areas and travelling conditions.
Target: V. cholera serogroup O1 (Classical, El Tor – Ogawa and Inaba)
Mechanism of action: The vaccine contains killed whole V. cholerae O1 bacteria and the recombinant non-toxic B-subunit of the cholera toxin (CTB). Bacterial strains of both Inaba and Ogawa serotypes and of El Tor and Classical biotypes are included in the vaccine. Dukoral is taken orally with bicarbonate buffer, which protects the antigens from the gastric acid. The vaccine acts by inducing antibodies against both the bacterial components and CTB. The antibacterial intestinal antibodies prevent the bacteria from attaching to the intestinal wall thereby impeding colonisation of V. cholerae O1. The anti-toxin intestinal antibodies prevent the cholera toxin from binding to the intestinal mucosal surface thereby preventing the toxin-mediated diarrhoeal symptoms. The heat-labile toxin (LT) of enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC ) is structurally, functionally and immunologically similar to CTB. The two toxins cross-react immunologically.
Key features and challenges:
The efficacy of Dukoral was compared with that of whole cell (WC) vaccine in a large double-blind placebo-controlled field trial in the Matlab district in rural Bangladesh. Children aged 2-15 years and women aged > 15 years received 3 doses of vaccine at intervals of 6 weeks. The study demonstrated that protection against cholera during the first 6 months after vaccination was 85% for Dukoral vaccinees compared with 58% for WC vaccinees. Overall protective efficacy for both vaccines was 60% during the 3-year follow-up and was similar against severe and mild disease.
WHO states that cholera vaccination is a complementary cholera prevention and control measure, secondary to improving access to clean potable water, adequate sanitation, and promotion of good water, sanitation and hygiene (WaSH) practices. For Dukoral, WHO recommends 3 doses should be given to children aged 2–5 years and 2 doses to children aged ≥6 years and adults, with an interval of 1–6 weeks between doses in both groups
Recent updates: Dukoral, a two-dose inactivated vaccine consisting of killed whole cells of Vibrio cholerae O1 and the B subunit of the cholera toxin, has been on the market since 1991. However, it is mainly used in developed countries as a traveler’s vaccine and has not been introduced in developing countries due to its relatively high cost

Name: Dydrogesterone - Endometriosis
Developers: Viatris (including Xixia Pharmaceuticals); Mylan Laboratories Ltd (previously Matrix Laboratories)
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of endometriosis associated pain, abnormal lesion/tissue growth, and sexual function.
Mechanism of action: Progesterone receptor agonist
Key features and challenges:
Dydrogesterone (6-dehydro-retroprogesterone) is a retroprogesterone structurally and pharmacologically similar to endogenous progesterone. It functions as a selective progesterone receptor agonist and has been marketed since the 1960s for hormone replacement therapy, menstrual disorders, infertility, and endometriosis (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0039128X11000833?via%3Dihub). 
As a progestogen, dydrogesterone exerts anti-proliferative effects on endometrial tissue and counteracts estrogen-driven stimulation, which is central to endometriosis pathophysiology.
Clinical evidence indicates that dydrogesterone may alleviate endometriosis-associated symptoms, promote regression of lesions, and improve pregnancy rates in women with infertility related to endometriosis (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8164626/). 
International guidelines support the use of progestogens for the management of dyspareunia, dysmenorrhea, and non-menstrual pelvic pain in endometriosis, including recommendations from the European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (https://www.eshre.eu/guideline/endometriosis
; https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2011/0101/p84.html).
Recent and ongoing clinical investigations continue to evaluate its role in endometriosis management.
A study initiated in 2018 is evaluating the effects of six months of dydrogesterone (Duphaston) administration in patients with confirmed endometriosis in a post-marketing context in the Russian Federation (NCT03690765; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03690765). 
A study initiated in 2023 is assessing the long-term efficacy and safety of dydrogesterone in managing ovarian endometriosis cysts following surgery (NCT05976529; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05976529). 
A real-world prospective study initiated in 2023 is assessing effectiveness and safety in treating endometriosis-associated pelvic pain over six months using clinical evaluation, imaging, and symptom rating scales (CTRI/2023/03/05077133; http://www.ctri.nic.in/Clinicaltrials/pmaindet2.php?trialid=77133). 
Additionally, a prospective Phase III randomized, double-blind, multicenter trial initiated in 2023 is comparing 30 mg sustained-release versus 10 mg conventional dydrogesterone tablets in endometriosis treatment, with evaluations at 30, 60, and 90 days (CTRI/2023/07/0581622; http://www.ctri.nic.in/Clinicaltrials/pmaindet2.php?trialid=81622).
Key challenges include variability in dosing regimens, duration of therapy, and heterogeneity in patient populations across studies. Long-term safety data, particularly regarding metabolic effects and recurrence rates after treatment discontinuation, require further clarification. While dydrogesterone is supported by guideline recommendations and ongoing clinical research, continued high-quality randomized controlled trials are needed to define optimal treatment protocols and long-term outcomes in diverse endometriosis phenotypes.

Name: Dydrogesterone - PCOS
Developers: Abbott Laboratories; Sohag University; Fayoum University
Indication: Treatment of PCOS infertility
Mechanism of action: Progesterone receptor agonist
Key features and challenges:
Dydrogesterone is an orally active synthetic progestogen structurally and pharmacologically similar to endogenous progesterone. It is non-sedative and non-thermogenic and does not suppress ovulation or gonadotropin release at therapeutic doses. Unlike certain other progestins, it exhibits negligible androgenic, glucocorticoid, or antimineralocorticoid activity, contributing to a favorable tolerability profile. Its role in PCOS is primarily related to menstrual cycle regulation, luteal phase support, and synchronization of the hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis, particularly in assisted reproductive technology (ART) settings.
A Phase 3 trial initiated in 2022 in Iran evaluated GnRH agonist-based pituitary suppression in women with PCOS undergoing frozen embryo transfer, within broader progesterone-supported ART protocols.
https://irct.behdasht.gov.ir/trial/65176
In 2023, a clinical trial investigated steroid pretreatment strategies, including dydrogesterone, to improve cycle synchronization and live birth outcomes in fresh embryo transfer cycles.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05300841
Another study completed in 2023 compared progesterone-primed ovarian stimulation (PPOS) protocols—where progestins such as dydrogesterone are used to prevent premature LH surge—with Cetrorelix-based GnRH antagonist protocols. The trial assessed LH suppression, prevention of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), and reproductive outcomes in women with PCOS-related infertility.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05939284
Ongoing trials through 2024–2025 continue to evaluate PPOS approaches using progestins, including dydrogesterone, against conventional GnRH antagonist protocols, focusing on IVF/ICSI outcomes, cost reduction, and optimization of ovarian stimulation strategies in PCOS populations.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05847660
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05751681
A 2024 multicenter retrospective real-world study in India involving 7,287 women assessed utilization patterns of dydrogesterone across obstetric and gynecological conditions, including PCOS. The study highlighted its frequent use for threatened abortion, common coexisting conditions such as PCOS and thyroid disorders, and its combination with supplements and other progesterone preparations.
https://journalrbgo.org/article/real-world-utilization-pattern-of-dydrogesterone-in-7287-indian-women-with-obstetric-and-gynecological-conditions-data-from-multicentric-retrospective-study/
Although dydrogesterone is widely used in reproductive medicine and ART protocols, its role in PCOS remains largely supportive rather than disease-modifying. It primarily addresses cycle control and luteal phase adequacy rather than core metabolic drivers such as insulin resistance, hyperandrogenism, or adiposity. Additionally, much of the available evidence focuses on ART settings rather than broader PCOS management, and comparative effectiveness data against other progestins or long-term metabolic outcomes remain limited.

The study concluded that the eazyplex® platform represents a useful rapid diagnostic option for point-of-care bacterial STI testing, particularly for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis, enabling prompt treatment initiation.
Key challenges include variable sensitivity across pathogens and specimen types, potential limitations in detecting low bacterial loads, and the need for validation in diverse clinical settings. Name: Eflornithine
Developers: Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS); Stiefel Laboratories; Vanderbilt University Medical Center
Indication: Treatment of PCOS hirsutism
Mechanism of action: Enzyme inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Eflornithine is an irreversible inhibitor of ornithine decarboxylase, an enzyme required for polyamine synthesis and hair follicle proliferation. It is marketed topically (e.g., Vaniqa) for the reduction of unwanted facial hair growth in women and systemically for the treatment of African trypanosomiasis. In dermatologic use, topical eflornithine slows hair growth by inhibiting cellular activity within the hair follicle, thereby reducing the rate of terminal hair development.
Hirsutism is one of the most distressing clinical manifestations of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), driven primarily by hyperandrogenism. Management strategies typically include hormonal therapies to suppress androgen production and cosmetic approaches to address visible hair growth. Topical eflornithine provides a non-hormonal, symptom-directed treatment option for facial hirsutism.
A 2022 review of pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions for PCOS highlights the role of topical eflornithine as part of an integrated management strategy for facial hirsutism. The review discusses its use alongside cosmetic procedures such as laser therapy and electrolysis, as well as complementary approaches including acupuncture and herbal medicine. Topical eflornithine is described as a supportive therapy that slows facial hair growth and may enhance outcomes when combined with physical hair removal techniques.
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1028455921003132?via%3Dihub
Eflornithine does not address the underlying endocrine or metabolic abnormalities of PCOS, including hyperandrogenemia, insulin resistance, or ovulatory dysfunction. Its effects are limited to localized reduction of hair growth, and continued application is required to maintain benefit. Adverse effects are generally mild and may include skin irritation or erythema at the application site.
Eflornithine represents a symptomatic, cosmetic adjunct in PCOS management rather than a disease-modifying therapy. While effective for reducing facial hirsutism, it does not modify hormonal drivers of PCOS and is typically used in combination with systemic treatments targeting hyperandrogenism.

Name: Elagolix - Endometriosis
Indication: Indicated for the prevention and treatment of endometriosis associated pain
Mechanism of action: Luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone receptor antagonists
Key features and challenges:
Elagolix is an oral, second-generation gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) receptor antagonist developed by AbbVie and Neurocrine Biosciences for the treatment of gynecological conditions, particularly endometriosis-associated pain. It competitively binds to GnRH receptors in the pituitary gland, leading to dose-dependent suppression of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) secretion. This suppression reduces ovarian production of estradiol and progesterone, thereby decreasing endometrial proliferation, inflammation, and pain associated with endometriosis (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/11250647
; https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB11979
; https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800020238).
Elagolix received US FDA approval in July 2018 for moderate to severe endometriosis-associated pain, with subsequent approvals in Canada (August 2018), Australia (January 2020), and Singapore (October 2020). AbbVie withdrew its European Union marketing application in 2019, and the drug has not been approved in Japan. It is marketed in North America for endometriosis pain and also indicated for menorrhagia associated with uterine fibroids.
Clinical investigations have evaluated elagolix both as monotherapy and in combination with hormonal add-back therapy to mitigate hypoestrogenic adverse effects such as bone mineral density loss (e.g., https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03213457). Additional studies have assessed elagolix combined with oral contraceptives (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04333576), its comparative efficacy versus placebo, long-term safety—particularly regarding bone mineral density—and real-world outcomes including treatment adherence and healthcare utilization. Across Phase III trials, elagolix demonstrated significant reductions in dysmenorrhea and non-menstrual pelvic pain compared with placebo, along with improvements in quality-of-life measures.
Key challenges include hypoestrogenic side effects, particularly dose-dependent decreases in bone mineral density, vasomotor symptoms, and potential mood changes. Long-term use requires careful monitoring and may necessitate add-back therapy. Regulatory variation across regions and cost considerations may affect access. While elagolix is an established, evidence-based oral GnRH antagonist for endometriosis pain management, balancing efficacy with long-term safety remains central to its clinical use.

Name: Elagolix - Uterine fibroids
Indication: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding Associated With Uterine Fibroids
Mechanism of action: LHRH receptor antagonists. Elagolix works by directly inhibiting the GnRH receptors in the pituitary gland, which leads to a reduction in the release of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). This, in turn, decreases ovarian production of estrogen and progesterone, leading to a reduction in fibroid size and related symptoms.
Key features and challenges:
Elagolix is an orally active, non-peptide gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) receptor antagonist. It suppresses pituitary secretion of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), thereby reducing ovarian estrogen and progesterone production. Because uterine fibroids (UF) are estrogen- and progesterone-responsive tumors, suppression of ovarian steroidogenesis reduces fibroid size and improves heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB). Elagolix is approved in the United States for the management of heavy menstrual bleeding associated with uterine fibroids.
https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800020238
Phase III ELARIS UF-I and UF-II trials demonstrated that elagolix significantly reduced menstrual blood loss compared with placebo. Hypoestrogenic adverse effects, including hot flushes and decreases in bone mineral density (BMD), were observed and were consistent with earlier phase studies. The addition of low-dose add-back therapy (estradiol 1 mg/norethindrone acetate 0.5 mg) mitigated bone loss and vasomotor symptoms without substantially compromising efficacy.
https://adis.springer.com/trials/700267034
http://adis.springer.com/downloads/mediarelease/1851/809254666.html
A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of four randomized controlled trials confirmed that elagolix effectively reduced heavy menstrual bleeding and improved hemoglobin levels. Elagolix monotherapy showed higher efficacy but was associated with more adverse events. Add-back therapy reduced side effects while maintaining clinical benefit.
https://mefj.springeropen.com/articles/10.1186/s43043-021-00064-5
Long-term safety data have been evaluated in Phase III and extension studies. A 24-month analysis demonstrated approximately 1% reduction in BMD at the lumbar spine, total hip, and femoral neck with elagolix plus add-back therapy, supporting extended use up to 24 months. Follow-up analyses reported consistent safety profiles with no new safety signals.
https://www.fertstert.org/article/S0015-0282(22)00684-7/fulltext
https://www.fertstert.org/article/S0015-0282(22)00683-5/fulltext
Data from a Phase 3b study (NCT03271489) assessing 36-month exposure indicated relative stability in BMD over time with add-back therapy, with mean percentage changes at 36 months comparable to 12- and 24-month findings. The study has been completed, with final results pending further updates.
https://www.fertstert.org/article/S0015-0282(23)01410-3/fulltext
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03271489
Although effective, elagolix therapy is generally recommended for limited duration (up to 24 months) due to concerns about long-term bone health. Additional considerations include hypoestrogenic symptoms, cost, and recurrence of symptoms after discontinuation. Intrinsic class effects of GnRH antagonism require monitoring of bone density and careful patient selection.
Elagolix represents a clinically validated, orally administered hormonal therapy for heavy menstrual bleeding associated with uterine fibroids. Its efficacy is well established, particularly when combined with add-back therapy to improve tolerability and bone safety. Long-term management considerations and symptom recurrence after cessation remain important clinical factors.

Name: Ellavi Uterine Balloon Tamponade (UBT)
Developers: PATH (including Meningitis Vaccine Project (MVP) and Malaria Vaccine Initiative (MVI)); Sinapi Biomedical; South African Medical Research Council (SAMRC)
Indication: Indicated for the temporary control or reduction of postpartum uterine bleeding when conservative management of uterine bleeding is warranted.
Mechanism of action: Provides direct intrauterine pressure/tamponade to promote haemostasis.
Key features and challenges:
The Ellavi Uterine Balloon Tamponade (UBT) was developed by PATH in partnership with Sinapi Biomedical for the management of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH), particularly in low-resource settings. It is a fully assembled device that can be inserted and activated in less than one minute. Once trained, maternal healthcare providers at various levels are able to insert the device. The Ellavi UBT uses a free-flow pressure-controlled system in which fluid moves freely between the uterine balloon and an external supply bag. As uterine contractility improves, fluid is displaced back into the bag, providing a visual indication of recovery and facilitating timely removal. Balloon pressure is adjusted by altering the vertical height of the fluid bag, ensuring intrauterine pressure remains slightly above uterine arterial pressure to control bleeding. With an estimated cost of US$5–15, the device is designed to be substantially more affordable than many commercial balloon tamponade systems.
A 2021 case series conducted in South Africa evaluated the Ellavi UBT in 10 patients with PPH (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34082561/). Bleeding was stopped in seven patients, markedly reduced in one, reduced in one, and unchanged in one case. All patients were referred to Nelson Mandela Academic Hospital, and outcomes were favourable. The study suggested that insertion and referral using Ellavi UBT were feasible in a rural regional hospital setting.
A 2023 implementation research study assessed adoption, sustainability, fidelity, acceptability, and feasibility of Ellavi UBT in health facilities in Ghana and Kenya (https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/13/2/e066907). The findings indicated that the device was appropriate and feasible for use by obstetric staff and could be integrated into maternal healthcare services in both countries. Additional programmatic documentation has supported its potential for scale-up (https://media.path.org/documents/DFID-DAWN-UBT-fs-Oct2019.pdf).
The device is classified as a Class II medical device. In February 2018, Sinapi Biomedical obtained a certificate of free sale from the South African National Department of Health, permitting sale in South Africa and export internationally. In February 2019, the device received CE marking with requirements for post-market clinical feedback, enabling commercialization in jurisdictions recognizing CE certification.
Key challenges include reliance on limited case series and implementation data rather than large randomized controlled trials, variability in training and health system readiness across settings, and the need for sustained procurement and supply chain integration. Continued evaluation is required to strengthen the evidence base and support broader regulatory and guideline inclusion.
