Name: Eptacog alfa
Indication: Treatment or control of postpartum haemorrhage, when uterotonic medicines are not effective at controlling the bleeding.
Mechanism of action: Promoting coagulation via Factor VIIa and Factor X-mediated pathways
Key features and challenges:
Eptacog alfa is a recombinant factor VIIa product developed by Novo Nordisk for the treatment of bleeding episodes in patients with acquired haemophilia or factor VII deficiency, Glanzmann’s thrombasthenia, and in patients with haemophilia A or B who have developed inhibitors to factor VIII or factor IX. The agent is also indicated among these patient populations for the prevention of bleeding in surgical interventions or invasive procedures. Eptacog alfa has been widely launched worldwide for these indications, and is also available in Japan, the EU and the US for the treatment of bleeding episodes in Glanzmann's thrombasthenia. Additionally, a heat-stable formulation and a pre-filled syringe formulation of eptacog alfa have been approved. 

Eptacog alfa was first used for PPH in early 2000s, with demonstrated effectiveness in controlling PPH. A case review of 118 cases of massive postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) treated with rFVIIa shows that at a median dose of 71.6 μg/kg, rFVIIa was effective in stopping or reducing bleeding in nearly 90% of the reported cases (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18393147/).
In 2010, Novo Nordisk and the Centre Hospitalier Universitaire de Nimes completed the clinical trial that evaluated the efficacy of eptacog alfa as salvage therapy, combined with standard of care (SOC) versus SOC alone in 84 women with severe postpartum haemorrhage, in whom uterotonics (sulprostone) had failed (PHRC-I/2005/GL-01; EudraCT2005-005801-40; NCT00370877). In 2020 , eptacog alfa was being investigated as a treatment for patients with severe postpartum haemorrhage in a retrospective cohort study in Switzerland (https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT04444856). 

Following the release of study results in April 2022, the EMA's Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) adopted a positive opinion, recommending an extension of eptacog alfa (NovoSeven) label to include treatment of women suffering from severe haemorrhage after giving birth, when medications used to induce uterine contractions and reduce bleeding (uterotonics) were insufficient to stop the bleeding. It is currently listed as authorised under this indication in the EU (https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/human/EPAR/novoseven). In February 2023, Novo Nordisk announced that the EMA approved eptacog alfa for the use in women with severe postpartum hemorrhage. There are currently ongoing post-marketing studies of its use, including health economics evaluations.

Name: Ergometrine/methylergometrine - PPH
Indication: Prevention and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage in patients with uterine atony.
Target: Alpha-1A adrenergic receptors; ; Dopamingeric receptors; Serotonin receptors
Mechanism of action: Stimulating uterine smooth muscle contraction
Key features and challenges:
Ergometrine (methylergometrine) is an ergot alkaloid with potent uterotonic and vasoconstrictive properties, used in the prevention and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) and postabortion haemorrhage associated with uterine atony. First identified in 1932, ergometrine is included on the World Health Organization’s Model List of Essential Medicines. It directly stimulates uterine smooth muscle, increasing the force and frequency of contractions, with heightened uterine sensitivity toward the end of pregnancy. In addition to its uterotonic effect, ergometrine induces arterial vasoconstriction through stimulation of alpha-adrenergic and serotonin receptors and inhibition of endothelial-derived relaxation factor release. Absorption is rapid and complete following oral or intramuscular administration.
The World Health Organization recommends ergometrine (200 μg IM/IV) as a uterotonic for the prevention and treatment of PPH in settings where hypertensive disorders can be excluded and where other uterotonics are not available. However, its use is associated with adverse effects including nausea, vomiting, hypertension, headache, and abdominal pain. Due to the risk of hypertension, administration requires skilled health personnel. Additional limitations include the need for cold storage and careful transport conditions.
A 2018 network meta-analysis evaluating uterotonic agents for prevention of PPH reported that ergometrine was effective in reducing PPH ≥500 mL compared with placebo or no treatment, but did not demonstrate effectiveness for PPH ≥1,000 mL. The analysis found that ergometrine plus oxytocin may reduce PPH ≥500 mL compared with oxytocin alone, although high-certainty evidence suggested little or no difference between ergometrine plus oxytocin and oxytocin alone for PPH ≥1,000 mL. Low-certainty evidence indicated that ergometrine alone may make little or no difference compared with oxytocin for both thresholds (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29693726/). 
Ergometrine remains widely used globally, and further clinical investigations continue to refine its role within uterotonic regimens.
Key challenges include its hypertensive effects, contraindication in women with pre-eclampsia or other hypertensive disorders, and logistical requirements for cold-chain storage. Comparative effectiveness against other uterotonics such as oxytocin and misoprostol varies depending on bleeding thresholds and study quality. Ongoing evaluation is required to optimize positioning within evidence-based PPH management protocols.

Name: Erythromycin
Developers: AbbVie; Mylan Laboratories Ltd (previously Matrix Laboratories)
Indication: Treatment of acne associated with PCOS
Mechanism of action: Protein synthesis inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Erythromycin, a macrolide antibiotic, stops the growth of acne-causing bacteria by inhibiting protein synthesis. Benzoyl peroxide is an antibacterial, keratolytic, sebostatic peroxide which decomposes to release oxygen that is lethal to the bacteria Proprionibacterium acnes. Due to its irritant effect, benzoyl peroxide increases turnover rate of epithelial cells, thereby peeling the skin and promoting the resolution of comedones. Benzoyl peroxide/ erythromycin topical gel is launched in the US. (https://adisinsight.springer.com/drugs/800054398)

A 2021 review aimed to highlight treatment options for acne associated with PCOS, emphasizing the importance of individual factors such as age, clinical presentation, medication history, and patient preferences in selecting the appropriate therapy. The review notes that in addition to its antibiotic activity against P. acnes, erythromycin has indirect anti-inflammatory properties. It is recommended to use benzoyl peroxide with erythromycin to decrease the development of P. acnes resistant and increase its efficacy. 
(https://doi.org/10.31838/ijpr/2021.13.03.156).

Name: Estetrol + Drospirenone (E4/DRSP)
Indication: Treatment PCOS - Menstrual cycle regulation; Metabolism; Hyperandrogenism
Target: Estrogen receptors (E4); progesterone receptors (drospirenone); mineralocorticoid receptors.
Mechanism of action:
This combination contains estetrol (E4), a naturally occurring fetal estrogen with a lower hepatic and hemostatic impact than ethinyl estradiol, and drospirenone (DRSP), a progestin with antiandrogenic and antimineralocorticoid activity.
E4 acts as a selective tissue estrogen with reduced stimulation of liver proteins involved in clotting, offering a more favourable cardiovascular and thrombotic risk profile.
DRSP suppresses ovulation, reduces androgen production, improves acne/hirsutism, and provides antimineralocorticoid activity that may improve fluid balance and BP.
Together, E4/DRSP provides ovulation suppression, improves menstrual regularity, and reduces hyperandrogenic symptoms, clinically relevant in PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
Estetrol + Drospirenone (E4/DRSP) is a next-generation combined oral contraceptive (COC) developed to provide effective ovulation suppression with reduced hepatic and hemostatic impact compared to traditional ethinyl estradiol (EE)-containing COCs. Estetrol (E4) is a naturally occurring estrogen produced by the fetal liver during pregnancy and is characterized by selective tissue activity and a comparatively lower effect on hepatic protein synthesis, including coagulation factors. This profile suggests a potentially more favourable cardiovascular and thrombotic risk profile relative to EE-based formulations. Drospirenone (DRSP), a synthetic progestin with antiandrogenic and antimineralocorticoid properties, contributes benefits relevant to polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), including reduction of acne, hirsutism, and improvement in menstrual irregularity.
E4/DRSP has been approved for contraceptive use in multiple regions, including the United States (Nextstellis®), the European Union (Drovelis®), and Japan (Alyssa®), based on Phase 3 programs demonstrating high contraceptive efficacy, favorable cycle control, and a safety profile associated with lower hepatic stimulation compared to EE/DRSP combinations. These characteristics make E4/DRSP a biologically and clinically plausible option for women with PCOS, who frequently present with elevated cardiometabolic and thrombotic risk factors.
A PCOS-specific clinical evaluation is currently underway in Thailand (TCTR20250319011), assessing the effects of E4/DRSP on menstrual cycle regulation, androgen levels, ovulatory markers, mood and quality of life, and metabolic parameters including insulin resistance and lipid profiles. This study reflects a targeted effort to evaluate the formulation beyond contraception and to determine its utility in managing PCOS-related menstrual dysfunction and hyperandrogenism.
https://www.thaiclinicaltrials.org/show/TCTR20250319011
Despite strong mechanistic rationale and established contraceptive approval, PCOS-specific evidence remains limited. Most available data derive from large contraceptive trials rather than from dedicated PCOS populations. Long-term metabolic safety in high-risk PCOS cohorts has not yet been fully characterized. Additional considerations include cost, variable access across settings, and regulatory labeling that currently focuses on contraception rather than expanded gynecologic or endocrine indications. Robust, PCOS-specific randomized controlled trials with longer follow-up will be necessary to establish its role in evidence-based PCOS management beyond contraceptive use.
Recent updates:
2021: FDA and EMA approvals for contraception (Nextstellis/Drovelis).
2024–2025: PCOS-targeted clinical trial registered in Thailand (https://www.thaiclinicaltrials.org/show/TCTR20250319011).

Name: Estetrol/drospirenone
Developers: Mithra; Fuji Pharmaceutical; Gedeon Richter plc
Indication: Indicated for the prevention and treatment of endometriosis associated pain and abnormal tissue growth
Target: Estrogen receptor; Mineralocorticoid receptor; Progesterone receptor; Testosterone congener
Mechanism of action: Estrogen receptor agonists; Hormone replacements; Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists; Progesterone receptor agonists; Testosterone congener inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Estetrol/drospirenone is a fifth-generation combined oral contraceptive developed by Mithra Pharmaceuticals and marketed under the brand Nexstellis. It contains estetrol (15 mg), a plant-synthesised analogue of the naturally occurring fetal estrogen, and drospirenone (3 mg), a well-established progestin. The product is approved for contraception in several countries, including parts of the European Union and Russia, and has undergone regulatory review in additional markets. A related formulation (PeriNesta) for menopausal symptoms was discontinued in 2021 (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800034634).
Combined oral contraceptives are recommended for the management of endometriosis-associated pain by professional societies, including the European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, reflecting their role in suppressing ovulation and stabilising hormonal fluctuations that contribute to endometriosis symptoms (https://www.eshre.eu/guideline/endometriosis
; https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2011/0101/p84.html).
Clinical development specific to endometriosis has progressed in recent years. Phase II and Phase III trials (including FSN-013P-04) conducted by Fuji Pharmaceutical evaluated the combination of estetrol and drospirenone in women with endometriosis, demonstrating effective bleeding control, improved cycle regulation, and quality-of-life benefits 
(https://adis.springer.com/trials/700346472
; https://adis.springer.com/trials/700366279). 
In September 2024, the combination received official registration for dysmenorrhoea in Japan under the name FSN-013, marking a regulatory milestone in this indication. Additionally, a Phase IV study initiated recruitment in 2024 to assess the effectiveness of estetrol/drospirenone in reducing ovarian endometriomas over 3 and 6 months (https://adis.springer.com/trials/700363827).
Key challenges include differentiation from numerous existing combined oral contraceptives already used off-label or on-label for endometriosis-related pain. Long-term comparative effectiveness data versus progestin-only therapies, GnRH analogues, and newer oral GnRH antagonists will be important in defining its positioning. Regulatory approvals to date have primarily focused on contraception and dysmenorrhoea, with broader endometriosis-specific labeling potentially requiring further evidence.
Overall, estetrol/drospirenone builds on an established hormonal strategy for endometriosis symptom control, supported by recent clinical trials and regulatory progress in Japan. Its ultimate role in endometriosis management will depend on demonstrated advantages in safety, tolerability, or quality-of-life outcomes compared with existing hormonal options.

Name: Estimated fetal weight (EFW)
Developers: Karolinska Institute, Karolinska Institutet; University of Texas, Houston
Indication: Diagnosis and prediction of IUGR.
Target: fetal biometric parameters (biparietal diameter, head circumference, abdominal circumference and femur diaphysis length)
Mechanism of action: Calculates fetal weight from biometric ultrasound measurements to detect deviation from expected growth trajectories indicative of restriction.
Key features and challenges:
​Estimated fetal weight (EFW) can be calculated using various formulae, that incorporate a variety of fetal biometric parameters, including biparietal diameter (BPD), head circumference (HC), abdominal circumference (AC), and femur diaphysis length (FL). SGA fetuses typically have EFW or AC below the 10th percentile, although 5th centile, 3rd centile, –2SD and Z-score deviation have also been used as cut-offs in the literature. Given an IUGR fetus is one that has not achieved its growth potential, reaching a consensus regarding a clinically useful definition is difficult; however, EFW may be one of the tools used to detect IUGR. 
 
The method used in Sweden to detect IUGR is repeated measurements of pregnant women's symphysis-fundus measure (SF measure). Weight estimation with ultrasound is performed only on indication, stagnant or deplaning SF dimensions, or in the event of complications. Only high-risk pregnancies have repeated growth checks during pregnancy from the beginning. A retrospective cohort study of all pregnancies in Stockholm from 2014 to 2017 utilised repeated ultrasound measurements to detect IUGR prior to labour. It aimed to evaluate the benefits of early detection and care of SGA/IUGR fetuses and to increase knowledge about this patient group. Results of the study are unknown (NCT05142644). 
 
Another study by researchers at the University of Texas Medical School Houston sought to apply customised standards to ultrasound-derived EFW and assess the frequency of abnormal growth when compared to population-based standards. Researchers also evaluated association with adverse perinatal outcomes. Results demonstrated that customised EFW was a better predictor of abnormal birthweight and adverse outcomes compared to traditional population EFW standards (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22835492/).

Name: Estradiol - PCOS
Indication: Treatment of PCOS infertility
Mechanism of action: Estrogen receptor agonist
Key features and challenges:
Estradiol is a naturally occurring estrogen steroid hormone, primarily produced in the ovaries. It regulates the menstrual cycle, supports the development of secondary sexual characteristics, and helps maintain bone density. Estradiol is often used in hormone replacement therapy (HRT) for managing symptoms of menopause, and can also be used in conditions like polycystic ovary syndrome to regulate menstrual cycles and support fertility treatments.
A 2022 randomised controlled trial compared the effects of hormone replacement therapy (HRT) protocols and GnRH agonist-HRT protocols on perinatal outcomes in 132 PCOS patients undergoing frozen-thawed embryo transfer (FET). No significant differences were observed between groups in neonatal birth weight, preeclampsia, gestational diabetes, or neonatal anomalies. The findings suggest that estradiol-based HRT without GnRH agonists is effective, less burdensome, and cost-effective for PCOS patients undergoing FET, providing similar outcomes to GnRH agonist protocols but with fewer complications. (https://www.pnrjournal.com/index.php/home/article/view/5513)
A study published in 2021 aimed to assess the impact of early versus late onset estrogen supplementation on immature oocyte retrieval, fertilization, and clinical pregnancy rates in PCOS patients undergoing follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) and human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) primed in vitro maturation (IVM) cycles. A retrospective analysis of 161 patients showed no significant differences between the two groups in fertilization, clinical pregnancy, or live birth rates. However, the early onset estrogen group had a significantly higher number of metaphase II oocytes and a lower number of germinal vesicle oocytes, suggesting improved oocyte quality. The findings indicate that early onset estrogen supplementation enhances oocyte maturation and quality in stimulated IVM cycles for PCOS patients. (https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jog.14858)

Name: Estradiol valerate
Indication: Treatment of PCOS infertility
Mechanism of action: Estradiol valerate can help manage menstrual irregularities and improve endometrial function.
Key features and challenges:
Estradiol valerate is a synthetic form of estrogen. It acts by binding to estrogen receptors in tissues that respond to estrogen, such as the reproductive system. It is used in hormone replacement therapy (HRT) to regulate menstrual cycles, improve endometrial lining in preparation for IVF, and alleviate symptoms of estrogen deficiency. In the context of PCOS, estradiol valerate can help manage menstrual irregularities and improve endometrial function.
The clinical trial NCT05227391 compares two endometrial preparation protocols for women with PCOS undergoing their first frozen embryo transfer (FET) cycle: one using estradiol valerate as part of hormone replacement treatment (HRT) and the other using letrozole. With 1,078 participants, the trial aims to assess pregnancy rates, live birth rates, and other perinatal outcomes to determine the most effective protocol for PCOS patients. The use of estradiol valerate in the HRT group is a key focus of the study. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05227391)
The trial (NCT05300841) is evaluating the effects of Estradiol valerate on women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). It aims to investigate its impact on hormonal and metabolic parameters such as insulin resistance, testosterone levels, and menstrual regularity. The study is designed to assess how Estradiol valerate could help in managing the symptoms and underlying dysfunctions of PCOS. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05300841)
A 2020 trial compared two endometrial preparation protocols for frozen-thawed embryo transfer (FET) in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). The study, which was Phase III, and completed, aimed to compare the efficacy of hormone replacement therapy versus mild ovarian stimulation. Drugs used included estradiol valerate, gonadotropins, letrozole, and progesterone. The trial focused on the therapeutic application for women with PCOS undergoing fertility treatments, specifically assessing outcomes related to endometrial preparation for FET. (https://adisinsight.springer.com/trials/700326197)

Name: Ethinylestradiol/cyproterone acetate
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Target: Estrogen receptors; progesterone receptors; androgen receptor
Mechanism of action: Ethinylestradiol (EE) and cyproterone acetate (CPA) are synthetic hormones combined in contraceptives. EE activates estrogen receptors and lowers free androgen levels, while CPA, a progestin, activates progesterone receptors and blocks androgen receptors, with stronger antiandrogen effects at higher doses. Together, they suppress ovulation and reduce ovarian androgen production, enhancing their antiandrogenic effects.
Key features and challenges:
Combined oral contraceptive pills (COCPs) are commonly prescribed for adults and adolescents with PCOS to ameliorate the hormonal disturbances and clinical features. International guidelines state that the COCP could be recommended in reproductive age adults with PCOS for management of hirsutism and/or irregular menstrual cycles. The effects of COCPs on menstrual cycle, hirsutism, weight loss, waist/hip ratio (WHR), testosterone concentrations, lipid profile and blood sugar levels are variably reported and depend on preparation, duration of use, severity of presentation, and adherence among other factors. Different combinations of COCPs are available with heterogeneous estrogen [natural estrogen or synthetic ethinyloestradiol (EE)] and progestin preparations with varying pharmacological and clinical properties. Thus, efficacy and side-effects of COCPs in PCOS may vary. The optimal COCP preparation, formulation, or dosing regimen remains unclear.  (https://www.monash.edu/medicine/mchri/pcos/guideline) 
Ethinylestradiol (EE) and cyproterone acetate (CPA) are synthetic hormones used together in contraceptives. EE, a synthetic estrogen, activates estrogen receptors and reduces free androgen levels, providing antiandrogenic effects. CPA, a synthetic progestin, activates progesterone receptors and blocks androgen receptors, though its antiandrogen effects are stronger at higher doses. Together, EE and CPA suppress ovulation and decrease ovarian androgen production through their antigonadotropic effects, which further enhances their antiandrogenic impact.
A 2023 study investigated the effects of letrozole combined with ethinylestradiol and cyproterone acetate on hormone and lipid profiles in PCOS patients. It found that this combination improved treatment efficacy compared to ethinylestradiol and cyproterone alone, significantly reducing levels of testosterone, luteinizing hormone, triglycerides, and LDL cholesterol, while increasing HDL and estrogen. It also enhanced follicle maturation, ovulation, and pregnancy rates. Independent factors for less effective treatment included higher fasting glucose, increased hirsutism, single-drug treatment, higher blood pressure, and lower baseline estrogen. Adverse reaction rates were similar in both groups. (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10006778)
A 2021 study evaluated the effects of Diane-35 and pioglitazone on endocrine, blood lipid, and glucose metabolism in PCOS patients. The combination therapy showed improvements over Diane-35 alone, significantly reducing hormone levels, blood glucose, insulin resistance, and LDL cholesterol, while increasing HDL. Patients receiving both treatments had lower BMI, waist-hip ratio, and Ferriman-Gallwey scores, indicating reduced hirsutism. These findings suggest that adding pioglitazone to Diane-35 may offer enhanced benefits in managing PCOS-related metabolic and endocrine symptoms. (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8661247/)
GLP-1RA + Metformin effectively reduced weight, BMI, waist circumference, fasting glucose, insulin levels, total cholesterol, IL-6, and improved insulin sensitivity and ovulation. In contrast, CPA/EE + Metformin was more effective in lowering hyperandrogenemia markers like testosterone and improving the LH/FSH ratio and SHBG. Both treatments affected proteins related to detoxification and immune response (e.g., PRDX6, FN1, SERPINB9), indicating their potential as biomarkers for assessing PCOS risk and treatment effectiveness.
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03151005 and https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12020-023-03487-4)

Name: Ethinylestradiol/desogestrel
Developers: Merck (also known as Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany), including Sigma-Aldrich, MilliporeSigma and EMD Serono; Health Research Council of New Zealand (HRC); Uppsala University Hospital; Swedish Society of Medicine
Indication: Treatment of PCOS.
Mechanism of action: Estrogen receptor agonists; Progesterone receptor agonists
Key features and challenges:
Combined oral contraceptive pills (COCPs) are widely prescribed for adolescents and adults with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) to manage hormonal disturbances and associated clinical features. International guidelines recommend COCPs for reproductive-age individuals with PCOS to address hirsutism and irregular menstrual cycles. COCPs may improve menstrual regularity, reduce androgen levels, and alleviate symptoms such as acne and excess hair growth. However, reported effects on weight, waist-to-hip ratio, lipid profile, glucose metabolism, and testosterone concentrations vary depending on formulation, duration of use, adherence, and baseline disease severity. Preparations differ in estrogen type (natural estrogen or synthetic ethinylestradiol [EE]) and progestin component, resulting in variability in efficacy and side-effect profiles. The optimal formulation and dosing regimen for PCOS management remain unclear.
(Source: International PCOS Guideline, Monash University)
A 2020 randomized clinical trial evaluated two combined oral contraceptives—ethinylestradiol/cyproterone acetate (EE/CPA) and ethinylestradiol/desogestrel (EE/DES)—with or without metformin in 107 women with PCOS over 12 months. Both regimens significantly improved hirsutism markers, including hair density and modified Ferriman-Gallwey scores. The addition of metformin did not confer significant additional benefit. Both COC formulations demonstrated comparable effectiveness in reducing hirsutism symptoms and improving patient perception of symptom severity.
(https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7492016/)
A 2021 population-based cohort study using Swedish national registry data examined the impact of early anti-androgen treatment initiation on fertility outcomes in women with PCOS. Among 15,106 women with PCOS followed for up to 10 years, those who initiated anti-androgen therapy during adolescence demonstrated higher spontaneous conception rates compared to later initiators. These findings suggest that early management of hyperandrogenism may improve long-term reproductive outcomes.
(https://academic.oup.com/humrep/article/36/5/1427/6102682)
A 2023 study reported that desogestrel/ethinyl estradiol combination oral contraceptives effectively improved hyperandrogenemia in PCOS by increasing sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) and reducing free androgen index (FAI). However, mild effects on glucose metabolism, lipid profiles, and inflammatory markers were observed, underscoring the need for long-term studies to assess metabolic safety and cardiovascular risk compared with alternative contraceptive routes.
(https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/12/8/2827)
Earlier clinical trials have also evaluated ethinyl estradiol/desogestrel alone or in combination with agents such as simvastatin or metformin for PCOS symptom management.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00365638
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00283816

Name: Ethinylestradiol/dienogest
Developers: Health Research Council of New Zealand (HRC); Uppsala University Hospital; Swedish Society of Medicine; Bayer Healthcare
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: Estrogen receptor agonists; Progesterone receptor agonists
Key features and challenges:
Combined oral contraceptive pills (COCPs) are commonly prescribed for adults and adolescents with PCOS to ameliorate the hormonal disturbances and clinical features. International guidelines state that the COCP could be recommended in reproductive age adults with PCOS for management of hirsutism and/or irregular menstrual cycles. The effects of COCPs on menstrual cycle, hirsutism, weight loss, waist/hip ratio (WHR), testosterone concentrations, lipid profile and blood sugar levels are variably reported and depend on preparation, duration of use, severity of presentation, and adherence among other factors. Different combinations of COCPs are available with heterogeneous estrogen [natural estrogen or synthetic ethinyloestradiol (EE)] and progestin preparations with varying pharmacological and clinical properties. Thus, efficacy and side-effects of COCPs in PCOS may vary. The optimal COCP preparation, formulation, or dosing regimen remains unclear. However, health professionals could consider that there is no clinical advantage of using high dose ethinylestradiol (>0.03mg) versus low dose ethinylestradiol (<0.03mg) when treating hirsutims in adults with PCOS. (https://www.monash.edu/medicine/mchri/pcos/guideline) 

Dienogest in combination with ethinyl estradiol (EE) is a commonly prescribed anti-androgenic combined oral contraceptive (aaCOC) used to manage hyperandrogenism in women with PCOS. Dienogest, a fourth-generation progestin, exhibits anti-androgenic properties, effectively reducing symptoms such as hirsutism and acne. Alongside EE, which stabilizes the endometrium and suppresses ovarian androgen production, this combination has been included in Swedish contraceptive policy guidelines for managing PCOS-associated hyperandrogenism.

A 2021 population-based study investigated whether early anti-androgenic treatment during adolescence improves spontaneous conception rates leading to childbirth in women with PCOS. Using linked Swedish national registries, 15,106 women with PCOS and 73,786 controls were followed from age 18 for up to 10 years. Women treated with anti-androgenic medications, such as aaCOCs or other anti-androgens, were categorized as hyperandrogenic, with further classification into mild or severe groups based on treatment type. Results showed that early anti-androgenic treatment significantly increased the probability of spontaneous conception leading to childbirth compared to late treatment or no treatment, highlighting the potential benefits of early intervention in managing PCOS-related infertility. (https://academic.oup.com/humrep/article/36/5/1427/6102682#236126388)

Name: Ethinylestradiol/drosperinone/levomefolic acid
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Target: Estrogen receptors; Mineralocorticoid receptors; Progesterone receptors; Testosterone congeners
Mechanism of action: Estrogen receptor agonists; Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists; Progesterone receptor agonists; Testosterone congener inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Combined oral contraceptive pills (COCPs) are commonly prescribed for adults and adolescents with PCOS to ameliorate the hormonal disturbances and clinical features. International guidelines state that the COCP could be recommended in reproductive age adults with PCOS for management of hirsutism and/or irregular menstrual cycles. The effects of COCPs on menstrual cycle, hirsutism, weight loss, waist/hip ratio (WHR), testosterone concentrations, lipid profile and blood sugar levels are variably reported and depend on preparation, duration of use, severity of presentation, and adherence among other factors. Different combinations of COCPs are available with heterogeneous estrogen [natural estrogen or synthetic ethinyloestradiol (EE)] and progestin preparations with varying pharmacological and clinical properties. Thus, efficacy and side-effects of COCPs in PCOS may vary. The optimal COCP preparation, formulation, or dosing regimen remains unclear. (https://www.monash.edu/medicine/mchri/pcos/guideline) 

Drospirenone/ethinylestradiol/levomefolic acid (EE/DRSP/LMF), is a combination of ethinylestradiol (EE), an estrogen, drospirenone (DRSP), a progestogen, antimineralocorticoid, and antiandrogen, and levomefolic acid (LMF), a form of vitamin B9, which is used as a birth control pill to prevent pregnancy. The formulation contains folate as the calcium salt of levomefolic acid to lower the risk of complications such as fetal neural tube defects should the medication fail as a form of birth control.

A completed Phase IV study compares the effects of a 6-month regimen of a low-dose oral contraceptive containing drospirenone (3 mg), ethinylestradiol (0.02 mg), and levomefolate calcium (0.451 mg) on androgen profiles, cardiometabolic measures, B-vitamin status, and menstrual regulation in women with PCOS. Participants are divided into three BMI-based groups: normal (18–24.9 kg/m²), overweight (25–29.9 kg/m²), and obese (30–35 kg/m²). The study aims to assess how body weight influences the contraceptive’s effectiveness in managing PCOS symptoms and metabolic factors. Results are yet to be published. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01360996)

Name: Ethinylestradiol/drospirenone (Yaz) - PCOS
Developers: Inonu University; Exeltis USA; Chittaranjan Seva Sadan Hospital
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Target: Mineralocorticoid receptor; Progesterone receptor; Testosterone congener
Mechanism of action: Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists; Progesterone receptor agonists; Testosterone congener inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Ethinylestradiol/drospirenone is a combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP) widely used for contraception and management of hyperandrogenic symptoms. International evidence-based guidelines recommend COCPs for reproductive-age women with PCOS to manage irregular menstrual cycles and hirsutism, while acknowledging that effects on weight, metabolic parameters, lipid profiles, and insulin resistance vary by formulation, duration, and patient phenotype. The optimal preparation remains uncertain due to heterogeneity in estrogen and progestin components.
https://www.monash.edu/medicine/mchri/pcos/guideline

Drospirenone is a synthetic progestin with anti-androgenic and anti-mineralocorticoid properties, which can reduce acne, hirsutism, and fluid retention. Its relatively neutral or potentially favorable metabolic profile compared with other progestins makes it attractive in PCOS populations where insulin resistance and cardiometabolic risk are concerns. Bayer Schering Pharma developed ethinylestradiol 20 µg/drospirenone 3 mg formulations, marketed globally as Yaz (24-day regimen) and Yasminelle (21-day regimen), with additional flexible-cycle formulations such as Flexyess in the EU.
https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800017043

Clinical studies continue to explore its comparative efficacy and metabolic effects in PCOS. A Turkish trial (2021–2023) compared drospirenone-containing COCs with cyproterone acetate-containing COCs, incorporating metabolomics analyses to better understand biochemical pathway changes in PCOS.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04831151

Name: Ethinylestradiol/gestodene
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: Regulates hormone levels to suppress ovulation and reduce androgen production.
Key features and challenges:
Ethinylestradiol/gestodene is a combined oral contraceptive (COC) containing synthetic estrogen (ethinylestradiol) and the progestin gestodene. It primarily functions by inhibiting ovulation, altering cervical mucus, and modifying endometrial receptivity. In women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), COCs are commonly prescribed to regulate menstrual cycles, suppress ovarian androgen production, and reduce clinical manifestations of hyperandrogenism such as acne and hirsutism.

International guidelines recommend combined oral contraceptive pills (COCPs) for reproductive-age individuals with PCOS to manage irregular menses and hirsutism. The metabolic and endocrine effects of COCs—including impacts on testosterone levels, lipid profile, glucose metabolism, body weight, and waist-to-hip ratio—vary depending on formulation, duration of use, baseline metabolic status, and adherence. Differences in estrogen type and progestin pharmacology contribute to heterogeneity in efficacy and adverse-effect profiles. Current guidelines do not endorse a specific COC formulation for PCOS due to insufficient comparative evidence.
https://www.monash.edu/medicine/mchri/pcos/guideline
A 2023 model-based meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy of oral contraceptives in managing oligomenorrhea and biochemical hyperandrogenism in women with PCOS. The analysis supported the effectiveness of OCs in improving menstrual irregularity and reducing androgen levels, consistent with prior clinical evidence. However, it also highlighted uncertainty regarding differences between specific OC formulations, noting a lack of definitive comparative data. The study examined cardiometabolic effects, reporting that while OCs may worsen lipid parameters, they have minimal impact on insulin sensitivity, body mass index (BMI), or blood pressure in most women with PCOS. Lipid changes were less pronounced in women with more severe baseline dyslipidemia, possibly reflecting underlying metabolic disturbances intrinsic to PCOS.
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0928098723002075?via%3Dihub
Although ethinylestradiol/gestodene is widely used for cycle regulation and androgen suppression, it does not address the underlying metabolic drivers of PCOS, such as insulin resistance or adipose dysfunction. Potential risks associated with COCs—including thromboembolic events, alterations in lipid profile, and hormonal adverse effects—require individualised risk assessment, particularly in women with obesity or cardiometabolic risk factors.
Ethinylestradiol/gestodene represents a standard symptomatic therapy in PCOS management, primarily targeting menstrual irregularity and hyperandrogenism. While supported by substantial class-wide evidence for COCs, no data currently demonstrate superiority of this specific formulation over alternative estrogen–progestin combinations in PCOS.

Lipid changes were less pronounced in women with more severe baseline dyslipidemia, potentially reflecting intrinsic metabolic abnormalities associated with PCOS.

Although ethinylestradiol/levonorgestrel is widely used for menstrual regulation and androgen suppression, it does not address underlying insulin resistance or long-term metabolic risk in PCOS. Ethinylestradiol/levonorgestrel represents a standard symptomatic therapy in PCOS management, primarily targeting cycle irregularity and hyperandrogenism. Source: https://www.monash.edu/medicine/mchri/pcos/guideline
Ethinylestradiol/norethisterone acetate (EE/NETA) combines synthetic estrogen (EE) with the progestin norethisterone acetate (NETA). Periodontal health parameters, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP) levels, and quality-of-life measures were assessed. After six months, significant improvements in periodontal parameters and hsCRP levels were observed across all groups. While systemic inflammation reduction did not significantly differ between intervention arms, greater improvement in gingival inflammation was noted in the group receiving dental scaling in combination with EE/NETA.

Name: Etonogestrel Contraceptive Implant
Developers: Jiaxing Maternal and Child Health Hospital; Zhejiang University; University of Naples "Federico II"
Indication: Treatment of endometriosis pain
Mechanism of action: Progesterone receptor agonists
Key features and challenges:
The etonogestrel contraceptive implant is a subdermal, long-acting progestin-only device inserted in the upper arm, releasing a low and steady dose of etonogestrel for up to three years. Etonogestrel binds to progesterone receptors in target tissues, including the reproductive tract, hypothalamus, and pituitary gland, suppressing gonadotrophin-releasing hormone (GnRH) and luteinising hormone (LH) secretion, thereby inhibiting ovulation and reducing endometrial proliferation (https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB00294). The implant is marketed in several countries under brand names such as Implanon NXT and Nexplanon, with ongoing evaluations of extended duration of use and drug–drug interactions (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800011815).
Clinical investigation of etonogestrel implants in endometriosis has accumulated over time. A 2018 study conducted at the University of Naples reported improvements in pain symptoms, mental health, and sexual function after 12 months in women with endometriosis-related pain and ultrasound features of endometrioma; however, no significant change in cyst diameter was observed (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00404-018-4851-0). 
In 2021, a study from Zhejiang University demonstrated significant reductions in pelvic pain visual analogue scale (VAS) scores and menstrual volume over 24 months of treatment in women with endometriosis or adenomyosis, although adverse effects such as irregular bleeding, amenorrhea, weight gain, and acne were reported (https://journals.lww.com/md-journal/fulltext/2021/02120/Effects_of_Etonogestrel_implants_on_pelvic_pain.54.aspx?context=LatestArticles). 
A 2022 publication further reported improvements in cyclical and non-cyclical pelvic pain, mental health, and sexual function with long-term etonogestrel use, with effects comparable to depot medroxyprogesterone acetate or the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35048754/).
More recently, a study conducted between April 2022 and July 2023 at Jiaxing Maternal and Child Health Hospital evaluated the efficacy and safety of etonogestrel subcutaneous implants for long-term management of endometriosis following surgery, comparing outcomes with a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device. Key endpoints included dysmenorrhea relief, recurrence rates, and menstrual pattern changes (https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=143064).
Although the implant is not formally approved for endometriosis treatment, it is used off-label in clinical practice (https://srh.bmj.com/content/31/1/67.short). 
Its use for reduction of endometriosis-associated pain is supported in clinical guidelines, including those from the European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology (https://www.eshre.eu/guideline/endometriosis).
Key challenges include irregular bleeding patterns, amenorrhea, weight gain, and dermatologic adverse effects, which may affect acceptability and continuation. As an off-label therapy for endometriosis in many jurisdictions, regulatory labeling and reimbursement may limit uptake despite supportive guideline recommendations.
Overall, the etonogestrel contraceptive implant represents a long-acting, progestin-based option with evidence supporting pain reduction in endometriosis. Its clinical role is shaped by tolerability, off-label status in many settings, and comparison with other hormonal long-acting therapies.

Name: Eurartesim®
Indication: Treatment of uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria in adults and children weighing 20 kg or more (except pregnant women in their first trimester), 3-day cure
Target: Free radical; Hemozoin; Protein synthesis; Sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium-transporting ATPase
Mechanism of action: Dihydroartemisinin is able to reach high concentrations within erythrocytes infected with parasites. Its endoperoxide bridge is thought to be essential for its antimalarial activity, causing free-radical damage to parasite membranes including: inhibition of Plasmodium falciparum sarcoplasmic-endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase; interference with mitochondrial electron transport; interference with parasite transport proteins; and disruption of parasite mitochondrial function. While the exact mechanism of action of piperaquine is unknown, it likely is similar to that of chloroquine (i.e. close structural analogue). Chloroquine binds to toxic haem (derived from patient's haemoglobin) within the malaria parasite, preventing its detoxification via a polymerisation step. Conversion from haem (also called heme) to hemozoin is how malaria protects itself from the toxicity of haem, therefore, inhibiting this conversion is considered a potential target for antimalarials.
Key features and challenges: 3-day cure, artemisinin-based combination therapies (TPP-1) with a comparatively long post-treatment protection and a two-year shelf life. Confirmed piperaquine resistance in Greater Mekong Subregion (GMS). Dihydroartemisinin/piperaquine (Eurartesim®) is a fixed-dose combination therapy being developed by sigma-tau (a subsidiary of Alfasigma), Chongqing Holley Holding, Oxford University and Medicines for Malaria Venture (MMV) for uncomplicated malaria. Dihydroartemisinin is a derivative of artemisinin, and such Artemisinin Combination Therapies (ACTs) are now the recommended treatment for drug-resistant malaria by the WHO, and many countries in sub-Saharan Africa and Asia have adopted it as a first-line treatment. Artemisinin/piperaquine is registered in the EU and has been launched initially in the UK, Ireland, Czech Republic, Netherlands, France, Germany, Belgium and Portugal. Launch of the product is also being prioritised, in malaria-endemic countries with marketing authorisation from the EMA (e.g. initially Cambodia). Ghana is the first African country to approve the product, followed by Burkina Faso, Tanzania, Kenya, Nigeria, Zambia and Mozambique. The product is in phase IV trials in these countries as part of the INESS (INDEPTH Effectiveness and Safety Studies of Anti-malarial drugs in Africa) programme. The therapy is also approved for use in China.

Name: Every Second Matters for Mothers and Babies - Uterine Balloon Tamponade (ESM-UBT) device
Developers: Massachusetts General Hospital (including CAMTech and the General Hospital Corporation); Vayu Global Health Innovations
Indication: Indicated for the temporary control or reduction of postpartum uterine bleeding when conservative management of uterine bleeding is warranted.
Mechanism of action: Provides direct intrauterine pressure/tamponade to promote haemostasis.
Key features and challenges:
The ESM-UBT device is an ultra-low-cost, high-quality, US FDA approved, easy to use condom-catheter UBT. It consists of a size-24 silicone urinary catheter, condoms, O-rings, a Luer-lock one-way valve, a 60 mL syringe, and a highly adherent adhesive to secure the ESM-UBT device. The ESM-UBT device components are packaged in a kit that additionally contains an illustrated checklist and data collection card. To place an ESM-UBT device, the condom is rolled out and secured to the end of the catheter with four twists of the O-ring, the balloon is then placed inside the uterus and rapidly filled with clean water using the 60 mL syringe until the bleeding stops. The device is carefully secured with the adhesive. A dose of a broad-spectrum prophylactic antibiotic is recommended, and providers are instructed to leave the ESM-UBT device in place for 6–24 h after placement. ESM-UBT devices are removed after a mother is stable by slow deflation with simultaneous close monitoring for potential resumption of bleeding. It is designed for low-resource settings, where commercial UBT devices may be unaffordable. It can be produced and distributed for less than $10 USD (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35212417/). 

A quasi-experimental, difference-in-difference (DID) design study compared changes in the rates of a composite outcome (PPH-related maternal death and/or artery ligation, uterine compression sutures, or hysterectomy) among women delivering in nine intervention facilities compared with those delivering in two control facilities, before and after the introduction of ESM-UBT. The study sample included 214 123 deliveries (n = 78 509 before ESM-UBT introduction; n = 47 211 during ESM-UBT introduction; and n = 88 403 after ESM-UBT introduction). After introduction of ESM-UBT, there was a significant decline in the rate of the primary composite outcome in intervention facilities (21.0–11.4 per 10 000 deliveries; difference −9.6, 95% confidence interval −14.0 to −5.4). Change in the rate of the primary composite outcome was not significant in control facilities (11.7–17.2 per 10 000 deliveries; difference 5.4, 95% confidence interval −3.9 to 14.9). DID analyses showed there was a significant reduction in the rate of the primary composite outcome in intervention facilities relative to control facilities (adjusted DID estimate −15.0 per 10 000 points, 95% confidence interval −23.3 to −6.8; P = 0.005) (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35212417/).
