Key features and challenges:
Ferric carboxymaltose is a non-dextran, intravenous iron replacement product initially developed by Vifor (International). It is a newer formulation of intravenous iron. It may be administered quickly and in higher doses than other intravenous irons, as a bolus injection of 200mg iron, and up to 1000mg of iron by intravenous infusion over 15 minutes. Moreover, the drug is not a contrast agent and does not interfere with MRI tests. (https://adisinsight.springer.com/drugs/800026927)

In a study by the University of Bern Switzerland, the side-effects and tolerance of IV ferric carboxymaltose was compared to IV iron sucrose. A retrospective analysis of 206 pregnant women who had received IV irons was performed. The study demonstrated that ferric carboxymaltose administration in pregnant women is well tolerated and is not associated with any relevant side effects. Furthermore, it demonstrated that ferric carboxymaltose has a comparable safety profile to iron sucrose but offers the advantage of a much higher iron dosage at a time reducing the need for repeated applications and increasing patient comfort. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22945271/).

A recent open label, individually randomised controlled trial tested a single dose of ferric carboxymaltose for anaemia treatment in Malawian pregnant women. Women with a singleton pregnancy of 13–26 weeks' gestation in primary care and outpatient settings across two regions in southern Malawi were enrolled. Women were eligible if they had capillary haemoglobin of less than 10·0 g/dL and negative malaria rapid diagnostic test. Participants were given ferric carboxymaltose up to 1000 mg, or standard of care (60 mg elemental iron twice daily for 90 days), along with intermittent preventive malaria treatment. The primary maternal outcome was anaemia at 36 weeks' gestation. The primary neonatal outcome was birthweight. The study demonstrated that treatment of anaemic pregnant women with ferric carboxymaltose was safe but did not reduce anaemia prevalence at 36 weeks' gestation or increase birthweight. (https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(23)00278-7/fulltext)

Name: Ferric citrate hydrate
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Measures serum prolactin to detect hyperprolactinemia contributing to menstrual irregularities and PCOS-like endocrine features.
Key features and challenges:
Ferric citrate hydrate (Riona) has been approved in Japan as an oral iron-based phosphate binder that effectively controls serum phosphate concentrations in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), including dialysis- and non-dialysis-dependent patients. Furthermore, ferric citrate hydrate increased haemoglobin levels in patients with iron-deficiency anaemia with or without CKD and has been approved to treat iron-deficiency anaemia in Japan. Riona has approximately 60 mg elemental iron per 250 mg tablet (https://rrtjournal.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s41100-022-00454-z#:~:text=Conclusions,of%20the%20presence%20of%20HF.)

Its safety in pregnant patients with iron deficiency anaemia has recently been tested in an observational study by Japanese Tobacco Inc., the company that markets Riona. Results of the study are unknown. (https://jrct.niph.go.jp/latest-detail/jRCT2031210322)

Name: Ferric derisomaltose (IV)
Developers: University of Copenhagen, Kobenhavens Universitet (UCPH); Thomas Jefferson University; Falun Hospital; Pharmacosmos
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Rapid molecular assay detecting gonococcal genetic markers to provide near-patient identification of infection.
Key features and challenges:
Ferric derisomaltose (formerly Iron isomaltoside 1000), is an intravenously administered colloidal matrix of iron (III) molecules and isomaltoside 1000. The drug is based on ironMatrix technology, consisting of interchanging iron(III) and isomaltoside 1000 molecules which are strongly bound together, allowing controlled-release of iron to iron-binding proteins in the body, with little risk of free iron. The low toxicity of this method of administration enables ferric derisomaltose to be given as a single high dose with no test dose requirement, meaning patients with iron deficiency anaemia can complete iron correction in one visit. It is marketed in many countries for iron deficiency anaemia. (https://adisinsight.springer.com/drugs/800036570)

A retrospective study in Sweden evaluated the efficacy and safety for mother and child of using intravenous iron isomaltoside (IV-IIM) during pregnancy. All pregnant women who received a single dose of 1000 or 1500 mg IV-iron isomaltoside (IV-IIM) in the maternity ward of Falu Hospital and subsequently gave birth between August 6, 2013, and July 31, 2018 were included. Women who received IV-IIM (case group) were individually matched with pregnant women who did not receive IV-IIM (control group) by delivery date, maternal age (± 2 years), and parity. Results supported the convenience, safety, and efficacy of a single high-dose (up to 1500 mg) infusion of IV-IIM for iron deficiency or iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32270330/)

The RAPIDIRON Trial (NCT05358509) in India is a 3-arm, randomised-controlled trial designed to assess if a single dose of an intravenous (IV) iron formulation, administered early in the second trimester of pregnancy for treatment of moderate IDA, results in a greater proportion of participants in the IV iron arms achieving a normal hemoglobin concentration in the third trimester when compared to participants randomised to receive oral iron. This trial was also designed to test the hypothesis that the low birth weight (LBW) rate for participants randomised to the IV iron arms will be lower when compared to the LBW rate of those randomly assigned to the oral iron arm. The three arms include two IV iron arms (arm 1 - ferric carboxymaltose, arm 2 - iron isomaltoside, also known as ferric derisomaltose) and an active, comparator arm receiving oral iron, which is the standard of care. The trial is expected to be completed in 2024.

Name: Ferrimanitol ovalbumin
Developers: University Rovira i Virgili, Universitat Rovira i Virgiliv (URV)
Indication: Indicated for the prevention and treatment of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Detects disease-associated biomarkers in noninvasive biological samples to identify molecular signatures consistent with endometriosis.
Key features and challenges:
Ferrimanitol ovalbumin (FMOA) is an adduct between ovalbumin and the complex Fe(III)-mannitol. Ovalbumin is the main protein found in egg white. It is a dark-red, homogeneous substance with appearance of powder or flakes. It is difficult to formulate as a solid dosage form, so it has been marketed as a granular composition which has to be dissolved in water. (https://patents.google.com/patent/US9173925B2/en). It is marketed as Profer and Ferroprotina for iron deficiency anaemia.

Ferrimanitol ovalbumin was tested in the ECLIPSES trial (NCT03196882). This trial was designed to determine the iron supplementation dose that is most beneficial for maternal and offspring health during gestation. Non-anaemic pregnant women were given 20mg/day, 40mg/day or 80mg/day in the form of ferrimanitol ovalbumin, from the 12th week of gestation to birth. Outcomes included anaemia and other anthropometric parameters of the newborn. The trial is completed; however, results are unknown.

Name: Ferrous acetyl aspartate
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Detects mutations in the ParC gene associated with fluoroquinolone resistance to inform antimicrobial susceptibility in Mycoplasma genitalium.
Key features and challenges:
Iron acetyl aspartate is a formulation of iron conjugated to one N-acetyl-aspartylated derivative of casein (Fe-ASP) that has recently been developed. Due to the casein coating, it is anticipated that iron is converted to a smaller extent in the stomach into insoluble salts. In this way, more iron reaches the duodenum to become absorbed whereas GI side effects are less common. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37022473/)

A clinical study in Greece investigated the efficacy of acetyl aspartate iron protein supplement in the treatment of anaemia in pregnant women after the first trimester. 28 pregnant women at 12 weeks gestation with haemoglobin <10.5 gr/dL-initiated acetyl aspartate protein iron at a daily dose of 80g elemental iron. Similarly, 35 women were studied who received different iron supplements at the same daily dose. After 30 days, haemoglobin values were measured. Results demonstrated that treatment with acetyl aspartylated iron led to higher levels of haemoglobin after four weeks of treatment. The difference was statistically significant with p < 0.0001. (https://www.imrpress.com/journal/CEOG/47/4/10.31083/j.ceog.2020.04.5310/htm#b15) (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02957643)

Name: Ferrous asparto glycinate
Indication: Indicated for the prevention and treatment of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Multiplex molecular assay detecting Mycoplasma genitalium DNA and macrolide resistance mutations to guide targeted therapy.
Key features and challenges:
Ferrous asparto glycinate is an iron-amino acid chelate in which aspartic acid and glycine are bonded to iron. It is reported that the intestinal iron absorption from iron- amino acid chelate is significantly higher compared with inorganic iron salts. Asparagine and glycine are known to enhance the transport of iron from the duodenum. In fact, absorption of iron-asparagine or iron-glycine chelate is more than double that of iron-ascorbate salt. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24959663/).

In a double blind, prospective, randomised, multicentre, parallel group comparative clinical study at three different centres in India, the efficacy and safety of oral ferrous asparto glycinate was compared to ferrous ascorbate in pregnant women with iron deficiency anaemia. A total of 73 pregnant women at 12-26 weeks' gestation were divided into two arms of ferrous ascorbate and ferrous asparto glycinate for a period of 28 days. The results showed that ferrous asparto glycinate is an effective iron-amino acid chelate in the management of iron deficiency anaemia in pregnant women as compared with ferrous ascorbate. However, additional large scale trials are warranted to confirm the findings. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24959663)

Name: Ferrous bisglycinate
Developers: University of British Columbia; Mahidol University; Næstved Hospital; Assiut University; HaEmek Medical Center
Indication: Indicated for the treatment and prevention of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Increases iron levels
Key features and challenges:
Ferrous bisglycinate consists of one molecule of ferrous iron bound to two molecules of glycine to form two heterocyclic rings. For food fortification and dietary supplementation, ferrous bisglycinate is formulated containing 77% ferrous bisglycinate, food-grade citric acid (17%), maltodextrin (2%), silicon dioxide (0.01%), and water (4%). The absorption of iron from ferrous bisglycinate is regulated through the same physiological mechanisms as other inorganic forms of iron. Following oral administration, ferrous bisglycinate adds to the intestinal intraluminal pool of inorganic, non-haem iron and is absorbed intact into the mucosal cells of the intestine and is subsequently hydrolysed into its iron and glycine components. (https://www.efsa.europa.eu/en/efsajournal/pub/299)

Ferrous bisglycinate has been studied for its use in the treatment and prevention of iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy. A clinical study by Assiut University (NCT02590224) compared the efficacy and tolerability oral ferrous bisglycinate (27mg tablets) to oral ferrous glycine sulphate (567.6mg tablets) in the treatment of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy. Patients received tablets once daily for eight consecutive weeks. The primary outcome was the rate of increase of Hb level over the eight weeks. Results of the study demonstrated that ferrous bisglycinate was more efficient in increasing Hb levels in pregnant women with second trimester iron deficiency anaemia. Moreover, it had more tolerable adverse effects and higher compliance than ferrous glycine sulphate. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29843553/).

Another study in Israel aimed to compare the efficacy of a single dose of intravenous iron sucrose versus a single dose of iron sucrose and 6 weeks of treatment with oral iron supplement i.e. ferrous bisglycinate. (https://classic.clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT02458625). Results showed that intravenous 500 mg iron sucrose treatment alone is sufficient to treat postpartum anaemia without the necessity of adding oral iron treatment ferrous bisglycinate. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34171389/)

A Danish study compared the effects of oral ferrous bisglycinate 25 mg iron/day versus ferrous sulphate 50 mg iron/day in the prevention of iron deficiency and iron deficiency anaemia in pregnant women. 80 healthy ethnic Danish women were included in the study. The study demonstrated that ferrous bisglycinate was not inferior to ferrous sulphate, and ferrous bisglycinate in a low dose of 25 mg iron/day appeared to be adequate to prevent IDA in more than 95% of Danish women during pregnancy and postpartum. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24152889/)

Name: Ferrous fumarate
Developers: University of Copenhagen, Kobenhavens Universitet (UCPH); University of Buenos Aires (Universidad de Buenos Aires); Martini Hospital; Ain Shams University; Gentofte Hospital; University of Toronto; Somdejprasangkharaj 17 Hospital
Indication: Indicated for the treatment and prevention of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Combines anatomical measurements and clinical risk factors to stratify likelihood of endometriosis.
Key features and challenges:
Ferrous fumarate is a ferrous salt. Like other ferrous salts, it has a low and variable absorption rate. In the acid conditions of the gastric contents, ferrous fumarate is dissociated, and ferrous ions are liberated. These irons are absorbed in the proximal portion of the duodenum. It may come in a tablet, liquid or capsule formulation, and is marketed under multiple names, including Ferro Tab, Fersamal and Galfer (https://www.medicines.org.uk/emc/product/2821/smpc and https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/ferrous-fumarate/about-ferrous-fumarate/).

Ferrous fumarate has been tested in trials for the prevention or treatment of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy. A study in the Netherland (NCT05278793) evaluated the intermittent dosage of 200mg Ferrous Fumarate supplementation three times a week compared to daily 200mg Ferrous Fumarate supplementation in anaemic pregnant women due to iron deficiency. The primary outcome was haemoglobin level after six weeks, and secondary outcomes included side effects and compliance. The trial was completed at the end of 2022; however, results are unknown.

Another trial in Denmark utilised ferrous fumarate to determine the optimal dose of iron prophylaxis in pregnancy. The study comprised 427 healthy pregnant women allocated to four groups taking ferrous fumarate in doses of 20mg, 40mg, 50mg and 80mg from 18 weeks gestation. The study demonstrated that a supplement of 40 mg ferrous iron/day from 18 weeks of gestation appears adequate to prevent iron deficiency in 90% of the women and iron deficiency anaemia in at least 95% of the women during pregnancy and postpartum. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15715531/)

Name: Ferrous gluconate
Indication: Indicated for the prevention and treatment of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Microfluidic platform performing loop-mediated isothermal amplification of Trichomonas vaginalis DNA for rapid molecular detection.
Key features and challenges:
Ferrous gluconate is a ferrous salt. It contains approximately 10% to 14% elemental iron per mg ferrous gluconate salt. Like other ferrous salts, it has a low and a variable absorption rate. Its absorption can be limited by mucosal luminal damage as well as by the ingestion of certain foods; so, it is indicated that administration one hour before meals on an empty stomach with a glass of orange juice or another form of vitamin C to enhance absorption. It is available in a liquid formulation as Floradix, or in tablet formulations as Ferate or Fergon to prevent or treat iron deficiency anaemia.  (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7477519/)

A Phase IV, multi-centre, randomised, open label study aimed to investigate the efficacy and safety of Floradix mit Eisen and ferro sanol duodenal mite 50 mg in pregnant women with diagnosed iron deficiency anaemia. However, only 26 women were recruited, and results were not formally published. (https://www.clinicaltrialsregister.eu/ctr-search/trial/2010-018940-15/DE)

Name: Ferrous gluconate (IV)
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Blood-based biomarker assay quantifying inflammatory and hormonal markers to identify endometriosis-related pathophysiology.
Key features and challenges:
Sodium ferric gluconate complex is an iron replacement product for treatment of iron deficiency anaemia. The stable macromolecular complex is negatively charged at alkaline pH with an apparent molecular weight of 289,000 – 440,000 daltons on gel chromatography. It is composed of iron (III) oxide hydrate directly bonded to sucrose with a chelating gluconate function in a molar ratio of two iron molecules to one gluconate. It is used in adult and in paediatric patients over the age of 6 years with chronic kidney disease (CKD) receiving haemodialysis and supplemental epoetin therapy. (https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB09517)

In the US, IV ferrous gluconate is not approved for use outside of patients with chronic kidney disease receiving haemodialysis and supplemental epoetin therapy. However, it is mentioned in review articles (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6142528/ and https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6020007/#CR34) looking at the treatment of iron deficiency in gynaecology and obstetrics, and the use of intravenous iron. It is unclear whether IV ferrous gluconate has been tested in clinical studies to evaluate its ability to treat iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy.

Name: Ferrous glycine sulphate
Developers: Assiut University; Tehran University of Medical Sciences (TUMS); Salus Haus
Indication: Indicated for the prevention and treatment of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Isothermal amplification coupled with CRISPR/Cas13a cleavage enables sequence-specific detection of Trichomonas vaginalis RNA via lateral flow readout.
Key features and challenges:
Ferrous glycine sulphate is an organic complex of glycine and ferrous sulphate. It has a bioavailability of at least 11% from a single daily dose of 100mg Fe. In Egypt, ferrous (II) glycine sulphate complex is marketed as Ferro Sanol Duodenal. (https://www.thieme-connect.com/products/ejournals/abstract/10.1055/s-0031-1296875).

Ferrous glycine sulphate has been studied for its use in the prevention and treatment of iron deficiency anaemia. A clinical study by Assiut University (NCT02590224) compared the efficacy and tolerability of oral ferrous bisglycinate (27mg tablets) to oral ferrous glycine sulphate (567.6mg tablets) in the treatment of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy. Patients received tablets once daily for eight consecutive weeks. The primary outcome was the rate of Hb increase over the eight weeks. Results of the study demonstrated that ferrous glycine sulphate was inferior to ferrous bisglycinate in increasing Hb levels in pregnant women with second trimester IDA. Moreover, ferrous bisglycinate had more tolerable adverse effects and higher compliance than ferrous glycine sulphate. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29843553/)

Another study by the Tehran University of Medical Sciences compared the influence and tolerability of two types of ferrous glycine sulphate supplements versus ferrous sulphate in both anaemic and non-anaemic pregnant women. Pregnant women were given Ferrofort Duodenal, Ferrofort Gyn or ferrous sulphate for two months. Outcomes included haemoglobin, serum ferritin, digestive complications, and compliance. Results of the study are unknown. (https://en.irct.ir/trial/38887)

Name: Ferrous succinate
Developers: Ocean University of China; China Medical University
Indication: Indicated for the prevention and treatment of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Increases iron levels
Key features and challenges:
Ferrous succinate is a ferrous salt. It involves iron bonded with succinic acid. Studies have previously shown that more iron is absorbed from ferrous succinate than multiple other iron compounds, including ferrous sulphate. Ferrous succinate is marketed in China. (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/003693306701200503?journalCode=scma)

In a study conducted by Shengjing Hospital, China, the effect of oral iron administration on iron deficiency anaemia in twin pregnancies was studied (NCT04975074). Women with twin pregnancies were given oral iron, including ferrous sulphate, polyferose, ferrous succinate, and Chinese medicine filling iron agent, according to the current recommended dose.  Routine bloods and ferritin were monitored every 2-4 weeks during pregnancy to understand the therapeutic effect of oral iron on iron deficiency anaemia and iron deficiency in pregnant women with twin pregnancies. After delivery, neonatal ferritin and haemoglobin status was tested. However, results of the study are unknown.

Name: Ferrous sulfate
Developers: The Walter and Eliza Hall Institute of Medical Research; Thomas Jefferson University; University of Texas Medical Branch, Galveston; University Medical Centre Ljubljana; Harvard University; Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Zurich (ETH Zürich)
Indication: Indicated for the treatment and prevention of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Analyzes biochemical spectral signatures of biological samples to identify molecular composition patterns associated with endometriosis.
Key features and challenges:
Ferrous sulphate is a bivalent ferrous salt. It is the gold standard of oral iron therapy in the UK and many other countries, given its acceptable tolerability, high-effectiveness and low cost. It has a bioavailability of between 10-15%. Prolonged-release preparations are available, which may improve gastrointestinal tolerability and enhance the bioavailability. This includes Tardyferon, a prolonged-release ferrous sulphate tablet containing 80 mg of elemental iron. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22654638/)

There are multiple studies evaluating the use of ferrous sulphate in the treatment and prevention of iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy. Given ferrous sulphate is the standard of care, it is frequently used as a comparator against other oral or IV iron preparations. The RAPIDIRON Trial (NCT05358509) in India is a 3-arm, randomised-controlled trial. It is designed to assess if a single dose of an intravenous (IV) iron formulation, administered early in the second trimester of pregnancy for treatment of moderate iron deficiency anaemia, will result in a greater proportion of participants in the IV iron arms achieving a normal haemoglobin concentration in the third trimester when compared to participants randomised to receive oral ferrous sulphate. The three arms include two IV iron arms (ferric carboxymaltose and ferric derisomaltose) and an active, comparator arm receiving oral ferrous sulphate, the standard of care. The trial is expected to be completed in 2024.

As part of a collaboration between the Harvard School of Public Health in Boston, and Muhimbili University of Health and Allied Sciences in Dar es Salaam Tanzania, a randomized clinical trial among 1,5000 pregnant women in Tanzania evaluated the safety and efficacy of prenatal iron supplementation with ferrous sulphate for prevention of maternal anaemia. Evidence for this practice was limited to areas of high malaria burden and among women who were not anaemic. Participants were randomised to receive 60 milligrams of ferrous sulphate or placebo daily and were followed up through the postpartum period. Women who were anaemic or iron deficient were not enrolled in the trial. The primary aims were to determine the safety and efficacy of iron supplementation among pregnant Tanzanian women, as measured by the incidence and density of placental malaria infection, and maternal haemoglobin concentrations, and infant birth weight, compared to placebo. Secondary aims were to examine the efficacy of iron supplements on the incidence of maternal anaemia, low birth weight, and maternal malaria infection, compared to placebo. (3U01HD061232-05S1 NIH REPORTER; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01119612). Results showed prenatal iron supplementation among iron replete non-anaemic women was not associated with an increased risk of placental malaria or other adverse events. (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4904713/). A secondary analysis of this data also showed that iron supplementation is effective even among pregnant women with non-iron deficiency anaemia. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36344770/)

Name: Ferumoxytol (IV)
Developers: University of Arizona; Thomas Jefferson University; Stanford University (including the Center for Innovations in Global Health); AMAG Pharmaceuticals Inc.
Indication: Treatment of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Measures selected serum biomarkers to detect biological changes associated with the presence of endometriosis.
Key features and challenges:
Fermoxytol is an intravenously administered iron preparation approved for the treatment of iron deficiency anaemia in adult patients with and without chronic kidney disease (CKD). Since ferumoxytol is administered intravenously, it does not cause common adverse events associated with oral iron preparations. In addition, it offers more flexibility in administration and dosages than other intravenous iron replacement products available on the market. It is approved by the US FDA, however, has been withdrawn from Austria, Canada, Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, the UK, Czech Republic, and Switzerland markets, along with the withdrawal of marketing authorisation in the EU due to commercial reasons (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/6432052 and https://adisinsight.springer.com/drugs/800014223)

Ferumoxytol is currently being tested in a Phase IV clinical trial by Thomas Jefferson University. The randomised, controlled multi-site trial of iron therapy is studying whether second trimester initiation of intravenous (IV) iron therapy is better than oral iron therapy (ferrous sulphate) for the treatment of anaemia in pregnancy by improving blood count, quality of life and reducing side effects. The trial is expected to be completed at the end of 2023 (NCT04278651). 

A 2023 study demonstrated that IV ferumoxytol was well tolerated, and was associated with statistically significant increases in maternal hemoglobin, hematocrit, iron, and ferritin compared to oral ferrous sulfate. The study also demonstrated that neonates of participants who received intravenous ferumoxytol were born with higher ferritin concentrations in cord blood, at the same gestation with the same birthweight. (https://www.ajogmfm.org/article/S2589-9333(23)00206-9/abstract#%20 and https://www.ajogmfm.org/article/S2589-9333(23)00205-7/abstract)

Name: Fetal Medicine Foundation algorithm - PE
Indication: Diagnosis and prediction of preeclampsia
Target: Combination of medical history and biomarkers (mean arterial pressure (MAP), uterine artery pulsatility index (PI), and serum placental growth factor) to predict PE
Mechanism of action: Ultrasound identification of structural or vascular cord abnormalities associated with impaired placental perfusion and preeclampsia.
Key features and challenges:
The Fetal Medicine Foundation’s Bayes theorem-based model for predicting preeclampsia uses a mix of maternal characteristics, medical history, mean arterial pressure (MAP), uterine artery pulsatility index (PI), and serum markers like placental growth factor (PlGF), PAPP-A, or sFlt-1 to estimate the risk in the first trimester.

The model looks at several maternal factors like age, weight, Afro-Caribbean or South Asian background, past pregnancy with preeclampsia, IVF conception, and smoking habits. It also takes into account medical history such as chronic high blood pressure, type I or II diabetes, lupus, or antiphospholipid syndrome. In pregnancies affected by preeclampsia, MoM values for uterine artery PI and MAP tend to be higher, while serum PLGF levels are lower. These differences are more noticeable in early-onset cases, making screening generally more effective the earlier delivery is needed for mother or baby. Between 11 and 14 weeks of pregnancy, adding PlGF to the model can detect around 90% of early-onset and 75% of preterm preeclampsia, with a screen positive rate of 10.(https://fetalmedicine.org/research/assess/preeclampsia/background).
 
This test is considered adopted because of its recommendation by the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics(https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ijgo.12802) and the implementation of its use in clinical practice in the UK via a dedicated app, the Tommy’s Clinical Decision Tool (https://bmcpregnancychildbirth.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12884-022-04867-w).                                            The International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology (https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/uog.20105) and the International Society for the Study of Hypertension in Pregnancy (https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/HYPERTENSIONAHA.117.10803) have also recommended multiparametric first trimester screening including maternal factors, BP, uterine artery Doppler, and PlGF, without mentioning the FMF. (https://www.thelancet.com/journals/ebiom/article/PIIS2352-3964(21)00574-0/fulltext). 

The algorithm designed for the prediction of PE has been used in studies that were also investigating IUGR as a potential outcome of PE. (https://ClinicalTrials.gov/show/NCT02189148 and https://www.clinicaltrialsregister.eu/ctr-search/search?query=eudract_number:2013-004241-17).​

Name: Fetal Medicine Foundation algorithm - PTL
Indication: Prediction of PTL
Target: Combination of obstetrical history, maternal characteristics and cervical length
Mechanism of action: Quantifies circulating fructose as a marker of altered carbohydrate metabolism associated with insulin resistance in PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
The Fetal Medicine Foundation (FMF) provides two models for the prediction of preterm birth. 
The first calculates the risk for spontaneous birth at <34 weeks and combines maternal characteristics and medical history (but no biomarker unlike their prediction models for IUGR and PE). 
The characteristics taken into account are: 
Maternal age, BMI, racial origin, method of conception (spontaneous, ovulation drugs or IVF), and smoking status during pregnancy 
Previous obstetric history: 
No previous pregnancies ≥16 wks 
Previous pregnancies with only iatrogenic deliveries <37 wks 
Spontaneous delivery only at 16-30 wks (one event) 
Spontaneous delivery only at 16-30 wks (two events) 
Spontaneous delivery at 16-30 wks (one event) plus spontaneous delivery 31-36 wks 
Spontaneous delivery at 16-30 wks (one event) plus delivery ≥ 37 wks 
Spontaneous delivery at 16-30 wks (two events) plus delivery ≥ 37 wks 
Spontaneous delivery only at 31-36 wks 
Deliveries only ≥37 wks 
(https://www.fetalmedicine.org/research/assess/preterm) 
A 2011 UK study on 34025 pregnancies found that this model could detect 38.2% of the preterm deliveries in women with previous pregnancies at or beyond 16 weeks and 18.4% in those without, at a false positive rate (FPR) of 10%. This study was also the basis for the exclusion of biomarkers. 
(https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/pd.2662) 
 
The second calculates the risk for spontaneous birth at <28, <31, <34 or <37 weeks and combines obstetric history (nulliparous or gestational age at delivery) and cervical length measurement at 20-26 weeks. 
(https://www.fetalmedicine.org/research/assess/preterm/cervix).                                                        This algorithm has been incorporated in the Tommy's Clinical decision Tool currently implemented in the UK and is thus considered adopted: (https://bmcpregnancychildbirth.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12884-022-04867-w).​

Name: Fetal femur length (FL) - IUGR
Developers: Medical University of Vienna, Medizinische Universitaet Wien; University of Toronto
Indication: Diagnosis and prediction of IUGR
Mechanism of action: Calculates matrix metalloproteinase-9 to TIMP-1 ratio to assess extracellular matrix remodeling and inflammatory activity associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
Fetal femur length (FL) is a basic biometric parameter to assess fetal size. Femur length, together with biparietal diameter, head circumference, and abdominal circumference, are computed to produce an estimate of fetal weight. In the second trimester, this may be extrapolated to an estimate of gestational age and an estimated due date (EDD). Femur length can be used to calculate fetal length, another predictor of fetal growth, with the following equation. Fetal length in centimetres = 6.18 + 0.59 x femur length in millimetres. 
Measurement criteria: 
measure with the transducer aligned along the long axis of bone - perpendicular to the shaft 
measure where the ends of the bones are blunt and not pointed 
measure from the blunt end of the proximal femoral epiphysis to the blunt end of the distal femoral epiphysis 
measure post 32-34 weeks when the distal femoral epiphysis can be seen (although not measured) 
never measure when there is excessive bowing, demineralisation or shortened length (https://radiopaedia.org/articles/femur-length-obstetric-ultrasound?lang=gb).

A fetus is SGA when its size (biometric evaluation) falls below a predefined threshold for its gestational age. The most common definition of SGA is EFW or AC below the 10th percentile of given reference ranges. While SGA and IUGR are not the same, fetuses with birth weight below the 10th percentile are at increased risk of stillbirth and perinatal mortality, with those with birth weight below the 3rd percentile being at the highest risk. For this reason, fetal size at the lower extreme of the growth charts, for example AC or EFW (calculation involving femur length) below the 3rd percentile for given growth charts, can be used as an isolated criterion to define FGR at any gestational epoch. 
 
A study in 2010 found that incorporation of femur length leads to underestimation of fetal weight in asymmetric preterm growth restriction (https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/uog.7605). 
A 2022 study compared femur growth parameters in normal pregnancies and pregnancies with IUGR associated with placental insufficiency using MRI rather than ultrasound (https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/uog.26133).

Name: Fetal fractional limb volume (FLV)
Developers: Baylor College of Medicine; University of Colorado, Denver
Indication: Prediction and diagnosis of IUGR
Target: fractional arm volume (AVol) or fractional thigh volume (TVol)4
Mechanism of action: Measurement of the foetus' arm or thigh correlates with estimated foetal weight.
Key features and challenges:
Fractional limb volume is a fetal soft tissue parameter that may be measured on 2D or 3D ultrasound. It involves fractional arm volume (AVol) or fractional thigh volume (TVol)4 and is based on 50% of the long bone diaphysis length. Such measurements are reproducible among blinded examiners and can be manually calculated from three-dimensional (3D) volume datasets within approximately 2 minutes. Normal reference ranges for AVol and TVol have been established and fractional limb volume has been used with conventional fetal biometry to improve the precision of estimated foetal weight (EFW) (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3601845/). 
 
The International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology (ISUOG) guidelines 'Ultrasound assessment of fetal biometry and growth' states that FLV may be used as an additional approach to assessing foetal growth and development. The guidelines outline that FLV - can serve as an index of fetal nutritional status and there are studies suggesting that combining fractional limb volume with 2D biometry improves the precision of EFW with some improvement in detection of late-onset FGR at 34–36 weeks (https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/uog.20272). 
 
A study sought to compare FLV measurements in fetuses with fetal growth restriction (FGR) versus small for gestational age (SGA) defined by the ISUOG-supported international Delphi consensus and to also correlate FLV findings with birth metrics. The study hypothesised that FLV measurements would be significantly smaller in FGR versus SGA fetuses and would correlate closer with Ponderal index (PIx) in the neonate than abdominal circumference (AC). The study demonstrated that both the AC and FLV measurements were significantly reduced in FGR fetuses compared to SGAs. While the AC outperformed FLV in predicting FGR, the FLV correlated best with PIx, which holds investigative promise. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34580892/).

Name: Fetal middle cerebral artery (MCA) indices - IUGR
Developers: Maulana Azad Medical College (including associated hospitals); Fudan University
Indication: Diagnosis of IUGR
Target: velocity of blood flow in the fetal middle cerebral artery
Mechanism of action: Doppler measurement of cerebral artery flow velocity and resistance to identify compensatory brain-sparing responses in growth-restricted fetuses.
Key features and challenges:
Fetal middle cerebral arterial (MCA) Doppler assessment is an important part of assessing fetal cardiovascular distress, fetal anaemia, or fetal hypoxia. Reduced fetal MCA-PI is a consequence of vasodilatation, the so called ‘brain-sparing’ effect. This represents a haemodynamic response to fetal hypoxemia, via direct vascular sensing of oxygen tension in the cerebral circuit, and in other vascular beds; a consequent redistribution of fetal cardiac output occurs preferentially to the coronary arteries and adrenal glands. In the appropriate situation it is a useful adjunct to umbilical artery doppler assessment. It is also used in the additional work up of intra-uterine growth restriction (IUGR), twin to twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS), and twin anaemia polycythaemia sequence (TAPS). 
 
For an accurate measurement, the fetal head should be in the transverse plane. An axial section of the brain, including the thalami and the sphenoid bone wings, should be obtained, and magnified. The MCA vessels are often found with colour or power doppler ultrasound overlying the anterior wing of the sphenoid bone near the base of the skull. The reading should be obtained close to its origin in the internal carotid artery as the systolic velocity decreases with distance from the point of origin of this vessel. An angle of insonation of <15° should be used; typically, an angle that approximates 0° can be achieved by moving the transducer on the maternal abdomen. Parameters used include fetal MCA pulsatility index (PI), fetal MCA peak systolic velocity (PSV) (the highest velocity should be recorded), and the fetal MCA systolic/diastolic (S/D) ratio (a normal fetal MCA S/D ratio should always be higher than the umbilical arterial S/D ratio) (https://radiopaedia.org/articles/fetal-middle-cerebral-arterial-doppler-assessment?lang=gb).

Name: Finasteride
Developers: Health Research Council of New Zealand (HRC); Swedish Society of Medicine; Uppsala University Hospital; Merck (also known as Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany), including Sigma-Aldrich, MilliporeSigma and EMD Serono; Gedeon Richter plc
Indication: Treatment of PCOS-related hirsutism
Mechanism of action: Cholestenone 5 alpha-reductase inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Finasteride is a selective type II 5α-reductase inhibitor developed by Merck & Co. and marketed for benign prostatic hyperplasia and androgenic alopecia (Propecia). By inhibiting the conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT), it reduces androgenic activity in target tissues.
https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800003853
In polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), finasteride is used off-label as a second-line therapy for hyperandrogenic manifestations such as hirsutism. Its mechanism specifically targets peripheral androgen action rather than ovarian androgen production, making it particularly relevant for symptoms mediated by DHT.
https://globalresearchonline.net/journalcontents/v73-1/18.pdf
Comparative evidence, however, suggests that its clinical impact may be more modest than other anti-androgens. A 2023 meta-analysis evaluating anti-androgens for PCOS found that while spironolactone and flutamide demonstrated moderate improvements in free androgen index, finasteride did not show comparable effectiveness.
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0928098723002075
Beyond symptomatic management, a 2021 Swedish population-based registry study explored whether early anti-androgen treatment influences long-term fertility outcomes. Among over 15,000 women with PCOS, early initiation of anti-androgen therapy during adolescence was associated with a higher probability of spontaneous childbirth compared to later treatment, particularly in hyperandrogenic phenotypes. Although this study did not isolate finasteride specifically, it highlights the potential broader reproductive implications of timely androgen suppression.
https://academic.oup.com/humrep/article/36/5/1427/6102682
International guidelines recommend that anti-androgens, including finasteride, may be considered in combination with effective contraception for women with persistent hirsutism after at least six months of combined oral contraceptive (COCP) therapy and/or cosmetic interventions. They may also be trialed for female pattern hair loss, though PCOS-specific evidence remains limited.
https://www.monash.edu/__data/assets/pdf_file/0003/3379521/Evidence-Based-Guidelines-2023.pdf
Despite its targeted mechanism, finasteride has important limitations. It is not approved specifically for PCOS, and its efficacy for improving overall endocrine or metabolic dysfunction in PCOS is limited. Its benefits appear confined largely to androgen-mediated dermatologic symptoms, with minimal impact on menstrual irregularity, ovulation, or insulin resistance. Furthermore, due to teratogenic risk (particularly concerning male fetal development), strict contraception is required during use.
Finasteride represents a mechanistically logical but symptom-focused adjunct therapy for hyperandrogenism in PCOS. Its role remains secondary to first-line hormonal therapies, and its clinical utility is primarily in managing hirsutism and androgenic alopecia rather than modifying the underlying metabolic or reproductive pathology of PCOS.

Name: Flutamide
Developers: Merck (also known as Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany), including Sigma-Aldrich, MilliporeSigma and EMD Serono; Schering-Plough Corporation; University of Virginia; University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA)
Indication: Treatment of PCOS-related hirsutism
Target: Androgen receptor; GnRH pulse generator; glucose metabolism; lipid metabolism; endometrium
Mechanism of action: Androgen receptor analogue; GnRH pulse generator inhibition; glucose/lipid metabolism modulator; endometrial imitochondria; anti androgen
Key features and challenges:
Flutamide is a non-steroidal anti-androgen that acts by competitively inhibiting androgen receptors, thereby reducing the biological effects of circulating androgens. Although not approved specifically for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), international evidence-based guidelines indicate that anti-androgens, including flutamide, may be considered in combination with effective contraception for women with persistent hirsutism after at least six months of combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP) therapy and/or cosmetic treatment. Given the significant psychological burden of hirsutism and female pattern hair loss, anti-androgens may also be trialed alongside COCPs in selected cases, though PCOS-specific evidence remains limited.
https://www.monash.edu/__data/assets/pdf_file/0003/3379521/Evidence-Based-Guidelines-2023.pdf
Clinical evidence demonstrates that flutamide can meaningfully reduce hyperandrogenic parameters. A 2022 meta-analysis reported that flutamide at 250 mg twice daily significantly reduced total testosterone compared to finasteride and increased sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) levels, while also lowering dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS) and androstenedione. However, when compared to placebo or other medications overall, the effect on total testosterone was not consistently significant, and the certainty of evidence for several hormonal outcomes was low.
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00404-022-06549-6
Beyond biochemical improvements, flutamide has been shown to improve clinical features such as hirsutism and acne and may enhance GnRH pulse generator sensitivity and lipid profiles. Experimental studies further suggest that flutamide can prevent dihydrotestosterone (DHT) and insulin-induced defects in endometrial receptivity, potentially improving implantation and pregnancy outcomes in hyperandrogenic environments.
https://joe.bioscientifica.com/view/journals/joe/255/1/JOE-22-0059.xml
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00109-021-02104-z
More recent research has explored possible metabolic benefits. A 2023 study reported reductions in abdominal fat and lipid accumulation in newly formed adipocytes among women treated with flutamide, suggesting potential effects beyond androgen suppression.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01889199
https://www.fertstert.org/article/S0015-0282(22)01745-9/fulltext
Ongoing investigations are examining flutamide’s influence on pituitary function, LH pulse dynamics, sleep-wake hormonal relationships, and gut microbiome alterations in PCOS models.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04597099
https://reporter.nih.gov/project-details/10546503
https://academic.oup.com/jes/article/7/Supplement_1/bvad114.1680/7291617
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00930228
Despite these promising mechanistic and clinical findings, flutamide’s role in PCOS remains constrained by important safety considerations. Hepatotoxicity is a well-documented risk, particularly at higher doses or prolonged use, necessitating careful liver function monitoring. It is not FDA-approved for the treatment of PCOS or hirsutism, and its risk–benefit profile has limited widespread adoption compared with other anti-androgens such as spironolactone. Additionally, while flutamide effectively addresses hyperandrogenic symptoms, it does not correct the underlying metabolic dysfunction of PCOS and is not considered a disease-modifying therapy.
Overall, flutamide is a potent anti-androgen with demonstrated efficacy in reducing biochemical and clinical manifestations of hyperandrogenism in PCOS. However, concerns regarding hepatotoxicity, limited regulatory endorsement, and modest evidence quality position it as a secondary, carefully monitored adjunct option rather than a first-line therapy in routine PCOS management.

Name: Folic acid-iron - fixed combined
Indication: Indicated for the treatment and prevention of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Increases iron/folic acid levels
Key features and challenges:
Daily iron and folic acid supplementation is currently recommended by WHO as part of antenatal care, to reduce the risk of low birth weight, maternal anaemia, and iron deficiency. Folic acid supplementation (with or without iron) provided before conception and during the first trimester of pregnancy is also recommended for decreasing the risk of neural tube defects. It is suggested that supplements contain 30-60 mg of iron, with the higher dose preferred in settings where anaemia in pregnant women is a severe public health problem (≥40%), along with 400 µg of folic acid. Daily supplementation throughout pregnancy, beginning as early as possible after conception, is recommended in all settings. Despite its proven efficacy and wide inclusion in antenatal care programmes, the use of iron and folic acid supplementation has been limited in programme settings. Possible reasons for this include a lack of compliance, concerns about the safety of the intervention among women with an adequate iron intake, and variable availability of the supplements at community level. Intermittent use of iron and folic acid supplements by non-anaemic women is a recommended alternative to prevent anaemia and improve gestational outcomes in areas where the prevalence of anaemia among pregnant women is lower than 20%. The suggested dose is 120 mg elemental iron and 2800 µg (2.8 mg) folic acid provided weekly throughout the pregnancy, beginning as early as possible after conception. (https://www.who.int/data/nutrition/nlis/info/antenatal-iron-supplementation)

Given its widespread use and WHO recommendation, combination iron and folic acid supplements have been widely studied for the treatment and prevention of iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy. A double-blind, randomised controlled trial in Tanzania examined the efficacy of pre-pregnancy supplementation with iron and multivitamins to reduce the prevalence of anaemia during the periconceptional period among rural Tanzanian women and adolescent girls. Participants were individually randomised to receive daily oral supplements of folic acid alone, folic acid and iron, or folic acid, iron, and vitamins A, B-complex, C, and E at approximately single recommended dietary allowance (RDA) doses for six months. In total, 561 participants completed the study and were included in the intention-to-treat analysis. Haemoglobin levels were not different across treatments; however, compared with the folic acid arm, there was a significant reduction in the risk of hypochromic microcytic anaemia in the folic acid and iron arm, and the folic acid, iron, and multivitamin arm. Overall, the study demonstrated that daily oral supplementation with iron and folic acid among women and adolescents prior to pregnancy reduces risk of anaemia. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25905863/)

The use of iron and folic acid has also been compared to multiple micronutrient supplementation. Meta-analyses have found that antenatal multiple micronutrient supplementation compared with iron and folic acid alone reduce adverse birth outcomes. (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/mcn.13509).

Name: Follitropin alfa - PCOS
Indication: Treatment of PCOS infertility
Mechanism of action: Chorionic gonadotropin stimulants; Ovarian follicle stimulants
Key features and challenges:
Follitropin alfa is a recombinant human follicle-stimulating hormone (r-FSH) used for ovulation induction and controlled ovarian stimulation (COS) in assisted reproductive technologies (ART). In women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), it is primarily indicated for ovulation induction in those resistant to first-line oral agents such as clomiphene citrate. Administered via subcutaneous injection under specialist supervision, follitropin alfa stimulates multiple follicular development to improve ovulation and pregnancy rates.
A completed Phase III study compared laparoscopic ovarian electrocautery with recombinant FSH (follitropin alfa) for ovulation induction in women with clomiphene citrate–resistant PCOS. The trial evaluated therapeutic efficacy in restoring ovulation and improving fertility outcomes; however, detailed results have not been fully disclosed.
https://adis.springer.com/trials/700145603
Two Phase IV studies further evaluated follitropin alfa in PCOS populations. One study in China explored the relationship between PCOS symptom profiles and the risk of ovarian over-response during ART using the Gonal-f pen. The trial was completed in 2017, but results have not been publicly published.
https://adis.springer.com/trials/700263360
Another Phase IV study aimed to individualize recombinant FSH treatment using the Gonal-f prefilled pen in women with chronic anovulation. This study was discontinued in 2016 due to manufacturing delays in sourcing the investigational product.
https://adis.springer.com/trials/700230992
More recently, a 2023 registered study is evaluating the similarity in efficacy, safety, immunogenicity, and pharmacokinetics between a biosimilar recombinant FSH injection (LZ-B-01) and Gonal-f in controlled ovarian hyperstimulation. The primary endpoint is the number of retrieved oocytes during ART.
https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=198565
Follitropin alfa is an established gonadotropin therapy used within fertility treatment protocols rather than as a disease-modifying therapy for PCOS. Its therapeutic role focuses on inducing ovulation and supporting ART cycles, without directly addressing the metabolic or endocrine drivers of PCOS.
Key challenges include the elevated risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) in women with PCOS, who often exhibit exaggerated ovarian response. Careful dose titration and close ultrasound monitoring are essential. Comparative evidence against alternative stimulation strategies (e.g., letrozole-based regimens or other gonadotropins) remains limited in PCOS-specific subgroups. Additionally, cost, injectable administration, and need for specialized reproductive services may limit accessibility in certain settings.
Overall, follitropin alfa remains a standard recombinant FSH option for ovulation induction and ART in PCOS-related infertility. While effective in promoting follicular development, optimal outcomes depend on individualized dosing strategies and vigilant monitoring to balance efficacy with safety in this high-response population.

Name: Follitropin beta
Developers: Merck (also known as Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany), including Sigma-Aldrich, MilliporeSigma and EMD Serono
Indication: Treatment of PCOS-related infertility
Mechanism of action: Ovarian follicle stimulants
Key features and challenges:
Follitropin beta is a recombinant human follicle-stimulating hormone (r-FSH) produced in genetically engineered Chinese hamster ovary cell lines. It consists of alpha- and beta-glycoprotein subunits and is used in assisted reproductive technologies to stimulate follicular development. In women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), follitropin beta is employed for ovulation induction and controlled ovarian stimulation (COS), particularly in those with anovulation or failure of first-line oral agents.

As with other gonadotropins, follitropin beta stimulates multiple follicle growth to increase the likelihood of conception. However, women with PCOS are at increased risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) due to heightened ovarian sensitivity, necessitating careful dose titration and monitoring.

The randomized clinical trial NCT03197077 evaluated follitropin delta versus follitropin beta in women with PCOS undergoing controlled ovarian stimulation for IVF. The study compared outcomes including oocyte yield and safety parameters, particularly the incidence of OHSS. The objective was to determine whether individualized dosing with follitropin delta could reduce OHSS risk compared with standard follitropin beta protocols. Results have not yet been published.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03197077
An additional ongoing trial is comparing low-dose gonadotropin therapy with follitropin beta (Puregon) versus clomiphene citrate as first-line treatment for infertility in women with PCOS. Participants undergo up to three treatment cycles, with ultrasound monitoring and hCG administration based on follicular response. The study aims to assess comparative ovulation and pregnancy outcomes.
https://onderzoekmetmensen.nl/en/trial/29131
Follitropin beta is an established fertility medication rather than a disease-modifying therapy for PCOS. Its role is limited to ovulation induction and assisted reproduction, without direct impact on underlying metabolic or endocrine abnormalities.
Key challenges include the elevated OHSS risk inherent to gonadotropin therapy in PCOS, the need for intensive monitoring, and cost considerations relative to oral ovulation induction agents. Additionally, comparative evidence between recombinant FSH preparations in PCOS-specific populations remains limited, and optimal stimulation protocols require individualized clinical judgment.
Overall, follitropin beta remains a standard gonadotropin option for ovulation induction and IVF in women with PCOS-related infertility. While effective in promoting follicular development, its use requires careful protocol management to balance efficacy and safety in this high-response population.

Name: Follitropin delta - PCOS
Indication: Treatment of infertility in PCOS
Mechanism of action: Acts as a follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) analog, binding to FSH receptors in ovarian follicles to promote follicular growth and development.
Key features and challenges:
Follitropin delta is a recombinant human follicle-stimulating hormone (r-FSH) used for controlled ovarian stimulation (COS) in assisted reproductive technologies, including in vitro fertilization (IVF) and intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI). Unlike conventional fixed-dose FSH regimens, follitropin delta is administered using an individualized dosing algorithm based on patient-specific parameters such as body weight and anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) levels. This individualized approach aims to optimize follicular response while reducing the risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), a complication to which women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) are particularly susceptible.
A 2021 retrospective study evaluated the effectiveness and safety of individualized follitropin delta dosing in 74 women with PCOS diagnosed according to the 2003 Rotterdam criteria. Participants underwent ovarian stimulation for IVF, ICSI, or oocyte cryopreservation. The study reported a high number of pre-ovulatory follicles and retrieved oocytes, with a satisfactory proportion of mature oocytes. Notably, no cases of moderate or severe OHSS were observed, suggesting that algorithm-based dosing may improve safety in this high-response population.
https://ovarianresearch.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s13048-021-00773-5
These findings support the potential role of follitropin delta in individualized ovarian stimulation strategies for women with PCOS. By tailoring dosing to ovarian reserve markers, follitropin delta may help balance adequate follicular development with mitigation of excessive ovarian response.
However, several challenges remain. Available evidence in PCOS populations is limited, largely retrospective, and based on relatively small cohorts. Direct comparisons with other recombinant FSH preparations or urinary gonadotropins in randomized controlled trials specific to PCOS are limited. As with other gonadotropins, careful monitoring remains essential to minimize the risk of OHSS and multiple gestation. Additionally, the cost of recombinant preparations and the need for advanced fertility infrastructure may limit accessibility in some settings.
Follitropin delta represents an individualized gonadotropin option for controlled ovarian stimulation in women with PCOS undergoing IVF/ICSI. While early evidence suggests a favorable safety profile with reduced OHSS risk, larger prospective studies are required to confirm its comparative effectiveness and long-term reproductive outcomes in this population.

Name: Free Androgen Index (FAI)
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS via detection of hyperandrogenism
Mechanism of action: Calculates ratio of total testosterone to sex hormone–binding globulin to estimate biologically active androgen levels.
Key features and challenges:
The Free Androgen Index (FAI) is a key diagnostic tool for assessing androgen excess in Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS). It is calculated by dividing total testosterone by sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) and multiplying by 100. Elevated FAI indicates hyperandrogenism, a hallmark of PCOS, and is used alongside the Rotterdam Criteria for diagnosis. FAI also helps monitor treatment effectiveness and provides a clearer androgen status than total testosterone alone, especially in patients with low SHBG due to insulin resistance. However, FAI must be interpreted with clinical symptoms and other tests for accuracy.

International guidelines for PCOS recommend assessing biochemical hyperandrogenism through tests like calculated free testosterone or the FAI. 
(https://academic.oup.com/jcem/article/106/3/e1071/5992309) 
(https://academic.oup.com/humrep/article/38/9/1655/7241786)
(https://annals.edu.sg/polycystic-ovary-syndrome-v-2023-simplified-diagnostic-criteria-for-an-east-asian-phenotype/)

The FAI plays a crucial role in assessing metabolic and anthropometric abnormalities in PCOS, particularly in women with hyperandrogenism. FAI has been identified as a strong predictor of issues such as visceral adiposity and lipid accumulation, both of which are associated with increased cardiovascular risk. A 2021 study emphasised the significance of FAI in predicting metabolic disorders, making it a valuable diagnostic marker for PCOS. Furthermore, recent studies (2022, 2024) have highlighted the utility of FAI in diagnosing PCOS in adolescents, showing its importance alongside other markers like AMH and the LH/FSH ratio. In these studies, FAI was found to be significantly elevated in PCOS patients compared to controls, reinforcing its diagnostic value. Additionally, AMH was identified as the most reliable marker in diagnosing PCOS across different age groups. These findings suggest that FAI, together with other biomarkers, can enhance the accuracy of PCOS diagnosis and improve patient management.
(https://www.thieme-connect.de/products/ejournals/abstract/10.1055/a-1422-3243)
(https://academic.oup.com/ejendo/article/188/6/494/7181126)
(https://dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/tchd/issue/82606/1347807)

Name: Free testosterone
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS via detection of hyperandrogenism
Mechanism of action: Measures unbound testosterone fraction to detect biologically active hyperandrogenism associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
Free testosterone is the unbound, biologically active form of testosterone in the bloodstream, capable of directly interacting with cells and tissues. It contrasts with bound testosterone, which is attached to proteins like sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) or albumin and is inactive. Total testosterone includes both free and bound testosterone.

Free testosterone is used in PCOS diagnosis, particularly in the Rotterdam criteria, to assess hyperandrogenism. Due to the complexity of measuring free testosterone directly, the Free Androgen Index (FAI) is often used, calculated as the ratio of total testosterone to SHBG. Elevated free testosterone or FAI levels indicate androgen excess, a key feature of PCOS.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14688154/)
(https://academic.oup.com/ejendo/article/189/2/G43/7242362)

A 2023 study used cluster analysis in adolescents to identify subgroups with and without PCOS, determining cut-offs for diagnostic features like free testosterone, FAI, and menstrual cycle length. Free testosterone and FAI were most effective in distinguishing groups. The study found that the identified cut-offs were lower than the conventional 95th percentile thresholds, suggesting the need for more accurate diagnostic methods beyond arbitrary cut-offs. (https://academic.oup.com/ejendo/article/188/6/494/7181126)

Name: Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) (incl cryoprecipitate)
Indication: Treatment and cessation of severe postpartum haemorrhage
Mechanism of action: FFP contains all coagulation factors except platelets, supplying hemostasic processes with the necessary factors to stop bleeding
Key features and challenges:
Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) is a blood product made from the liquid portion of whole human blood. As it is derived from human blood, it contains all coagulation factors except platelets. A standard dose of 10 to 20 mL/kg (4 to 6 units in adults) will raise factor levels by approximately 20%. An increase of roughly 10% of several factors is enough to effect haemostasis. 
There are few specific indications for FFP. These generally are limited to the treatment of deficiencies of coagulation proteins for which specific factor concentrates are unavailable or undesirable, for example replacement of isolated factor deficiencies; reversal of warafin effect; antithromin III deficiency; immunodeficiencies; thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura treatment. However it is also indicated and used as plasma replacement due to haemorrhage (of any type). As such, FFP is commonly used in urgent treatment/control of bleeding in women with severe postpartum haemorrhage, often where uterotonics have failed, where it is a standard inclusion the the 'massive transfusion pack' (along with blood and platelets). Treatment with FFP has a dual benefit of promoting coagulation and stopping bleeding while also helping to restore blood volume and replenish spent clotting factors. 
Cryoprecipitate, also called cryo for short, is a frozen blood product prepared from blood plasma. To create cryoprecipitate, fresh frozen plasma is thawed to 1–6 °C is then centrifuged and the precipitate is collected. The precipitate is resuspended in a small amount of residual plasma and is then re-frozen for storage. Because of this, cryo is quite high in fibrinogen. But it is unavailable in many European countries. Trials in FFP and cryoprecipitate are geared towards protocol optimisation (e.g. https://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN12146519).
Proper storage of FFP and cryo is essential. If thawed and not used within 24 hours, the FFP should be discarded. Once thawed, the activity of clotting factors, particularly factor V and factor VIII, decline gradually. Both FFP and cryoprecipitate also require cross-matching before infusion, with known potential transfusion-related complications and risks. Given this, plus its resource intensive preparation, FFPs viability is reduced considerably in resource poor settings, such as developing countries.

Mechanism of action:
**Mechanism of Action (MOA) of GBP510**  

GBP510 is a recombinant protein-based COVID-19 vaccine that uses the receptor-binding domain (RBD) of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein as its antigen. When administered, the vaccine introduces the RBD protein to the immune system, mimicking the structure of the virus's spike protein without causing disease.  

This stimulates the immune system to produce neutralizing antibodies specifically targeting the RBD, which is critical for the virus to bind to human cells. Additionally, the vaccine activates T-cell responses, which enhance immunity and provide long-term protection. By generating both antibody and cellular immunity, GBP510 equips the body to recognize and neutralize SARS-CoV-2 upon exposure, preventing infection and severe disease.
Key features and challenges:
Vx Schedule: Day 0 + 21 +51
**Key Features and Challenges of GBP510**  

GBP510 is a recombinant protein-based COVID-19 vaccine developed by SK Bioscience in collaboration with global partners. The vaccine uses a stabilized spike protein receptor-binding domain (RBD) as its antigen, designed to elicit a strong and targeted immune response. A notable feature of GBP510 is its use of a proven vaccine platform, which enhances safety and scalability for global manufacturing. It is stable at standard refrigeration temperatures, making it easier to store and distribute compared to vaccines requiring ultra-cold storage. GBP510 has shown promising immunogenicity and safety in Phase I/II clinical trials and is currently undergoing Phase III trials in Europe and Southeast Asia, supported by CEPI.  

However, GBP510 faces challenges common to recombinant protein vaccines, including potentially slower production timelines compared to mRNA vaccines. Additionally, gaining emergency use authorization and WHO prequalification will require comprehensive efficacy data from Phase III trials. Another challenge is ensuring equitable distribution to low-income regions, as global demand for COVID-19 vaccines remains high. Despite these hurdles, GBP510 holds significant promise as a safe, effective, and accessible vaccine option for combating COVID-19 globally.
Recent updates: Dec 2024: As of June 2022, GBP510 received approval for use in South Korea. However, in November 2022, production was indefinitely suspended due to low demand. In September 2023, SK bioscience withdrew its application for marketing authorization in the European Union. No other updates.

Name: Gauze (non-medicated)
Developers: University Hospital Mongi Slim Hospital la Marsa; Tunis El Manar University
Indication: Indicated for the temporary control or reduction of postpartum uterine bleeding when conservative management of uterine bleeding is warranted.
Mechanism of action: Gauze works to control PPH through mechanical compression, adhesion of the gauze and improved local primary haemostasis.
Key features and challenges:
Uterovaginal packing with non-medicated sterile gauze has long been used as a mechanical method to control postpartum haemorrhage (PPH). Standard sterile cloth gauze or sponges are inserted into the uterine cavity and vagina to exert direct pressure on bleeding surfaces, promoting haemostasis through tamponade. The approach is simple, low cost, rapidly deployable, and widely available. However, concerns have been raised regarding potential infection risk, inadequate tamponade, and the possibility of concealed haemorrhage if bleeding continues behind the packing (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1140727/
; https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0002937823005501). Gauze used for intrauterine packing is regulated as a non-active medical device; in the European Union, relevant standards include BS EN 14079:2003.
A retrospective study conducted in Tunisia evaluated intrauterine packing (IUP) with gauze for PPH due to uterine atony following vaginal delivery, unresponsive to first-line medical treatment (2023: https://www.panafrican-med-journal.com/content/article/45/192/full/). Over a two-and-a-half-year period, 63 patients were included. Gauze packing was used as a second-line intervention. The primary outcome was successful control of haemorrhage; secondary outcomes included vital signs, transfusion requirements, haemoglobin changes, and maternal morbidity. No major complications were reported. Three patients required laparotomy with conservative surgical management, but no hysterectomies or maternal deaths occurred. The study concluded that intrauterine gauze packing can be an effective and valuable tool for managing atonic PPH, particularly where balloon tamponade devices are unavailable.
Key challenges include limited high-quality comparative data against commercial balloon tamponade systems, risk of retained gauze if removal protocols are not strictly followed, and infection concerns in prolonged placement. While cost-effective and accessible, careful monitoring and standardized protocols are required to mitigate safety risks and ensure timely escalation when bleeding persists.

Name: Goserelin - Endometriosis
Indication: management of endometriosis symptoms
Mechanism of action: LHRH receptor agonists
Key features and challenges:
Goserelin is a synthetic decapeptide analogue of luteinising hormone-releasing hormone (LHRH) developed by AstraZeneca. It is a gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonist that binds to and activates GnRH receptors, leading to downregulation of pituitary gonadotropin secretion and reduced estradiol levels. By inducing a hypoestrogenic state, goserelin suppresses endometrial proliferation and reduces endometriosis-associated pain. It is also used in prostate and breast cancers, uterine fibroids, and assisted reproduction (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800015280).
Goserelin was first approved in the United States in 1989, with a supplemental NDA for endometriosis treatment approved in 1993. A further supplemental NDA for endometrial thinning prior to ablation was approved in 1997. It was launched in India for endometriosis in 2002. In the United Kingdom, the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) approved goserelin acetate in November 2005 for endometrial thinning prior to ablation and in June 2008 for managing endometriosis symptoms. In February 2012, AstraZeneca completed a study in China involving 426 patients with moderate to severe endometriosis, and the product was subsequently launched there for adjuvant treatment. In July 2021, goserelin acetate was launched in Canada for hormonal management of endometriosis and as an endometrial thinning agent. 
As of March 2022, it is authorized in several EU countries, including the Netherlands, Germany, and Sweden (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800015280).
A clinical study initiated in 2020 is evaluating the efficacy and use of goserelin as a comparator in trials assessing new or repurposed endometriosis medications (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05013242).
A 2021 review highlighted that GnRH analogues have documented effects on pelvic pain reduction and decreased symptom recurrence following surgical management of endometriosis (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S2468784720301410). 
However, a 2023 report noted that prolonged use is associated with bone mineral density loss and vasomotor symptoms, and treatment is generally recommended to be limited to 12 months to mitigate hypoestrogenic adverse effects (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2666334122001209).
Although goserelin is an established and widely approved therapy for endometriosis-associated pain, its hypoestrogenic side-effect profile limits long-term use. While it remains a standard treatment and comparator in clinical research, safety concerns related to bone density and vasomotor symptoms underscore the need for alternative long-term therapeutic strategies.

Name: Gynomax XL vaginal ovule
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Trichomoniasis.
Target: ferredoxin-mediated electron transport system; 14-α demethylase; Sodium channels; DNA synthesis
Mechanism of action: Reduction by ferredoxin-mediated electron transport system; inhibits ergosterol synthesis; Sodium channel antagonists; DNA synthesis inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Gynomax XL vaginal ovule is indicated for the treatment of bacterial vaginosis, candidal vulvovaginitis, trichomonal vaginitis, and mixed vaginal infections. The formulation contains tinidazole (300 mg), tioconazole nitrate (200 mg), and lidocaine (100 mg), and is administered once daily for three consecutive days.
Tinidazole is a nitroimidazole antimicrobial used to treat trichomoniasis and other protozoal infections. Its mechanism involves reduction of the nitro group within Trichomonas species via a ferredoxin-mediated electron transport system, generating reactive nitro radicals that cause DNA damage and cell death (https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB00911). 
Tioconazole is an imidazole antifungal that inhibits ergosterol synthesis by targeting 14-α demethylase, thereby disrupting fungal cell membrane integrity (https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB01007). 
Lidocaine is a local anesthetic that stabilizes neuronal membranes and inhibits nerve impulse conduction, providing symptomatic relief (https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB00281).
A single-arm clinical study involving 98 women evaluated the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of Gynomax XL for common vaginal infections (https://www.jcog.com.tr/article/en-the-efficacy-and-safety-of-gynomax-xl-vaginal-ovule-in-the-treatment-of-common-vaginal-nfections-a-single-arm-clinical-trial-gyno-turk-97675.html). 
The intervention was reported to be effective and well tolerated for bacterial vaginosis, candidal vulvovaginitis, and mixed infections. However, only one participant (1.0%) was diagnosed with trichomoniasis, and this diagnosis was not microbiologically confirmed. Consequently, no definitive conclusions regarding safety or efficacy for trichomoniasis can be drawn. No serious or non-serious adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation were reported.
Key challenges include limited clinical evidence specifically for trichomoniasis, absence of microbiological confirmation in reported cases, and the need for controlled comparative studies to establish efficacy for this indication. Further robust clinical evaluation is required to define its role in the management of trichomonal vaginitis.

Name: Head circumference (HC)
Developers: Dudley Group of NHS Foundation Trust; University of Toronto
Indication: Diagnosis and prediction of IUGR
Mechanism of action: Combines ALG2 biomarker levels with testosterone measurements to improve detection of biochemical hyperandrogenism and PCOS risk.
Key features and challenges:
Head circumference (HC) is one of the basic biometric parameters used to assess fetal size. HC together with biparietal diameter (BPD), abdominal circumference (AC), and femur length (FL) are computed to produce an estimate of fetal weight. In the second trimester, this may be extrapolated to an estimate of gestational age and an estimated due date (EDD). Measurement: HC is measured on the same plane as BPD, that is on an axial plane that traverses the thalami and cavum septum pellucidum. The transducer must be perpendicular to the central axis of the head, and thus the hemispheres and calvaria should appear symmetric. The cerebellar hemispheres should not be in the plane of the image, or the probe too caudal, giving an inaccurate size of the fetal head. If the available ultrasound equipment allows for the measurement of an ellipse, this may be drawn around the outside of the calvarium. Alternatively, HC may be calculated from BPD and occipitofrontal diameter (OFD) as:  HC = 1.62 × (BPD + OFD) (https://radiopaedia.org/articles/head-circumference?lang=gb).

A fetus is SGA when its size (biometric evaluation) falls below a predefined threshold for its gestational age. The most common definition of SGA is EFW or AC below the 10th percentile of given reference ranges. While SGA and IUGR are not the same, fetuses with birth weight below the 10th percentile are at increased risk of stillbirth and perinatal mortality, those with birth weight below the 3rd percentile being at the highest risk. For this reason, fetal size at the lower extreme of the growth charts, for example AC or EFW (calculation utilises head circumference) below the 3rd percentile for given growth charts, can be used as an isolated criterion to define FGR at any gestational epoch.
