Name: Hexoprenaline - PTL/PTB
Indication: Prolonging gestation in threatened preterm labour
Mechanism of action: Reducing uteral contractility via selective agonism of beta-2-adrenoreceptors
Key features and challenges:
Hexoprenaline is a selective beta-2-adrenergic agonists indicated for acute tocolysis during labour for uterine tachysystole or suspected foetal distress. 

Hexoprenaline’s mechanism of action is well known due to its extensive clinical use in airway smooth muscle to treat asthma and bronchospasms. It selectively agonises beta-2-adrenoreceptors, which goes to avoid the adverse events typically associated with beta-1-adrenoceptor agonism. 

The success rate for hexoprenaline tocolysis is 34-78%, dependent on the patient’s initial tocological condition. The advantage of hexoprenaline compared with other tocolytics based on experience made so far seems to relate to the smaller increase in chronotropy and the better tolerability when compared to other sympathomimetic tocolytics.

Uterine tachysystole (more than 5 contractions per 10 minutes in 2 consecutive intervals) is common during labour, particularly with use of labour‐stimulating agents. Tachysystole may reduce foetal oxygenation by interrupting maternal blood flow to the placenta during contractions. By reducing uterine contractions, beta-2-adrenergic agonists may improve placental blood flow, improving foetal oxygenation. 

A 2018 Cochrane review evaluated the use of tocolytics to reduce or stop uterine contractions for improvement of the condition of the fetus in utero. They found eight relevant studies, two of which investigated hexoprenaline. These concluded that receiving hexoprenaline whilst awaiting emergency delivery for foetal distress could improve foetal heart rate tracing, but did not improve other outcomes (mortality and morbidity, Apgar scores, umbilical artery pH or NICU admission). Compared to atosiban, hexoprenaline was also associated with higher rate of maternal palpitations or tachycardia, with no differences detected between the two across other outcomes. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29971813/)

Hexoprenaline is used in some countries (such as Russia and Switzerland) as a tocolytic agent but it is not approved by FDA for the US market. Interest in hexoprenaline as a tocolytic seems to have diminished significantly since the 80's and 90's.
Recent updates: May 2012: Study finds that intrauterine exposure to the β-2-sympathomimetic hexoprenaline might increase the occurrence of infantile haemangioma in preterm infants. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22611112/)

Name: Human chorionic gonadotropin - PCOS
Indication: Treatment of PCOS infertility
Mechanism of action: Chorionic gonadotropin stimulants; Ovarian follicle stimulants
Key features and challenges:
Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is a glycoprotein hormone structurally and functionally similar to luteinizing hormone (LH). It is widely used in assisted reproductive treatments to induce ovulation by mimicking the physiological LH surge required for final follicular maturation and oocyte release. In women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), hCG is typically administered after exogenous follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) stimulation or following ovulation induction protocols when at least one dominant follicle reaches approximately 17 mm in diameter.
In PCOS-related infertility management, gonadotropins are generally introduced when first-line ovulation induction therapies, such as clomiphene citrate or letrozole, are unsuccessful. Exogenous FSH stimulates follicular development, and hCG (commonly 5,000 IU) is subsequently administered to trigger ovulation. However, in women with PCOS who often exhibit multifollicular ovarian response, hCG administration must be carefully timed and may be withheld if multiple follicles (>14 mm) are present to reduce the risk of multiple gestations and ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS).
https://journals.lww.com/rdm/fulltext/2024/03000/an_overview_of_the_physiopathology_and_various.7.aspx
A completed clinical study (NCT02436226) evaluated the impact of low-dose hCG administration following clomiphene citrate in infertile women with clomiphene-resistant PCOS. Participants were randomized to receive clomiphene citrate alone or in combination with hCG, with follicular development monitored via transvaginal sonography to assess ovulation rates. The study aimed to determine whether adjunctive hCG improves ovulatory outcomes in this treatment-resistant subgroup.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02436226
While hCG is an established and effective ovulation trigger in fertility management, it is not a disease-modifying therapy for PCOS. Its use is limited to facilitating ovulation in controlled settings rather than addressing underlying metabolic, inflammatory, or endocrine dysfunction.
Key challenges include the elevated risk of OHSS in women with PCOS, who frequently demonstrate exaggerated ovarian response to stimulation. Careful monitoring of follicular number and estradiol levels is essential to mitigate complications. Additionally, hCG administration increases the risk of multiple pregnancy when multiple mature follicles are present. The agent is typically used within structured fertility protocols and requires close clinical supervision.
Overall, hCG remains a standard ovulation-triggering agent in PCOS-related infertility treatment, particularly in assisted reproduction or gonadotropin-based induction cycles. Its role is procedural and supportive within fertility management rather than therapeutic for core PCOS pathophysiology.

Name: Human menopausal gonadotropin - Menotropin
Developers: Affiliated Hospital of Jinggangshan University; Cairo University (including Faculty Of Medicine, Kasr Al Ainy); Ferring Pharmaceuticals ; Bharat Serums and Vaccines Limited
Indication: Treatment of infertility in PCOS
Mechanism of action: Stimulating ovulation by promoting the development of mature follicles
Key features and challenges:
Human menopausal gonadotropin (HMG), also known as menotropin, is a urinary-derived gonadotropin preparation containing both follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) activity, typically in a 1:1 ratio. It is extracted from the urine of postmenopausal women and used for ovulation induction and controlled ovarian stimulation (COS) in infertility treatment. In women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), HMG is employed to stimulate follicular growth and promote ovulation, particularly when first-line oral agents are ineffective or when assisted reproductive technologies (ART) are indicated.
Highly purified subcutaneous formulations (e.g., Menopur, Repronex; Ferring Pharmaceuticals) contain 75 IU FSH and 75 IU LH per vial and are marketed for female infertility, including PCOS in some jurisdictions. Late-stage clinical development for infertility indications is ongoing in certain markets.
https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800032232
Additional formulations, such as freeze-dried intramuscular HMG (HUMOG; Bharat Serums and Vaccines), also contain FSH and LH activity and are used for ovulation induction and follicular maturation.
https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800051017
A large 2023 retrospective study of 2,710 women with PCOS compared maternal and neonatal outcomes among patients treated with HMG alone, letrozole + HMG, or hormone replacement therapy (HRT). The HMG group demonstrated lower cesarean section rates and reduced incidence of large-for-gestational-age (LGA) infants compared with HRT. The combination of letrozole + HMG further reduced risks of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) and LGA, suggesting improved maternal and neonatal outcomes relative to either HMG or HRT alone.
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10815-023-02956-z
A separate 2023 study evaluating minimal ovarian stimulation protocols reported that menotropin-based minimal stimulation resulted in favorable estradiol levels on trigger day, optimal oocyte and embryo yield, acceptable clinical pregnancy rates, and reduced risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) in women with PCOS.
https://bmcwomenshealth.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12905-023-02473-2
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03876145
Another 2023 retrospective study comparing ovulation induction regimens (letrozole + HMG, clomiphene + HMG, and HMG alone) in women undergoing intrauterine insemination (IUI) found that letrozole + HMG achieved higher mature follicle numbers, ovulation rates, clinical pregnancy rates, and improved endometrial receptivity without increased adverse events.
https://accp1.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jcph.2318
Despite demonstrated effectiveness in ovulation induction and ART, HMG is not a disease-modifying therapy for PCOS. Its use is procedural, targeting ovulation and fertility rather than underlying metabolic or endocrine dysfunction.
Key challenges include the heightened risk of OHSS in women with PCOS, necessitating careful monitoring and individualized dosing. Variability in ovarian response requires frequent ultrasound and hormonal monitoring. Cost, injection burden, and access to fertility services also limit widespread applicability. Additionally, comparative effectiveness among different gonadotropin formulations in PCOS-specific populations remains incompletely defined.
Overall, menotropin (HMG) is a well-established gonadotropin option for ovulation induction and assisted reproduction in PCOS-related infertility. When used within carefully managed stimulation protocols; particularly in combination with agents such as letrozole, it may optimize reproductive outcomes while mitigating OHSS risk in this high-response population.

Name: Indomethacin
Developers: MetroHealth Medical Centre; University of Newcastle
Indication: Prevention or treatment of preterm labour/birth through tocolytic/relaxant effects on myometrial contraction
Mechanism of action: Non-selective inhibition of cyclooxygenase 1 and 2 to arrest myometrial contractions
Key features and challenges:
Indomethacin is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) and cyclooxygenase (COX) inhibitor widely used for acute pain management. It is commonly used off-label as a tocolytic agent in preterm labour. Indomethacin reduces prostaglandin synthesis, thereby decreasing uterine contractions and potentially prolonging pregnancy. Its use in preterm contractions dates back to the 1970s, with early studies suggesting that it was more effective than placebo in delaying delivery for 7–10 days, prolonging pregnancy beyond 37 weeks in some cases, and reducing rates of small-for-gestational-age neonates.
Preclinical studies published in 2001 and 2004 supported the use of COX inhibitors, particularly indomethacin, for inhibition of myometrial contractions associated with preterm labour (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11385116/
; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15300521/). 
These mechanistic findings reinforced the biological rationale for prostaglandin pathway inhibition in tocolysis.
However, clinical evidence has been mixed. Comparative studies evaluating rectal indomethacin versus oral nifedipine produced inconclusive results, although it has been hypothesized that local administration may offer theoretical advantages due to prostaglandin synthesis in the uterus and cervix. A 2015 Cochrane review evaluating COX inhibitors for treatment of preterm labour found no clear evidence of superiority over placebo or other tocolytic agents, and no consistent improvement in clinically meaningful neonatal outcomes (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26042617/).
More recently, a 2022 study from the University of Newcastle compared the tocolytic potency of several novel compounds with established agents including nifedipine and indomethacin. In decreasing order of contraction-blocking potency, agents ranked as nifedipine > rolipram > glycyl-H-1152 > HC-067047 > 2-APB > indomethacin > aminophylline, suggesting that indomethacin may be less potent than some alternative agents in experimental models (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9810572/).
Key challenges with indomethacin include concerns regarding fetal adverse effects, particularly when used beyond 32 weeks’ gestation, such as premature ductus arteriosus constriction and oligohydramnios. While indomethacin remains a short-term option for acute tocolysis, especially in early gestations, evidence does not clearly demonstrate superiority over other agents, and safety considerations limit its duration and timing of use.

Name: Intrauterine pressure catheter (IUPC)
Developers: CERVOCHECK, LLC; Johns Hopkins University School of Biomedical Engineering
Indication: An internal contraction monitoring device to predict delivery after spontaneous or artificial rupture of the membranes
Mechanism of action: Invasive catheter-based measurement of intrauterine pressure to directly quantify contraction strength and frequency during labour.
Key features and challenges:
The first measurement of intrauterine pressure to record uterine contractions was performed in 1872 by Friedrich Schatz. His method for assessing uterine contractions used a small bag of fluid introduced between the membranes and the lower segment of the uterus, connected to a mercury manometer.
Currently, use of the IUPC requires its placement within the intraamniotic cavity following either spontaneous or artificial rupture of the membranes, and is therefore limited to only when delivery is desired. 
There are 3 types of IUPCs: fluid-filled, transducer-tipped, and sensor-tipped. The fluid-filled catheter has a column that connects a balloon in the amniotic cavity to an external pressure monitor, and the water column in the catheter transmits the intrauterine pressure to a transducer on the monitor that converts the resulting electrical signal to contraction waveforms. 
The 2 more modern systems are one in which both the pressure sensor and the transducer are at the intrauterine tip, and one in which the transducer is extrauterine. Both transducer- and sensor-tipped systems are connected to the fetal heart rate monitor, obviating the need for a fluid-filled catheter. 
No significant difference has been demonstrated between the different types of IUPCs in relation to maternal and fetal complications. 
(https://www.ajog.org/article/S0002-9378(22)00724-4/fulltext)
The routine use of IUPC in laboring patients should be avoided because of an increased risk of maternal fever.

Key features and challenges:
Iodine is an essential trace element. Iodine is required to produce thyroid hormones, which are essential for normal brain development, and the fetus, newborn, and young child are particularly vulnerable to iodine deficiency.  The iodine requirement increases during pregnancy and recommended intakes are in the range of 220-250 microg/day. New recommendations from the World Health Organization suggest that a median urinary iodine concentration >250 microg/L and <500 microg/L indicates adequate iodine intake in pregnancy. Based on this range, it appears that many pregnant women have inadequate intakes. (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/Iodine)

Iodine is not known to impact iron absorption or metabolism. However, given the need to supplement iodine in iodine-deficient populations, iron and iodine may be given in the same supplement (e.g. Triferdine). A randomised controlled trial in Thailand is using a combined iodine, iron and folate supplement to test the effectiveness of daily versus intermittent oral iron supplementation in pregnancy. Participants are assigned to one of three groups: Daily medication group (1 tablet Triferdine each day), three days per week group: (1 tablet of Triferdine every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday) and the once weekly group (1 tablet of Triferdine and 1 tablet of Ferrous fumarate). The concentration of blood, iron, and thyroid hormones will be tested, alongside a urine test for iodine levels. The trial is expected to be completed in 2024. (https://www.thaiclinicaltrials.org/show/TCTR20230310002)

Name: Iron acetyl-transferrin hydroglycerin
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Paper-based nucleic acid amplification test enabling low-cost amplification and detection of Trichomonas vaginalis DNA at the point of care.
Key features and challenges: Iron acetyl-transferrin hydroglycerin is an oral iron supplement. It was tested in a multi-centre, prospective, randomised, open-label trial (NCT00802139) and compared against iron sucrose for the treatment of iron deficiency anaemia in pregnant women. Women in their 30th-32nd week of gestation were given iron sucrose once weekly or iron acetyl-transferase hydroglycerin solution twice daily (40mg iron) for five weeks. Outcomes included change in Hb levels, target Hb achievement rate (11g/dL), transferrin saturation (%), ferritin(ng/mL), TIBC (ug/dL), MCV(fl), MCH(pg) and change in reticulocyte count. Results of the study are unknown.

Name: Iron dextran (IV/IM)
Developers: University of Texas Medical Branch, Galveston; Indiana University Bloomington; Brown University; Kasturba Medical College; Maulana Azad Medical College (including associated hospitals)
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Analyzes circulating or endometrial biomarkers to detect molecular signatures associated with endometriotic lesions.
Key features and challenges:
Iron dextran is a dark brown, slightly viscous liquid complex of ferric hydroxide and dextran for intravenous or intramuscular use. It is used for treatment of patients with documented iron deficiency in whom oral administration is unsatisfactory or impossible. It is also used to replenish body iron stores in chronic kidney disease. It is a slow-release formulation. Due to the concern for anaphylaxis, its accessibility varies. The older iron dextran preparation was linked to rare anaphylactic reactions but is no longer used. The newer low molecular weight iron dextran (brand name INFeD™) formulation has a much lower risk of anaphylaxis and is approved by the US FDA. (https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/pharmacology-toxicology-and-pharmaceutical-science/iron-dextran and https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB00893).

In a prospective, partially randomised study in 2004, 148 pregnant women received daily oral doses of iron and folic acid, and 106 pregnant women received 3 intramuscular doses of 250 mg elemental Fe as iron dextran at 1-mo intervals and oral doses of folic acid twice weekly. One hundred women in each group completed the study. Changes in haemoglobin, iron indicators, pregnancy outcomes, and birth weight were compared between the 2 groups. The study concluded that 3 doses of 250mg IM Fe (iron dextran) at monthly intervals appears to have good compliance and efficacy and may be used in women who cannot tolerate oral administration of iron. However, it also concluded that intramuscular administration of iron is appropriate only in hospital settings well equipped to treat anaphylactic crises. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14684407/)

In 2022, a randomized controlled trial in the US tested how effective and safe IV low-molecular weight iron dextran is compared to oral iron for improving perinatal outcomes in pregnant women with IDA. The main focus was on maternal anemia at delivery (hgb < 11 g/dL). Early results suggested that IV iron lowered anemia rates at admission for delivery, but the study ended early due to logistical issues.(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34839481/).

A clinical trial which started in 2021 in the US by the University of Texas Medical Branch, Galveston (NCT05047211) is comparing oral daily versus IV iron in anaemic postpartum patients. The trial has a pragmatic, open label randomised controlled trial study design. Outcomes include haemoglobin levels, as well as side-effects, including arthralgia, back pain, fever, nausea or vomiting, and myalgia. The trial is expected to conclude at the end of 2023 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05047211)

Name: Iron dextran- Oral
Developers: Ocean University of China; Qingdao University
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Increases iron levels
Key features and challenges: Iron dextran is a new oral formulation of iron made from ferric iron instead of divalent iron. It is compounded to reduce the production of free iron, and to improve iron absorption. In a study in Shandong Province in China, the safety of oral iron therapy, including iron dextran oral solution, in pregnant women with iron-deficiency anaemia was investigated. Patients taking iron dextran oral solution had 0.05g twice a day. The study demonstrated all the adverse reactions of oral iron were mainly gastrointestinal adverse reactions, and no heavy adverse reactions were found. (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/20420986231181335)

Name: Iron liposome
Developers: General University Hospital of Alicante; Lifepoint Multispeciality Hospital; University of Milan
Indication: Indicated for the treatment and prevention of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Near-patient molecular assay detecting pathogen-specific nucleic acids to identify Trichomonas vaginalis infection.
Key features and challenges:
Liposomal iron, a preparation of ferric pyrophosphate associated with ascorbic acid and conveyed within a phospholipid membrane, is a new-generation oral iron that shows a high bioavailability and a low incidence of side effects, due to lack of any direct contact with the intestinal mucosa. Therefore, liposomal iron presents good tolerability and better compliance than iron salts. Minimal data are available about its use during pregnancy. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32953141/)

Liposomal iron has been studied for its use in the prevention and treatment of iron deficiency anaemia in pregnant women. In a recent clinical study in India, the efficacy and safety of iron liposome (emulsified ferric pyrophosphate) is being tested in pregnant women with iron deficiency anaemia. Study participants are given 30mg iron liposome once a day or 60mg iron liposome once a day for 16 weeks. Outcomes include change in Hb levels, ferritin levels, fatigue severity, serum iron, symptoms of iron deficiency and gastrointestinal side-effects of iron supplementation. Results of the study are unknown. (https://www.ctri.nic.in/Clinicaltrials/pmaindet2.php?trialid=77005)

Another study by the University of Milan compared different regimens of iron supplementation, including iron liposome, on maternal haematological status and pregnancy outcome in a cohort of healthy pregnant women. Eighty non-anaemic women with a normal singleton pregnancy were recruited at 11-13 weeks and randomised into controls and groups supplemented with ferrous iron 30 mg, liposomal iron 14 mg, and liposomal iron 28 mg/daily up to 6 weeks post-partum. The results demonstrated the effectiveness of 28 mg and 14 mg liposomal iron on maternal anaemia prevention. It also showed that 28mg and 14mg of liposomal iron has similar effects to higher doses of ferrous iron on maternal haematological parameters, thus allowing the reduction of iron doses and side-effects. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27588568/)

Name: Iron polymaltose
Developers: KOC Ahmadi Hospital; University of Buenos Aires (Universidad de Buenos Aires); University of Zurich
Indication: Indicated for the treatment and prevention of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Increases iron levels
Key features and challenges:
Iron-polymaltose complex (IPC) contains non-ionic polynuclear iron (III)-hydroxide cores. It is superficially surrounded by several non-covalently bound polymaltose molecules, forming a stable complex that is highly water soluble within a wide range of pH levels.  It aims to address two problems: firstly, the low and variable absorption, chelation by food products and free radical-mediated mucosal luminal damage of ferrous salts; secondly, the low solubility at physiologic pH and tendency for intraluminal precipitation as hydroxide or phosphate of ferric compounds. It is marketed as Maltofer in 80 countries. (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7811280/ and https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1924983/)

Oral iron polymaltose has been studied for its efficacy in treating and preventing iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy. A study in Colombia evaluated the efficacy and safety of iron(III) polymaltose complex versus ferrous sulphate in pregnant women with iron deficiency anaemia using recommended doses. The study was open label, randomised, controlled, multi-centred. 80 pregnant women with iron-deficiency anaemia were randomised 1:1 to oral iron(III) polymaltose complex or ferrous sulphate (each 100 mg iron twice daily) for 90 days. The study demonstrated that oral iron(III) polymaltose complex offers at least equivalent efficacy and a superior safety profile compared to ferrous sulphate for the treatment of iron-deficiency anaemia during pregnancy. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21859366/)

Another study by the University of Zurich (NCT02487719) was registered in 2015 to evaluate different iron supplements for prevention of anaemia in pregnancy. According to the study design, study participants were given iron sulphate, iron polymaltose or routine supplementation of a multivitamin from less than 16 weeks gestation to birth. Outcomes included haemoglobin before delivery, birthweight, gestational age at birth, discontinuation of iron or multimineral supplementation, and ferritin before delivery. Results of the study are unknown.

Name: Iron polymaltose (IV)
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Amplifies and detects pathogen-specific nucleic acids to enable fast and accurate molecular diagnosis of gonorrhea.
Key features and challenges:
Iron polymaltose (Ferrosig) contains a macromolecular spherocolloidal complex of iron(III) hydroxide and the carbohydrate ligand polymaltose. It is an aqueous, approximately isotonic solution for intramuscular injection or intravenous administration. The complex is stable over a wide pH range (1 - 14) and each ampoule contains the equivalent of 50 mg iron per mL. It is the only parenteral iron formulation suitable for total iron replacement in one single infusion. However, due to the risk of infusion related adverse reactions, it must be given as a slow infusion over several hours. (https://www.schn.health.nsw.gov.au/_policies/pdf/2020-224.pdf and https://www.medsafe.govt.nz/profs/datasheet/f/ferrosiginj.pdf)

An open-labelled prospective RCT in Launceston, Tasmania compared the efficacy and safety of ferric carboxymaltose (FCM), against IV iron polymaltose (IPM), and standard oral iron (ferrous sulphate) for the treatment of iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy.  A single IV infusion of 1000mg of FCM (n = 83 patients) over 15 minutes was compared against a single IV infusion of 1000mg of IPM (n = 82) over 2 hours and 325mg daily oral ferrous sulphate (n = 81) until delivery. The overall cost utility of IV FCM and IV IPM appear to be similar to oral iron. There were no differences in the fetal outcomes between the 3 trial arms. In conclusion, this study demonstrates that a single IV iron infusion is an effective and safe option for treatment of IDA during pregnancy. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30502851/)

Name: Iron polysaccharide
Developers: China Medical University; Guangzhou University of Traditional Chinese Medicine
Indication: Indicated for the prevention and treatment of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Point-of-care nucleic acid amplification test detecting Trichomonas vaginalis–specific genetic sequences for rapid diagnosis.
Key features and challenges:
Iron polysaccharide complex (polyferose) capsules are a novel oral iron trivalent supplement with higher iron content and lower gastrointestinal irritation. The iron content is approximately 40-46%. It is absorbed in molecular form and does not contain free iron ions, resulting in the reduced gastrointestinal irritation. It is marketed as Nifirex in China. (https://patents.google.com/patent/CN101003580A/en and https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8503988/)

Polyferose was studied in a clinical trial conducted by Shengjing Hospital in China (NCT04975074). In this study, the effect of oral iron administration on iron deficiency anaemia in twin pregnancies was evaluated. Women with twin pregnancies were given oral iron, including ferrous sulfate, polyferose, ferrous succinate, and Chinese medicine filling iron agent, according to the current recommended dose.  Routine bloods and ferritin were monitored every 2-4 weeks during pregnancy to understand the therapeutic effect of oral iron on iron deficiency anaemia and iron deficiency in pregnant women with twin pregnancies. After delivery, neonatal ferritin and haemoglobin status was tested. However, results of the study are unknown.

Another study in China (NCT05804071) is investigating the effect of iron polysaccharide complex (Niferex) 150mg or 300mg daily compared with IV ferric derisomaltose on iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy. Participants are in their second trimester of pregnancy and outcomes include haemoglobin, ferritin, serum iron, transferrin saturation, and reticulocyte count. The study is estimated to be completed in 2025.

Name: Iron protein succinylate
Developers: Elpen Pharmaceutical Co. Inc.; Nanjing Medical University; Santa Lucía University Hospital
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Increases iron levels
Key features and challenges:
Iron protein succinylate is a highly soluble complex of iron bound to succinylated milk proteins. The whole complex precipitates at pH<4, allowing iron to pass through the stomach inside a protein shell and, therefore, avoiding direct contact with the gastric mucosa. Once the complex reaches the duodenum, it resolubilises and is hydrolysed by pancreatic enzymes, thus releasing iron molecules in the gut lumen. This uptake pathway reduces the gastrointestinal adverse effects typically associated with iron supplementation. The product is unsuitable for people with hypersensitivity to milk proteins. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31944128/)

A study in Greece compared IV LMW iron-dextran to oral iron protein succinylate for the treatment of postpartum anaemia. Women received a total amount of 1000 mg of LMW iron-dextran intravenously in two doses (n = 109 women) or 800 mg daily for 30 days of iron protein-succinylate orally. Three weeks later women of both groups underwent a full blood count analysis. Results demonstrated that Haemoglobin and ferritin levels increased significantly the IV LMW iron dextran group compared to the oral iron protein succinylate group (p < 0.0001). (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21793279/.)

Name: Iron sorbitol (IM)
Developers: Maulana Azad Medical College (including associated hospitals); Sarojini Naidu Medical College
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Laboratory-developed molecular or immunoassay detecting disease-associated biomarkers to support diagnosis of endometriosis.
Key features and challenges:
Iron sorbitol is an intramuscular formulation that contains a complex of iron, sorbitol and citric acid. Absorption from the muscle takes place rapidly; two-thirds of the iron is removed within 3 hours, and there is a very rapid increase in the serum-iron concentration. About 30% of the total dose of iron is excreted through the kidneys during the first 24 hours after injection. Intramuscular iron aims to avoid the side-effects seen with oral iron. It is marketed in India as Jectofer/Jectocos. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14465561/)

A study in India in 2005 aimed to compare the effect of daily oral iron supplementation with two injections of high dose IM iron sorbitol for the treatment of iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy. A total of 220 pregnant women with a singleton pregnancy and haemoglobin between 8 to 11 g% at 16-24 weeks gestation were identified and randomly divided into two groups. Group A was started on daily oral iron therapy of 100 mg of elemental iron. Group B was given 250 mg of iron sorbitol intramuscularly and repeated at an interval of 4-6 weeks. Blood indices were evaluated at the beginning of study and at 36 weeks. Results demonstrated that the two treatment regimens were biologically equivalent in terms of haematological response. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15777891/)

Name: Iron sucrose (IV)
Developers: Public Health Foundation of India (PHFI); University of Bern; HaEmek Medical Center
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Bench-top nucleic acid amplification test providing accelerated detection of Neisseria gonorrhoeae DNA from clinical samples.
Key features and challenges:
Iron sucrose is composed of a polynuclear iron(III)-hydroxide core surrounded by a large number of non-covalently bound sucrose molecules. The complex has a weight average molecular weight (Mw) of approximately 43 kDa. The polynuclear iron core has a structure similar to that of the core of the physiological iron storage protein ferritin. The formulation is developed as CSL Vifor and is marketed as Venofer in over 80 countries worldwide. (https://www.medicines.org.uk/emc/product/5911/smpc#gref) 

There have been numerous studies evaluating the safety and efficacy of iron sucrose in pregnancy. A study in India evaluated the safety and effectiveness of intravenous iron sucrose versus standard oral iron therapy in pregnant women with moderate-to-severe anaemia in a multicentre, open-label, phase 3, randomised, controlled trial. Between 2014, and 2017, 2018 women were enrolled, and 999 were randomly assigned to the intravenous iron sucrose group and 1019 to the standard therapy group. However, the study was stopped due to futility, as there was insufficient evidence to show the effectiveness of intravenous iron sucrose in reducing clinical outcomes compared with standard oral iron therapy in pregnant women with moderate-to-severe anaemia. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31708151/)

Studies have also compared different intravenous iron formulations, including a study in Switzerland which compared high-dose ferric carboxymaltose to iron sucrose (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22945271/).

Name: Is It Typhoid Antigen
Disease: Typhoid and paratyphoid fever (S. Typhi, S. Paratyphi A)
Indication: Diagnosis of acute typhoid and paratyphoid fever caused by Salmonella typhi and paratyphi infection respectively.
Target:
Salmonella typhi (S. typhi) and Salmonella paratyphi (S.
paratyphi) antigens

Name: Is It Typhoid IgG/IgM
Disease: Typhoid and paratyphoid fever (S. Typhi, S. Paratyphi A)
Indication: Indicated for the qualitative detection and differentiation of anti-Salmonella Typhi IgG and IgM antibodies.
Target: IgG/IgM against various antigens (including LPS and OMP)
Key features and challenges:
Also includes SD Bioline Salmonella typhi IgG/IgM Fast (detects IgM and IgG antibodies to unspecified S. Typhi antigens), Zephyr Biologicals Enteroscreen® (detects IgM and IgG antibodies to S. typhi LPS antigen), Mega Diagnostics Mega Salmonella (detects IgM/IgG antibodies to unspecified S. Typhi antigens), Typhidot Malaysian Bio-Diagnostics Research (detects IgM and IgG to Anti-OMP) and CTK Biotech Typhoid IgG/IgM Combo Rapid Test CE.
Sensitivity and specificity for TYPHIDOT Rapid IgG/IgM (Combo) are 84% and 79% respectively. Miniaturised dot-blot enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) format. The test is considered positive if the IgM is positive, and indeterminate if the IgG is positive but IgM negative.

Name: Isotretinoin
Developers: Al-Azhar University; Sun Pharma (including Ranbaxy); Roche (including InterMune)
Indication: Indicated for PCOS acne.
Mechanism of action: Ornithine decarboxylase inhibitors; Retinoic acid receptor agonists
Key features and challenges:
Isotretinoin is an oral retinoid widely used for the treatment of moderate to severe acne, where it can induce long-term remission. It reduces sebaceous gland activity, normalizes follicular keratinization, and exerts anti-inflammatory effects. Mechanistically, isotretinoin promotes apoptosis of sebocytes and modulates transcription factors such as p53, FoxO1, and FoxO3. The drug is, however, well known for its teratogenicity and other adverse effects, requiring strict pregnancy prevention programmes during treatment.
Beyond dermatologic indications, isotretinoin has been observed to influence androgen-related pathways. It has been shown to reduce insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), which in turn may decrease 5-α reductase activity and limit conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT). Through upregulation of p53 expression, isotretinoin may indirectly reduce circulating testosterone levels, offering a mechanistic rationale for its potential benefit in hyperandrogenic states such as PCOS.
A 2024 study evaluated the effectiveness of oral isotretinoin in female subjects with acne and PCOS, highlighting possible modulatory effects on the pituitary–ovarian axis. The findings suggested potential benefits in hyperandrogenic women, including improvements in acne severity and hormonal parameters. However, the authors emphasized the need for larger, multicentre controlled trials to confirm these effects and to clarify endocrine outcomes.
https://ovarianresearch.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s13048-024-01347-x#Sec8
Despite theoretical and preliminary clinical promise, isotretinoin faces significant limitations in the PCOS context. Its teratogenic risk necessitates strict contraceptive measures, making it unsuitable for women actively attempting conception. Evidence remains limited to small or exploratory studies, with no robust long-term data on ovulatory function, metabolic outcomes, or fertility. Furthermore, isotretinoin does not address the underlying metabolic drivers of PCOS, such as insulin resistance.
Isotretinoin may provide symptomatic benefit for acne in hyperandrogenic PCOS phenotypes and could exert modest endocrine effects; however, its role remains adjunctive and highly restricted due to safety considerations and insufficient evidence for broader PCOS management.

Name: Isoxsuprine
Indication: Pevention of preterm labour
Mechanism of action: β2 adrenoreceptor agonist that causes direct relaxation of uterine and vascular smooth muscle.
Key features and challenges:
Isoxsuprine is a beta-adrenergic agonist that causes direct relaxation of uterine and vascular smooth muscle. Its vasodilating actions are greater on the arteries supplying skeletal muscle than on those supplying skin. It is used in the treatment of peripheral vascular disease, and in premature labour. It is not FDA approved for preterm labour, but appears to be marketed elsewhere for this condition.
The mechanism of action of isoxsuprine hydrochloride is controversial, because isoxsuprine has beta-adrenergic activities that could not be offset by beta-adrenergic blockers. Although stimulation of the beta-adrenergic receptor increases blood flow to produce vasodilation, this agent may also have direct effects on the contractility of smooth muscle.
In 2010, a systematic review finds preliminary evidence that isoxsuprine administered acutely (intravenous administration) and as maintenance therapy (oral or intramuscular administration) is effective in prolonging pregnancy in women at risk of abortion or premature delivery (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27725717/). The review found, through combination of two analysis undertaken in the review, a beneficial effect of isoxsuprine in 77.3% of cases at risk of abortion and 89% for risk of premature delivery.
A 2021 study into the safety of isoxsuprine as a tocolytic agent found that it was safe and effective. Maternal tachycardia and vomiting (8% each) were the commonly reported adverse drug reactions, which were resolved with dose adjustment (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31550735/). Post marketing, multicentre observational studies are also underway.
Recent updates:
February 2021: Isoxsuprine was found to be an effective and well-tolerated tocolytic agent in arresting PTL, in turn resulting in the overall improvement in maternal and perinatal outcomes (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31550735/).

2010: Systematic review finds with a combination of individual and general data that there is a beneficial effect of isoxsuprine in 77.3% of cases at risk of abortion and 89% for risk of premature delivery (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20712130/)

Name: Itraconazole
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Mycetoma.
Mechanism of action: Lanosterol 14-alpha demethylase inhibitor.
Key features and challenges:
Itraconazole is a triazole antifungal agent used to treat various fungal infections.  First synthesized in the early 1980s, itraconazole is a broad-spectrum triazole antifungal agent used to treat a variety of infections. It is a 1:1:1:1 racemic mixture of four diastereomers, made up of two enantiomeric pairs, each possessing three chiral centres. Itraconazole was first approved in the US in 1992 and is available orally. While the intravenous formulation of the drug was formerly available, it was discontinued in the US in 2007 (https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB01167).

Current recommended therapy for Eumycetoma is itraconazole for 9-12 months, but cure rates as low as 26% have been reported, and fungi can often still be cultured from lesions post-treatment. Surgical excision is often used with itraconazole to obtain better treatment outcomes. Amputation may be required if the combination of antifungals and surgical excision fails. Fosravuconazole was investigated as a potentially more effective antifungal treatment with itraconazole as an active comparator (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03086226).

Name: Itraconazole
Developers: University of Alabama at Birmingham; Janssen Pharmaceutical NV
Indication: Treament of histoplasmosis infection
Mechanism of action: Itraconazole interacts with 14-α demethylase, a cytochrome P-450 enzyme necessary to convert lanosterol to ergosterol
Key features and challenges:
A Phase 2/3 prospective, multi-center, randomized, open-label parallel arm study involving patients with proven or probable invasive endemic fungal infection evaluated the pharmacokinetics, safety, efficacy, tolerability and health economics of oral SUBA-itraconazole compared to conventional itraconazole.
Results posted: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03572049.

Name: Ivermectin
Developers: Murdoch Children's Research Institute (MCRI); Bordeaux Hospital University Center, Centre Hospitalier Universitaire (CHU) de Bordeaux; University of Oxford (including Oxford University Clinical Research Unit Vietnam (OUCRU), Nuffield Department of Women's and Reproductive Health (NDWRH)); MSD (also known as Merck & Co)
Indication:
1.Treatment of scabies
2. MDA chemoprophylaxis
Mechanism of action: Binds to glutamate-gated chloride ion channels of invertebrate nerve and muscle cells
Key features and challenges: Approved for scabies treatment in Japan, MDA drug in highly endemic settingshttps://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa1500987. Contraindicated in children below 15kg and pregnant women
Recent updates:
Recommendation for use of Invermectin both as treatment (IDM) and MDA (WHO Informal Consultation on a Framework for Scabies Control)
Oral ivermectin is recommended, but contraindicated for pregnant women and children who weigh less than 15 kg.
24/01/25:
- Ivermectin Therapy for Scabies Infection in Children Younger Than 5 Years of Age (ITCHY Study) (ITCHY) (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05500326).
- Oral Ivermectin Versus Topical Permethrin to Treat Scabies in Children and Adults (SCRATCH) (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02407782)
- Ivermectin Safety in Small Children (ISSC) (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04332068)
- Evaluating Pediatric Ivermectin in Children Under 15 kg (EPIC-15) (EPIC-15) (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06404333).

Name: JYNNEOS® / IMVAMUNE® / IMVANEX®
Indication: Active immunization for the prevention of mpox in adults
Mechanism of action: Immunostimulant
Key features and challenges:
Modified vaccinia Ankara is a third-generation, live, non-replicating, prophylactic vaccine, developed by Bavarian Nordic as an intradermal and subcutaneous injection for the prevention of smallpox bioterror attack, monkeypox and vaccinia virus infections. This product consists of a highly attenuated strain of Modified Vaccinia Ankara (MVA) virus that does not replicate in human cells, thus alleviating the safety concerns of previous smallpox vaccines that were based on various replicating vaccinia virus strains. IMVAMUNE® is expected to be effective and offer protection against smallpox in 3 days following a single injection, compared with traditional vaccines that only show protection after 10-14 days. The vaccine is launched in the US and Canada for prevention of smallpox and monkeypox disease. The vaccine is available in the European Union, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and approved in Switzerland for prevention of small pox, monkeypox and for the prevention of disease caused by vaccinia virus. The subcutaneous liquid-frozen formulation is available in the US, Canada and approved in the United Kingdom for the prevention of small pox and monkeypox. The vaccine is also approved for use as under emergency use authorization for the prevention of monkeypox infection in Democratic Republic of the Congo and Nigeria. The vaccine is approved in Singapore for the prevention of small pox and monkeypox. The freeze-dried formulation of the vaccine is under regulatory review in the US for the prevention of small pox and monkeypox. Clinical development is underway in Mexico, South Korea, Germany, Puerto Rico.

Bavarian Nordic is working with the Biomedical Advanced Research and Development Authority (BARDA) to further improve modified vaccinia Ankara vaccine by developing a freeze-dried version of the vaccine, which will have a longer shelf-life and simplified shipment and storage logistics.
Recent updates: In Sept 2024, the vaccine received WHO PQ status

Name: Janssen - Ad26.COV 2.S
Indication: Prevention of disease caused by SARS CoV-2 infection in persons 18 years and older
Mechanism of action: The Janssen COVID-19 Vaccine is a monovalent vaccine composed of a recombinant, replication-incompetent human adenovirus type 26 (Ad26) vector that encodes a SARS-CoV-2 spike (S) protein in a stabilized conformation. The S protein on the surface of the coronavirus binds to the Angiotensin Converting Enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptor of a host cell allowing the virus to infect the cell. Vaccination with the Janssen COVID-19 Vaccine leads to humoral and cellular immune responses directed against the S protein and in particular the production of neutralizing and other functional S antibodies which may block ACE2 receptor binding to the S protein, contributing to protection against COVID-19.

Name: K-Othrine (IRS)
Indication:
Prevention and control of malaria in children and adults living in areas with ongoing malaria transmission.
WHO policy: strong recommendation, low certainty evidence
Mechanism of action: Sodium channel modulator
Key features and challenges:
Initially recommended by WHOPES and later converted to WHO prequalification on 29/01/2018

K-Othrine® Polyzone, developed by Bayer (now part of Covestro), is a cutting-edge residual insecticide spray that offers long-lasting vector control through innovative polymer technology. Its active ingredient, deltamethrin, a pyrethroid insecticide, is protected by a polymer film that adheres to treated surfaces. This technology prevents environmental degradation, ensuring consistent effectiveness for up to 90 days, even in challenging conditions like high temperatures or humidity.  

Designed for versatility, K-Othrine® Polyzone works on a variety of surfaces, including porous materials, maintaining its efficacy across diverse environments. Its extended residual action makes it an excellent choice for malaria vector control and other public health applications. Prequalified by the **World Health Organization (WHO)**, it meets rigorous global standards for safety and performance, establishing it as a trusted tool for integrated vector management programs.  

Despite its advantages, K-Othrine® Polyzone faces some challenges. The advanced formulation may come at a higher cost compared to traditional insecticides, potentially limiting its accessibility for resource-constrained programs. Effective application requires trained personnel to ensure optimal coverage and performance, which may be a barrier in certain regions. Additionally, as with all pyrethroid-based products, ongoing monitoring is essential to address potential resistance among vector populations.

Name: LH/FSH ratio (serum or urinary point-of-care)
Developers: Ankara Bilkent City Hospital; Tokushima University; All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS); The West China School of Public Health
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS
Mechanism of action: Calculates luteinizing hormone to follicle-stimulating hormone ratio to identify gonadotropin imbalance characteristic of PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
The LH/FSH ratio is a long-established biochemical marker used in the evaluation of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Many women with PCOS exhibit increased LH pulsatility and relative FSH suppression, resulting in an elevated LH/FSH ratio, which reflects the neuroendocrine dysregulation underlying chronic anovulation. The Japan Society of Obstetrics and Gynecology (JSOG) recommends the LH/FSH ratio as part of the biochemical evaluation of PCOS, particularly in Asian populations where hormonal profiles may differ from Western cohorts.
(https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jog.15423).
Studies consistently show that women with PCOS often have an elevated Recent studies continue to demonstrate diagnostic utility of the LH/FSH ratio. A 2024 adolescent study showed significantly higher LH/FSH ratios in PCOS versus controls, supporting the ratio as a helpful discriminator in early-life PCOS presentations.
(https://dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/tchd/issue/82606/1347807).
Another study (Thieme, 2022) demonstrated that combining LH/FSH with AMH and the Free Androgen Index (FAI) improves diagnostic accuracy, consistent with guideline recommendations emphasizing multimodal assessment rather than reliance on a single hormonal parameter.
(https://www.thieme-connect.de/products/ejournals/abstract/10.1055/a-1880-1264).
Multiple 2022–2023 studies have established laboratory-specific cut-off values for clinical use. For example, using ARCHITECT and ECLusys platforms, LH/FSH cut-offs of 1.21–1.51 effectively distinguished PCOS from controls in Japanese and Asian cohorts.
(https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jog.15423).
A separate cross-sectional analysis showed the LH/FSH ratio was highest in PCOS (1.3) compared with congenital adrenal hyperplasia (0.8) and idiopathic hyperandrogenism (0.6), reaffirming its diagnostic specificity toward PCOS-related gonadotropin dysfunction.
(https://rs.yiigle.com/cmaid/1350488).
A urinary FSH/LH diagnostic test kit is now being evaluated in a registered clinical study (ChiCTR #276706) as a point-of-care screening tool for PCOS.
(https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=276706).
The test is designed to measure urinary LH and FSH concentrations semi-quantitatively and calculate the ratio as a non-invasive, rapid, and accessible screening tool. This has potential advantages for:
-Primary care and community-level PCOS screening,
-Adolescent and young adult populations,
-Settings with limited access to serum hormone testing, and
-Large-scale population screening programs.
If validated, urinary LH/FSH testing could support low-cost, decentralized early PCOS detection, reducing delays in diagnosis; an issue highlighted in recent international PCOS reports (e.g., Monash PCOS Guidelines, WHO).
Guideline reference: https://www.monash.edu/medicine/mchri/pcos/guideline
Challenges and limitations:
-High interpersonal and inter-cycle variability: LH pulsatility, obesity, menstrual phase, and stress can affect serum and urinary LH levels.
-Diminished utility in obesity and adolescents: Obesity blunts LH elevation, and adolescents may show overlapping gonadotropin profiles even without PCOS.
-Not recommended as a standalone diagnostic test: The International Evidence-Based PCOS Guideline states that hormonal tests (including LH/FSH) cannot be used alone to diagnose PCOS.
-Urinary test kits are still experimental: Clinical validation, cut-off standardization, and assay reproducibility for urinary LH/FSH remain unestablished.
Overall, the LH/FSH ratio remains a useful supportive biomarker, and emerging urinary POC technology may expand access to early PCOS screening. However, interpretation must be cautious, context-dependent, and integrated with clinical signs, androgen markers, AMH, and ultrasound.
Recent updates:
2025: A urinary LH/FSH diagnostic test is being evaluated as a point of care screening test for PCOS.

Name: LNG-IUD - Endometriosis
Indication: Treatment of endometriosis-related menorrhagia and pain and prevention of recurrence post surgery
Mechanism of action: Progesterone receptor agonists
Key features and challenges:
The levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) is a T-shaped intrauterine device that releases approximately 20 µg of levonorgestrel daily for up to five years. Levonorgestrel is a synthetic progestogen widely used in contraception and hormone therapy. The device has been marketed globally since its European launch in 1997 and is approved for contraception, treatment of menorrhagia, and endometrial protection during hormone replacement therapy. Its primary mechanisms include endometrial suppression, thickening of cervical mucus, and inhibition of sperm motility. Variants with lower hormone release profiles, such as Kyleena and Skyla, have also been developed (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800011854).
The use of LNG-IUDs for endometriosis-associated pain is recommended in clinical guidelines, including those from the European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, reflecting their role in suppressing endometrial proliferation and reducing menstrual-related pain 
(https://www.eshre.eu/guideline/endometriosis
; https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2011/0101/p84.html).
Clinical evidence has been evolving. A 2021 systematic review evaluating the LNG-IUD as postoperative therapy for endometriosis found uncertainty regarding its impact on dysmenorrhoea and overall pain relief due to limited high-quality randomized controlled trial data, highlighting the need for further research (https://academic.oup.com/humrep/article/36/Supplement_1/deab130.301/6343830). 
In 2022, a study involving 80 patients compared GnRH agonist therapy alone with GnRH agonist plus LNG-IUD (Mirena) and reported improved clinical efficacy, reduced sex hormone and CA125 levels, lower pain scores, and reduced recurrence rates in the combination group (https://cellmolbiol.org/index.php/CMB/article/view/4449).
Most recently, a clinical trial completed in 2024 evaluated the efficacy and quality-of-life outcomes of levonorgestrel IUD (Mirena), medroxyprogesterone injection, and combined oral contraceptives compared with untreated controls in preventing recurrence after conservative surgery for endometriosis-associated pain (https://adis.springer.com/trials/700238519). 
Looking ahead, a prospectively registered trial expected to commence in 2026 will investigate the addition of norethisterone acetate (NETA) to LNG-IUD therapy in adolescents and young adults to improve bleeding control, pain outcomes, and continuation rates 
(NCT04948489; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04948489).
Key challenges include variability in reported pain outcomes, irregular bleeding patterns, and limited robust comparative data versus other hormonal strategies. While guideline-endorsed, the LNG-IUD may have variable effectiveness as a standalone therapy in some populations, prompting exploration of combination regimens.
Overall, the LNG-IUD is an established, guideline-supported hormonal option for endometriosis-associated pain with extensive real-world use. Ongoing and future studies aim to clarify its optimal positioning, particularly in postoperative and adolescent populations.

Name: Labetalol
Indication: Management of hypertension in preeclampsia
Mechanism of action: Labetalol non-selectively antagonizes beta-adrenergic receptors, and selectively antagonizes alpha-1-adrenergic receptors
Key features and challenges:
Labetalol is a combined alpha- and beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist used in the management of hypertension. It non-selectively blocks β-adrenergic receptors and selectively antagonizes α1-adrenergic receptors. Alpha-1 blockade results in vasodilation and reduced peripheral vascular resistance, while beta-adrenergic antagonism contributes to blood pressure reduction. As with other beta-blockers, potential adverse effects include bronchospasm, particularly due to β2-receptor blockade.
In the context of pre-eclampsia, labetalol is widely used to control maternal hypertension. It addresses the symptomatic elevation of blood pressure but does not modify the underlying pathophysiology of the disorder, which involves placental dysfunction and angiogenic imbalance. Despite this limitation, labetalol plays an essential role in clinical management and has been used for many years as a first-line antihypertensive agent in pre-eclampsia, particularly in the United Kingdom. Historical comparisons indicate that seizure rates were not significantly different from those observed in settings where magnesium sulfate is routinely used for seizure prophylaxis.
A study started in 2024 to examine the Effect of Intravenous Infusion of Labetalol Versus Hydralazine on Cerebral Hemodynamics of Preeclampsia Patients is on-going.
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06360601).
Key challenges include its inability to address disease progression, the need for careful maternal and fetal monitoring, and potential contraindications in patients with asthma or certain cardiac conditions. While labetalol remains a cornerstone for blood pressure control in pre-eclampsia, comprehensive management requires additional interventions targeting seizure prevention and timing of delivery.
Recent updates:
2024: The Effect of Intravenous Infusion of Labetalol Versus Hydralazine on Cerebral Hemodynamics of Preeclampsia Patients Prospective Randamized Study. It's an ongoing study. https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06360601?term=Labetalol&cond=preeclampsia&rank=1

Despite strong evidence supporting its first-line role in ovulation induction, letrozole is not a disease-modifying therapy for PCOS and does not directly address metabolic dysfunction. Resistance may occur in a subset of patients, and optimal dosing strategies remain under investigation. Long-term reproductive safety data are reassuring but continue to be monitored, particularly in higher-dose or combination protocols.
Letrozole is currently the preferred first-line pharmacologic agent for ovulation induction in women with PCOS seeking pregnancy, demonstrating superior live birth outcomes compared with clomiphene citrate and a favorable safety profile. Ongoing research focuses on optimizing dosing strategies and combination regimens to enhance outcomes in resistant or metabolically complex PCOS phenotypes.

Name: Leuprorelin Depot - Endometriosis
Developers: AbbVie; Takeda Pharmaceutical Company; Daewoong Therapeutics; Camurus
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of endometriosis
Mechanism of action: Gonadotropin releasing hormone stimulants
Key features and challenges:
Leuprorelin depot is a sustained-release formulation of the gonadotrophin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonist leuprorelin. It initially stimulates luteinising hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) secretion, followed by pituitary desensitisation and downregulation with continued use, resulting in suppression of ovarian estrogen production. This hypoestrogenic effect underpins its established role in the treatment of endometriosis and other hormone-dependent conditions. Leuprorelin depot is marketed globally under various brand names, including Enantone, and is available in multiple formulations across key markets (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800009297).
Clinical investigations in endometriosis have spanned more than a decade. In 2012, a study was initiated to evaluate the efficacy of leuprorelin with differing add-back therapy regimens to mitigate estrogen deficiency symptoms (https://adis.springer.com/trials/700197521). Also initiated in 2012 was a trial assessing the effects of norethisterone acetate in combination with leuprorelin on symptom control and bone mineral density in women with endometriosis (https://adis.springer.com/trials/700022554). In 2013, a study began evaluating the efficacy and tolerability of anastrozole plus leuprorelin compared with leuprorelin monotherapy in women with recurrent endometriosis (https://adis.springer.com/trials/700228340).
Subsequently, completed clinical trials have examined the suppressive effects of orally administered leuprolide on gonadotropins and gonadal steroids compared with intramuscular depot injection, although results have not yet been published (https://adis.springer.com/trials/700353250). 
More recent evidence published in 2023 reported continued use of GnRH agonists with steroid add-back beyond the recommended 12-month duration in adolescents, highlighting considerations around prolonged therapy (https://www.jpagonline.org/article/S1083-3188(23)00103-1/abstract
). Another 2023 publication found no significant difference in therapeutic effectiveness or safety between postoperative dienogest and leuprorelin in women with endometriosis (https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jog.15585).
Key challenges associated with leuprorelin depot include hypoestrogenic adverse effects such as vasomotor symptoms and bone mineral density loss, necessitating add-back therapy for longer-term use. Recurrence of symptoms following treatment discontinuation remains common. Although leuprorelin is well established in clinical practice, ongoing research continues to optimise combination strategies and long-term management approaches.
Overall, leuprorelin depot is a long-standing, globally available GnRH agonist with extensive clinical use in endometriosis. Current research focuses on improving tolerability and refining adjunctive strategies rather than establishing primary efficacy.

Name: Linzagolix - Endometriosis

Mechanism of action: Luteinizing hormone receptor hormone antagonists
Key features and challenges:
Linzagolix choline is an oral, non-peptide GnRH receptor antagonist, developed to address estrogen-dependent conditions such as endometriosis, adenomyosis, and uterine fibroids. It functions by binding to and blocking GnRH receptors in the pituitary gland, which inhibits the secretion of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). This suppression results in a decrease in estrogen levels, which is beneficial for managing symptoms related to endometriosis.
Linzagolix has been proposed to manage symptoms of endometriosis symptoms by lowering estrogen to a level that alleviates pain and reduces the growth of endometrial lesions, while maintaining estradiol within a target range of 20 to 60 pg/mL. This balance helps relieve symptoms without causing the significant bone loss or other adverse effects associated with full estrogen suppression.
The drug was approved in the European Union in June 2022 for managing symptoms of uterine fibroids and is currently under regulatory review in the US for similar indications. Clinical development for endometriosis is ongoing in several countries, reflecting its potential as a treatment option for this condition.
Linzagolix choline is similar to other GnRH receptor antagonists, such as cetrorelix, relugolix, and elagolix, and works by inhibiting GnRH receptor signaling to prevent estrogen production. In addition to its use for endometriosis, ObsEva is also exploring its potential for treating hormone-dependent prostate cancer and is seeking commercial partners for further development and commercialization. 
(https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800032710)

Name: Luteinizing hormone

Mechanism of action: Measures serum luteinizing hormone concentrations to detect hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis dysregulation associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
Luteinizing hormone (LH) is a hormone produced by the pituitary gland that regulates the menstrual cycle and ovulation in women. It stimulates the ovaries to release estrogen and trigger ovulation. LH levels are elevated in many women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), leading to irregular ovulation and increased androgen production, which can cause symptoms like hirsutism and acne. The LH/FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) ratio is a key diagnostic tool for PCOS, but it's not definitive on its own, especially in adolescents or overweight individuals. PCOS diagnosis typically relies on the Rotterdam criteria, but LH levels are recommended as a diagnostic biomarker for PCOS by the Japan Society of Obstetrics and Gynecology (JSOG).

A study published in 2022 aimed to establish cut-off values for LH and the LH/FSH ratio in diagnosing PCOS using two assay systems. The study found that the cut-off values for LH were 7.1 mIU/mL and 9.9 mIU/mL, and for LH/FSH ratio, 1.21 and 1.51, in the ARCHITECT and ECLusys systems, respectively. These values were consistent across both systems and effectively identified endocrinological abnormalities in PCOS, providing useful criteria for diagnosis, especially in Japan and Asian populations. Name: M. genitalium ddPCR assay
Developers: Thermo Fisher Scientific (including Life Technologies and Mesa Biotech); Bio-Rad Laboratories (including Bio-Rad AbD Serotec GmbH)
Indication: Detection of Mycoplasma geniutalium.
Mechanism of action: Droplet Digital PCR
Key features and challenges:
Droplet digital polymerase chain reaction (ddPCR) is a molecular amplification technique based on water–oil emulsion droplet technology, in which a sample is partitioned into approximately 20,000 individual droplets prior to PCR amplification. Each droplet functions as an independent reaction chamber, enabling absolute quantification of target nucleic acid without reliance on standard curves. ddPCR utilizes reagents and workflows similar to conventional TaqMan probe-based assays, with extensive sample partitioning representing a key distinguishing feature. The technology has been approved for use in in vitro diagnostic applications.
A 2023 study developed and evaluated a ddPCR assay for the quantification of Mycoplasma genitalium (https://academic.oup.com/lambio/article/76/6/ovad064/7180972). 
The assay demonstrated precise and reproducible quantitation across multiple template types. Findings suggest that ddPCR may be a useful tool for assessing bacterial load in patient samples and for investigating associations between pathogen burden and clinical outcomes, including symptom severity, sequelae, and treatment response.
Key challenges include the requirement for specialized laboratory equipment, trained personnel, and higher operational costs compared to routine nucleic acid amplification tests. While ddPCR offers high precision and absolute quantification capabilities, its role in routine clinical diagnosis of M. genitalium may be limited by infrastructure and scalability considerations.

Name: Magnesium sulphate - PE/E
Indication: Prevention and treatment of severe preeclampsia/eclampsia
Mechanism of action: Magnesium may act to increase the seizure threshold by inhibiting NMDA receptors, thereby limiting the effect of glutamate
Key features and challenges:
Magnesium sulphate (MgSO₄) is an inorganic magnesium salt widely used in obstetric practice for the prevention and treatment of seizures associated with severe preeclampsia and eclampsia. It exerts anticonvulsant effects primarily through central nervous system mechanisms, including inhibition of N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors, thereby increasing the seizure threshold and limiting glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity. Magnesium sulphate also functions as a calcium antagonist and smooth muscle relaxant, contributing to its cardiovascular and neuromodulatory effects.
Magnesium sulphate is the first-line therapy for seizure prophylaxis and treatment in severe preeclampsia and eclampsia and is included in the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines. A Cochrane systematic review, incorporating the large Magpie Trial and additional studies across varying disease severity, demonstrated that magnesium sulphate approximately halves the risk of eclampsia compared with placebo or no treatment (https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD000025.pub2/full).
Adverse effects are dose-dependent and relate to its smooth muscle–relaxant properties. Serious complications such as respiratory depression or cardiac arrest are rare but more likely in women with renal impairment, as magnesium is excreted almost exclusively via the kidneys. Careful clinical monitoring of respiratory rate, reflexes, and urine output is essential to minimize toxicity. Despite challenges related to administration protocols and monitoring requirements, magnesium sulphate remains inexpensive, widely available, and particularly suitable for low-resource settings.
Current research focuses on dose-optimization strategies to improve safety, simplify regimens, and enhance feasibility of use in resource-limited environments. Although magnesium sulphate has indications for fetal neuroprotection and was previously used for tocolysis, it is now primarily reserved for management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/bmjopen/7/1/e013952.full.pdf).
Key challenges include ensuring safe administration in settings with limited monitoring capacity and determining optimal low-dose regimens without compromising efficacy. Nonetheless, magnesium sulphate remains the global standard of care for seizure prevention and management in preeclampsia and eclampsia.

Name: Magnesium sulphate - PTL/PTB
Developers: Assiut University; Shaheed Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto Medical University
Indication: Delaying preterm labour/birth through tocolytic/relaxant effects on myometrial contraction
Mechanism of action: Magnesium sulfate inhibits Ca2+ influx through dihydropyridine-sensitive, voltage-dependent channels, therefore reducing myometrial contractions
Key features and challenges:
Magnesium sulfate is a medication used to manage and treat multiple clinical conditions and holds several on and off-label uses. FDA approved indications include constipation, hypomagnesemia, prevention of seizures in eclampsia/preeclampsia, acute nephritis (pediatric patients), cardiac arrhythmias secondary to hypomagnesemia, and soaking minor cuts or bruises. Non-FDA approved indications however include tocolysis for preterm labour, and was until recently the most frequently used tocolytic. Due to limited evidence of benefit, maternal risk of toxicity, and poor tolerance,  use of magnesium in preterm labour is decreasing in favour of calcium channel blockers.

Despite many years of research, the precise mechanism of action is not completely understood. Magnesium sulfate appears to function in a similar manner by competitively blocking intracellular calcium channels, decreasing calcium availability and thus inhibiting smooth muscle contractility. It also competes with calcium at the motor end plate, where it reduces excitation by inhibiting acetyl choline release. This then decreases myometrial contractions. In a 2014 systematic review that compared magnesium sulfate with no treatment or placebo, magnesium sulfate did not statistically decrease the rate of PTL/PTB less than 48 hours after initial presentation. In addition, it did not improve neonatal and maternal outcomes, and the incidence of PTL/PTB 48 hours after initial presentation and less than 37 weeks’ gestation was similar between the magnesium treated and untreated groups. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the Society for Maternal-Foetal Medicine consider magnesium sulfate a reasonable option for prolongation of pregnancy in the setting of preterm labour of up to 48 hours to give adequate timing for administration of antenatal corticosteroids. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25126773/)

A 2015 Cochrane review on different treatment regimens of magnesium sulphate for tocolysis in women in preterm labour (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26662716/) showed magnesium sulphate to be of benefit in a wide range of obstetric settings.

In 2023, Shaheed Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto Medical University is undertaking an RCT assessing HCG versus MgSO4 as a tocolytic agent in Pakistan (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05828966#study-overview). 

Another study investigated the uterus relaxant effect of the coadministration of β2-mimetic terbutaline and magnesium sulfate (MgSO4) in an isolated organ bath and to perform in vivo smooth muscle electromyographic (SMEMG) studies in pregnant rats. The study also investigated whether the tachycardia-inducing effect of terbutaline can be reduced by the presence of magnesium, due to the opposite heart rate modifying effects of the two agents. Both MgSO4 and terbutaline reduced uterine contractions in vitro and in vivo, furthermore, the administration of a small dose of MgSO4 significantly enhanced the relaxant effect of terbutaline, especially in the lower range. However, in Ca2+-poor environment, MgSO4 was not able to increase the effect of terbutaline. In the cardiovascular studies, MgSO4 significantly decreased the tachycardia-inducing effect of terbutaline in late pregnant rats (https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/aogs.14532).
Recent updates:
Phase II 2022 study planned to investigate high versus low dose of magnesium sulfate as initial tocolytic agent for preterm labour in symptomatic placenta previa (even though MgSO4 is prescribed to women with PE to stop or slow preterm birth and to protect the preterm foetal brain (https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT04599868).

2014: Cochrane review finds magnesium sulphate ineffective at delaying birth or preventing preterm birth, has no apparent advantages for a range of neonatal and maternal outcomes as a tocolytic agent and its use for this indication may be associated with an increased risk of total fetal, neonatal or infant mortality (in contrast to its use in appropriate groups of women for maternal, fetal, neonatal and infant neuroprotection where beneficial effects have been demonstrated) .(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25126773/)

Dec 2015: Cochrane review on Different treatment regimens of magnesium sulphate for tocolysis in women in preterm labour (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26662716/). Magnesium sulphate has been shown to be of benefit in a wide range of obstetric settings, although it has not been recommended for tocolysis. In clinical settings where health benefits are established, further trials are needed to address the lack of evidence regarding the optimal dose (loading dose and maintenance dose), duration of therapy, timing of therapy and role for repeat dosing in terms of efficacy and safety for mothers and their children.

Name: Mean arterial blood pressure measurement
Indication: Diagnosis of preeclampsia
Mechanism of action: Combines maternal serum HtrA4 levels with uterine artery Doppler resistance to identify impaired placentation associated with preeclampsia.
Key features and challenges:
The gold standard for the diagnosis of preeclampsia is the new onset of hypertension and proteinuria, or the new onset of hypertension and significant end-organ dysfunction with or without proteinuria after 20 weeks of gestation, or postpartum in a previously normotensive patient. Hypertension can be measured using auscultatory measurement of systolic and diastolic pressures, with the mean arterial pressure estimated by using a formula in which the lower (diastolic) blood pressure is doubled and added to the higher (systolic) blood pressure and that composite sum is then divided by 3 to estimate MAP. 
 
During pregnancy, hypertension is defined as systolic blood pressure ≥140 mmHg and/or diastolic blood pressure ≥90 mmHg. Severe hypertension is defined as systolic blood pressure ≥160 mmHg and/or diastolic blood pressure ≥110 mmHg. 
 
MAP is often used in studies as a comparator (e.g. https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04943133).

Key challenges include the reliance on antibody detection, which may not differentiate between active and past infection, and the need for further validation against molecular diagnostic standards. Additional clinical performance data and implementation research are required to establish its role within routine trichomoniasis screening strategies.

Medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) functions as a synthetic progesterone, mimicking the action of natural progesterone in the body.
