Name: Medroxyprogesterone depot - Endometriosis
Indication: Indicated for the prevention and treatment of endometriosis associated pain
Mechanism of action: Interleukin 6 receptor antagonists; Progesterone receptor agonists
Key features and challenges:
Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) subcutaneous formulation is a long-acting progestin therapy developed for contraception and management of endometriosis-associated pain. It suppresses ovulation, reduces estrogen production, and induces endometrial atrophy, mechanisms that are also therapeutically relevant in endometriosis, where ectopic endometrial tissue growth is estrogen-dependent. The subcutaneous formulation contains approximately 30% less medroxyprogesterone acetate than the intramuscular presentation (Depo-Provera) and provides contraceptive protection for up to 13 weeks. It has also been developed in a self-injectable format to improve accessibility and patient autonomy.
In the United States, the subcutaneous formulation (Depo-SubQ Provera 104) was approved by the FDA in March 2005 for contraception and for the management of pain associated with endometriosis. In Australia, it received approval in June 2011 for both contraception and endometriosis management. In the European Union, the product is widely available for contraception under the brand name Sayana Press, with endometriosis use more commonly occurring off-label depending on national regulatory frameworks (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800043972). The product is also available in multiple African and Asian countries, including Kenya, primarily for contraceptive use.
The therapeutic rationale in endometriosis is based on suppression of ovulation and hypoestrogenic effects, leading to reduced stimulation of ectopic endometrial implants and improvement in pelvic pain symptoms. The subcutaneous formulation offers lower dosing, improved convenience, and potential for self-administration, which may enhance adherence compared with intramuscular administration.
Key challenges include adverse effects associated with long-term progestin use, such as irregular bleeding, weight gain, mood changes, and potential reductions in bone mineral density with prolonged therapy. Fertility delay after discontinuation may also influence patient acceptability. While the formulation is approved for endometriosis-associated pain in certain jurisdictions, regulatory indications vary globally, and comparative effectiveness against other hormonal treatments requires continued evaluation. Long-term safety, patient adherence, and individualized risk–benefit assessment remain important considerations in endometriosis management.

Key features and challenges:
Metformin is a well-known, affordable medicine originally used for type 2 diabetes. It’s now also widely used to treat polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), especially because many people with PCOS have insulin resistance, when the body does not respond well to insulin. This can affect weight, hormones, blood sugar, and fertility. Metformin helps the body use insulin more effectively. This can improve blood sugar levels, reduce weight, and regulate periods. It’s often recommended for adults with PCOS who have a BMI of 25 or higher, and sometimes for others, including teenagers, although the evidence is still growing. Metformin is most effective when combined with lifestyle changes like exercise and healthy eating and is often combined with other medicines like clomiphene citrate (Clomid) to boost fertility. Evidence from multiple RCTs shows that combining metformin with clomifene or combined oral contraceptives yields synergistic benefits in women with PCOS, enhancing ovulation and pregnancy rates as well as improving biochemical hyperandrogenism and insulin resistance beyond the effects of either drug alone.

Name: Methyldopa
Indication: Management of hypertension in preeclampsia
Mechanism of action: Methyldopa stimulates the central alpha-adrenergic receptors by a false neurotransmitter (α-methylnorepinephrine), which results in a decreased sympathetic outflow of norepinephrine to the heart, kidneys, and peripheral vasculature
Key features and challenges:
Methyldopa is an antihypertensive medication used for managing high blood pressure.  It is widely marketed and used for this indication. It is also one of the most commonly used first-line treatments of hypertension during pregnancy, and widely used off-label to manage preeclampsia-associated hypertension.
Women destined to develop gestational hypertensive complications often exhibit deviant hemodynamic adaptation patterns before overt clinical disease. Gestational hypertension and late onset preeclampsia are associated with an exaggerated rise in cardiac output on top of a higher prepregnant value, whereas a shallow rise in cardiac output and the lack of a peripheral resistance drop predisposes to the much less common early onset-preeclampsia along with impaired foetal growth. Early treatment of altered cardiac output and peripheral resistance adjustments with a drug such as methyldopa can prevent development of gestational hypertensive complications.
A clinical trial investigating early vascular adjustments using labetalol, methyldopa, or nifedipine in high-risk women (women with preeclampsia in their first pregnancy). (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04216706). 
The study found that tailored circulatory normalisation of non-physiological hemodynamic changes during pregnancy halves the risk of recurrent preeclampsia, without disadvantageous effects on offspring outcome (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33813842/).
Recent updates: 2021: A clinical trial investigating early vascular adjustments using labetalol, methyldopa, or nifedipine in high-risk women (women with preeclampsia in their first pregnancy) (NCT04216706) found that tailored circulatory normalization of non-physiological hemodynamic changes during pregnancy halves the risk of recurrent preeclampsia, without disadvantageous effects on offspring outcome (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33813842/).

Name: Metronidazole - Trichomoniasis
Developers: Appili Therapeutics; Tulane University of Louisiana; Peking University First Hospital
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of confirmed trichomoniasis.
Mechanism of action: DNA synthesis inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Metronidazole is a nitroimidazole antimicrobial widely used for the treatment of anaerobic bacterial and protozoal infections, including trichomoniasis, giardiasis, and amebiasis. It is available in oral, topical, and suppository formulations and has been used clinically for several decades (https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB00916). 
For trichomoniasis, metronidazole is indicated for the treatment of confirmed infection caused by Trichomonas vaginalis, except during the first trimester of pregnancy.
Although metronidazole remains a standard treatment, cure rates are suboptimal in some settings and recurrence rates can be high. A 2022 comparative study of four 5-nitroimidazole agents found that T. vaginalis isolates were less susceptible to metronidazole (61%) compared with tinidazole (80%), secnidazole (75%), and ornidazole (89%) (https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/spectrum.00912-22). Resistance levels were higher for metronidazole (11%) than for tinidazole (2%) and secnidazole (1%), with no resistance observed for ornidazole in the study population.
The exact mechanism of action of metronidazole has not been fully elucidated. Following passive diffusion into susceptible organisms, its nitro group is reduced by anaerobic electron transport proteins such as ferredoxin or flavodoxin, generating reactive nitro radicals. These metabolites interact with DNA and other macromolecules, disrupting nucleic acid synthesis and leading to cell death. Ongoing studies are evaluating alternative dosing strategies and comparative effectiveness of nitroimidazole regimens for refractory trichomoniasis, including multi-dose metronidazole and comparisons with secnidazole. 
(https://adis.springer.com/trials/700352303
; https://adis.springer.com/trials/700371166).
Key challenges include emerging resistance, treatment failures and recurrence, and safety considerations. Metronidazole has been associated with peripheral neuropathy and convulsions at higher doses, and carcinogenicity has been observed in animal models, although the relevance to humans remains unclear. Continued surveillance of resistance patterns and optimization of treatment regimens are critical to maintaining its role in trichomoniasis management.

Name: Mifepristone
Developers: Nanavati Max Super Speciality Hospital; Gedeon Richter Group; sanofi-aventis
Indication: Indicated to manage pain and heavy menstrual bleeding associated with fibroids.
Mechanism of action: Glucocorticoid receptor antagonists; Progesterone receptor antagonists
Key features and challenges:
Mifepristone is a synthetic steroid that functions primarily as a progesterone receptor antagonist. It is best known for its use in combination with misoprostol for medical abortion, but it also has other medical applications due to its ability to block the effects of progesterone. Off-label, mifepristone is being investigated for reducing fibroid size and managing symptoms such as heavy menstrual bleeding and pelvic pain. Mifepristone's primary action in treating uterine fibroids is through its antagonistic effects on progesterone receptors in the uterine tissue. By blocking progesterone, it can reduce fibroid growth, induce cell death in fibroid tissue, and alleviate symptoms associated with fibroids, such as heavy menstrual bleeding and pelvic pain. 
(https://adisinsight.springer.com/drugs/800001657). 
While the benefits of mifepristone for pain and heavy bleeding are documented, its effect on fibroid volume remains uncertain with conflicting results and there are concerns regarding endometrial hyperplasia.
(https://www.emas-online.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/fibroids.pdf)
The use of Mifepristone to reduce pain and heavy menstrual bleeding is recommended by the European Menopause and Andropause Society and the American Academy of Family Physicians.
(https://www.emas-online.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/fibroids.pdf; https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2017/0115/p100.html#:~:text=Management%20of%20uterine%20fibroids%20should,therapy%3B%20and%20the%20physician's%20experience.&text=Expectant%20management%20is%20appropriate%20for%20women%20with%20asymptomatic%20uterine%20fibroids.)
A preclinical study from 2021 showed syndecan-1 silencing enhanced the efficacy of mifepristone on the uterine leiomyoma cell proliferation and ECM formation. (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10616-021-00455-6)
In 2022 a CT was registered to examine the effects of low dose mifepristone combined with high intensity focused ultrasound in the treatment of uterine fibroids. (https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=169335)
A 2024 study was found that mifepristone significantly reduced uterine volume by 75%, with hemoglobin levels substantially improving from 9 gm/dL initially to 12.51 gm/dL after six months. Pain intensity, assessed using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) score, gradually decreased from baseline to three-month, with all 20 patients reporting the complete absence of pelvic pain by six months. (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13224-023-01903-3)
Recent updates: No recent clinical trials. The previous one was in 2009

Indication:

Target: cytochrome-c oxidase,  phosphatidylcholine biosynthesis,  inhibition of Akt
Mechanism of action: Within the mitochondria, miltefosine inhibits cytochrome-c oxidase leading to mitochondrial dysfunction and apoptosis-like cell death. Antineoplastic mechanisms of action are related to antileishmanial targets and include inhibition of phosphatidylcholine biosynthesis and inhibition of Akt (also known as protein kinase B), which is a crucial protein within the PI3K/Akt/mTOR intracellular signalling pathway involved in regulating the cell cycle
Key features and challenges:

Miltefosine is ether phospholipid derivative (alkylphosphocholine) is developed by MegaPharm and AEterna Zentaris (now Zentaris) for the treatment of cancer metastases, cutaneous leishmaniasis, leishmaniasis, visceral leishmaniasis. Miltefosine is the first drug ether phospholipid derivative which has shown antitumour activity to be developed for use in the treatment of patients with cancer. Ether lipids constitute a new group of drugs with antineoplastic activity, possibly due to inhibition of protein kinase C and other membrane-associated enzymes like phospholipase C. Miltefosine is available in multiple countries worldwide for cancer metastases, cutaneous leishmaniasis, leishmaniasis and visceral leishmaniasis.

Name: Mineral - Calcium - PE/E
Indication: Prevention of preeclampsia
Target: Unclear, primary target involved in parathyroid hormone and vitamin D homeostasis
Mechanism of action: Calcium reduces parathyroid hormone and 1,25-OH-vitD levels and thus reduces peripheral vascular resistance
Key features and challenges:
Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the human body and plays a critical role in muscle contraction, vascular tone regulation, bone metabolism, and hormone and enzyme function. Low calcium intake during pregnancy has been hypothesized to stimulate parathyroid hormone release, increase intracellular calcium concentrations in vascular smooth muscle, and activate the renin–angiotensin system, contributing to vasoconstriction, sodium retention, and fluid imbalance. These mechanisms are thought to increase the risk of preeclampsia.
(Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28867880/)
A 2012 meta-analysis of 15 randomized controlled trials reported that calcium supplementation during pregnancy (0.5–2 g/day) reduced the risk of preeclampsia by approximately 52% and severe preeclampsia by 25%.
(Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22742607/)
A 2013 World Health Organization (WHO) guideline recommended daily calcium supplementation (1.5–2.0 g) from 20 weeks’ gestation onward in populations with low dietary calcium intake to prevent preeclampsia, particularly among women at higher risk of hypertension. The recommendation was based on moderate-quality evidence from randomized trials demonstrating a substantial reduction in preeclampsia incidence.
(Source: https://www.who.int/nutrition/publications/micronutrients/guidelines/calcium_supplementation/en/)
Subsequent analyses indicated that low-dose calcium supplementation may also reduce preeclampsia risk; however, the quality of supporting clinical trials was considered low.
(Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24621141/)
Implementation challenges in low-income settings include uncertainty regarding optimal dosing strategies, as WHO’s recommended dosage range should not be interpreted as either the minimal effective or optimal dose. Calcium supplementation may interfere with iron absorption, and excessive intake has been associated in some studies with increased risks such as hypercalcemia, HELLP syndrome, postnatal bone resorption, and potential cardiovascular effects. To minimize adverse outcomes, total daily calcium intake is generally recommended not to exceed 2,500 mg.
A clinical trial completed in 2022 compared 500 mg versus 1,500 mg calcium supplementation during pregnancy to assess differential impact on preeclampsia outcomes; results have not yet been published.
(Source: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03350516
Recent updates:
AAA: Phase III trial was completed in 2022

Phase III non-inferiority Ca dosing regimen trial (NCT03350516) is recruiting as of April 2020.

In 2018, WHO published a guideline named "WHO recommendation: Calcium supplementation during pregnancy for prevention of pre-eclampsia and its complications".

Name: Misoprostol
Indication: Prevention and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage
Mechanism of action: PGE2 receptor agonist
Key features and challenges:
Misoprostol is a synthetic prostaglandin PGE1 analogue medication used and widely marketed to prevent and treat stomach ulcers. In some countries, it is also marketed and indicated for use in medical termination of pregnancy. Misoprostol is taken by mouth when used to prevent gastric ulcers in persons taking NSAIDs. For abortions it is used by itself and with mifepristone or methotrexate. It is also used for labor induction or abortion, taken by mouth, dissolved in the mouth, or placed in the vagina. 

Misoprostol binds to smooth muscle cells in the uterine lining to increase the strength and frequency of contractions as well as degrade collagen and reduce cervical tone. As such, it is also used extensively off-label to induce labour, and manage and treat postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) due to uterine atony, where it is often administered rectally, sublingually or orally. The off-label use of misoprostol for PPH is considered routine for this indication with high quality evidence to support its use. It is recommended by the WHO for the prevention and treatment of PPH, and listed on the Essential Medicines List (EML)

Misoprostol has been found to be inferior to oxytocics in efficacy in preventing PPH but is superior in that it is heat stable and easily transported and stored. Because of this, WHO guidelines for PPH management recommend the use of misoprostol in the absence of oxytocics, especially in resource-challenged developing countries. Misoprostol should not be used during pregnancy or for women of childbearing age as it is a well-known and used abortifacient agent. 

A 2018 Cochrane review investigating multiple uterotonic agents found misoprostol plus oxytocin reduces the use of additional uterotonics (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.73, high certainty) and probably also reduces the risk of blood transfusion (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.37 to 0.70, moderate certainty) when compared with oxytocin. High‐certainty evidence suggests that ergometrine plus oxytocin (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.03) and misoprostol plus oxytocin (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.11) make little or no difference in the outcome of PPH ≥ 1000 mL compared with oxytocin alone (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33232518/). 

Clinical investigations of misoprostol for PPH are ongoing, often in combination with other uterotonics including carbetocin and oxytocin, or as a comparator with other uterotonics (e.g. https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT05077540), or haemostatic medications such as tranaxemic acid (e.g. https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT03870256)

Name: Moderna - Spikevax
Indication: Prevention of disease caused by SARS CoV-2 infection in persons 12 years and older
Mechanism of action:
Spikevax (elasomeran) contains mRNA encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles. The mRNA encodes for the full-length SARS-CoV-2 spike protein modified with 2 proline substitutions within the heptad repeat 1 domain (S-2P) to stabilise the spike protein into a prefusion conformation. After intramuscular injection, cells at the injection site and the draining lymph nodes take up the lipid nanoparticle, effectively delivering the mRNA sequence into cells for translation into viral protein.
The delivered mRNA does not enter the cellular nucleus or interact with the genome, is non-replicating, and is expressed transiently mainly by dendritic cells and subcapsular sinus macrophages. The expressed, membrane-bound spike protein of SARS-CoV-2 is then recognised by immune cells as a foreign antigen. This elicits both T-cell and B-cell responses to generate neutralising antibodies, which may contribute to protection against COVID-19.
Key features and challenges:
In a phase III clinical study  (Study P301) the vaccine efficacy of SPIKEVAX to prevent COVID-19, regardless of prior SARS-CoV-2 infection (determined by baseline serology and nasopharyngeal swab sample testing) from 14 days after Dose 2 was 93.6% in persons aged ≥ 18yrs.
Study P203 is an ongoing phase II/III clinical study to evaluate the safety, reactogenecity and effectiveness of Spikevax in adolescents aged 12-17yrs in the United States. In this study, there were 2 COVID-19 cases in the SPIKEVAX group and 13 cases in the placebo group, with avaccine efficacy of 92.7% (95% confidence interval of 67.8% to 99.2%).
The paediatric study is an ongoing Phase 2/3 randomised, placebo-controlled, observer-blind, clinicaltrial to evaluate the safety, reactogenicity, and effectiveness of the SPIKEVAX in children ages 6 through 11 years in the United States and Canada. Participants will befollowed for effectiveness and safety until 1 year after the second dose.
In June 2021, UNICEF and Moderna Therapeutics signed a agreement to supply mRNA 1273 vaccine, on behalf of the COVAX facility. Under the agreement, Moderna will supply up to 34 million doses of mRNA 1273 vaccine, to be delivered in the fourth quarter 2021 and up to 500 million doses of the vaccine in 2022 to UNICEF and its procurement partners including the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO). In December 2021, Moderna announced an amendment to its existing contract with Gavi to accelerate supply of 20 million doses to COVAX by December 31, 2021 for a total of 54 million doses made available to COVAX in 2021. These doses are included in Moderna’s previously announced agreement with Gavi and were originally scheduled for delivery in the first quarter of 2022. Gavi retains the option to procure 233 million additional doses in 2022 under the original agreement.

Name: Modified Ferriman–Gallwey (mFG) hirsutism score
Indication: Tool used to assess hirsutism in PCOS
Mechanism of action: Clinical scoring of androgen-dependent hair growth to assess phenotypic hyperandrogenism associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
A scoring system to quantify hirsutism was developed in 1961 by Ferriman and Gallwey, incorporating eleven androgen dependent specific body areas. The scoring system was later modified incorporating only nine sites and this modified Ferryman–Gallwey (mFG) scoring system is considered the standard scoring system that defines hirsutism quantitatively. Scores range from 0 (no hair) to 4 (severe hair growth), with a total score of 8 or higher indicating hirsutism. In PCOS, the mFG score helps measure androgen excess, one of the diagnostic criteria, aiding in both diagnosis and management of the condition.

A 2023 study used cluster analysis to define normative cut-offs for PCOS diagnostic features in adolescents, including the modified Ferriman–Gallwey (mFG) score, free testosterone, and menstrual cycle length, establishing lower cut-offs than conventional standards. The study called for redefining PCOS diagnostic criteria in adolescents. 
(https://academic.oup.com/ejendo/article/188/6/494/7181126)

A 2019 study found a higher mFG score in PCOS women compared to non-PCOS women, with a score of 7 or higher associated with hirsutism and elevated free testosterone, suggesting its use as a marker for hyperandrogenism. 
(https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6935772/)

A 2017 study showed a significant link between hirsutism, metabolic syndrome, and PCOS, with women having an mFG score ≥8 more likely to have metabolic syndrome, highlighting the need for metabolic syndrome evaluation in women with hirsutism due to its cardiovascular risks.
(https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5514800/)

Mechanism of action: RTS,S induces immune responses in humans that are believed to protect against infection with malaria sporozoites. These include high levels of antibodies against circumsporozoite protein capable of inhibiting sporozoite infection of liver cells in vitro. RTS,S/AS01 is the first malaria vaccine to be tested in Phase 3 clinical trials and the first to be assessed in routine immunization programs in malaria-endemic areas.
Results of Phase 3 testing show that among children aged 5–17 months who received 4 doses of RTS,S/AS01, vaccine efficacy against malaria was 36% over 4 years of follow-up.
Phase 3 efficacy was lower among infants who received the vaccine with other childhood vaccines at 6, 10 and 14 weeks of age, and did not justify further use in this age group.
RTS,S/AS01 shows the most benefit in areas with intense malaria transmission, including reductions in malaria cases, overall hospital admissions, and the need for blood transfusions.
WHO recommended widespread use of RTS,S/AS01 among children in sub-Saharan Africa and in other regions with moderate to high P. falciparum malaria transmission
Significant hurdles for integration of RTS,S into a country’s vaccination schedule include the need for vaccination during non-routine visits and requirement for at least four doses, including a booster given 18 months after the first dose.

Name: Moxifloxacin
Indication: Treatment of Mycoplasma genitalium infection (macrolide-resistant)
Target: Macrolide-resistant Mycoplasma genitalium strains, particularly those with and without parC S83 mutations.
Mechanism of action: Fluoroquinolone antibiotic inhibiting bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV.
Key features and challenges:
Moxifloxacin is a broad-spectrum fluoroquinolone antibiotic commonly used to treat various bacterial infections, including respiratory, skin, and sexually transmitted infections. It works by inhibiting bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, enzymes essential for DNA replication, transcription, and repair. Moxifloxacin is particularly effective against Mycoplasma genitalium (MG), a sexually transmitted pathogen that has shown increasing resistance to other antibiotics like macrolides. It was shown to be more effective than azithromycin at eradicating M. genitalium infections, which supports its preferential use as a first-line treatment.
(https://www.mdpi.com/2079-6382/11/3/353)
However, rising resistance to fluoroquinolones, particularly mutations in the parC gene, has raised concerns about its long-term efficacy.

Its use is recommended in national and international clinical guidelines for the treatment of MG, including the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology (as a second line treatment), the US Center for Disease Control and the Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine  (combined with Doxycycline in cases of macrolide resistance).
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35182080/ ; https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/mycoplasmagenitalium.htm ; https://sti.guidelines.org.au/sexually-transmissible-infections/mycoplasma-genitalium/)

A study conducted at the Melbourne Sexual Health Centre between August 2019 and December 2020 evaluated the efficacy of resistance-guided combination therapies for Mycoplasma genitalium infections. Patients with macrolide-susceptible infections were treated with doxycycline and azithromycin, while those with macrolide-resistant infections received doxycycline and moxifloxacin. Results showed that the doxycycline-azithromycin combination achieved a cure rate of 92.1%, while doxycycline-moxifloxacin achieved 85% cure, with significant variations based on parC mutations. Although combination therapy showed some benefit, it was not more effective than sequential monotherapy, and high levels of quinolone resistance, particularly parC mutations, limited moxifloxacin's efficacy. Additionally, adverse effects were common, primarily mild gastrointestinal symptoms.
(https://www.publish.csiro.au/sh/pdf/SHv18n4abs)

Name: Multiple micronutrient supplement - fixed combined
Developers: George Washington University; Hospital for Sick Children; Harvard University; Medical Research Council Unit (MRC), The Gambia
Indication: Indicated for the prevention of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Increases iron levels
Key features and challenges:
Multiple micronutrient supplement (MMS) contain combinations in a fixed dose formulation of vitamins and minerals including iron, folic acid vitamin A, calcium, vitamin B2, vitamin B3, zinc, and more. The United Nations International Multiple Micronutrient Antenatal Preparation (UNIMMAP) is an established multiple micronutrient formulation that is widely available and contains 15 micronutrients, including iron and folic acid (IFA) in doses of 30mg and 0.4mg, respectively. (https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240007789). 

Several trials have addressed the question of whether an antenatal MMN with various vitamins and minerals, including IFA, would be more appropriate than the currently recommended IFA supplements, especially in low and middle-income countries (LMICs). In 2016, evidence from a Cochrane review suggested that MMN (containing 13 to 15 micronutrients, including IFA) were associated with an average 11% reduction in low birthweight compared with IFA supplements. However, lack of other beneficial effects, the added cost of MMN, equivocal evidence on neonatal mortality related to the dose of iron in IFA supplements, possibility of unknown harms, lack of evidence on cost-effectiveness, and concerns about feasibility led the Guideline Development Group of the WHO to decide not to recommend a change from existing IFA supplements strategies at the time.

Since 2016, the Cochrane review was updated to include four additional
trials (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30873598/). Review of the updated evidence resulted in a context-specific recommendation that antenatal multiple micronutrient supplements that include iron and folic acid are recommended instead of existing IFA supplements. The recommendation is based on evidence derived from trials using MMN containing 13 to 15 micronutrients (including IFA) and UNIMMAP, which contains 15 micronutrients. As the evidence was mainly derived from LMICs, its applicability to high-income countries or to populations not at risk of micronutrient deficiencies is unclear. (https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240007789)

Name: NG-penA-LAMP3 assay
Indication: Detection of gonorrhoea and antimicrobial susceptibility
Target: pecific regions of the N. gonorrhoeae penA
Mechanism of action: loop-mediated isothermal amplification
Key features and challenges:
NG-penA-LAMP3 assay is a loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP)–based molecular diagnostic designed to predict cefixime (CFM) susceptibility in Neisseria gonorrhoeae by detecting allele-specific nonmosaic penA variants. The assay was developed as a nonculture method to support antimicrobial resistance–guided therapy.
A 2022 study reported the development and validation of NG-penA-LAMP3 alongside the previously described NG-penA-LAMP1 assay to improve specificity and avoid cross-reactivity with commensal Neisseria species (https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/spectrum.02335-22). 
The combined assay demonstrated 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity for identifying N. gonorrhoeae strains carrying nonmosaic penA alleles. Validation was performed using isolated strains and clinical specimens confirmed positive by culture and real-time PCR.
Key challenges include the need for broader validation across diverse geographic strain distributions, assessment of performance in low bacterial load samples, and integration into routine point-of-care workflows. Ongoing surveillance will also be required to account for emerging resistance-associated penA variants.
Overall, the NG-penA-LAMP3 assay represents a rapid, culture-free diagnostic approach for predicting cefixime responsiveness in gonorrhea. Further implementation studies are needed to support its role in resistance-guided treatment strategies.

Indication: Indicated for the treatment of endometriosis-associated pelvic pain
Mechanism of action: Inhibit cyclooxygenase enzymes to reduce prostaglandin synthesis, thereby decreasing inflammation and endometriosis-associated pain.
Key features and challenges:
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as aspirin, ibuprofen and naproxen are commonly used to reduce pain,  inflammation, fever, and prevent blood clots. Potential side effects include an increased risk of gastrointestinal ulcers and bleeds, heart attack, and kidney disease. NSAIDs work by inhibiting the activity of cyclooxygenase enzymes (the COX-1 and COX-2 isoenzymes). They are available in many doses and forms, including chewable tablets, injections, suppositories, extended release formulations, and others.

The use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs to treat endometriosis related pain is recommended by the European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists.
(https://www.eshre.eu/guideline/endometriosis; https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2011/0101/p84.html) 
Although widely used to treat endometriosis-related pain symptoms, current evidence to support the use of NSAIDs is of low-quality.
(https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S109888232300031X)

A study started in 2021 aims to assess the efficacy and safety of low-dose aspirin (75 mg/day) compared to Yasmin (Drospirenone ethinyl estradiol) in controlling endometriosis-associated pelvic pain. The randomized, controlled trial will enroll 220 patients, measuring pain reduction after 24 weeks using the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) and monitoring lesion progression and coagulation function.
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05156879)

Key features and challenges:
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as aspirin, ibuprofen, mefenamic acid and naproxen are commonly used to reduce pain,  inflammation, fever, and prevent blood clots. Potential side effects include an increased risk of gastrointestinal ulcers and bleeds, heart attack, and kidney disease. NSAIDs work by inhibiting the activity of cyclooxygenase enzymes (the COX-1 and COX-2 isoenzymes). They are available in many doses and forms, including chewable tablets, injections, suppositories, extended release formulations, and others.

The use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs to treat uterine fibroids-related pain and heavy bleeding is recommended by the American Academy of Family Physicians.
(https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2017/0115/p100.html#:~:text=Management%20of%20uterine%20fibroids%20should,therapy%3B%20and%20the%20physician's%20experience.&text=Expectant%20management%20is%20appropriate%20for%20women%20with%20asymptomatic%20uterine%20fibroids.)

In addition to their antalgic effect, NSAIDs may help reducing blood loss. In a 2019 meta-analysis on heavy menstrual bleeding (non-specific for uterine fibroids), NSAIDs reduced heavy menstrual bleeding when compared with placebo, but were less effective than tranexamic acid, danazol or LNG IUS. In the limited number of small studies suitable for evaluation, there was no clear evidence of a difference in efficacy between NSAIDs.

Name: Nifedipine - PE/E
Indication: Management of blood pressure in preeclampsia
Mechanism of action: Nifedipine induces vasodilatation by blocking calcium entry into smooth muscle cells.
Key features and challenges:
Nifedipine is a calcium channel blocker that induces arteriolar vasodilation by inhibiting calcium influx into vascular smooth muscle cells. It is used in the management of hypertension in preeclampsia and is considered first-line therapy when intravenous access is not feasible. It is also used alongside other antihypertensive agents such as hydralazine and prazosin.
Early preclinical studies in animal models demonstrated that nifedipine reduced maternal arterial pressure. In pregnant sheep, nifedipine lowered maternal blood pressure without significant changes in arterial blood gases, although heart rate increased.
(Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3674140/)
Another experimental study reported reductions in placental blood flow, fetal weight, and placental weight following nifedipine exposure.
(Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1765309/)
Subsequent animal data indicated that maternal nifedipine infusion was associated with fetal hypoxia and acidosis in sheep, though without persistent reductions in uteroplacental or fetoplacental blood flow or blood pressure. These findings highlight the need for careful maternal–fetal monitoring during therapy.
(Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9125622/)
In clinical settings, nifedipine retard has demonstrated higher rates of successful blood pressure control without adverse events compared to labetalol or methyldopa when used as monotherapy.
(Source: https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(19)31282-6)
Caution is advised when nifedipine is administered concurrently with intravenous magnesium sulphate due to the risk of excessive hypotension, which may adversely affect maternal and fetal hemodynamics.
A 2024 preclinical study evaluated nifedipine in combination with olive leaf extract (OLE) in an L-NAME–induced rat model of preeclampsia. The combination therapy significantly reduced systolic and diastolic blood pressure and improved biomarkers associated with oxidative stress and renal function, including reductions in malondialdehyde (MDA), proteinuria, and serum creatinine levels. These findings suggest potential synergistic effects in experimental models.
(Source: https://pharmacia.pensoft.net/article/122471/element/8/202242//)
Overall, nifedipine is an established antihypertensive agent in the management of preeclampsia. While animal studies highlight potential fetal considerations, clinical evidence supports its effectiveness for blood pressure control. Ongoing research continues to explore adjunctive strategies to enhance therapeutic outcomes.
Recent updates:
2023: Effectiveness of nifedipine, labetalol, and hydralazine as emergency antihypertension in severe preeclampsia: a randomized control trial.  Nifedipine is the most effective drug to reduce the blood pressure when single dose administration is used, but requires more doses to further reduce the blood pressure.

A 2019 randomised trial reported superiority of nifedipine retard in blood pressure control as single agents, compared to labetalol or methyldopa.

Name: Nifedipine - PTL/PTB
Indication: Prolonging gestation in threatened preterm labour/birth
Mechanism of action: Nifedipine suppresses myometrial contraction via calcium channel inhibition
Key features and challenges:
Nifedipine is a calcium channel blocker that acts as an effective smooth muscle relaxant by inhibiting the inward flow of calcium ions across uterine smooth muscle cells, thereby reducing uterine contractility. It is widely used off-label as a tocolytic agent in the management of preterm labour.
A 2011 systematic review confirmed that nifedipine is superior to β2-adrenergic receptor agonists and magnesium sulphate for tocolysis in women in preterm labour. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21284967). 
In 2014, a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials comparing calcium channel blockers with placebo or no treatment found that calcium channel blockers significantly decreased the risk of preterm birth within 48 hours (RR 0.30; 95% CI 0.21–0.43). However, when compared with other classes of tocolytics, there was no statistically significant reduction in this outcome (RR 0.86; 95% CI 0.67–1.10). Compared specifically with betamimetics, calcium channel blockers demonstrated advantages in prolongation of pregnancy (mean difference 4.38 days), reduction in serious neonatal morbidities, and improved maternal safety profile. Overall, nifedipine and other calcium channel blockers were found to have more favourable maternal tolerance, fewer adverse effects, and easier administration compared with betamimetics (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24901312).
Between 2012 and 2017, the Indiana University–Purdue University Indianapolis conducted studies focusing on individualization of nifedipine dosing strategies for preterm labour, reflecting efforts to optimize therapeutic response and minimize adverse events. In 2022, a randomized clinical trial in Egypt was initiated to compare nifedipine plus magnesium sulphate versus magnesium sulphate alone for tocolysis in threatened preterm labour; results are pending (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05345132).
Most recently, a 2025 clinical trial comparing nifedipine and nicorandil for tocolysis demonstrated that both agents were equally effective in delaying labour for 48 hours, although nicorandil was associated with fewer adverse effects (https://www.clinicaterapeutica.it/2025/176/3/05_1048_Adel.pdf).
Key challenges include its off-label status, variability in dosing regimens, and limited evidence for improvement in long-term neonatal outcomes despite short-term pregnancy prolongation. Nevertheless, nifedipine remains one of the most widely used first-line tocolytics due to its favorable maternal safety profile and comparable efficacy to other established agents
Recent updates:
2025: Clinical trial, published in 2025, demonstrated Nicorandil and Nifedipine are equally effective as tocolytic drugs in postponing labor in women who have preterm labor that has already started for 48 hours after administration. (https://www.clinicaterapeutica.it/2025/176/3/05_1048_Adel.pdf)

Name: Nifuratel
Indication: Nifuratel is a nitrofuran derivative indicated in the treatment of leucorrhea, vulvovaginal infections, and urinary tract infections.
Mechanism of action: Interferes with DNA Synthesis
Key features and challenges:
Nifuratel is a nitrofuran derivative indicated for the treatment of leucorrhoea, vulvovaginal infections, and urinary tract infections. It has broad-spectrum antibacterial, antifungal, and antiprotozoal activity, making it suitable for mixed vaginal infections, including those involving Trichomonas vaginalis and bacterial vaginosis (https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB13724). 
Regulatory approval and clinical use appear to be concentrated in parts of Europe and selected other regions.
Nifuratel exerts its antiprotozoal effects through multiple mechanisms. These include reduction by microbial nitroreductases to form reactive intermediates that damage protozoal DNA, interference with membrane lipids and proteins leading to increased permeability and cell lysis, and inhibition of key enzymatic pathways involved in metabolic and biosynthetic processes. These combined effects limit replication and survival of susceptible organisms. Clinical reports have described its utility in treating mixed infections, particularly in settings where combined antimicrobial and antiprotozoal coverage is desirable (https://journals.eco-vector.com/0300-9092/article/view/626065).
Key challenges include limited global availability, variable regulatory approval across regions, and the potential for antimicrobial resistance with prolonged or widespread use. Although generally well tolerated, adverse effects may include gastrointestinal disturbances, allergic reactions, and rare neurological symptoms. Use during pregnancy and breastfeeding requires clinical supervision, as safety data remain limited. Further comparative studies are needed to define its role relative to standard nitroimidazole therapies in trichomoniasis management.

Name: Non-pneumatic Anti-shock Garment (NASG)
Indication: Indicated as an fist aid intervention for the control or reduction of atonic postpartum haemorrhage until subsequent standard treatment is initiated.
Mechanism of action: Provides pressure directly to pelvic organs including the uterus and acts as a partial abdominal tourniquet to control pelvic blood flow.
Key features and challenges:
The Non-pneumatic Anti-Shock Garment (NASG) is a low-cost first-aid device designed to stabilize women experiencing hypovolemic shock secondary to postpartum haemorrhage (PPH). Adapted from anti-gravity suit technology originally developed by the United States National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), the NASG applies circumferential external pressure to the lower body, redirecting blood flow to vital organs. By reducing blood flow to the pelvis and uterus, it helps stabilize hemodynamics while definitive treatment is arranged. The garment is lightweight, washable, and reusable for up to 144 applications, supporting its suitability for low-resource settings.
A cluster-randomized trial conducted in Zambia and Zimbabwe evaluated NASG use at 38 primary health care centres, comparing standard obstetric hemorrhage and shock protocols with and without early NASG application prior to referral (2013: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24194839/). All women received the NASG at referral hospitals. Although the planned sample size for statistical power was not reached, early NASG application was associated with a non-significant 54% reduction in the odds of extreme adverse outcome (a composite of mortality and severe morbidity) and significantly faster shock recovery. The findings suggested potential benefit when applied early, particularly in settings where delays to definitive care are common.
The World Health Organization recommended the NASG in 2012 as a temporary stabilizing measure until appropriate treatment is available. In 2015, it was included in the WHO, UNICEF, and UNFPA interagency list of medical devices for essential reproductive, maternal, newborn, and child health interventions (https://www.unicef.org/innovation/non-pneumatic-anti-shock-garment-nasg). The NASG has since been scaled in multiple countries as part of comprehensive PPH management strategies.
Key challenges include limited statistical power in some trials, reliance on referral systems for definitive treatment, and the need for training to ensure correct application. While not a definitive treatment for haemorrhage, its role as a temporizing stabilization tool is supported in settings with delayed access to surgical or transfusion services. Further large-scale studies could strengthen evidence on mortality impact and cost-effectiveness.

Name: Norethindrone Acetate
Indication: Indicated for treatment of endometriosis (pain and bleeding management, menstrual regulation)
Mechanism of action: progesterone receptor agonist
Key features and challenges:
Norethindrone acetate (NETA), also known as norethisterone acetate, is a synthetic progestin derived from norethisterone by esterification of the hydroxyl group. It binds to progesterone receptors in the pituitary and reproductive tissues, suppressing luteinizing hormone (LH) secretion, inhibiting ovulation, and inducing decidualization and atrophy of endometrial tissue. These mechanisms reduce estrogen-driven proliferation of ectopic endometrial implants and alleviate endometriosis-associated pain. NETA is also used in oral contraceptives and other gynecologic indications (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/5832).
Norethindrone acetate has been approved for endometriosis management by major regulatory authorities. In the United States, the FDA approved its use for endometriosis several decades ago (historically available since at least the 1990s). The European Medicines Agency (EMA) has authorized its use across multiple European countries, with approval timelines varying by member state. In Japan, the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) approved norethindrone acetate for endometriosis management in the early 2000s. These approvals reflect established evidence of efficacy in reducing dysmenorrhea, pelvic pain, and lesion progression.
Current clinical investigations aim to optimize its therapeutic use. A trial registered as NCT04948489, planned to begin in 2026, is evaluating whether combining norethindrone acetate with an intrauterine device (IUD) improves bleeding patterns, pain control, and treatment continuation rates in women with endometriosis (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04948489).
Another randomized study initiated in 2021 (NCT05476172) compares daily 5 mg doses of dienogest and norethindrone acetate, with pain scores assessed at six and twelve months to determine comparative effectiveness (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05476172).
Key challenges include potential progestin-related adverse effects such as breakthrough bleeding, mood changes, weight gain, and metabolic effects. Long-term use requires monitoring, particularly in patients with cardiovascular risk factors. Developmental toxicity considerations necessitate appropriate contraceptive counseling during treatment. While norethindrone acetate remains a well-established, guideline-supported therapy for endometriosis-associated pain, ongoing trials aim to refine dosing strategies and combination approaches to improve tolerability and long-term adherence.

Name: Omega-3 Screening
Developers: University of Adelaide; South Australian Health and Medical Research Institute (SAHMRI)
Indication: A biochemical laboratory test measuring omega-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (LCPUFAs) in maternal serum to identify pregnant women with low omega-3 status who are at increased risk of preterm birth. Integrated into antenatal screening to guide targeted omega-3 supplementation for PTL prevention.
Target: Total serum omega-3 fatty acids (% of total fatty acids), including DHA and EPA
Mechanism of action: The test quantifies serum omega-3 fatty acid concentrations using gas chromatography to classify women as having low, moderate, or sufficient omega-3 levels. Low omega-3 status has been associated with increased risk of early preterm birth. Screening allows targeted supplementation for those most likely to benefit. Laboratory processes include sample receipt, fatty acid extraction, chromatographic quantification, and reporting through existing antenatal screening systems.
Key features and challenges:
Omega-3 Screening is a population-level antenatal biochemical screening initiative designed to identify pregnant women with low omega-3 status. The program has been integrated into South Australia’s South Australian Maternal Serum Antenatal Screening (SAMSAS) program, representing one of the first large-scale implementations of omega-3 status screening in routine antenatal care.
The screening uses serum samples collected before 20 weeks’ gestation and analysed using validated gas chromatography methods. Omega-3 levels are classified as low (<3.7%), moderate (3.7–4.3%), or sufficient (>4.3%), based on thresholds derived from whole-blood to serum conversion equations from the ORIP trial. These thresholds are intended to support targeted supplementation strategies.
In the first 14 months of implementation, 4,801 tests were completed, with 97.6% analysed within 72 hours, demonstrating high operational feasibility. Early adopters were reported to be demographically representative of the broader antenatal population (page 9; Table 2).
(Source: https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.06.12.25329455v1.full.pdf)
The screening approach is designed to enable precision supplementation by identifying women most likely to benefit from omega-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (LCPUFA; DHA + EPA) to reduce the risk of preterm labour.
However, implementation requires access to laboratory infrastructure capable of gas chromatography analysis and effective coordination between pathology services and antenatal screening systems. Interpretation guidance is necessary due to variability in omega-3 cutoff definitions and safety thresholds (e.g., <1% considered deficient; >10% potentially excessive intake). Successful integration also depends on clinician awareness, consistent ordering practices, and alignment with existing antenatal workflows.
Evidence for clinical impact on reducing preterm labour is pending final evaluation; current data primarily address feasibility, uptake, and early implementation outcomes.
Recent updates:
2021–2022: Omega-3 Test-and-Treat Program implemented in South Australia across 18,362 antenatal referrals, with 4,801 omega-3 tests completed.
2025: Preprint describes feasibility, early adoption, uptake trends, fidelity, and demographic representativeness (Best KP et al., 2025).

Name: Orlistat
Developers: Roche (including InterMune); Yildirim Beyazit University; Shandong University; Capital Medical University; University of Hull
Indication: Treatment of PCOS-related obesity
Mechanism of action: Lipase inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Orlistat is an orally active gastrointestinal lipase inhibitor derived from lipstatin, a compound produced by Streptomyces toxytricini. It reduces dietary fat absorption by approximately 30% by inhibiting pancreatic and gastric lipases. Orlistat was developed by Roche for the treatment of mild to moderate obesity and is indicated for individuals with a body mass index (BMI) ≥30 kg/m², or ≥28 kg/m² in the presence of comorbid risk factors such as hypertension, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidaemia, or excess visceral adiposity. The product has been widely launched internationally.
https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800003007
A 2021 meta-analysis of 80 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) concluded that orlistat reduces BMI compared with placebo, although it did not demonstrate superiority over metformin in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Its use was noted to be limited by gastrointestinal adverse effects.
https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/cen.14663
A separate 2021 meta-analysis of 28 RCTs reported no significant differences in fasting insulin, HOMA-IR, or fasting glucose levels with orlistat treatment, suggesting modest metabolic benefits beyond weight reduction.
https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/cen.14623
A 2021 review of weight management strategies in PCOS described orlistat as an advanced pharmacologic option for further weight reduction, particularly in overweight or obese women, with demonstrated short-term benefits.
https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/17446651.2021.1896966
Combination regimens have also been evaluated. Studies published in 2022–2023 demonstrated that ethinyl-estradiol/drospirenone (EE/DRSP) combined with orlistat significantly reduced lipoprotein(a) and other cardiovascular risk markers in overweight or obese women with PCOS.
https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/09513590.2022.2078805
https://www.maturitas.org/article/S0378-5122(23)00296-7/fulltext
A 2022 study reported that orlistat combined with drospirenone/ethinylestradiol was superior to contraceptive therapy alone in reducing visceral fat area, body weight, free testosterone, blood pressure, and fasting plasma glucose, suggesting additive metabolic and endocrine benefits.
https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/09513590.2022.2089108
Preclinical evidence from a 2023 rodent model indicated that orlistat may exert therapeutic effects in PCOS by modifying gut microbiota composition and metabolite profiles, suggesting potential microbiome-mediated mechanisms.
https://ovarianresearch.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s13048-023-01193-3
The 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of PCOS supports consideration of anti-obesity medications, including orlistat, in addition to lifestyle intervention, for weight management in adults with PCOS according to general population obesity guidelines.
https://academic.oup.com/humrep/article/38/9/1655/7241786
Despite its established role in obesity treatment, orlistat is not a primary endocrine therapy for PCOS. Its benefits are largely mediated through weight reduction rather than direct ovarian or hormonal modulation. Gastrointestinal side effects, including steatorrhea and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption, may limit adherence. Additionally, its metabolic impact appears modest compared with newer agents such as GLP-1 receptor agonists.
Orlistat is a guideline-supported anti-obesity agent that may provide adjunctive benefit in overweight or obese women with PCOS by improving weight-related metabolic and cardiovascular risk factors. Its therapeutic value is primarily weight-mediated rather than disease-modifying for core PCOS pathophysiology.

Name: Ornidazole
Developers: University of KwaZulu-Natal, Durban, Republic of South Africa
Indication: Treatment of trichomoniasis
Mechanism of action: DNA synthesis inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Ornidazole is a 5-nitroimidazole derivative used in the treatment of susceptible protozoal and anaerobic bacterial infections. It has antiprotozoal, antibacterial, and antitrichomonal activity and is structurally related to metronidazole (https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB13026
; https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/28061). 
Ornidazole is selectively taken up by anaerobic organisms and protozoa, where intracellular reduction of its nitro group generates reactive intermediates that damage DNA and inhibit nucleic acid synthesis, ultimately leading to cell death.
A 2022 in vitro study assessing susceptibility of Trichomonas vaginalis isolates from South African women reported that 89% of isolates were susceptible to ornidazole, with no resistance detected (https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/spectrum.00912-22). 
In comparison, metronidazole demonstrated higher resistance rates (11%) and lower overall susceptibility. The findings suggest that ornidazole, alongside tinidazole and secnidazole, may represent a potential alternative to metronidazole for the treatment of trichomoniasis, pending further clinical validation.
Common adverse effects include gastrointestinal disturbances (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea), headache, dizziness, and metallic taste. Rare but serious effects may include peripheral neuropathy or seizures. As ornidazole is hepatically metabolized, dose adjustments and monitoring may be required in individuals with liver impairment. Although widely used in several countries for protozoal infections, ornidazole has not received specific approval for trichomoniasis from major regulatory agencies such as the U.S. Food and Drug Administration or the European Medicines Agency.
Key challenges include limited high-quality clinical trial data for trichomoniasis, regional variability in regulatory approval, and the need for further comparative studies against established therapies. While in vitro data are promising, robust clinical efficacy and safety data are required to clarify its role in routine trichomoniasis management.

Name: Oxytocin - PPH
Indication: Prevention and treatment of PPH due to uterine atony
Mechanism of action: Oxytocin receptor agonism leads to an increase in myometial tone and muscle contraction
Key features and challenges:
Recombinant oxytocin is a synthetic cyclic peptide form of the naturally occurring posterior pituitary hormone oxytocin. Oxytocin is an oxytocic - it binds to oxytocin receptors in the uterine myometrium, which triggers the G-protein coupled receptor signal transduction cascade that causes increased intracellular calcium concentrations. Increased calcium concentration levels activate myosin light chain kinase which, in turn, induces the formation of the contractile protein actomyosin. This stimulates uterine smooth muscle contractions. In its synthetic, medication form, it is therefore used to cause contraction of the uterus to start labour, increase the speed of labour, and to prevent or treat postpartum haemorrhage (PPH). 
A 2018 Cochrane review found that oxytocin when compared to placebo or no-treatment found PPH ≥ 1000mL was significantly reduced (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33232518/). It is used largely as a comparator in ongoing clinical studies into effective uterotonics, and in dose and sub-population-specific studies. Oxytocin is the gold standard drug recommended for the prevention and treatment of PPH. Oxytocin (10 IU, IV/IM) is strongly recommended by the WHO as the first-line uterotonic drug for the prevention of PPH. Intravenous oxytocin alone is also the WHO recommended uterotonic drug for the treatment of PPH.  In 2019, the Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) for World Health Organization (WHO) maternal and perinatal health recommendations prioritised the updating of the existing WHO recommendations for intravenous (IV) versus intramuscular (IM) oxytocin for prevention of PPH after vaginal birth in response to the availability of new evidence (https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240013926). There are multiple ongoing studies on the use of oxytocin, including in combination with other uterotonics, including misoprostol, methylergometrine, carboprost and carbetocin. 
The challenge with oxytocin is its need for cold storage and transport, and (largely) intravenous administration, requiring skilled health workers for it use. These are challenges in low resource settings. There are therefore often quality issues with oxytocin. Oxytocin also has a fairly short half like: uterine response occurs almost immediately and subsides within 1 hour following IV administration. Following intramuscular injection of the drug, uterine response occurs within 3-5 minutes and persists for 2-3 hours. 
To improve usability, sublingual tablets containing oxytocin have been marketed in the past. However, these products were withdrawn from the market as their administration was considered to be more unpredictable, and the pharmacokinetic profile to have an unfavourable latent period. Also, sublingual tablets were not stable enough under tropical conditions. Heat-stable, sublingual, fast dissolving tablets and a heat-stable, inhaled oxytocin are now in development. Oxytocin in a single use, easy to use Uniject system has also been developed, and although not heat-stable, does include a time-temperature indicator (TTI) to maximise field utility.

Name: Oxytocin/ergometrine - fixed dose combination
Indication: Prevention and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage
Mechanism of action: Oxytocin receptor and alpha-1A adrenergic receptor agonists
Key features and challenges:
Oxytocin/ergometrine (also called Syntometrine) is an obstetric combination drug. The components are synthetically produced oxytocin, a hypothalamic hormone and oxytocin receptor agonist, and ergometrine, an ergot alkaloid, and alpha-adrenergic, dopaminergic and serotonin (5-HT2) receptor agonist. Both drugs can - and are often - used alone for the prevention and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH). Both drugs cause the uterus to contract. Oxytocin (10 IU, IV/IM) alone is the first-line recommended uterotonic drug for the prevention and treatment of PPH  and in the active management of labour globally. However, in settings where appropriately stored and maintained  oxytocin is not available, the WHO recommends use of other uterotonics, including ergometrine alone, and an oxytocin/ergometrine fixed drug combination (Syntometrine), where hypertensive disorders can be safely excluded (and other uterotonics are not available). 

A 2020 Cochrane review found moderate-certainty evidence suggesting that oxytocin plus ergometrine probably reduces PPH ≥1000 ml and ≥500mL compared with no treatment, and compared with oxytocin alone has desirable effects. While the combination of ergometrine plus oxytocin may be more effective than oxytocin alone for some desirable outcomes, this combination also increases important side-effects for the woman. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33232518/). 

Downsides to the combination include side effects associated with ergometrine in particular - including nausea, vomiting, hypertension, headache and abdominal pain, as well as the need for cold storage and transportation. Because of the increased likelihood of hypertension, ergometrine products also required the presence of skilled health personnel for its safe use (WHO, 2018). Clinical trials are largely comparator studies and protocol/dose optimisation.

Key features and challenges:

(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33914327/)
The test is performed using a vaginal swab collected for approximately 15 seconds, with results available within 10 minutes. PREMAQUICK is positioned as a rapid, point-of-care diagnostic tool intended to improve identification of women at risk of preterm labour among those presenting with threatened PTL.
Overall, PREMAQUICK provides a multi-marker diagnostic approach combining structural (IGFBP-1) and inflammatory (IL-6) biomarkers. While early diagnostic performance appears promising, broader validation and real-world implementation data remain important for confirming its clinical utility.

In 2023, a prospective, double-blinded cohort study of women with a singleton gestation and TPTL symptoms presenting to a tertiary hospital in Hong Kong between 24 + 0 to 33 + 6 weeks was performed. Name: Platelets
Developers: Grupo Mexicano para el Estudio de la Medicina Intensiva
Indication: Indicated for the treatment and prevention of postpartum haemorrhage.
Mechanism of action: Supplement of platelets to stop bleedng.
Key features and challenges:
Platelets are circulating blood components essential for primary haemostasis. Upon vascular injury, they become activated, adhere to damaged endothelium, and aggregate to form a platelet plug, initiating the mechanical phase of the coagulation cascade. In the context of major haemorrhage, including postpartum haemorrhage (PPH), coagulopathy may arise from activation of coagulation and fibrinolytic pathways as well as dilutional effects from large-volume transfusion of red blood cells and crystalloids that lack clotting factors and platelets. Although platelet counts typically remain above the generally accepted haemostatic threshold of 50 × 10⁹/L until substantial blood volume replacement has occurred, in actively bleeding patients platelet levels are generally maintained above this threshold to support haemostasis.
Platelet transfusion is a standard component of massive transfusion protocols across clinical contexts, including obstetric haemorrhage. In cases of massive PPH, platelets are routinely administered as part of balanced transfusion strategies alongside red blood cells and fresh frozen plasma to mitigate dilutional coagulopathy and support clot formation.
A comparator study (NCT03784794) is evaluating two coagulation management algorithms in massive obstetric haemorrhage: one guided by thromboelastometry and hemostatic agents (prothrombin complex concentrate and fibrinogen concentrate), and the other guided by standard coagulation testing and conventional blood components, both including platelet transfusion (https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT03784794). Primary outcomes include the number of allogeneic blood products transfused intraoperatively, within 24 hours, and during hospital stay. Secondary outcomes assess mortality, intensive care unit admission duration, hysterectomy and surgical reintervention rates, transfusion-associated circulatory overload, transfusion-related acute lung injury, and healthcare-associated infections.
Key challenges include risks inherent to platelet transfusion, such as transfusion reactions, alloimmunization, infection transmission, and resource constraints related to storage and shelf-life. Optimal transfusion thresholds and timing in PPH remain areas of active investigation, particularly with increasing interest in goal-directed, viscoelastic-guided resuscitation strategies.

Name: Pneumatic Anti-shock Garment (PASG)
Developers: University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust
Indication: Indicated as an fist aid intervention for the control or reduction of atonic postpartum haemorrhage until subsequent standard treatment is initiated.
Mechanism of action: Provides pressure directly to pelvic organs (e.g. uterus) and acts as a partial abdominal tourniquet to control pelvic blood flow.
Key features and challenges:
The Pneumatic Anti-Shock Garment (PASG) was introduced into civilian emergency medicine in 1973 and was historically used in the management of trauma and shock, including pelvic and lower-limb fractures, hypovolemic shock, and septic shock. The device consists of inflatable compartments that apply circumferential pressure to the lower body, thereby increasing central blood volume and stabilizing hemodynamics. While no randomized controlled trials have evaluated PASG specifically for obstetric haemorrhage, case reports have described its use as a temporizing intervention in severe bleeding (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18805742/).
Evidence over the past two decades has been limited, as clinical focus has shifted toward the non-pneumatic anti-shock garment (NASG), which is easier to apply and more suitable for low-resource settings. However, earlier case studies suggest potential benefit in selected obstetric scenarios. A 2004 case report described PASG use in a woman following caesarean section for abdominal pregnancy who remained hypotensive and coagulopathic despite intravenous fluids, repeat surgery, blood transfusion, and abdominal packing (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14709462/). Following PASG application, bleeding decreased, blood pressure improved, and coagulation parameters stabilized, with survival of both mother and infant.
Key challenges include the absence of randomized controlled trial data in obstetric haemorrhage, potential complications associated with prolonged use, and practical limitations compared with newer non-pneumatic alternatives. As a result, PASG is generally considered a temporizing or last-resort intervention rather than a standard component of contemporary postpartum haemorrhage management protocols.

Name: PreTRM blood test
Indication: Prediction of risk of premature birth at 18-20 weeks of gestation in asymptomatic singleton pregnancies.
Mechanism of action:
This blood test uses proteomics -- a high-throughput protein analysis that uses mass spectrometry to analyze peptides and protein expression in pregnancy. Specifically measuring two proteins:
1. Insulin-like growth factor binding protein (IBP4)
2. Sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG)
Detection can predict a higher risk of premature birth in asymptomatic singleton pregnancies.
Key features and challenges:
​PreTRM is a blood test developed by Sera Prognostics that is used during weeks 18 through 20 of pregnancy to measure protein biomarkers that inform the risk of premature birth in asymptomatic singleton pregnancies. 
 
This blood test uses proteomics, a high-throughput protein analysis that uses mass spectrometry to analyse peptides and protein expression in pregnancy. It specifically measures two proteins: Insulin-like growth factor binding protein (IBP4) and sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG). 
 
The PreTRM test has been clinically validated in two U.S clinical studies (PAPR & TREETOP) in more than 10,500 patients. A prospective, randomised intervention trial demonstrated an 85% reduction in newborn intensive care unit (NICU) length-of-stay for spontaneous preterm deliveries admitted to the NICU – from 45.5 to 6.8 days. A cost-effectiveness study projected $863 net savings ($1,608 gross savings) per pregnant woman, a $54 million reduction in total costs over the study population. 
 
The challenge with this test is that the blood draw must occur during the 18th through 20th week of pregnancy. This test is only available in the U.S.; samples must be shipped to Sera Prognostics, who will provide results through a portal in an average of 7 business days. An access program is available to offset costs. (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6381594/) 
 
From a regulatory approval point of view, PreTRM is not FDA cleared or approved but it was granted a clinical laboratory permit by the state of New-York (New York’s Clinical Laboratory Reference System). New York’s Clinical Laboratory Reference System has requirements that are equal to or more stringent than the Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments of 1988 (CLIA), the program was granted exempt status by the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) in 1995. With New York State approval of Sera’s laboratory and PreTRM® test, Sera is permitted to provide its innovative laboratory testing services for intended use by pregnant women in all states nationwide.​

Name: Pregnolia System
Indication: The prediction of the start of delivery, and risk of preterm birth based on cervical stiffness measurements.
Mechanism of action: The Pregnolia System consists of a single-use sterile probe and a control unit. The probe is placed in contact with the anterior lip of the cervix and a small vacuum inside the probe tip gently pulls on the tissue. The control unit displays the cervical stiffness index (CSI) within seconds.
Key features and challenges:
The Pregnolia System is a medical device designed to quantitatively assess cervical softening through measurement of tissue elasticity. Cervical softening precedes cervical shortening, effacement, and dilatation, and is considered an early biomechanical marker associated with risk of preterm birth.
The system consists of a single-use sterile probe connected to a control unit. The probe is positioned against the anterior lip of the cervix using a speculum, and cervical tissue stiffness is measured through controlled application of negative pressure. The device provides an objective elasticity value intended to support clinical risk assessment.
Early validation studies demonstrated that quantitative measurement of cervical stiffness is more reliable than digital palpation and may provide more informative assessment than cervical length alone in certain contexts. These findings support the concept that biomechanical cervical properties may enhance prediction of preterm birth risk.
(https://en.pregnolia.com/_files/ugd/bb77a3_9ad7505ac1404e64b623e6747c2cfd4b.pdf)
The technology was developed as a spin-off from research conducted at ETH Zürich and the University Hospital Zürich investigating cervical stiffness changes during pregnancy. The Pregnolia device is CE-certified and has received European Union co-funding to support further development toward scalable implementation.
(https://en.pregnolia.com/)
Overall, the Pregnolia System represents a device-based, quantitative approach to early cervical assessment. While preliminary data support its potential utility, further prospective clinical validation is required to determine its predictive performance for preterm labour and birth across diverse populations.
