Name: Progesterone - PCOS
Developers: Besins Healthcare; Mansoura University; National University of Malaysia
Indication: Treatment of PCOS infertility
Mechanism of action: Progesterone receptor agonists
Key features and challenges:
Progesterone is a naturally occurring steroid hormone and therapeutic agent used in reproductive medicine, hormone therapy, and obstetric care. In women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), progesterone is commonly used to regulate menstrual cycles, provide endometrial protection in anovulatory patients, support luteal phase function during assisted reproduction, and manage infertility. It may also indirectly improve symptoms associated with unopposed estrogen exposure.
A 2021 pilot study evaluated cyclic oral micronized progesterone in women with PCOS who were intolerant of combined hormonal contraceptives. The study reported improvements in menstrual cycle regularity and reductions in estradiol-related symptoms such as fluid retention, breast tenderness, and cervical mucus changes, suggesting potential benefit as an alternative hormonal approach in selected patients.
https://www.mdpi.com/1648-9144/57/10/1024
A 2021 registered feasibility study investigated the combined use of cyclic progesterone and spironolactone in women aged 19–40 years with androgenic PCOS. The study aimed to assess improvements in quality of life, menstrual regularity, fertility, weight management, and hyperandrogenic symptoms such as hirsutism and acne over a six-month period.
https://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN99343883
In assisted reproductive contexts, a 2023 study compared different luteal phase support agents during frozen–thawed embryo transfer cycles. Intramuscular (IM) progesterone was associated with higher pregnancy rates compared to vaginal progesterone gel, particularly in women under 30 and over 35 years of age.
https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1155/2023/8157210
While progesterone plays an essential role in managing menstrual irregularity and providing luteal support, it does not address the underlying metabolic or androgen-excess drivers of PCOS. Its therapeutic effect is primarily regulatory and supportive rather than disease-modifying.
Key challenges include variability in administration routes (oral, vaginal, intramuscular), differences in bioavailability, and potential side effects such as mood changes or sedation with certain formulations. Long-term efficacy for hyperandrogenic symptoms remains limited, and progesterone is often used as part of combination regimens rather than monotherapy for comprehensive PCOS management.
Progesterone is an established and widely used component of PCOS management, particularly for menstrual regulation and fertility support. However, its role is supportive rather than corrective of core endocrine–metabolic abnormalities associated with PCOS.

Name: Progesterone, natural, micronized (vaginal/topical) - PTL/PTB
Developers: Catalent, Inc. (including Swindon UK facilities, Juniper Pharmaceuticals, Inc.); Dare Bioscience, Inc.; Actavis; Besins Healthcare; Columbia Laboratories, Inc.
Indication: Reducing risk of preterm labour in women with history of preterm birth or women with short cervix
Mechanism of action: Progesterone reduces risk of subsequent preterm delivery by modulating levels of HLA-G, which is linked to spontaneous preterm birth and intra-amniotic inflammation or infections.
Key features and challenges:
Progesterone is a medication and naturally occurring steroid hormone. It is often used in combination with estrogens in hormone therapy for menopausal women. It is also used to support pregnancy and fertility and to treat gynaecological disorders. Because of its anti-inflammatory properties, vaginal progesterone is considered potentially beneficial in preventing preterm labour in women at risk.
A 2013 Cochrane review (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23903965) examined evidence on use of progestogen for women at risk of preterm birth either because of a previous preterm birth or a short cervix. The OPPTIMUM trial was one of the largest to test whether vaginal progesterone prophylaxis prevents preterm labour. However, it showed no significant beneficial or harmful effects on primary obstetric, neonatal or childhood outcomes (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29945711/). Results from another study  in 2021 however noted that combined treatment with vaginal progesterone could prolong the latency period in preterm labour when compared with none (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33900515/). A systematic review in 2021 evaluating progestogens for preventing preterm birth showed both vaginal progesterone and injectable 17-OHPC reduced birth before 34 weeks' gestation in high-risk singleton pregnancies, with particular utility for women with a short cervix (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33773630/). 
Despite conflicting results, use of vaginal progesterone to prevent preterm labour in women with a short cervix is  recommended across the world (UK, Europe, Australia) and widely used off label for this indication. However (and in contrast to injectable 17‐OHPC), vaginal progesterone is not licensed for preventing preterm birth in the USA. 
Commercially available formulations include vaginal tablet or suppository containing micronized progesterone by Besins Healthcare. A bioadhesive gel containing natural progesterone is developed by Catalent, where progesterone is delivered vaginally in a single-use, pre-filled, tampon-like applicator. A sustained-release intravaginal ring is in development by Catalent and Dare Bioscience for women with a short cervical length mid-pregnancy. (https://reporter.nih.gov/project-details/10004392)
The Menoufia University in Egypt has in 2023 completed a phase IV trial to detect the efficacy and safety of vaginal progesterone alone or combined with aspirin in prevention of recurrent PTB. Women were randomly allocated to prophylactically receive either vaginal progesterone at a dose of 200 mg (prontogest 200mg every 12 hr) combined with oral aspirin at a dose of 100mg once daily both at the same time (group1), or vaginal progesterone (prontogest 200mg every 12 hr) and oral placebo (manufactured in a standard way to have the same size and shape of asprin tablet) also at the same time (group 2). Results have not been published (NCT05319834).

Name: Progestin - PCOS
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: Progestins bind to the progesterone receptor and act as an agonist; however, they also bind to other steroid receptors: the estrogen receptor, androgen receptor, glucocorticoid receptor, and mineralocorticoid receptor. All progestins have only one effect in common, the progestogenic activity on the estrogen-primed endometrium. However, there are considerable differences between progestins in the other biological elicited effects related to the agonist or antagonist effect on various receptors
Key features and challenges:
Progestin, a synthetic form of progesterone, interacts with progesterone receptors in tissues like the uterus to mimic progesterone’s effects, supporting pregnancy-related functions. For managing PCOS, progestin can be taken 10–14 days every 1–3 months to induce menstruation, reducing the risk of endometrial cell overgrowth and hyperplasia. 
Current investigations of progestin focus on its supportive role in fertility treatments:
A 2021 published study evaluates the feasibility and outcomes of the progestin-primed ovarian stimulation (PPOS) regimen in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) patients, finding that it resulted in superior oocyte and embryo quality compared to controls, with no significant differences in pregnancy outcomes or risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS). (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1642431X21000619?via%3Dihub)
A 2023 systematic review comparing progestin-primed ovarian stimulation (PPOS) and GnRH antagonist protocols in preimplantation genetic testing (PGT) cycles, the cumulative live birth rate for PPOS in PCOS patients was lower than for GnRH antagonists, though this difference wasn’t statistically significant. The findings suggest a careful approach when choosing PPOS, especially for those with normal or high ovarian reserve.(https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/endocrinology/articles/10.3389/fendo.2023.1117513/full)
Another 2023 systematic review analysed PPOS for PCOS patients undergoing IVF and found that PPOS did not reduce the risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) or improve pregnancy outcomes compared to GnRH protocols. However, PPOS may still be viable for frozen embryo transfers due to its efficiency and safety, though long-term child safety and cost-effectiveness remain to be studied. (https://www.phdynasty.ru/en/catalog/magazines/gynecology-obstetrics-and-perinatology/2021/volume-20-issue-5/42563)

Name: Progestin - Uterine fibroids
Indication: Heavy menstrual bleeding associated with uterine fibroids and fibroid growth
Mechanism of action: progeterone receptor agonist
Key features and challenges:
Progestins are synthetic analogues of progesterone used in the management of uterine fibroids, primarily to control symptoms such as heavy menstrual bleeding rather than to reduce fibroid size.
A 2017 Cochrane systematic review by Lethaby et al. concluded that there was insufficient high-quality evidence to support the use of progestogens for treating premenopausal women with uterine fibroids.
(Source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7762035/)
Clinical guidance from the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada includes progestins among medical options for managing abnormal uterine bleeding associated with fibroids, reflecting their role in symptom control.
(Source: https://www.jogc.com/article/S1701-2163(15)30338-8/fulltext)
A 2020 study similarly reported insufficient evidence to confirm meaningful clinical benefit of progestogens in reducing fibroid size, reinforcing that their primary utility lies in symptom management rather than disease modification.
(Source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7762035/)
Clinical reviews have described progestins as part of conservative management strategies for abnormal uterine bleeding associated with fibroids. They are available in multiple formulations, including oral tablets (e.g., norethindrone or desogestrel-containing “mini-pills”), intrauterine devices (IUDs), injections, and implants, providing flexibility in administration.
(Source: https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jog.15591
; https://www.jptcp.com/index.php/jptcp/article/view/3385/3313)
More recent literature (2024) highlights that while progestins may alleviate bleeding symptoms, their effectiveness in reducing fibroid volume remains uncertain and inconsistent across studies.
(Source: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/13543784.2024.2343786)
Overall, progestins are considered a symptomatic management option rather than a curative treatment. Treatment response varies between individuals, and long-term hormonal exposure may raise concerns, particularly in individuals with hormone-sensitive conditions.

Name: QUiPP app
Indication: The QUIPP tool integrates obstetrical history information, quantitative fetal fibronectin (qfFN), and cervical length to predict the risk of spontaneous preterm birth in asymptomatic high-risk women.
Mechanism of action: An online tool/app that integrates obstetrical history information, quantitative fetal fibronectin (qfFN), and cervical length to predict the risk of spontaneous preterm birth in asymptomatic high-risk women.
Key features and challenges:
The QUiPP app is a clinical decision-support tool designed to predict the risk of spontaneous preterm birth (PTB) in both symptomatic women and high-risk asymptomatic women. It integrates quantitative fetal fibronectin (fFN) testing results with cervical length measurements and obstetric history to generate individualized risk estimates for delivery within specified timeframes. The application is classified as a regulated medical device within the United Kingdom and is intended to support clinical decision-making regarding hospital admission, corticosteroid administration, and transfer to higher-level care.
A 2021 randomized clinical trial involving 258 participants evaluated the impact of the QUiPP tool on clinical outcomes and healthcare resource utilization (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8291648/). 
Perinatal outcomes were comparable between the intervention group (managed using the QUiPP tool) and the control group receiving standard care. However, the intervention group demonstrated reduced utilization of medical resources, including fewer unnecessary admissions and interventions, suggesting that the tool may enhance efficiency in care delivery. These findings indicate potential value in optimizing resource allocation, particularly in lower-resource healthcare settings where over-triage can strain capacity.
The QUiPP app is freely available online and through app distribution platforms (https://quipp.org/). While it is regulated within the United Kingdom, it has not undergone formal regulatory approval processes in many other international jurisdictions.
Key challenges include variability in availability and standardization of fetal fibronectin testing and cervical length measurement across healthcare settings. Additionally, clinical effectiveness depends on proper training, accurate data input, and adherence to local clinical protocols. Although the tool has demonstrated safety and resource efficiency, ongoing validation in diverse populations and health systems is important to support broader implementation.

Name: Recombinant Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (rFSH)
Developers: Guangdong Provincial People's Hospital; Amsterdam UMC, including Emma Kinderziekenhuis
Indication: Used to stimulate follicular development in anovulatory or oligo-ovulatory women with PCOS, alone or in combination with oral ovulation-induction agents or in assisted reproduction cycles.
Target: FSH receptor on granulosa cells in ovarian follicles → stimulation of follicular growth, aromatase activity and estradiol production.
Mechanism of action: rFSH binds to FSH receptors on granulosa cells, promoting follicular recruitment, growth and estrogen production. In PCOS, where endogenous LH is often elevated and endogenous FSH insufficient to support normal follicle maturation, exogenous rFSH can induce mono- or limited multi-follicular development, restoring ovulation in women who do not respond adequately to oral ovulation-induction agents. The goal in PCOS is low-dose titration to avoid ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) and excessive multi-follicular recruitment.
Key features and challenges:
Recombinant FSH is an established gonadotropin used worldwide for ovulation induction and controlled ovarian stimulation. In PCOS, rFSH is generally considered a second-line therapy, especially for women who do not respond to first-line oral agents such as letrozole or clomiphene. International guidelines recognise the efficacy of low-dose, step-up rFSH protocols in inducing mono-follicular ovulation while reducing the risk of ovarian hyperstimulation in this high-risk population.
(https://www.monash.edu/medicine/mchri/pcos/guideline).
A number of studies have demonstrated that rFSH is highly effective in inducing ovulation and achieving pregnancy in PCOS when careful titration and monitoring are used. Meta-analyses show higher ovulation rates compared with clomiphene, and comparable or improved pregnancy rates, though at higher cost and with more intensive monitoring. (https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD010290.pub3/full).
The ChiCTR study (ChiCTR-PRC-249245) evaluates the use of rFSH in PCOS ovulation induction, comparing different low-dose titration strategies to optimise follicular response, avoid multi-follicular development and minimise OHSS risk. (https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=249245)
Clinical evidence outside China also supports low-dose rFSH protocols. Randomised trials have shown that beginning with very low doses (37.5–50 IU) and adjusting slowly reduces the risk of overstimulation in PCOS without compromising pregnancy outcomes.
Despite its efficacy, rFSH faces several challenges. First, OHSS risk remains higher in PCOS due to increased follicle sensitivity, requiring intensive monitoring and specialist expertise. Second, cost and injectable administration limit accessibility compared with oral agents. Third, the need for frequent ultrasound and blood-test monitoring makes rFSH less feasible in low-resource settings. Finally, international guidelines still recommend letrozole as first-line therapy, with rFSH positioned as a secondary option for selected cases.
(https://www.asrm.org/practice-guidance/practice-committee-documents/ovulation-induction-in-pcos/).
The new EU Clinical Trial EUCTR 2024-519354-36-00 includes rFSH as an active comparator in women with PCOS undergoing ovulation induction, reflecting the continued relevance of rFSH as a reference standard in fertility treatment research.
(https://euclinicaltrials.eu/search-for-clinical-trials/?lang=en&EUCT=2024-519354-36-00)
Overall, rFSH is a highly effective but resource-intensive option for PCOS-related infertility, well-established in reproductive medicine but requiring careful dose titration to minimise the risks inherent to PCOS physiology.
Recent updates:
Recent trials continue to use rFSH as a standard active comparator in PCOS ovulation-induction studies, including the 2024 EUCTR study (https://euclinicaltrials.eu/search-for-clinical-trials/?lang=en&EUCT=2024-519354-36-00). Ongoing protocol optimisation efforts focus on ultra-low-dose step-up regimens to minimise OHSS risk in PCOS. 
New trial in China (https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=249245) also reflects continued evaluation of rFSH dosing strategies in anovulatory PCOS populations.

Name: Recombinant von Willebrand factor
Indication: Prevention and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage (in women with Von Willebrand Disease)
Mechanism of action: Supply of von Willebrand factor to promote coagulation and stop bleeding in women with von Willebrand disease
Key features and challenges:
Recombinant von Willebrand factor (rVWF) is a replacement therapy indicated for the on-demand treatment and control of bleeding episodes in adults with von Willebrand disease (VWD), the most common inherited bleeding disorder, affecting approximately 1% of the population. VWD is characterized by quantitative or qualitative defects in von Willebrand factor (VWF), resulting in impaired hemostasis. rVWF is marketed as vonicog alfa (Takeda) and received U.S. FDA approval in December 2015 (https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB12872).
It is used across bleeding contexts in VWD, including management of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) in affected women.
Women with VWD have an estimated 1.5-fold increased risk of PPH, with reported incidence ranging from 40% to 60%. Early identification of pregnant women with undiagnosed VWD is therefore important for risk stratification and prevention planning. VWF replacement therapy may involve either plasma-derived VWF (pdVWF) or recombinant VWF (rVWF). A comparative study has reported differences in clinical effect between plasma-derived and recombinant VWF in women experiencing PPH (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32692849/), highlighting potential considerations in product selection.
The VWD-WOMAN trial (NCT04344860) is recruiting participants to evaluate recombinant von Willebrand factor in combination with tranexamic acid versus recombinant von Willebrand factor alone for reducing postpartum haemorrhage in women with VWD (https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT04344860). 
This study aims to further define optimal management strategies for obstetric bleeding in this high-risk population.
Key challenges include limited high-quality comparative data between recombinant and plasma-derived products in obstetric settings, variability in access and cost of recombinant therapies, and the need for timely diagnosis of VWD during pregnancy. Evidence specific to PPH prevention and treatment remains evolving, and clinical protocols require further standardization.

In November 2017, the Phase III SPIRIT-2 trial (NCT03204331; EudraCT2017-001588-19) was initiated to evaluate relugolix with and without low-dose estradiol (E2) and norethindrone acetate (NETA) in women with endometriosis-associated pain; the study was completed in May 2021 (https://adis.springer.com/trials/700286445
; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03204331). 
In May 2019, ASKA initiated a Japan-based Phase III trial (TAK385-3-A; NCT03931915) comparing relugolix 40 mg once daily with leuprorelin in premenopausal patients; ASKA completed this study in September 2020 (https://adis.springer.com/trials/700306885). 
In parallel, the SPIRIT-1 trial (NCT03204318) evaluated relugolix 40 mg once daily co-administered with low-dose E2/NETA versus placebo for 24 weeks; the trial was completed in 2021 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03204318).
Evidence published in 2022 supports efficacy for endometriosis-associated pain. SPIRIT-1 results published in 2022 reported that once-daily relugolix combination therapy significantly improved endometriosis-associated pain and was generally well tolerated (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35717987/). 
Separately, results from the Japan Phase III comparison with leuprorelin (published in 2022) showed relugolix was noninferior to leuprorelin for endometriosis-associated pelvic pain, with comparable safety; return of menses occurred earlier with relugolix, which may be relevant for individuals planning conception after treatment (https://www.fertstert.org/article/S0015-0282(21)02214-7/fulltext). 
As of September 2022, ASKA Pharmaceutical received marketing approval for relugolix to treat endometriosis (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800028257).
Longer-term data and additional studies have continued to refine use. An extension study related to the SPIRIT program was completed in 2023, with results published in 2024 demonstrating sustained improvements in endometriosis-associated pain over 104 weeks, including high responder rates for dysmenorrhea and non-menstrual pelvic pain, with stable bone mineral density and a tolerable safety profile (https://www.clinicaltrialsregister.eu/ctr-search/trial/2017-004066-10/results
; https://adis.springer.com/trials/700298398
; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38243752/). 
In 2023, additional clinical research was initiated to explore alternative dosing (every-other-day relugolix 40 mg) and comparative sequencing strategies versus dienogest (https://jrct.niph.go.jp/latest-detail/jRCTs031220707
; https://jrct.niph.go.jp/latest-detail/jRCTs061230064). 
A Phase 3 single-arm open-label study updated in March 2024 is assessing the relugolix combination tablet in the context of pregnancy prevention (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04756037
; https://adis.springer.com/trials/700333754), and a Phase 3B study (estimated completion 2029) is evaluating bone mineral density with long-term use in women with uterine fibroids or endometriosis (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05862272).
Key challenges include managing hypoestrogenic adverse effects and ensuring bone health over prolonged treatment, which drives the need for add-back therapy and long-term monitoring. Differentiation versus other hormonal options (e.g., progestins such as dienogest, GnRH agonists, and other oral GnRH antagonists), tolerability, cost, and local regulatory/labeling variability may influence uptake and positioning. Continued comparative effectiveness evidence and long-term safety data (particularly for bone mineral density) remain important for sustained adoption in endometriosis care.
Overall, relugolix combination therapy has robust Phase III evidence and post-trial extension data supporting sustained pain reduction with an acceptable safety profile, alongside marketing approval for endometriosis in Japan. Ongoing studies are focused on optimising dosing, comparative positioning, and long-term bone safety to strengthen real-world use.

Name: Relugolix combination tablet - Endometriosis
Developers: Sumitomo Pharma America; Gedeon Richter plc; ASKA Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd.; Pfizer; TAKEDA PHARMACEUTICALS INTERNATIONAL AG; University of Michigan
Indication: Indicated for the prevention and treatment of endometriosis associated pain
Target: Estrogen receptor; LHRH receptor; Progesterone receptor
Mechanism of action: Estrogen receptor agonists; LHRH receptor antagonists; Progesterone receptor agonists
Key features and challenges:
Relugolix combination therapy is an oral fixed-dose regimen consisting of relugolix (a non-peptide gonadotropin-releasing hormone [GnRH] receptor antagonist), estradiol (1 mg), and norethindrone acetate (0.5 mg). Relugolix suppresses pituitary release of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), leading to reduced ovarian estradiol production. The addition of low-dose estradiol and norethindrone acetate serves as add-back therapy to maintain sufficient estrogen levels to preserve bone mineral density and mitigate hypoestrogenic side effects, such as vasomotor symptoms, while maintaining therapeutic efficacy in reducing endometriosis-associated pain (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800058162).
In 2022, the Phase III SPIRIT 1 and SPIRIT 2 trials evaluated relugolix combination therapy (Relugolix-CT) in women with endometriosis-associated pain (https://academic.oup.com/humrep/article/36/Supplement_1/deab126.057/6344062).
The studies demonstrated significant improvements in dysmenorrhea and non-menstrual pelvic pain (NMPP) compared with placebo. A greater proportion of treated participants achieved analgesic- and opioid-free status. Results were consistent across both the overall study population and European subpopulations, confirming robust pain reduction and decreased reliance on rescue medication.
Regulatory approvals followed these pivotal findings. The US Food and Drug Administration approved the combination therapy in August 2022 for moderate to severe endometriosis-related pain. In September 2023, the European Commission approved RYEQO for endometriosis treatment in women with prior treatment history. Health Canada approved MYFEMBREE in October 2023. These approvals established relugolix combination therapy as a commercially available oral GnRH antagonist regimen for endometriosis management.
A 2024 retrospective cohort study (NCT05739136) is evaluating fetal and infant outcomes following in utero exposure to relugolix combination therapy, using secondary de-identified electronic healthcare data (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05739136). 
This study reflects ongoing pharmacovigilance efforts to assess safety in cases of inadvertent exposure during pregnancy.
Key challenges include management of hypoestrogenic risks despite add-back therapy, including potential long-term effects on bone density with extended use. Treatment duration limitations and recurrence of symptoms following discontinuation remain considerations. Cost and accessibility may also influence uptake in certain healthcare settings. Continued post-marketing surveillance and long-term safety data will be important to define optimal duration of therapy and clarify reproductive safety outcomes.
Recent updates: TM 14/12/2025: Trial identified from JRCT (https://jrct.mhlw.go.jp/latest-detail/jRCT2031250206) and CT.gov (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07100782).

Name: Relugolix combination tablet- Uterine fibroids
Developers: Sumitomo Pharma America; Myovant Sciences; Pfizer; University Hospital, Geneva
Indication: Uterine fibroid heavy menstrual bleeding
Target: Estrogen receptor; LHRH receptor; Progesterone receptor
Mechanism of action: Estrogen receptor agonists; LHRH receptor antagonists; Progesterone receptor agonists
Key features and challenges:
Relugolix combination therapy (relugolix/estradiol/norethindrone acetate; Rel-CT) is a once-daily, fixed-dose oral tablet developed by Sumitomo Pharma America (formerly Myovant Sciences) for heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) associated with uterine fibroids (uterine leiomyoma) and for endometriosis-associated pain. Relugolix is a gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) receptor antagonist that suppresses pituitary luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), thereby reducing ovarian estrogen production. Estradiol (E2) and norethindrone acetate (NETA) are included as add-back therapy to maintain estradiol in a therapeutic range, mitigate hypoestrogenic symptoms (e.g., vasomotor symptoms), and preserve bone mineral density (BMD) while maintaining symptom control. The combination is approved in multiple jurisdictions for uterine leiomyoma and/or endometriosis-related pain, with ongoing global development.
https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800058162
In 2021, pivotal evidence showed that once-daily Rel-CT significantly reduced menstrual bleeding compared with placebo and preserved bone mineral density in women with uterine fibroids.
https://www.nejm.org/doi/10.1056/NEJMoa2008283
Also in 2021, pooled analyses from the LIBERTY and SPIRIT programs (n≈2019) reported that BMD changes with Rel-CT were minimal and plateaued early, with approximately –0.66% change at Week 52. In contrast, relugolix monotherapy showed greater early BMD loss (approximately –1.84%), stabilizing to around –1.31% by Week 52, supporting the bone-sparing rationale for add-back therapy.
https://www.fertstert.org/article/S0015-0282(21)00743-3/fulltext
A further 2021 report evaluating longer exposure indicated durability of effect over two years, including maintenance of low menstrual blood loss (MBL) volume in women with symptomatic uterine fibroids. The study also noted that heavy menstrual bleeding commonly returned after treatment cessation and improved again upon re-treatment with Rel-CT, highlighting the chronic management nature of therapy.
https://www.fertstert.org/article/S0015-0282(21)00613-0/fulltext
In 2022, patient-experience evidence expanded beyond bleeding endpoints. LIBERTY trial data published in 2022 demonstrated that over 24 weeks, Rel-CT significantly reduced moderate-to-severe uterine leiomyoma–associated pain, with the greatest effect observed for menstrual pain, indicating clinically meaningful improvements in symptom burden.
https://journals.lww.com/greenjournal/fulltext/2022/06000/relugolix_combination_therapy_for_uterine.13.aspx
Also in 2022, expert reviews characterized relugolix/E2/NETA as a well-tolerated, non-invasive pharmacologic option for uterine fibroids, emphasizing the importance of add-back therapy to reduce hypoestrogenic adverse effects and BMD loss. The reviews also noted that symptoms are likely to recur soon after discontinuation, consistent with trial observations.
https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14656566.2022.2030705
https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14740338.2022.1989409
In 2022, a prospective study was completed to evaluate patient-reported quality of life and perceived effectiveness in controlling HMB among women treated with GnRH antagonist plus add-back therapy (elagolix + E2/NETA). While this study is not specific to relugolix, it reflects broader interest in add-back GnRH-antagonist strategies for fibroid-associated HMB.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05026502
In 2023, a study in European women compared once-daily Rel-CT with placebo and reported improvements in uterine fibroid–associated symptoms with preservation of bone mineral density, supporting generalizability of trial findings across populations.
https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/09513590.2023.2249107
Relugolix combination therapy is clinically validated for reducing HMB and improving fibroid-associated symptoms while mitigating hypoestrogenic adverse effects through add-back therapy. Key ongoing considerations include cost and access, the likelihood of symptom recurrence after discontinuation, and long-term safety monitoring; particularly bone health, when used for chronic symptom control.

Name: Remdesivir
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of non-severe at highest risk of hospitalisation (WHO definition) adults and paediatric patients (28 days of age and older and weighing at least 3 kilograms)
Mechanism of action: Remdesivir is an inhibitor of the SARS-CoV-2 RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), which is essential for viral replication. Remdesivir is an adenosine nucleotide prodrug that distributes into cells where it is metabolized to a nucleoside monophosphate intermediate by carboxyesterase 1 and/or cathepsin A, depending upon the cell type. The nucleoside monophosphate is subsequently phosphorylated by cellular kinases to form the pharmacologically active nucleoside triphosphate metabolite (GS-443902). Remdesivir triphosphate (RDV-TP) acts as an analog of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and competes with high selectivity (3.65-fold) over the natural ATP substrate for incorporation into nascent RNA chains by the SARS-CoV-2 RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, which results in delayed chain termination during replication of the viral RNA. RDV-TP can also inhibit viral RNA synthesis following its incorporation into the template viral RNA as a result of read-through by the viral polymerase that may occur at higher nucleotide concentrations. When remdesivir nucleotide is present in the viral RNA template, the efficiency of incorporation of the complementary natural nucleotide is compromised, thereby inhibiting viral RNA synthesis.
Key features and challenges: First granted emergency use authorisation by FDA in 01/05/2020, approved on date listed. Study published in NEJM demonstrated that remdesivir was superior to placebo in shortening time to recovery and having evidence of lower LRTI. In Nov 2020, WHO recommended against its use due to lack of evidence that it improves survival and other outcomes in patients.

Name: ResistancePlus GC - SpeeDx
Indication: Detection of gonorrhoeae and antimicrobial susceptibility
Target: Neisseria gonorrhoeae DNA and mutations linked with susceptibility or resistance to ciprofloxacin
Mechanism of action: multiplex qPCR
Key features and challenges:
ResistancePlus® GC, developed by SpeeDx, is a multiplex quantitative PCR (qPCR) assay powered by proprietary PlexPCR technology. The test simultaneously detects Neisseria gonorrhoeae and mutations associated with ciprofloxacin susceptibility or resistance. The PlexPrime design enhances allele-specific detection by generating distinct amplicons in a multiplexed format, improving specificity and reducing primer competition. The assay has been validated for use with a range of specimen types and is compatible with multiple extraction platforms, with amplification and detection performed on instruments such as the LightCycler® 480 Instrument II and the cobas® z 480 Analyzer (https://diagnostics.roche.com/global/en/products/params/resistanceplus-gc.html).
A 2021 study published in the Journal of Antimicrobial Chemotherapy evaluated the performance of ResistancePlus® GC for detecting N. gonorrhoeae and predicting ciprofloxacin susceptibility (https://academic.oup.com/jac/article/76/1/84/5905664). 
The assay demonstrated high concordance with phenotypic susceptibility testing, supporting its utility for resistance-guided therapy. In addition, a clinical study (NCT05286931) has investigated the impact of genotype-guided treatment strategies using ciprofloxacin for susceptible infections (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05286931). 
Findings support the potential for rapid molecular resistance detection to inform targeted therapy and reduce unnecessary use of broad-spectrum injectable antibiotics.
Key advantages include integration of pathogen detection and resistance profiling in a single assay, support for antimicrobial stewardship, and alignment with evolving international and regional guideline recommendations. Challenges include reliance on molecular detection of specific resistance markers, which may not capture all resistance mechanisms, and the need for laboratory infrastructure and technical expertise. Broader implementation will depend on cost-effectiveness, local resistance epidemiology, and integration into clinical workflows.

Name: ResistancePlus MG - SpeeDx

Target: Single well: M. genitalium (MgPa), A2058T, A2058C, A2058G, A2059G, Internal control
Mechanism of action: Multiplex molecular assay detecting Mycoplasma genitalium DNA and macrolide resistance mutations to guide targeted therapy.
Key features and challenges:
ResistancePlus MG simultaneously detects Mycoplasma genitalium and 4 mutations at positions 2058 and 2059 in the 23S rRNA gene (E. coli numbering) that are associated with resistance to azithromycin (macrolide-based antibiotic). A 2021 study compared three real-time PCR methods for the detection of macrolide resistance Mycoplasma genitalium strains: an in-house PCR described by Touati et al., ResistancePlus MG (SpeeDx), and S-DiaMGRes (Diagenode Diagnostics). They found that ResistancePlus MG falsely determined one sample as macrolide-sensitive, but this sample was determined as resistant when retested. The sensitivity of the methods was comparable, although there should be awareness of possible incorrect determination of macrolide resistance, especially of low-positive samples.
(https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0732889321000420?via%3Dihub).

A 2023 study compared the performance of AnyPlexTM II STI-7e with standard-of-care diagnostic methods (ResistancePlus MG for M. genitalium). Of the 1318 samples tested for M. genitalium, 83 (6.3%) were positive on the reference test (the quantitative PCR-based assay ResistancePlus MG). The positive % agreement (PPA) of AnyPlex II STI-7e compared to the reference assay was 96.4% (80/83) [95% confidence intervals (CI) 89.8–99.3].
(https://academic.oup.com/lambio/article/76/1/ovac002/6887826).

A 2021 study investigated detection and prevalence of macrolide and fluoroquinolone resistance (MLr/FQr) in Mycoplasma genitalium in Badalona, Spain. A total of 415 MG-positive samples by Allplex STI-7 (Seegene) were analyzed for MLr detection by pyrosequencing. From those, 179 samples were further analyzed for MG and MLr by ResistancePlus MG kit (SpeeDx) and 100 of them also for fluoroquinolone resistance (FQr) by sequencing the parC gene. Regarding MG detection, Allplex and Resistance Plus showed an overall agreement of 87%, but this value rose to 95.4% if we compare them for MLr detection.
(https://www.mdpi.com/2079-6382/11/4/485).

Name: Rotateq

The exact immunologic mechanism by which RotaTeq protects against rotavirus gastroenteritis is

Key features and challenges:

Name: S-DiaMGRes
Developers: Hologic, Inc. (including Cytyc Prenatal Products Corp.)
Indication: Detection of Mycoplasma genitalium and antimicrobial susceptibility
Mechanism of action: real-time PCR
Key features and challenges:
S-DiaMGRes™ (Diagenode Diagnostics, Belgium) is a commercially available real-time PCR assay designed to detect macrolide resistance–associated mutations in Mycoplasma genitalium. The increasing global prevalence of macrolide-resistant M. genitalium strains has significantly impacted treatment efficacy, prompting the development of molecular assays to guide resistance-informed therapy.
A 2021 study compared three real-time PCR methods for detection of macrolide resistance mutations: an in-house assay, ResistancePlus® MG (SpeeDx), and S-DiaMGRes™ (Diagenode Diagnostics) (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0732889321000420?via%3Dihub). 
The analysis included 100 M. genitalium-positive clinical samples collected in Sweden and a quantified DNA control. ResistancePlus® MG and S-DiaMGRes™ each incorrectly identified one resistant sample as macrolide-sensitive; upon retesting, the sample was confirmed as resistant. Overall, the assays demonstrated comparable sensitivity, although the findings highlighted the potential for misclassification, particularly in low-positive samples.
Key challenges include the possibility of false susceptibility results in samples with low bacterial load, the need for confirmatory testing in ambiguous cases, and reliance on laboratory-based PCR infrastructure. While S-DiaMGRes™ supports resistance-guided management of M. genitalium infection, careful interpretation of results and integration into broader diagnostic algorithms are essential to optimize clinical decision-making.

Name: Sacace Real-TM Kit - Gonorrhea
Indication: Detection of gonorrhoeae
Mechanism of action: PCR assay
Key features and challenges:
The Sacace Real-TM multiplex Real-Time PCR Kit is a laboratory-based molecular diagnostic assay designed for the simultaneous detection of sexually transmitted pathogens, including Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, Mycoplasma genitalium, and Trichomonas vaginalis. The assay enables multiplex real-time PCR detection, supporting syndromic testing approaches and comprehensive pathogen identification within a single test.
A 2023 study conducted at the National Reference Center for STIs in Havana, Cuba evaluated the use of pooled triple-site samples (genital and extragenital) for STI detection using the Sacace multiplex Real-TM PCR kit (https://academic.oup.com/ofid/article/10/4/ofad126/7078167). 
The findings demonstrated that pooled testing strategies could be implemented effectively to detect infections across multiple anatomical sites. This approach may enhance testing efficiency and reduce costs while maintaining diagnostic performance for N. gonorrhoeae and other STIs.
Key challenges include reliance on centralized laboratory infrastructure, the need for trained personnel, and further validation of pooled sampling strategies in varied epidemiological contexts. While multiplex PCR offers operational efficiencies and expanded anatomical site testing, additional data are required to confirm consistent sensitivity for gonorrhoea detection in routine clinical settings.

Secnidazole
Developers: Lupin; Evofem Inc.; Tulane University of Louisiana; University of KwaZulu-Natal, Durban, Republic of South Africa
Indication: Indicated for treating trichomoniasis in patients 12 years of age and older.
Target: Insufficiently established.  Presumed inhibitor of DNA synthesis.
Mechanism of action: Like other 5-nitroimidazole antimicrobials, the antibacterial and antiprotozoal activity of secnidazole is accounted for by the nitro group in the imidazole ring.  Upon entering the target pathogen, the nitro group of secnidazole is reduced by bacterial or parasitic nitroreductase enzymes, producing radical anions and reactive intermediates.  Radical anions and reactive intermediates cause the depletion of thiols, DNA helix damage, disruption of bacterial or parasitic protein synthesis and replication, and ultimately, cell death of susceptible isolates of Gram positive bacteria, Gram negative bacteria and T. vaginalis.
Key features and challenges:
Secnidazole is a broad-spectrum, second-generation 5-nitroimidazole antimicrobial agent structurally related to metronidazole and tinidazole. It demonstrates improved oral absorption and a longer terminal elimination half-life compared with other agents in this class. Secnidazole is active against anaerobic Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria as well as protozoa, including Trichomonas vaginalis. After entering susceptible organisms, it is reduced by microbial enzymes to form reactive intermediates that damage DNA and lead to pathogen death. Secnidazole has been used in multiple regions globally for decades and was approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in September 2017 under the brand name Solosec for the treatment of trichomoniasis and bacterial vaginosis (https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB12834).
A review evaluating secnidazole for the treatment of trichomoniasis in women and men reported favorable pharmacokinetics, including a prolonged half-life and lower minimal lethal concentration against T. vaginalis compared with metronidazole and tinidazole (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2050052122000038?via%3Dihub). 
Single-dose or short-course secnidazole demonstrated efficacy comparable to multi-dose metronidazole regimens, potentially reducing treatment burden and improving adherence. In addition, a study reported high efficacy of single-dose oral secnidazole in women co-infected with trichomoniasis and bacterial vaginosis (https://academic.oup.com/cid/article/73/6/e1282/6188734).
Secnidazole is typically administered as a single oral dose. Reported rates of de novo serum enzyme elevations are low (<0.5%), and no cases of clinically apparent liver injury were observed in prelicensure studies. Despite extensive global use, it has not been convincingly linked to clinically apparent hepatotoxicity (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/71815#section=Toxicological-Information). 
However, data on use during breastfeeding are limited, and potential risks, including Candida overgrowth and theoretical concerns regarding mutagenicity or carcinogenicity, warrant further study.
Key challenges include higher cost relative to metronidazole, limited data in pregnancy and lactation, and the need for continued monitoring of resistance patterns. While secnidazole offers simplified dosing and favorable pharmacokinetics, its comparative affordability and safety profile in specific populations remain important considerations in treatment decision-making.

Indication: Indicated for the prevention and treatment of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Measures serum alpha-fetoprotein as a biomarker reflecting metabolic or hepatic alterations associated with PCOS-related endocrine dysfunction.
Key features and challenges:
Aktiferrin-F or foliferrin contains ferrous sulphate, serine and folic acid. Serine, an amino acid, is thought to improve the absorption and bioavailability of iron in the body. Studies have previously demonstrated that the composition of the diet influences the amount of iron absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract. It has been shown that diets low in protein are associated with a low iron uptake and that the amount of iron absorbed is roughly dependent upon the amount of protein in the diet. Further, it was found that it is necessary for a diet to contain from 15–18 per cent protein for adequate iron absorption. The way protein exerts this effect is not known, but it has been suggested that one of the factors enhancing iron absorption could be the availability of increased amounts of amino acids derived from high dietary protein. (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0006497120807228#bib1)

A trial in Tel Aviv, Israel used aktiferrin or foliferrin to assess the efficacy of doubling the 30 mg dose of iron in women with iron deficiency anaemia (IDA) in singleton pregnancies. In all, 160 women were randomized to receive one capsule and 164 received two capsules. Both groups had similar Hb and ferritin at allocation. Hb concentration in both groups was similar at 35 weeks (10.8 g dl-1), and there were no significant differences in any of the secondary outcomes. Therefore, the study demonstrated that in IDA pregnant women, a single dose of iron is as effective as a double dose. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28383533/)

Name: Sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) - PCOS
Indication: Measurements used as individual biomarker and as part of the Free Androgen Index test for diagnosis of PCOS.
Mechanism of action: SHBG binds to sex hormones, particularly testosterone and estrogen, and regulates their bioavailability. Low SHBG levels can lead to higher free (unbound) testosterone, which is often associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
The Sex Hormone-Binding Globulin Receptor (SHBR) helps regulate sex hormone availability by binding to testosterone and estrogen. In women with PCOS, lower SHBG levels are often observed, leading to higher free testosterone and symptoms of hyperandrogenism. Low SHBG levels can indicate increased androgen activity and are commonly seen in insulin resistance, which is prevalent in PCOS. Measuring SHBG, alongside testosterone and insulin, can provide additional insights into the hormonal imbalances associated with PCOS. 

The Free Androgen Index (FAI) is a ratio used to assess androgen levels in the body. It is calculated by dividing total testosterone by SHBG (sex hormone-binding globulin) and multiplying by 100. A higher FAI indicates higher free testosterone, which is common in PCOS. FAI is used in the Rotterdam Criteria to help diagnose PCOS, particularly in assessing hyperandrogenism.

A  study published in 2024 found that higher SHBG levels are linked to a lower risk of PCOS. Using genetic variants associated with SHBG as instruments, the study showed that elevated SHBG concentrations reduced PCOS risk (odds ratio = 0.56). The results were consistent across multiple methods, supporting an inverse relationship between SHBG and PCOS. However, further research is needed to understand the underlying mechanisms. (https://bmcwomenshealth.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12905-024-03144-6)

Key features and challenges:
The bivalent inactivated whole-cell oral vaccine was initially developed by International Vaccine Institute. It transferred the technolgoy to Shantha Biotechnics (Sanofi Pasteur) to enable use of the vaccine, marketed as Shanchol, in countries outside of Vietnam.

A total of 66,900 subjects aged one year or older were administered twodoses of Shanchol or placebo at an interval of at least two weeks. The study demonstrated that Shanchol provided 65% protection against clinicalsignificant V. cholerae O1. Overall protection was sustained for 5 years follow-up.
Sanofi stopped producing Shanchol at the end of 2023.

Name: Sinopharm (Beijing) - BBIBP-CorV
Developers: China National Pharmaceutical Group Corporation (Sinopharm), including China National Biotec Group Company Limited (CNBG)
Indication: Prevention of disease caused by SARS CoV-2 infection in persons 18 years and older
Mechanism of action: BBIBP-CorV is an inactivated viral vaccine with an aluminium hydroxide adjuvant. It acts as an immunostimulant.
Key features and challenges:
First Chinese vaccine to be granted EUL by the WHO. *  

BBIBP-CorV, developed by Sinopharm, is an inactivated COVID-19 vaccine. It uses a chemically inactivated SARS-CoV-2 virus to stimulate an immune response without causing infection. A significant advantage of BBIBP-CorV is its well-established vaccine platform, which has been used for decades in other vaccines, ensuring safety and scalability. The vaccine is stable at standard refrigeration temperatures (2–8°C), making it easier to store and distribute, particularly in low-resource settings. BBIBP-CorV has demonstrated strong immunogenicity and safety in clinical trials, leading to emergency use authorization (EUA) in multiple countries and its inclusion in the World Health Organization (WHO) Emergency Use Listing (EUL).

However, the vaccine faces challenges, including reduced efficacy against emerging variants of concern compared to mRNA vaccines. Additionally, while it has been widely distributed in low- and middle-income countries, concerns about transparency in Phase III trial data and inconsistent efficacy rates have been raised. Another challenge is ensuring long-term protection and determining the need for booster doses, particularly in the face of waning immunity and new variants. Despite these hurdles, BBIBP-CorV remains a crucial tool in the global fight against COVID-19, particularly in regions where mRNA vaccines are less accessible.
Recent updates: On 7 May 2021 , the World Health Organization approved the BIBP vaccine for use in COVAX. Sinopharm has signed purchase agreements for 170 million doses from COVAX.

Key features and challenges:
The Solana Trichomonas Assay is a rapid in vitro diagnostic test for the qualitative detection of nucleic acids isolated from clinician-collected vaginal swab specimens or urine specimens obtained from asymptomatic or symptomatic patients to aid in the diagnosis of Trichomoniasis.

When performed on the Solana instrument, the allows for the rapid, accurate detection of Trichomonas. The assay utilises helicase-dependent amplification (HDA) and fluorescent probe-based detection in the Solana instrument to determine assay results.

A vaginal swab specimen or a urine specimen is lysed by simple heat treatment, diluted, and added to a reaction tube containing the lyophilised HDA reagents including primers specific for the amplification of a T. vaginalis-specific target sequence, as well as sequence specific probes. Competitive process control (PRC) is included in the lysis tube to monitor sample processing, inhibitory substances in clinical samples, reagent failure or instrument failure.

Results are displayed on the touchscreen, can be saved to the instrument, printed, and are capable of being sent to the LIS and exported through one of Solana’s five USB ports.

Spectinomycin was withdrawn from the U.S. market in 2007 and is no longer approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of gonorrhoea. It is also not routinely recommended in the European Union or Japan. However, it may remain available in certain countries and could serve as an alternative option in settings where resistance to first-line therapies complicates treatment.
Key challenges include limited global availability, absence from current major treatment guidelines, and reduced use due to evolving antimicrobial resistance patterns and the preference for cephalosporin-based regimens. While spectinomycin has historical utility in gonorrhoea management, its contemporary role is restricted and context-dependent.

Name: Spironolactone
Indication: Treatment of PCOS-related hirsutism
Mechanism of action: Aldosterone antagonists
Key features and challenges:
Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic with anti-androgenic properties that is widely used off-label for the management of hyperandrogenic symptoms in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), particularly hirsutism, acne, and androgenic alopecia. It exerts its therapeutic effect primarily by competitively blocking androgen receptors and inhibiting androgen production. Although not specifically approved for PCOS, international evidence-based guidelines recommend spironolactone as a second-line pharmacologic option for women who do not achieve adequate improvement with combined oral contraceptives and cosmetic therapies after at least six months, provided reliable contraception is used due to its teratogenic potential.
(Source: https://www.monash.edu/__data/assets/pdf_file/0003/3379521/Evidence-Based-Guidelines-2023.pdf)
Preclinical studies in PCOS animal models have demonstrated that spironolactone can reduce circulating androgen levels, improve lipid profiles, and attenuate inflammatory markers, suggesting benefits beyond cosmetic symptom control. In particular, rodent studies indicate improvements in hormonal balance and fat metabolism, supporting a broader metabolic rationale for its use.
(Source: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40200-022-01097-x)
Clinical data in adolescents have further expanded interest in spironolactone as part of combination regimens. The SPIOMET protocol (spironolactone, metformin, and pioglitazone) showed improvements in liver fat content, insulin sensitivity, and endocrine parameters compared with monotherapy, highlighting potential synergistic effects when spironolactone is integrated into metabolically targeted treatment strategies.
(Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-021-86317-9)
However, while spironolactone is consistently effective in reducing hirsutism severity, its impact on core reproductive outcomes such as ovulation and menstrual regularity remains limited when used alone. It does not significantly improve body mass index or restore ovulatory cycles in most patients, and therefore is not considered an ovulation-induction agent. Some evidence suggests potential fertility benefits in women with pronounced hyperandrogenism, but its primary clinical utility remains symptom-focused rather than disease-modifying.
(Source: https://academic.oup.com/humrep/article/36/5/1427/6102682)
Ongoing clinical trials are exploring its potential role in improving ovulatory function and addressing androgen excess in adolescents and pubertal girls, which may further clarify its positioning within early-intervention PCOS strategies.
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01422759)
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04075149)
Spironolactone represents a well-established anti-androgen adjunct therapy for PCOS, particularly effective for cosmetic manifestations of hyperandrogenism. Nevertheless, its limited effect on metabolic dysfunction, ovulation, and menstrual restoration, along with the requirement for strict contraception and monitoring for hyperkalemia, position it as a targeted adjunct rather than a comprehensive first-line therapy in PCOS management.

(https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB12708)
Sulprostone is used in clinical practice for management of severe postpartum hemorrhage (PPH), induction of labour in cases of intrauterine fetal death, and medical abortion. In the context of PPH, it is typically administered as a second-line agent when oxytocin fails to control bleeding.
In 2014, clinical data reported high efficacy rates for sulprostone in cases of uterine atony resistant to first-line oxytocics. In one series of 91 patients with atony unresponsive to oxytocin, the reported efficacy was 89%. In another series including 1,370 patients treated for atony-related hemorrhage, the reported success rate was 83.4%. However, no randomized trials comparing sulprostone with placebo have been conducted.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25447391/)
Clinical effectiveness appears to depend on timely administration. Recommendations suggest initiating sulprostone within 30 minutes of PPH diagnosis following oxytocin failure, with earlier administration considered in cases of severe bleeding.
Sulprostone is associated with potentially serious adverse effects, including hyperthermia, gastrointestinal disturbances, bronchospasm, and cardiovascular complications. Concerns regarding safety—particularly with intramuscular or intramyometrial administration—have led to market withdrawal in certain countries. The World Health Organization does not recommend injectable prostaglandins, including sulprostone, for routine PPH prevention, but they remain recommended as second-line therapy for treatment of established PPH.
In 2022, the French National Authority for Health issued a positive opinion confirming sulprostone’s role as a second-line treatment for PPH.
(https://www.has-sante.fr/upload/docs/application/pdf/2022-06/nalador_050122_summary_ct19450.pdf)
Ongoing research is investigating predictors of treatment failure with sulprostone in postpartum hemorrhage management.
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06164236)
Overall, sulprostone is an established second-line uterotonic for severe PPH with documented high success rates in observational studies. However, its safety profile and absence of placebo-controlled trials warrant cautious use, and its role continues to be evaluated alongside newer device-based and pharmacologic interventions.

Syntometrine is a fixed-dose combination uterotonic containing oxytocin and ergometrine, used in the prevention and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) due to uterine atony. Its key strength lies in the complementary pharmacology of its components: oxytocin provides a rapid onset of uterine contraction, while ergometrine induces more sustained and forceful uterine tone. This dual action can make Syntometrine more effective than oxytocin alone in achieving prolonged uterine contraction, particularly in cases where uterine atony persists. However, the clinical and programmatic use of Syntometrine is limited by significant safety and implementation challenges. The ergometrine component is associated with vasoconstriction and can cause acute hypertension, increasing the risk of serious adverse events such as stroke, myocardial ischemia, and seizures. As a result, Syntometrine is contraindicated in women with pre-eclampsia, eclampsia, chronic hypertension, cardiovascular disease, and certain hepatic or renal conditions—comorbidities that are common in obstetric populations and not always reliably identified in emergency or low-resource settings. Its use therefore requires prior blood pressure assessment and closer clinical monitoring, which may not be feasible during acute PPH management.

These safety concerns have influenced global guidance and practice. The World Health Organization recommends oxytocin alone as the first-line uterotonic for PPH prevention and treatment, with Syntometrine positioned as an alternative only where no contraindications exist. Compared with other options such as oxytocin alone or misoprostol, Syntometrine has a higher side-effect burden and is less amenable to task-shifting to lower-level health workers. Consequently, while Syntometrine remains an effective uterotonic in carefully selected patients, its role in modern PPH management is increasingly selective rather than frontline, particularly in settings with high prevalence of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

Name: The Jada System
Developers: Organon & Co.; Alydia Health (formerly InPress Technologies)
Indication: Indicated for the temporary control or reduction of postpartum uterine bleeding when conservative management of uterine bleeding is warranted.
Mechanism of action: The Jada System mimics postpartum physiology by applying low-level intrauterine negative pressure to induce collapse and contraction of the atonic postpartum uterus, constricting blood vessels to achieve haemostasis.
Key features and challenges:
The Jada® System is a U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)–cleared intrauterine, vacuum-induced hemorrhage control device designed for rapid treatment of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH). The device consists of a soft, silicone, teardrop-shaped loop that is placed within the uterine cavity. Gentle vacuum suction is applied to stimulate uterine contraction and collapse of the uterine cavity, thereby compressing bleeding vessels and promoting hemostasis.
In 2020, the PEARLE study evaluated the safety and effectiveness of the Jada System in a prospective, single-arm, multicenter trial involving 107 participants with primary postpartum hemorrhage or abnormal postpartum uterine bleeding. The comparator was a literature-based meta-analysis of outcomes associated with the Bakri balloon. The study reported a 94% treatment success rate (100/106 participants), with no adverse events judged to be definitively device-related and a low rate of possibly related adverse events.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32909970/)
In 2021, Alydia Health, the original developer of the Jada System, was acquired by Organon, a Merck spinoff, to expand global development and commercialization efforts.
(https://www.merck.com/news/merck-announces-acquisition-of-alydia-health-on-behalf-of-its-planned-spinoff-of-organon/)
A randomized controlled trial in Ghana (NCT05382403) is currently comparing the Jada System with standard-of-care management for postpartum hemorrhage, with completion expected in 2027.
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05382403)
In 2025, a retrospective cohort study compared maternal PPH outcomes between uterine balloon tamponade and vacuum-induced hemorrhage control devices, contributing further real-world comparative data.
(https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14767058.2025.2537225)
Overall, the Jada System represents an FDA-cleared, device-based intervention for rapid control of postpartum hemorrhage through vacuum-induced uterine contraction. While early prospective data demonstrate high effectiveness and favorable safety, ongoing randomized and comparative studies will further define its role relative to existing uterine tamponade techniques.
