Name: Tibolone - Endometriosis
Developers: Organon & Co.; Hanmi Pharmaceutical; Schering-Plough Corporation; MSD (also known as Merck & Co)
Indication: Indicated to mitigate the negative impact of hormonal treatment of endometriosis
Target: Estrogen receptor; Progesterone receptor; Testosterone congener
Mechanism of action: Estrogen receptor agonists
Key features and challenges:
Tibolone is a synthetic steroid classified as a selective tissue estrogenic activity regulator (STEAR). Although it does not contain estrogen or progestogen, it exhibits tissue-specific estrogenic, progestogenic, and androgenic effects. Tibolone is approved in more than 80 countries for the treatment of postmenopausal symptoms and prevention of postmenopausal osteoporosis at a dose of 2.5 mg/day; it is not approved in the United States, Canada, or Japan (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800008188).
In the context of endometriosis, tibolone has been referenced primarily as an add-back therapy. Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists are commonly used to suppress ovarian estrogen production in endometriosis management; however, prolonged hypoestrogenism may lead to bone loss and vasomotor symptoms. The European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology (ESHRE) guidelines identify tibolone as a potential add-back option to mitigate bone mineral density loss during GnRH agonist therapy. It is also described as a possible alternative to combined menopausal hormone therapy, given its estrogenic effects on vasomotor symptoms and bone, alongside progestogenic-like effects on the endometrium (https://www.eshre.eu/guideline/endometriosis).
In 2024, a Phase IV clinical trial was planned to evaluate tibolone as add-back therapy in patients with endometriosis and fibroids; however, the trial was withdrawn prior to enrollment due to prioritization of other projects (https://adis.springer.com/trials/700357494).
Key challenges include limited contemporary clinical trial data specifically evaluating tibolone in endometriosis populations. As tibolone has estrogenic activity in certain tissues, theoretical concerns remain regarding stimulation of residual endometriotic lesions, although its tissue-selective profile may mitigate this risk. Regulatory variation across countries and the absence of recent controlled trials further limit definitive conclusions. While tibolone may have a role as add-back therapy to reduce hypoestrogenic side effects during GnRH suppression, robust clinical data are needed to confirm safety and efficacy in endometriosis management.

Name: Tinidazole - Trichomoniasis
Developers: Mission Pharmacal; US National Institutes of Health (NIH); Peking University; University of KwaZulu-Natal, Durban, Republic of South Africa
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of trichomoniasis caused by T. vaginalis in both female and male patients.
Mechanism of action: DNA synthesis inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Tinidazole is a second-generation 5-nitroimidazole antimicrobial used in the treatment of trichomoniasis, giardiasis, amebiasis, and bacterial vaginosis. It was approved in the United States in 2004 for the treatment of trichomoniasis and related protozoal infections and has been widely used in Europe and other regions for several decades with established efficacy and acceptable tolerability (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0149291805003243). 
Its mechanism of action involves reduction of the nitro group within Trichomonas vaginalis by a ferredoxin-mediated electron transport system, generating reactive nitro radicals that damage DNA and result in cell death.
A 2022 in vitro study comparing three 5-nitroimidazoles (tinidazole, ornidazole, and secnidazole) with metronidazole found that 80% (75/94) of T. vaginalis isolates were susceptible to tinidazole, compared with 61% for metronidazole (https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/spectrum.00912-22). 
Reported resistance rates were 2% for tinidazole and 11% for metronidazole, suggesting improved in vitro susceptibility relative to conventional therapy. Refractory trichomoniasis, often associated with antimicrobial resistance, has emerged as a clinical challenge. A clinical trial due for completion in 2025 is evaluating two intensified oral tinidazole regimens combined with metronidazole for refractory trichomonas vaginitis (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05383521).
Tinidazole is typically administered as a short-course regimen. Reported adverse effects include possible serum enzyme elevations and hypersensitivity reactions such as urticaria, angioedema, and bronchospasm. Although transient liver enzyme elevations have been observed, tinidazole has not been convincingly linked to clinically apparent liver injury with jaundice despite extensive global use (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/5479#section=Toxicity).
Key challenges include emerging resistance, the management of refractory infections requiring higher-dose or combination regimens, and monitoring of safety in prolonged or intensified therapy. Tinidazole remains an important alternative to metronidazole, particularly in settings where resistance to first-line therapy is increasing.

Name: Tirzepatide
Developers: Eli Lilly and Company; Mitsubishi Tanabe Pharma Corporation; Rheinische Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universitaet Bonn
Indication: Treatment of obesity in PCOS
Target: Gastric inhibitory polypeptide receptor; Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor
Mechanism of action: Gastric inhibitory polypeptide receptor agonists; Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists
Key features and challenges:
Tirzepatide is a novel medication marketed for treating type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and obesity treatment. Tirzepatide is a dual agonist for the glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) and glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) receptors. The drug leads to significantly improved glycemic control and weight reduction in patients with T2DM, maximizing benefits similar to GLP-1 medications such as semaglutide.

A 2023 study reviewed the current therapies for the treatment of PCOS and evaluates the potential use of Tirzepatide to address the symptoms of PCOS, including reproductive dysfunction, obesity, and insulin resistance. They report that Tirzepatide is a newly approved FDA drug that significantly reduces weight loss and improves insulin sensitivity in patients with and without diabetes. While this drug has several gastrointestinal side effects, there is a reduction in their intensity (relative to GLP-1RA drugs alone) due to its dual mechanism of action. Tirzepatide could be a novel therapeutic strategy for PCOS, particularly in addressing weight gain and insulin sensitivity.
(https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/12/14/4575).

A 2023 single-center retrospective study showed the hazard ratio of weight loss is nearly 2 times higher in patients with PCOS taking COMBO treatment with metformin and a tirzepatide vs metformin alone. (https://www.fertstert.org/article/S0015-0282(23)01397-3/fulltext)
Recent updates:
2025: New EU Phase IV therapeutic-use trial (EUCTR 2024-515982-32-00) identified for tirzepatide in women with PCOS and overweight/obesity.
Source: https://euclinicaltrials.eu/search-for-clinical-trials/?lang=en&EUCT=2024-515982-32-00

Name: Tocilizumab
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of severe or critical (WHO definition) adults and paediatric patients 2 years of age or older
Mechanism of action: Tocilizumab binds specifically to both soluble and membrane-bound IL-6 receptors (sIL-6R and mIL6R), and has been shown to inhibit IL-6-mediated signaling through these receptors. IL-6 is a pleiotropic pro-inflammatory cytokine produced by a variety of cell types including T- and B-cells, lymphocytes, monocytes and fibroblasts. IL-6 has been shown to be involved in diverse physiological processes such as T-cell activation, induction of immunoglobulin secretion, initiation of hepatic acute phase protein synthesis, and stimulation of hematopoietic precursor cell proliferation and differentiation.

Name: Tocodynamometer (TOCO)
Developers: College of Engineering Guindy Anna University
Indication: Diagnosis and prediction of PTL
Mechanism of action: Measures testosterone not bound to SHBG to estimate biologically available androgen levels associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
Cardiotocography (CTG) is the most common method used for monitoring fetal heart rate (FHR) and uterine contractions during pregnancy and labor. This method detects mechanical activity of fetal heart and uterus; however, it provides low accuracy and sensibility, and hence more accurate methods are required. It is commonly used to diagnose preterm labor in clinical practice. 
 
Measuring uterine activity is important for diagnosing preterm labor, but the accuracy of the tocodynamometer (TOCO) can be affected by gestational age (GA). Uterine electromyography (EMG) offers a noninvasive way to monitor contractions. This study set out to compare how interpretable contraction patterns are in preterm patients when measured by EMG versus TOCO. In 2022, a prospective observational study followed 48 patients between 24w0d and 36w6d GA, recruited from June 2020 to May 2021. Participants were evaluated for preterm labor or induction/augmentation and monitored with both devices. Two blinded obstetricians reviewed the tracings, analyzing the relative rate (RR) of interpretable patterns, the number of contractions in the first 20 minutes, and total tracing duration. The average GA was 32.1 weeks; 45.8% were Black and 50% Hispanic. The RR for uninterpretable tracings comparing EMG to TOCO was 0.95 (P=0.75). EMG detected more contractions in the first 20 minutes (RR 2.7, P<0.01) and overall (RR 3.04, P<0.01), with even greater differences in patients under 33 weeks. However, neither device showed a statistically significant advantage in detecting true labor based on contractions in the first 20 minutes. While interpretability was similar, EMG tended to capture more contractions, especially in earlier gestations, suggesting it may be worth considering for use in these cases (https://www.ajog.org/article/S0002-9378(21)02099-8/fulltext).

Given its clinical use, most studies use TOCO as a comparator with newer more sensitive methods, such as EHH (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32040634/).

Name: Total testosterone
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS, specifically assessment of biochemical hyperandrogenism
Mechanism of action: Measures circulating total testosterone to identify biochemical hyperandrogenism associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
Total testosterone is the combined amount of testosterone in the blood, including both free (active) testosterone and testosterone that bounds to proteins like SHBG and albumin. In Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS), measuring total testosterone helps assess hyperandrogenism, which leads to symptoms like hirsutism, acne, and alopecia. Elevated levels support a PCOS diagnosis, alongside other clinical and hormonal evaluations. (https://journals.lww.com/rdm/fulltext/2024/03000/an_overview_of_the_physiopathology_and_various.7.aspx)

The 2023 International Evidence-based Guidelines for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) recommend the use of both total testosterone and free testosterone to assess biochemical hyperandrogenism, which is a key diagnostic feature of PCOS. (https://academic.oup.com/jcem/article/108/10/2447/7242360)
(https://academic.oup.com/jcem/article/106/3/e1071/5992309)

A 2023 study found that total testosterone (TT) levels were significantly higher in women with PCOS compared to healthy women, with an optimal cut-off of 0.82 mIU/L, showing a diagnostic accuracy of AUC = 0.852 and a Youden's index of 0.58%. (https://www.dovepress.com/diagnostic-performance-of-anti-mllerian-hormone-luteinizing-hormone-to-peer-reviewed-fulltext-article-IJWH)

Name: Tranexamic acid - PPH
Developers: London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine (LSHTM) (including MEIRU)
Indication: Prevention and treatment of Postpartum haemorrhage
Mechanism of action: Plasminogen receptor blockades
Key features and challenges:
Tranexamic acid (TXA) is an antifibrinolytic that competitively inhibits the activation of plasminogen to plasmin. It is approved for use to treat or prevent excessive blood loss from major trauma, surgery, dentistry, heavy menstruation and short-term use for haemophilia. TXA is relatively cheap in most contexts, often available in health care settings due to its use in trauma and surgery, has a shelf life of three years, and can be stored at room temperature (15–30 C) in many places. It does however require skilled health workers for administration (IV).
Based on evidence for the benefit of TXA in improving trauma care outcomes, WHO’s recommendations for prevention and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) issued in 2012 included a conditional recommendation to use TXA for treatment of PPH when uterotonics fail to control the bleeding or the bleeding is thought to be due to trauma. 
Results from the 2017 World Maternal Antifibrinolytic Trial (the WOMAN Trial) showed that early use of IV TXA (within three hours of birth and as soon as possible after onset of bleeding) reduces death due to bleeding in women with PPH, regardless of cause, and with no adverse maternal effects. WHO has since updated its recommendations for the use of TXA for treatment of PPH, where it is recommended to be considered as part of a comprehensive PPH package of care, especially where other uterotonics have failed to halt bleeding, or if it is thought that the bleeding may be partly due to trauma. 
The WOMAN-2 Trial investigated whether TXA can prevent women developing PPH in the first place. This trial recruited 15,000 women giving birth vaginally with anaemia across Asia and Africa. The trial was completed in 2023, however results are yet to be published. (https://woman2.lshtm.ac.uk/about-woman-2/the-woman-trials/; https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT03475342)
The VWD-WOMAN Trial is also comparing recombinant von Willebrand factor (rvWf) plus tranexamic acid vs. rvWf alone to reduce postpartum haemorrhage in women with von Willebrand disease. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT04344860) 
Several clinical trials are underway for TXA for the prevention and treatment of PPH. There is also ongoing NIH funded research into the use of tranexamic acid to treat PPH (https://reporter.nih.gov/project-details/9927496).

Name: Tranexamic acid - Uterine fibroids
Indication: Indicated to treat uterine fibroids to reduce bleeding.
Mechanism of action: By targeting plasminogen, the drug prevents its conversion into plasmin, which is responsible for breaking down fibrin in blood clots. This stabilization of clots helps to reduce excessive bleeding, providing significant symptom relief for women experiencing heavy menstrual flow due to fibroids.
Key features and challenges:
Tranexamic acid is a valuable option for managing heavy menstrual bleeding associated with uterine fibroids due to its antifibrinolytic properties. One of the key advantages of tranexamic acid is that it offers a non-hormonal approach to managing menstrual bleeding. This is particularly beneficial for women who either cannot or prefer not to use hormonal therapies. 
The use of Tranexamic acid to manage heavy menstrual bleeding associated with uterine fibroids is recommended by the American Academy of Family Physicians and the European Menopause and Andropause Society.
(https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2017/0115/p100.html#:~:text=Management%20of%20uterine%20fibroids%20should,therapy%3B%20and%20the%20physician's%20experience.&text=Expectant%20management%20is%20appropriate%20for%20women%20with%20asymptomatic%20uterine%20fibroids. ; https://www.emas-online.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/fibroids.pdf)

However, there are challenges associated with its use. Tranexamic acid addresses only the symptom of heavy bleeding and does not impact the fibroids themselves or their size. Therefore, while it helps manage bleeding, it does not provide a long-term solution for the underlying fibroid issues. Furthermore, potential side effects include gastrointestinal disturbances and, in rare cases, thromboembolic events due to its impact on blood clotting.

A 2020 Phase 4 clinical trial, with results first published in 2021, assessed the comparative effectiveness of Levonorgestrel Intrauterine System (LNG-IUS) to Tranexamic Acid (TA) for the treatment of heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) in women with clinically-significant fibroids. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03317795#study-record-dates).

A 2023 review comprehensively summarized the recent research advances on uterine fibroids, focusing on risk factors, development origin, pathogenetic mechanisms, and treatment options. Additionally, they described the current treatment interventions for uterine fibroids. Tranexamic acid is listed as a non-hormonal management option that is well tolerated and has a favorable safety profile. It is associated with rare and mild adverse effects including gastrointestinal and musculoskeletal symptoms, and it is contraindicated for patients with color blindness, active bleeding, a history of intravascular clotting, or hypersensitivity to the medication. 
(https://www.jptcp.com/index.php/jptcp/article/view/3385).

Name: Transvaginal Uterine Artery Clamp (TVUAC)
Developers: Kerala Federation of Obstetrics and Gynaecology
Indication: Indicated for the temporary control or reduction of postpartum uterine bleeding when conservative management of uterine bleeding is warranted.
Mechanism of action: TVUAC controls PPH through the bilateral occlusion of the uterine arteries.
Key features and challenges:
The Transvaginal Uterine Artery Clamp (TVUAC) is a modified stainless-steel instrument designed for mechanical occlusion of the uterine arteries in the management of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH). It is an extended (30.5 cm) adaptation of sponge-holding forceps, with the distal blades bent at right angles approximately 2.5 cm from the tip, resulting in an effective working length of 28 cm. The fenestrated blades have inner serrations to enhance grip and, when fully closed, maintain a 6 mm gap between the arms. A pair of TVUACs is used alongside vaginal retractors to allow adequate visualization of the cervix. The clamps are applied transvaginally at the 3 and 9 o’clock positions to compress the uterine arteries at the level of the uterine isthmus, thereby reducing uterine blood flow.
A retrospective chart review conducted at a tertiary care centre in South India evaluated the use of TVUAC in women who developed immediate atonic PPH following vaginal delivery between April 2015 and December 2020 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35276445/). Among 3,999 vaginal deliveries, 251 women developed primary atonic PPH. Of the 162 patients requiring intervention beyond medical management, haemostasis was achieved in 153 (94.4%) following TVUAC application. In 120 women (78.4%), bleeding was controlled with TVUAC alone, while 33 required additional second-line surgical procedures. The mean duration of clamp application was 25 ± 10 minutes. No procedure-related complications were reported up to six weeks of follow-up.
Key challenges include reliance on retrospective single-centre data, lack of randomized controlled trials comparing TVUAC with other surgical or tamponade interventions, and potential variability in operator skill. Broader evaluation across diverse clinical settings is needed to confirm safety, reproducibility, and comparative effectiveness within standardized PPH management protocols.

Name: Tretinoin (topical)
Indication: Indicated for acne treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: Protein synthesis inhibitors; Retinoic acid receptor agonists
Key features and challenges:
Tretinoin is a generic name for a medication derivative of vitamin A (retinol), also commonly known as all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA). Tretinoin can be given systemically or topically for various indications. Tretinoin is used to treat acne vulgaris and certain types of promyelocytic leukemia, as well as various skin conditions in over-the-counter medications.
The exact mechanism by which topical tretinoin functions are not completely understood, but current evidence suggests mediation through binding of retinoic acid receptors (RARs) alpha, beta, and gamma along with retinoid X receptors (RXRs) by blocking inflammatory mediators. By doing this, the production of procollagen increases to augment collagen type I and III formations.

A 2021 review aimed to point out the options for female patients to treat acne associated with PCOS. They point out that the correct selection of acne treatment depends on many factors such as patient’s age, clinical presentation, medication history, pregnancy, and patient preference. It reports that benzoyl peroxide is superior to topical tretinoin for inflammatory lesions.
(http://dx.doi.org/10.31838/ijpr/2021.13.03.156).

Mechanism of action: Acts on B-subtype nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR), depolarizing muscular nAChRs of helminthic parasite

Name: Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (combined)
Indication: Treatment of acne associated with PCOS
Mechanism of action: CYP2C9 inhibitor; anti-folate; pyrimidine inhibition; sulfamide inhibition
Key features and challenges:
Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole is a fixed antibiotic combination used to treat and prevent many bacterial infections. This drug is very cost-affordable and used for many types of illnesses.
Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole is a synthetic combination of two antibacterial agents, trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole. This synergistic combination, also known as Co-Trimoxazole, inhibits two sequential steps in the bacterial metabolism of folic acid. Trimethoprim is a pyrimidine inhibitor of dihydrofolate reductase; sulfamethoxazole is a sulfamide inhibitor of bacterial dihydrofolate synthase.

The FDA-Approved indications include acute infective exacerbation of chronic bronchitis, otitis media in pediatrics only, travelers diarrhea for treatment and prophylaxis, urinary tract infections, shigellosis, pneumocystis jirovecii, pneumonia/pneumocystis carinii pneumonia (PJP/PCP), and toxoplasmosis, both as prophylaxis and treatment. There are also non-FDA-approved indications, including for acne vulgaris.

A 2021 review aimed to point out the options for female patients to treat acne associated with PCOS. They point out that the correct selection of acne treatment depends on many factors such as patient’s age, clinical presentation, medication history, pregnancy, and patient preference. It reports that Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole combination is effective to use in acne. 
(http://dx.doi.org/10.31838/ijpr/2021.13.03.156).

Name: TrinScreen™
Indication: Diagnosis of HIV infection: adults, adolescents, children and infants > 18 months of age
Mechanism of action: The test operates through immunoassay technology, where the HIV antibodies in the sample bind to specific antigens coated on the test strip. This binding results in a visible signal (e.g., a color change) that indicates whether the sample is HIV positive or negative.
Key features and challenges:
TrinScreen™ HIV is a high-quality, single-use rapid point-of-care immunoassay designed to aid in the diagnosis of HIV. Its ease of use and robustness make it reliable in diverse testing settings. The test offers a quick result time of approximately 10 minutes using venous or capillary whole blood, with excellent sensitivity and specificity. Featuring simple procedures and easy interpretation, each test includes a built-in control to ensure accurate results, making it an ideal solution for efficient and reliable HIV testing in a variety of point-of-care environments.
(https://www.trinitybiotech.com/area/trinscreen/)

Name: Triptorelin - Endometriosis
Developers: Debiopharm ; Ferring Pharmaceuticals ; Actavis; Rumah Sakit Pusat Angkatan Darat (RSPAD) Gatot Soebroto
Indication: Indicated for the prevention and treatment of endometriosis associated growth and activity of endometrial tissue, pain and fertility
Mechanism of action: Gonadotropin releasing hormone stimulants
Key features and challenges:
Triptorelin, a gonadorelin analogue originally developed at Tulane University and licensed to Debiopharm, stimulates the release of pituitary gonadotrophins, affecting hormonal activity in the testes and ovaries. It is widely approved for treating conditions such as endometriosis, prostate cancer, breast cancer, precocious puberty, and more. Available in various formulations, including intramuscular and subcutaneous, it is marketed globally under names like Decapeptyl and Pamorelin. While some developments, like a four-month sustained-release formulation, have been discontinued, triptorelin remains a crucial therapeutic agent with ongoing clinical trials and market presence. Triptorelin works by suppressing the pituitary gland’s release of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), leading to a significant reduction in estrogen and testosterone levels. This hormonal suppression helps manage symptoms of endometriosis by reducing the growth and activity of endometrial tissue, thus alleviating pain and improving fertility outcomes. Decapeptyl is often used in assisted reproductive technologies to control ovarian function and optimize conditions for successful embryo implantation. (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800004444)
In November 2019, Ipsen completed a Phase III trial (D-CN-52014-220; NCT03232281) in China comparing two formulations of triptorelin for endometriosis: triptorelin pamoate 15mg administered every 3 months and triptorelin acetate 3.75mg administered monthly. The study evaluated estradiol suppression, efficacy, and safety and involved 300 patients. Additionally, clinical development of triptorelin for endometriosis is ongoing in China (NCT01942369). (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800004444)
A Phase 2 clinical trial is underway to assess the impact of various pre-treatment regimens, including Decapeptyl, Dienogest, and Oral Contraceptive Pill (OCP), on pregnancy outcomes in women with endometriosis undergoing in vitro fertilization (IVF). The trial, conducted at Shahid Beheshti and Amin Hospitals in Isfahan, involves 88 infertile women aged 30-45 who are randomly assigned to one of the four treatment groups. The study aims to determine which regimen is most effective in achieving positive pregnancy outcomes, measured by HCG positivity and endometrial thickness. Exclusion criteria include drug sensitivity, history of thromboembolic diseases, malignancy, and other factors that could affect the safety and efficacy of the treatments. (https://irct.behdasht.gov.ir/trial/65288)

Name: Triptorelin - PCOS
Indication: Treatment of PCOS infertility
Mechanism of action: Triptorelin is a synthetic agonist analog of gonadotropin releasing hormone
Key features and challenges:
Triptorelin is a synthetic decapeptide gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonist that reversibly suppresses pituitary secretion of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) following an initial stimulatory phase. Triptorelin acetate (marketed as Decapeptyl) is widely used in assisted reproductive technology (ART) cycles, particularly for pituitary downregulation in GnRH agonist long protocols and as an ovulation trigger in GnRH antagonist cycles. In women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), who are at elevated risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), GnRH-based strategies are central to balancing ovarian response with safety.
The 2023 International Evidence-Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of PCOS recommends a GnRH antagonist protocol for women with PCOS undergoing IVF/ICSI, as it permits the use of a GnRH agonist trigger and freeze-all strategy to reduce OHSS risk without compromising cumulative live birth rates. The guideline also notes that adjunct metformin therapy may be considered in women undergoing stimulation with a GnRH agonist long protocol to reduce the risk of OHSS and miscarriage.
https://academic.oup.com/humrep/article/38/9/1655/7241786
A 2022 study evaluating endocrine and reproductive outcomes in PCOS patients undergoing ART reported that women administered triptorelin achieved higher rates of fresh embryo transfer, clinical pregnancy, and live birth, alongside a lower ectopic pregnancy rate, compared with those receiving tripraline. These findings suggest potential advantages of triptorelin as part of ART protocols in PCOS.
https://rbej.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12958-022-01007-z
In 2023, a study comparing gonadotropin responses to triptorelin among healthy women, women with PCOS, and women with hypothalamic amenorrhea found that the FSH response to triptorelin was reduced in women with polycystic ovaries, irrespective of ovarian stimulation status. This highlights potential intrinsic differences in pituitary–ovarian axis responsiveness in PCOS.
https://academic.oup.com/jcem/article/108/7/1666/6991760
A 2024 study demonstrated that, in PCOS patients undergoing frozen embryo transfer (FET), endometrial preparation with GnRH agonist pretreatment prior to an artificial cycle improved implantation and clinical pregnancy rates compared with conventional artificial cycle protocols without GnRH-a pretreatment. However, confirmation through well-designed randomized controlled trials is required.
https://ovarianresearch.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s13048-024-01410-7
Another 2024 study reported that pretreatment with a long-acting GnRH agonist during the early follicular phase improved live birth rates in FET cycles. Age under 40 years, primary infertility, PCOS, and irregular menstruation were identified as effective indications for GnRHa pretreatment in endometrial preparation. Nonetheless, further randomized trials are necessary to validate these findings and clarify optimal patient selection.
https://ovarianresearch.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s13048-023-01277-0

Name: Triptorelin - Uterine Fibroids
Developers: Esfahan University of Medical Sciences; Debiopharm ; AbbVie; Arbor Pharmaceuticals
Indication: Uterine fibroid treatment for the size of fibroids and to manage symptoms; Preoperative treatment to reduce fibroid size, facilitating surgical procedures.
Target: GnRH receptors in the pituitary gland,
Mechanism of action: Triptorelin acts by binding to GnRH receptors in the pituitary gland, leading to a decrease in the release of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH). This reduction in FSH and LH subsequently leads to lower estrogen levels, which can reduce the size and symptoms of uterine fibroids.
Key features and challenges:
Triptorelin is a synthetic gonadorelin (GnRH) analogue originally synthesised at Tulane University and exclusively licensed worldwide to Debiopharm. It stimulates the release of pituitary gonadotrophins, resulting in modulation of hormonal secretory activity in the testes and ovaries. Through sustained administration, it suppresses gonadal steroid production via downregulation of GnRH receptors.
The agent has been approved and launched as an intramuscular formulation in multiple markets worldwide for a range of indications, including breast cancer, prostate cancer, precocious puberty, endometriosis, uterine leiomyoma, paraphilias, and female infertility.
Clinical studies have demonstrated that triptorelin can reduce fibroid size and alleviate symptoms such as heavy menstrual bleeding and pelvic pain. However, its therapeutic effect is typically considered short-term, as fibroid regrowth and symptom recurrence may occur after discontinuation of treatment.
A controlled-release intravenous formulation (Triptorelin ER) is marketed in Iran and the European Union for the treatment of uterine leiomyoma.

Name: Triptorelin ER - Endometriosis
Indication: Endometriosis hormonal dysregulation, pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, pain during intercourse, abnormal tissue growth
Mechanism of action: Gonadotropin releasing hormone stimulants; biosphere release
Key features and challenges:
Triptorelin ER is an extended-release injectable biosimilar of triptorelin being developed by Xbrane Biopharma using biodegradable microsphere technology. The formulation embeds triptorelin in biocompatible microspheres designed to provide sustained release of the active ingredient. Triptorelin is a gonadotrophin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonist that initially stimulates and subsequently downregulates pituitary GnRH receptors, leading to suppression of luteinising hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), and consequently reducing estrogen production in women. This hormonal suppression underlies its established use in managing endometriosis and other hormone-dependent conditions (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800043602).
In June 2019, Xbrane signed a non-binding agreement with STADA Arzneimittel for European development and commercialization of the triptorelin biosimilar, with plans for a pivotal Phase III trial in endometriosis, uterine myoma, and breast cancer (https://adis.springer.com/trials/700309828). 
The company has also granted exclusive marketing rights to China Resources Pharmaceutical Group for China and to BL&H for South Korea, alongside distribution agreements in Israel and Iran. GMP certification has been obtained in Italy to support manufacturing.
Regulatory and market milestones include filing for approval in Sweden for prostate cancer and endometriosis and launch of the product (Spherotide 3M) in Iran for prostate cancer, endometriosis, and uterine leiomyoma. The biosimilar is additionally under clinical development in Sweden for precocious puberty and breast cancer (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800043602). 
Planned pivotal Phase III studies remain central to broader European positioning.
Key challenges include demonstrating biosimilarity in terms of efficacy, safety, and pharmacokinetics compared with reference triptorelin products, as well as navigating complex regulatory requirements for long-acting injectable formulations. Market uptake may depend on pricing competitiveness, interchangeability policies, and clinician confidence in biosimilar extended-release technologies. As a GnRH agonist, class-related hypoestrogenic adverse effects and the need for add-back therapy remain relevant considerations in endometriosis management.
Overall, triptorelin ER represents a biosimilar strategy leveraging established GnRH agonist mechanisms with extended-release microsphere delivery. Its clinical and commercial impact in endometriosis will depend on successful completion of pivotal trials and competitive positioning within an established hormonal treatment landscape.

Name: Triptorelin Pamoate (prolonged release)
Indication: Endometriosis pain, hormone regulation, menstual regulation
Mechanism of action: Gonadotropin releasing hormone stimulants
Key features and challenges:
Triptorelin pamoate prolonged-release (PR) 3-month formulation (15 mg) was developed to provide therapeutic equivalence to the standard triptorelin acetate PR 1-month formulation (3.75 mg) while reducing injection frequency. Triptorelin is a gonadotrophin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonist that suppresses pituitary luteinising hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) secretion after initial stimulation, leading to decreased estrogen production and consequent reduction of endometriosis-related lesion activity and pain. The 1-month formulation, first introduced in France in 1996, has become standard of care for endometriosis in China and is approved in over 40 countries for multiple indications. One- and three-month formulations have also been launched in the Philippines for endometriosis, and a six-month sustained-release intramuscular formulation (Decapeptyl/Pamorelin 22.5 mg) has been launched in Europe (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800004444).
In 2022, a Phase III, randomized, open-label, multicenter trial was completed to demonstrate noninferiority of the triptorelin pamoate PR 3-month formulation compared with the 1-month regimen in Chinese women with endometriosis (https://adis.springer.com/trials/700287465). Conducted across 24 centers, the study enrolled 300 women aged 18–45 years who required GnRH agonist therapy for six months.
Results published in 2022 demonstrated that triptorelin pamoate PR 3-month was noninferior to the 1-month triptorelin acetate regimen in terms of clinical effectiveness, while reducing the number of injections and potentially lowering treatment burden (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12325-022-02264-5).
Key challenges include class-related hypoestrogenic adverse effects such as bone mineral density loss and vasomotor symptoms, which may limit duration of therapy without add-back regimens. Although reduced injection frequency may improve convenience and adherence, long-term safety and cost considerations remain relevant in routine clinical practice.
Overall, triptorelin pamoate PR 3-month offers a less frequent dosing alternative with demonstrated noninferiority to monthly formulations in endometriosis. Its value proposition centers on reduced treatment burden within an established GnRH agonist therapeutic class.

Name: Ulipristal acetate - Uterine fibroids
Developers: Gedeon Richter plc; Amsterdam UMC, including Emma Kinderziekenhuis; Medical University of Bialystok, Uniwersytet Medyczny w Bialymstoku; Polish Academy of Sciences; HRA Pharma; National Institute for Health Research (NIHR)
Indication: Treatment for uterine fibroids - reduces fibroid size and controls symptoms such as heavy menstrual bleeding.
Mechanism of action: Selective progesterone receptor modulators
Key features and challenges:
Ulipristal (CDB 2914), a synthetic selective progesterone receptor modulator (SPRM), was developed by HRA Pharma (a subsidiary of Perrigo) as an antiprogestogen for oral use as an emergency post-coital contraceptive. As an SPRM with antagonistic and partial agonistic effects at the progesterone receptor, ulipristal prevents progesterone from occupying its receptor. 
It has also been investigated and marketed for the treatment of uterine leiomyoma. 
The drug is under regulatory review in the US (for uterine leiomyoma). Phase III development for the treatment of uterine leiomyoma is under-way in Japan. 
However its use in Europe is limited by several pharmacovigilance agencies. The Medicines and Health Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) in the UK issued guidelines restricting the use of Ulipristal for uterine fibroids following several cases of liver failures. (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7854411/#:~:text=UPA%20is%20one%20of%20the%20selective%20progesterone%20receptor%20modulators%20that,life%20and%20better%20pain%20control.)
In September 2020, the Pharmacovigilance Risk Assessment Committee (PRAC) of the European Medicines Agency recommended the revocation of marketing authorisation of Ulipristal for the treatment of uterine leiomyoma due to risk of liver injury. Following this assessmen, the European Commission restricted the use of ulipristal acetate for uterine leiomyoma in the European Union in 2021. The medicine can now only be used to treat uterine fibroids in premenopausal women for whom surgical procedures (including uterine fibroid embolisation) are not appropriate or have not worked. The medicine must not be used for controlling symptoms of uterine fibroids while awaiting surgical treatment.(https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/human/referrals/ulipristal-acetate-5mg-medicinal-products).

A Phase III clinical trial that ended in 2021 investigated ulipristal acetate compared to conventional therapy for the management of heavy menstrual bleeding, including uterine fibroids. (https://adis.springer.com/trials/700254415).

A Phase III randomised control trial evaluated the efficacy and safety of ulipristal acetate (UPA) for uterine fibroids (UFs). The found that the effect of UPA on heavy menstrual bleeding was shown to be comparable with that of LEU in Japanese patients with symptomatic UFs. No notable AEs occurred because of the UPA treatment, and the incidence of AEs in the UPA group was comparable with that of AEs in the LEU group. This result demonstrates the clinical utility of UPA for Asians. (https://www.fertstert.org/article/S0015-0282(21)00044-3/fulltext).
Recent updates: On 12 November 2020, EMA’s human medicines committee (CHMP) recommended restricting use of medicines containing ulipristal acetate 5 mg (Esmya and generic medicines) as a result of cases of serious liver injury. The medicines can now only be used to treat uterine fibroids in premenopausal women for whom surgical procedures (including uterine fibroid embolisation) are not appropriate or have not worked. The medicines must not be used for controlling symptoms of uterine fibroids while awaiting surgical treatment.

-Assessment of calcification, degenerative changes, vascularization
-Pre- and post-procedure evaluation
Therapeutic ultrasound (HIFU):
-Delivers highly focused ultrasound beams to induce:
-Thermal coagulative necrosis (60–80°C)
-Cavitation and mechanical disruption
-Ablation of fibroid tissue without incisions
-NPVR (Non-Perfused Volume Ratio) is used to quantify ablation coverage.
-Evidence shows NPVR ≥ 70% is associated with optimal long-term outcomes.
Key features and challenges:
Ultrasound is a cornerstone diagnostic modality for uterine fibroids, offering real-time, non-invasive, and cost-effective imaging. Transvaginal ultrasound is widely regarded as the gold standard for fibroid detection and mapping. Two-dimensional (2D), three-dimensional (3D), Doppler, and elastography modalities enable assessment of fibroid size, vascularization, and tissue stiffness.
A 2022 study demonstrated a high correlation between ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in determining fibroid location and size, particularly for smaller fibroids.
(Source: https://ijrr.com/article-1-4464-en.html)
Another study reported strong concordance between ultrasound fibroid mapping and intraoperative findings, supporting its reliability for surgical planning.
(Source: https://www.jcdronline.org/admin/Uploads/Files/65adf1dc58eab1.93160149.pdf)
A 2023 study found that ultrasound-based assessment correlated strongly with MRI for fibroid characterization, and that emerging techniques such as contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) and shear-wave elastography improved diagnostic precision, particularly in differentiating fibroids from adenomyosis.
(Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-36313-y)
Three-dimensional ultrasound segmentation has also been shown to provide fibroid volume estimates comparable to MRI, supporting its utility in complex anatomical visualization.
(Source: https://www.jmig.org/article/S1553-4650(23)00348-5/pdf)
High-Intensity Focused Ultrasound (HIFU) represents the therapeutic extension of ultrasound technology, enabling non-invasive fibroid ablation through localized thermal necrosis and cavitation. HIFU provides a uterus-preserving treatment option without surgical incisions.
Large retrospective cohort analyses have demonstrated that HIFU achieves comparable long-term reintervention rates to transcervical resection of myoma (TCRM) when the non-perfused volume ratio (NPVR) is ≥70%, supporting NPVR as a key technical success threshold.
(Source: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1002/jum.70011)
More recent studies (2024–2025) report that HIFU is associated with effective symptom relief and fewer short-term complications compared to surgical alternatives. Predictors of optimal outcomes include higher NPVR, patient age, and baseline symptom profile.
(Sources: https://bmcwomenshealth.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12905-024-03093-0#
; https://bmcwomenshealth.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12905-025-03797-x)
Despite its advantages, limitations remain. Diagnostic ultrasound may have difficulty differentiating fibroids from adenomyosis in certain cases, although elastography has improved accuracy. HIFU outcomes are operator-dependent and influenced by fibroid location, vascularity, and accessibility. The procedure requires specialized equipment, trained clinicians, and high-quality imaging for accurate targeting. Long-term fertility outcomes and economic evaluations continue to require further investigation.

Name: Ultrasound: Follicle number per ovary (FNPO)
Developers: University of Oulu; University of Granada, Universidad de Granada
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS
Mechanism of action: Counts ovarian follicles by ultrasound to identify increased follicle number characteristic of polycystic ovarian morphology.
Key features and challenges:
The number of follicles per ovary (FNPO) is one of the criteria used in the Rotterdam criteria for diagnosing Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS). 

The 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for the assessment and management of PCOS reinforces that FNPO is considered the most effective ultrasound marker for detecting polycystic ovarian morphology (PCOM) in adults. According to the guideline:
FNPO should be counted as part of the diagnostic process, with 12 or more follicles per ovary (measuring 2-9 mm in diameter) being indicative of polycystic ovaries. This is a key feature for PCOS diagnosis when combined with other criteria such as irregular ovulation and clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism.
The guideline emphasizes that FNPO is the primary feature to assess on ultrasound for detecting PCOM, highlighting its role in clinical practice for diagnosing PCOS.
(https://www.monash.edu/__data/assets/pdf_file/0003/3379521/Evidence-Based-Guidelines-2023.pdf)
PolyCystic Ovary Morphology (PCOM) is assessed through ultrasound. Follicle number per ovary (FNPO) is evaluated using transvaginal or endovaginal ultrasound, while ovarian volume (OV) is measured using transvaginal, endovaginal, or transabdominal ultrasound. The assessment should also include specifications on transducer bandwidth and report parameters such as FNPO, ovarian dimensions and volume, endometrial thickness and appearance, and any ovarian or uterine pathology, including cysts and dominant follicles ≥10 mm. These evaluations must be performed by trained professionals. (https://www.mdpi.com/2075-4418/11/11/1953)

Recent studies have examined the role of ovarian follicle count in PCOS diagnosis:

Application of a New Ultrasound Criterion for the Diagnosis of PCOS (2022): This study evaluated updated ultrasound criteria for PCOM, suggesting that increasing the follicle count threshold may improve diagnostic specificity. (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/endocrinology/articles/10.3389/fendo.2022.915245/full)

Validation of an Anti-Müllerian Hormone Cutoff for Polycystic Ovarian Morphology (2024): Researchers assessed the correlation between serum anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) levels and PCOM, proposing that AMH could serve as a surrogate marker, potentially reducing the reliance on ultrasound (https://www.researchprotocols.org/2024/1/e48854/)

Name: Ultrasound: Ovarian volume
Developers: Tehran University of Medical Sciences (TUMS); Alborz University of Medical Sciences
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS
Mechanism of action: Non-invasive imaging method for measuring ovarian and uterine characteristics
Key features and challenges:
Ovarian volume is a key sonographic marker in the diagnosis of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). According to the Rotterdam criteria, an ovarian volume ≥10 cc is indicative of polycystic ovarian morphology (PCOM). Enlargement is typically attributed to increased stromal tissue and multiple immature follicles and has been associated with hyperandrogenism, menstrual irregularities, and infertility. Ultrasound assessment provides a non-invasive tool for both diagnosis and monitoring.
Ultrasound evaluation of PCOM includes measurement of follicle number per ovary (FNPO) and ovarian volume (OV). FNPO is assessed using transvaginal or endovaginal ultrasound, while ovarian volume can be measured via transvaginal, endovaginal, or transabdominal approaches. These assessments require trained professionals to ensure accuracy and reproducibility.
(Source: https://www.mdpi.com/2075-4418/11/11/1953)
A 2022 cross-sectional study involving 61 women aged 18–40 years with PCOS examined the relationship between ovarian morphology measured by transvaginal ultrasound and hormonal parameters. Ovarian volume was positively associated with total testosterone levels, free androgen index, and the LH/FSH ratio, even after adjusting for age, menstrual status, and BMI. Other parameters, such as antral follicle count and stromal area, were not significantly associated with androgen levels or insulin resistance.
(Source: https://bmcendocrdisord.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12902-022-01224-y)
A 2023 study conducted in Saudi Arabia among 73 participants diagnosed or suspected of having PCOS found that 68.5% had ovarian diameters exceeding 28 mm, while 31.5% had normal-sized ovaries. Larger ovarian size was significantly associated with PCOS diagnosis and irregular menstrual patterns.
(Source: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1687850723001152?via%3Dihub)
In another study of 100 women with suspected PCOS, 64% had ovarian volumes ≥10 cc, 67% had 12 or more follicles per ovary, and 91% exhibited follicles measuring 2–9 mm. Echogenic stroma was observed in 97% of participants, with 38% showing stromal thickness ≥10 mm. These sonographic features correlated strongly with clinical symptoms such as oligomenorrhea and biochemical markers including elevated free testosterone and BMI ≥25 kg/m², supporting ovarian volume as a significant diagnostic predictor of PCOS.
(Source: https://www.jcdronline.org/admin/Uploads/Files/644a2eee9b50a0.85904005.pdf

Name: Umbilical artery pulsatility indices (UA PI)
Developers: Hospital for Sick Children; Mayo Clinic (including Mayo Medical School)
Indication: Diagnosis of IUGR
Mechanism of action: Doppler measurement of umbilical artery pulsatility to assess placental vascular resistance and impaired fetoplacental perfusion.
Key features and challenges:
​Umbilical arterial (UA) doppler assessment is used in surveillance of fetal well-being in the third trimester of pregnancy. Abnormal umbilical artery doppler is a marker of placental insufficiency and consequent intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR). The umbilical arterial waveform usually has a ’sawtooth‘ pattern with flow always in the forward direction, that is towards the placenta. An abnormal waveform shows absent or reversed diastolic flow. Before the 15th week, the absence of diastolic flow may be a normal finding. The 95% confidence interval limit slowly decreases for both the resistive index (RI) and pulsatility index (PI) through the course of gestation due to progressive maturation of the placenta and increase in the number of tertiary stem villi. The commonly used parameters are umbilical arterial S/D ratio (SDR), systolic velocity/diastolic velocity, pulsatility index (PI) (Gosling index), (PSV - EDV)/TAV, resistive index (RI) (Pourcelot index), (PSV - EDV)/PSV, PSV, peak systolic velocity, EDV, end-diastolic velocity and TAV. and time-averaged velocity (https://radiopaedia.org/articles/umbilical-arterial-doppler-assessment). 
 
While umbilical artery doppler assessment is widely adopted, different techniques for blood flow assessment are being studied. A study by the Mayo clinic sought to establish the frequency of discordant blood flow patterns between right and left umbilical arteries at the abdominal wall insertion site (AWI). Secondary aims included determining the frequency of discordance between FL and AWI patterns and whether deterioration of Doppler waveforms occurred in a synchronous pattern. The study concluded that frequent variability exists between arterial umbilical doppler flow patterns in growth restricted fetuses, both at time of diagnosis and during subsequent measurements. Further investigations are needed to determine if umbilical artery doppler discordance could represent an additional parameter for antepartum monitoring in fetal growth restriction (https://www.ajog.org/article/S0002-9378(19)31866-6/fulltext#%20).

Name: Umbilicocerebral ratio (UCR)
Developers: Academic Medical Center (AMC), Academisch Medisch Centrum Amsterdam
Indication: Diagnosis of IUGR
Target: velocity flow profiles of the umbilical artery and the fetal middle cerebral artery
Mechanism of action: Ratio of umbilical to cerebral artery Doppler resistance indices to identify placental insufficiency and fetal circulatory redistribution.
Key features and challenges:
​Redistribution of the fetal circulation, signaled by an abnormal ratio of the Doppler velocity flow profiles of the umbilical artery and the middle cerebral artery, more specifically an increased umbilicocerebral ratio (UCR), is an adaptation to chronic hypoxaemia and nutritional scarcity with long-term consequences in survivors. The relevance of an abnormal UCR has been signaled extensively, and there is a consensus that it is a signal of FGR, independent of size, with a strong association with poor outcomes (https://trialsjournal.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s13063-022-06561-w). 
 
The Doppler Ratio In fetal Growth restriction Intervention Trial At (near) Term (DRIGITAT) is aiming to evaluate if the timing of the delivery based on an abnormal UCR in late preterm fetuses identified as SGA improves neurodevelopmental outcomes at 2 years of age. The study is a national multicentre cohort study of women with singleton pregnancies between 32 and 37 weeks of gestation identified as SGA, with a nested randomised controlled trial (RCT) in case of an abnormal UCR (> 0.8). In the nested RCT, women are randomised to either immediate induction of labour or expectant management from 34 weeks in case of severely abnormal size (EFW or FAC < p3) and from 36 weeks in case of mildly abnormal size (EFW or FAC p3–p10). The primary outcome measure is the 7-point average difference in the composite cognitive score (CCS) and composite motor score (CMS) on the Bayley-3 at 2 years. Secondary outcome measures include a composite outcome of neonatal morbidity, perinatal mortality, mode of delivery, maternal quality of life, costs, and predictive value of serum biomarkers. The study is ongoing (https://trialsjournal.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s13063-022-06561-w).

Name: Uric acid - PE
Developers: Morgan Innovation and Technology Ltd; Datta Meghe Institute of Medical Sciences; University of Athens; University of Buenos Aires (Universidad de Buenos Aires)
Indication: Diagnosis and prediction of PE
Mechanism of action: Exerts antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects to reduce cytokine-mediated uterine activation associated with preterm labour.
Key features and challenges:
Uric acid is the end product of purine metabolism, produced via the action of xanthine oxidase and plays a central role in free radical scavenging, presenting both pro-oxidant and antioxidant properties. During normal pregnancy, serum urate concentration is significantly decreased due to plasma volume expansion, while its clearance is amplified by the increased glomerular filtration rate and the uricosuric effects of estrogen. On the other hand, preeclampsia has been considered as a state of hyperuricemia, with uric acid excretion impaired and its production magnified by the increased trophoblast turnover. Uric acid may also have a role in the progression of the disease, since its elevated concentration may inhibit nitric oxide production, leading to inadequate trophoblast invasion and impaired endothelial repair. While uric acid has been routinely used in the clinic for the diagnosis of preeclampsia, there is some controversy around the utility of this test.
(https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1258/om.2011.110075)

A 2020 study showed that preeclampsia is associated with significantly higher serum uric acid levels during all trimesters, both in early preeclampsia and in late-onset preeclampsia. When the two forms of the disease were compared, early-onset preeclampsia was linked to higher uric acid concentration. In terms of severity, both mild and severe preeclampsia are associated with significantly higher uric acid levels compared with healthy pregnant controls, and the levels tend to increase with the severity. HELLP syndrome is also associated with elevated urate levels compared with uncomplicated preeclampsia. Diagnostic accuracy analysis demonstrated that evaluation of serum uric acid concentration during the 3rd trimester was able to detect preeclampsia with an estimated sensitivity of 76.7% (95% CI: 70.5-81.9) and specificity of 79.6% (95% CI: 74.2-84.1), while 2nd-trimester measurements predicted preeclampsia with sensitivity of 78.6% (95% CI: 52.4-92.4) and specificity of 61.6% (95% CI: 57.1-65.8)
(https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/jch.13865).

An Indian study compared salivary and serum uric acid with each other and between PE women and a control group. They found elevated levels of uric acid in both saliva and serum, with a correlation to the severity of PE (higher values for severe vs. non severe PE). Salivary uric acid and serum uric acid were correlated significantly indicating that salivary uric acid can function as a cost-effective, novel marker to provide an idea about serum uric acid levels (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35475103/).

Some point-of-care tests are under investigation, such as a testing platform designed for the digital quantification of salivary uric acid, based on a colorimetric reaction on an easy-to-build smartphone-assisted microfluidic paper-based analytical device (SμPAD). UA levels are quantified according to the colour intensity of Prussian blue on the SμPAD with the aid of a MATLAB code or a smartphone App. The assay time is less than 10 min. SμPADs demonstrate a correlation of 0.97 with a commercial UA kit for the detection of salivary UA in clinical samples. (https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/acssensors.2c00854

An additional project funded by UKRI started in 2023: Morgan Innovation and Technology (MIAT) are developing Salurate, a saliva sampling device testing saliva levels of uric acid for home monitoring use.  The funding will cover maximising performance of the device, concluding device associated software development and a clinical study on 4,000 participants to validate the data-learning algorithm from a representative UK population, as well as technical file compilation for regulatory approval (UKCA marking).
(https://gtr.ukri.org/projects?ref=10053908)

Name: Urine protein/Creatinine ratio - PE/E
Indication: Diagnosis of PE
Mechanism of action: Applies multivariable analysis of maternal biomarkers and clinical parameters to estimate risk of developing preeclampsia.
Key features and challenges:
The urine protein-to-creatinine ratio has been studied as an alternative to the 24-hour protein excretion test for diagnosing preeclampsia. A 2013 meta-analysis reviewed research on how well this ratio predicts significant proteinuria in patients at risk. The study pooled data from 24 trials with a total of 3,186 participants, finding sensitivities and specificities of 91.0% (95% CI 87.0–93.9) and 86.3% (95% CI 78.4–91.7), respectively. The pooled positive likelihood ratio was 6.7 (95% CI 4.1–10.9) and the negative likelihood ratio was 0.10 (95% CI 0.07–0.16). Meta-regression showed accuracy wasn’t influenced by any examined co-variables. The authors concluded that a random urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is useful for ruling out significant proteinuria in at-risk patients, with a cut-off value above 0.30 offering the best accuracy (http://www.annclinlabsci.org/content/43/2/211.short) 
 
The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists suggests checking proteinuria either with a 24-hour collection or by using a protein-to-creatinine ratio from a single urine sample to help diagnose preeclampsia.(https://journals.lww.com/greenjournal/citation/2013/11000/hypertension_in_pregnancy__executive_summary.36.aspx) 
 
These biomarkers are also the basis of the uCheck device developed by Biosense for the diagnosis of PE (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12553-018-0248-0).

Measuring urine protein is the gold standard for detecting proteinuria in preeclampsia (PE), but the 24-hour urine test can be time-consuming and inconvenient. A 2022 study looked at how accurate the protein/creatinine (P/C) ratio is in spotting significant proteinuria (> 1 g/24-hour urine) in PE. The study included 110 women with preeclampsia, admitted for blood pressure monitoring, 24-hour urine collection, fetal well-being checks, and a spot urine sample to measure the P/C ratio. After medical history and examination, routine antenatal tests were done per hospital protocol to rule out chronic kidney disease. The 24-hour urine collection began the morning after admission, and spot samples were taken just before starting the collection. Data analysis showed that a P/C ratio of 1.35 ± 2.54 had 94.4% sensitivity, 94.9% specificity, 97.1% positive predictive value, 90.2% negative predictive value, and 94.5% overall accuracy in detecting significant proteinuria. The study suggests the P/C ratio can be a practical alternative to the 24-hour urine test for diagnosing significant proteinuria in PE (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35156696/).

Name: Urofollitropin
Developers: Merck Serono; IBSA Institut Biochimique SA
Indication: Treatment of PCOS infertility
Mechanism of action: Ovarian follicle stimulants
Key features and challenges:
Urofollitropin is a highly purified urinary-derived follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) used in the management of infertility. FSH is a glycoprotein hormone that stimulates follicular development and is widely employed for ovulation induction and controlled ovarian stimulation (COS) in assisted reproductive technologies (ART), including in vitro fertilization (IVF) and intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI). In women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), FSH is primarily used when first-line ovulation induction agents fail or in ART settings requiring precise ovarian stimulation.
The 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of PCOS states that both urinary FSH (u-FSH, including urofollitropin) and recombinant FSH (r-FSH) are appropriate options for controlled ovarian stimulation in women with PCOS undergoing IVF/ICSI. However, current evidence does not demonstrate clear superiority of one FSH preparation over another, and further research is required to determine optimal preparation choice for this population.
A 2023 study comparing ovarian stimulation strategies in women with PCOS undergoing IVF evaluated minimal and mild stimulation protocols using recombinant FSH or urinary human menopausal gonadotropin (u-HMG). Minimal stimulation with u-HMG demonstrated advantages including reduced medication exposure, optimal oocyte and embryo yield, lower estradiol levels, and reduced risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), while maintaining similar fertilization and implantation rates. Clinical pregnancy and live birth rates were higher in the minimal stimulation u-HMG group. Conversely, a minimal-FSH protocol was associated with increased OHSS risk, highlighting the importance of protocol selection in PCOS patients who are particularly vulnerable to hyper-response.
https://bmcwomenshealth.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12905-023-02473-2
An ongoing randomized clinical trial initiated in 2023 (NCT05362799) is comparing four ovulation induction strategies in women with PCOS who did not achieve ovulation or pregnancy with clomiphene citrate. The study includes urofollitropin alone (75 IU subcutaneously or intramuscularly for five days) and urofollitropin combined with metformin, alongside letrozole-based comparators. Participants undergo ultrasound folliculometry with ovulation triggering based on follicular response, with up to three treatment cycles and follow-up for pregnancy outcomes.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05362799
Urofollitropin is an established fertility medication rather than a disease-modifying therapy for PCOS. Its use is focused on ovulation induction and fertility management rather than correction of underlying metabolic or endocrine dysfunction.
Key challenges include the heightened risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome in women with PCOS, who often demonstrate increased ovarian sensitivity to gonadotropins. Careful dose titration and monitoring are essential. Additionally, comparative effectiveness between urinary and recombinant FSH preparations remains inconclusive, and individualized protocol selection is required to balance efficacy with safety. Cost, monitoring intensity, and access to ART services also influence real-world applicability.
Urofollitropin represents a well-established gonadotropin option for ovulation induction and assisted reproduction in PCOS-related infertility. While effective in achieving follicular development and pregnancy, its role is confined to fertility treatment and requires cautious protocol optimization to mitigate OHSS risk in this high-response population.

Name: Uterine artery (UtA) indices - IUGR
Developers: University of Zurich; Academic Medical Center (AMC), Academisch Medisch Centrum Amsterdam
Indication: Diagnosis of IUGR
Target: blood flow in the uterine arteries
Mechanism of action: Measures telomerase activity as a marker of cellular stress and inflammatory/metabolic dysregulation associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
Assessment of uteroplacental blood flow using uterine artery Doppler is key to evaluating fetal well-being and predicting complications like pre-eclampsia and intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR). Normally, uterine artery resistance decreases as pregnancy progresses due to trophoblastic invasion of the myometrium. Persistently high resistance, indicated by increased pulsatility index (PI), resistive index (RI), or the presence of a diastolic notch, suggests impaired placental perfusion. A low-resistance waveform has a strong negative predictive value for IUGR or pre-eclampsia, while high resistance correlates with up to a 70% risk of pre-eclampsia and 30% risk of IUGR.
A 2008 meta-analysis including over 120,000 pregnancies found uterine artery Doppler most predictive in the second trimester, particularly when both elevated PI and notching were present. These parameters were the strongest indicators of pre-eclampsia and IUGR, especially in high-risk patients, highlighting the value of uterine artery Doppler as an important diagnostic and screening tool in pregnancy.(https://www.cmaj.ca/content/178/6/701.full).

A 2024 prospective study of 306 singleton pregnancies at ≥32 weeks’ gestation found a 4.9% prevalence of late-onset fetal growth restriction (FGR). Compared with normal pregnancies, those with FGR showed significantly higher uterine artery pulsatility index (UtA-PI) and lower cerebroplacental ratio (CPR), cerebral-placental-uterine ratio (CPUR), and umbilical vein blood flow normalized for abdominal circumference (UVBF/AC). These Doppler findings suggest that late-onset FGR is associated with mild placental insufficiency detectable through altered maternal and fetal vascular indices.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39966094/)

Name: VECTRON T500
Developers: Mitsui Chemicals, Inc.; Innovative Vector Control Consortium (IVCC)
Indication: Prevention and control of malaria in children and adults in areas with ongoing malaria transmission where the principal malaria vector(s) exhibit pyrethroid resistance.
Mechanism of action: GABA-gated chloride channel allosteric modulator
Key features and challenges:
In final stages of assessment for WHO pre-qualification, with PTQ/VC Ref Number P-03226.

VECTRON™ T500  is an innovative insecticide formulation developed by Mitsui Chemicals Agro, Inc. that utilizes broflanilide (Tenebenal™)  to combat malaria-transmitting mosquitoes. It offers a new mode of action by targeting the GABA receptor in mosquitoes, causing paralysis and death. This unique mechanism is particularly effective against both pyrethroid-susceptible and resistant mosquito populations, addressing a critical need in malaria vector control.  

Prequalified by the **World Health Organization (WHO)** for **indoor residual spraying (IRS)**, VECTRON™ T500 has demonstrated high efficacy, providing long-lasting residual activity on treated surfaces. Its introduction is an important step in resistance management, as it represents a novel chemical class distinct from existing insecticides. Additionally, its targeted use minimizes environmental impact compared to broad-spectrum alternatives.  

Despite its promise, VECTRON™ T500 faces challenges. Field trials are necessary to confirm its effectiveness under diverse environmental conditions. Furthermore, its expansion into **insecticide-treated nets (ITNs)** is still under evaluation, requiring further research to assess its suitability for this application. Adoption in malaria control programs will also depend on affordability and logistical feasibility, particularly in resource-constrained settings.  

VECTRON™ T500 represents a significant advancement in vector control, offering a powerful new tool to combat insecticide resistance and support global efforts to reduce the burden of malaria.

Indication: Treatment of endometriosis related pain and lesions
Mechanism of action: Progesterone receptor agonists
Key features and challenges:
Progesterone is a naturally occurring steroid hormone widely used in hormone therapy, fertility support, and the management of various gynecological disorders. When administered continuously, progesterone induces endometrial atrophy, suppresses ovulation, and reduces estrogen-driven proliferation. In endometriosis, long-term continuous progesterone therapy can thin the endometrial lining, suppress menstruation, and exert anti-proliferative effects on ectopic endometrial lesions.
The use of progestogens to reduce endometriosis-associated pain is recommended by the European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology (ESHRE) in its clinical guideline on endometriosis management (https://www.eshre.eu/guideline/endometriosis). 
Progestogen therapy is considered a first-line hormonal treatment option due to its efficacy in reducing dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and non-menstrual pelvic pain.
A vaginally administered tablet formulation of micronised progesterone was developed by Besins Healthcare and has been launched worldwide for indications including female infertility, menopausal syndrome, menstrual and premenstrual disorders, amenorrhoea, breast disorders, prevention of preterm labour, prevention and treatment of spontaneous abortion, and endometriosis (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800043105). 
Vaginal administration allows for targeted uterine delivery with reduced systemic exposure compared to oral formulations, potentially improving tolerability.
Although vaginal progesterone is an established hormonal option and is included within recommended progestogen therapies for endometriosis, its efficacy is comparable to other progestin-based treatments rather than disease-modifying. Long-term use may still be associated with irregular bleeding, mood changes, and other progestogenic side effects. Further comparative studies may help clarify its relative effectiveness versus other progestins and GnRH-based therapies in different endometriosis phenotypes.

Name: Visby Medical Sexual Health Test - Gonorrhea
Indication: Detection of gonorrhoeae
Mechanism of action: automated PCR amplification
Key features and challenges:
The Visby Medical Sexual Health Test is a rapid, single-use molecular point-of-care diagnostic designed to detect Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, and Trichomonas vaginalis from self-collected vaginal swabs in under 30 minutes (https://www.visbymedical.com/sexual-health-test/). The device integrates sample preparation, amplification, and detection within a compact platform intended for near-patient use, enabling same-visit diagnosis and treatment decisions.
A 2021 study conducted by investigators at Johns Hopkins Medicine evaluated the clinical impact of the Visby Medical point-of-care test compared with standard batched laboratory nucleic acid amplification testing. 
(https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laninf/article/PIIS1473-3099(20)30734-9/abstract). 
The study reported significantly shorter time to results (approximately 47 minutes versus 25 hours with standard-of-care testing), higher rates of appropriate treatment, and lower rates of overtreatment. Rapid availability of organism-specific results enabled guideline-concordant therapy for gonorrhoea rather than empiric antibiotic administration.
Key challenges include cost considerations, single-use consumable dependency, and scalability in resource-limited settings. While the platform offers rapid molecular detection and supports antimicrobial stewardship through targeted therapy, broader implementation will depend on affordability, regulatory approvals, and integration into routine sexual health services.

Name: Vitamin C and iron - fixed combined (+/- folic acid)
Developers: Fetal Medicine Foundation USA; Jawaharlal Institute of Postgraduate Medical Education & Research (JIPMER); Sri Dharmasthala Manjunatheshwara College of Ayurveda and Hospital (SDMCAH)
Indication: Indicated for the treatment and prevention of iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Enhances iron absorption; regulates cellular iron uptake and metabolism
Key features and challenges:
Vitamin C (ascorbate) is a six-carbon compound. It is the most potent enhancer of nonheme iron absorption. Furthermore, accumulating evidence strongly suggests that in addition to the known ability of dietary ascorbate to enhance nonheme iron absorption in the gut, ascorbate within mammalian systems can regulate cellular iron uptake and metabolism. Recent evidence also indicates that ascorbate is a novel modulator of the classical transferrin–iron uptake pathway, which provides almost all iron for cellular demands and erythropoiesis under physiological conditions. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25048971/ and https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/immunology-and-microbiology/vitamin-c)

Ferrous ascorbate is a synthetic chelate of iron in the ferrous state
with ascorbic acid. Ascorbic acid, in quantities greater than 200mg, increases the absorption of medicinal iron by at least 30%. Ferrous ascorbate has a high iron content of 12–15%. In the ascorbate preparation, iron is maximally absorbed due to inhibition of conversion of ferrous into ferric iron, inhibition of the effects of phytates, phosphates and oxalates on iron absorption, and inhibition of formation of insoluble iron complexes that interfere with absorption. (https://www.jsafog.com/doi/JSAFOG/pdf/10.5005/jp-journals-10006-1896)

Ferrous ascorbate has been tested in multiple studies in India and is available for use in maternal anaemia. One study by the Sri Venkateshwaraa Medical College Hospital and Research Centre evaluated the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of different iron supplements among antenatal women with iron deficiency. It compared over a period of 60 days, ferrous ascorbate 200mg BD with ferrous sulphate 200mg BD, ferrous fumarate 200mg BD and IV iron sucrose 200mg twice weekly. Results demonstrated that injectable iron sucrose showed a significant improvement in mean haemoglobin percentage compared to the various oral preparations. However, on analysing the cost-effectiveness ratio, it was found out that the cost incurred per increase in Hb% was less in the ferrous sulphate group, followed by iron sucrose, ferrous fumarate, and ferrous ascorbate. (https://www.njppp.com/fulltext/28-1662616460.pdf?1691362449)

Other studies are looking at iron supplements plus vitamin C supplements (i.e not combined). A study by the Fetal Medicine Foundation (NCT03564756) aimed to identify the effects of vitamin C on anaemia in pregnancy. It was planned that pregnant women of less than 20 weeks gestation with iron deficiency anaemia would be given one iron tablet plus 1000mg Vitamin C per day, or a control of one iron tablet plus a placebo tablet. However, the study was withdrawn due to difficulties with enrolment.

Another study in India aimed to determine the effect of iron and folic acid tablets taken with vitamin C tablets, compared to iron and folic acid tablets taken with vitamin C rich foods on the anaemia of pregnant women attending a tertiary care hospital in Puducherry. The outcome studied was the mean difference in haemoglobin level between the intervention and control arm. Results of the study are unknown. (https://www.ctri.nic.in/Clinicaltrials/pmaindet2.php?trialid=68281)

Name: Xpert® TV
Indication: Detection of T vaginalis
Mechanism of action: NAAT
Key features and challenges:
The Xpert® TV assay, performed on the GeneXpert® System, is an automated, cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) designed for the detection of Trichomonas vaginalis in symptomatic and asymptomatic individuals. The GeneXpert® platform integrates sample preparation, amplification, and detection within a single-use, self-contained cartridge. Each cartridge incorporates three internal controls: a Sample Adequacy Control (SAC) to confirm appropriate specimen collection, a Sample Processing Control (SPC) to verify correct processing, and a Probe Check Control (PCC) to monitor reagent integrity. 
(https://www.cepheid.com/en-AU/tests/blood-virology-womens-health-sexual-health/xpert-tv.html#nav-id-2).
The Xpert® TV assay provides molecular detection with high analytical sensitivity and specificity, enabling more accurate diagnosis compared with traditional microscopy-based methods. The platform is widely implemented in laboratory and near-patient settings and supports streamlined workflows through automated processing.
However, GeneXpert® systems require stable electricity, temperature-controlled environments, routine calibration, and cartridge supply chains, which may limit deployment in lower-level facilities in low- and middle-income countries. As a result, they are often considered more suitable for district-level hospitals and above, although ongoing efforts aim to expand access to more remote primary healthcare settings. 
(https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9035340/).
Key challenges include infrastructure dependence, equipment and cartridge costs, and sustainability of maintenance in resource-limited environments. While the Xpert® TV assay offers reliable molecular detection and quality control safeguards, broader decentralization will depend on addressing operational and cost constraints.

Key challenges include dependence on GeneXpert instrument infrastructure, cartridge-based consumables, and associated costs. While the test provides rapid, multiplex molecular detection suitable for near-patient use, scalability in resource-limited settings may depend on existing platform availability and sustainable procurement mechanisms.
