Name: Zhukovsky Double Balloon Obstetric Catheter
Indication: Indicated for the temporary control or reduction of postpartum uterine and vaginal bleeding when conservative management is warranted.
Mechanism of action: Provides direct intrauterine and intravaginal pressure to promote haemostasis.
Key features and challenges:
The Zhukovsky Double Balloon Obstetric Catheter is a dual-balloon tamponade device consisting of an intrauterine balloon and a vaginal balloon. It is primarily used in Russian-speaking countries and is also available in single-balloon configurations (uterine-only or vaginal-only). The design enables close apposition of the intrauterine balloon to the uterine walls, limiting blood accumulation within the cavity. The addition of a vaginal balloon generates multidirectional compression forces from both the uterus and vagina, potentially enhancing haemostasis through mechanisms such as lower uterine segment compression.
An observational controlled trial evaluated combined management including standard therapy (fresh frozen plasma, erythrocyte mass transfusion, uterotonics, and hemostatic agents), surgical hemostasis where required, and insertion of the Zhukovsky double balloon, compared with standard management alone (2019: https://mednexus.org/doi/full/10.1097/FM9.0000000000000002
). The combined approach was associated with a 1.5-fold reduction in blood loss and a 6.72-fold reduction in hysterectomy rates compared with controls. Additional investigation has assessed the use of the Zhukovsky balloon in women undergoing postpartum hysterectomy for severe bleeding (2019: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30614315/), suggesting potential utility in high-risk or refractory cases.
Key challenges include reliance on observational data without large randomized controlled trials, limited geographic adoption, and variability in comparative effectiveness against other commercially available balloon tamponade systems. Broader evaluation across diverse clinical settings is needed to clarify its role within standardized postpartum haemorrhage management algorithms.

Developers: Entasis Therapeutics; Global Antibiotic Research and Development Partnership (GARDP)
Indication: Treatment of uncomplicated gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: DNA gyrase inhibition
Key features and challenges:
Zoliflodacin is a first-in-class, orally administered antibiotic and novel DNA gyrase inhibitor targeting Neisseria gonorrhoeae. It was originally developed by AstraZeneca and is currently being advanced by Entasis Therapeutics for the treatment of uncomplicated gonorrhoea. An oral powder formulation is under clinical development. Zoliflodacin received Qualified Infectious Disease Product (QIDP) designation and Fast Track status from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in 2014.
In 2023, a global Phase III registration trial reported that zoliflodacin met its primary endpoint, demonstrating statistical non-inferiority for microbiological cure at the urogenital site compared with intramuscular ceftriaxone plus oral azithromycin. 
(https://adis.springer.com/trials/700286757
; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03959527). 
These findings support its potential as an effective oral alternative to current injectable first-line therapy.
A 2023 preclinical study further evaluated combination therapy including zoliflodacin and doxycycline, demonstrating enhanced bactericidal activity and suppression of resistance emergence compared with zoliflodacin monotherapy (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/pharmacology/articles/10.3389/fphar.2023.1291885/full). 
These data suggest potential benefits of combination strategies to optimize efficacy and mitigate resistance development.
Key challenges include the need for continued evaluation of resistance dynamics, assessment of activity at extragenital sites, and investigation of potential synergistic or antagonistic effects when co-administered with other antibiotics for gonorrhoea or concomitant STIs. While Phase III results are promising, regulatory approval, cost considerations, and post-marketing surveillance will be critical to defining its role in future gonorrhoea treatment guidelines.

The platform received CE marking in April 2019, clearance from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in August 2019, and CLIA-waived status in March 2021.
The system is designed for use with clinician- or self-collected female vaginal swabs obtained in clinical settings, as well as male urine specimens. It is intended to be user-friendly, requiring no calibration, preventive maintenance, or subjective interpretation of results, and can be operated by non-laboratory-trained personnel. 
(https://binxprod.blob.core.windows.net/uploads-mybinxhealth-com/binx_io_Brochure_bad11732c7/binx_io_Brochure_bad11732c7.pdf).
A 2021 clinical evaluation study assessed the performance of the binx io platform for CT/NG detection in point-of-care settings (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34225553/). 
The assay demonstrated sensitivity and specificity comparable to standard laboratory-based NAAT platforms, supporting its use as a near-patient molecular diagnostic alternative to centralized laboratory testing.
Key challenges include dependence on cartridge-based consumables, cost considerations relative to laboratory-based batch testing, and implementation logistics in resource-constrained settings. While the platform offers rapid turnaround time and decentralized testing capability, sustained uptake will depend on affordability, supply chain reliability, and integration into routine clinical workflows.

The cobas® CT/NG assay is a qualitative nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) designed for the detection of Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae on an automated molecular diagnostic platform. However, the assay’s validated performance across urogenital and extragenital specimen types supports its utility in comprehensive gonorrhoea screening strategies, particularly in high-prevalence and high-risk populations.

Mechanism of action: amplification reaction
Key features and challenges:
The eazyplex® STD complete test is a qualitative in vitro diagnostic assay designed for rapid detection of multiple sexually transmitted pathogens, including Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Ureaplasma urealyticum, Mycoplasma hominis, Mycoplasma genitalium, and Treponema pallidum, from swab specimens (https://www.eazyplex.com/en-gb/STDs). 
The assay delivers results within approximately 25 minutes and does not require prior DNA extraction. Sample preparation takes approximately 3 minutes, after which the specimen is directly added to a freeze-dried, ready-to-use amplification reaction. All necessary buffers and reagents are included in the kit, and real-time amplification results are displayed during the run.
A 2023 study evaluated the performance of the eazyplex® system compared with a reference diagnostic method (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s15010-023-01981-5#Ack1). 
Reported overall sensitivity and specificity were 88% and 98% for N. gonorrhoeae, 82% and 100% for C. trachomatis, 70% and >99% for U. urealyticum, and 85% and 98% for M. hominis. Sensitivity for N. gonorrhoeae and U. urealyticum in urethral samples reached 100%. Although specific performance metrics for M. genitalium were not detailed in the study summary, the multiplex platform includes its detection capability within the assay panel.
Key challenges include variability in sensitivity across pathogens and specimen types, limited publicly available performance data specifically for M. genitalium, and the need for further validation in diverse clinical settings. While the platform offers rapid turnaround time and simplified workflow suitable for point-of-care testing, comparative performance against high-sensitivity laboratory-based NAATs may influence its role in routine M. genitalium diagnosis.

Name: ebb Complete Tamponade System
Developers: The American Hospital of Paris; Clinical Innovations
Indication: Indicated for the temporary control or reduction of postpartum uterine and vaginal bleeding when conservative management is warranted.
Mechanism of action: Provides direct intrauterine and intravaginal pressure to promote haemostasis.
Key features and challenges:
The ebb Complete Tamponade System is a disposable, multi-lumen catheter with an integrated dual-balloon design intended for control of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) originating from the uterus and vagina. The system comprises an upper uterine balloon and a lower vaginal balloon that are permanently assembled and designed to function together. The uterine balloon includes separate lumens for inflation/deflation, irrigation, and drainage, while the vaginal balloon includes a lumen for inflation and deflation. The device may remain in situ for up to 24 hours during postoperative management.
A distinguishing feature of the ebb system is its malleable polyurethane balloon material, which allows the balloon to conform more effectively to uterine anatomy, including in the presence of fibroids or anatomical variations such as a uterine horn. The maximum recommended fill volumes are 750 mL for the uterine balloon and 300 mL for the vaginal balloon, although uterine balloon volumes may be exceeded when clinically necessary, such as in cases of global uterine atony. Inflation can be performed directly from an intravenous fluid bag without requiring syringes or stopcocks, facilitating rapid deployment (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29535559/).
A post-marketing surveillance study published in 2014 evaluated the device in 51 women with PPH due to uterine atony or abnormal placentation (https://www.ajog.org/article/S0002-9378(13)00956-3/fulltext). The median interval from delivery to balloon placement was 2.2 hours for the overall cohort and 1.3 hours in women with uterine atony only. Following placement, bleeding decreased in 43% of cases and ceased in 55%, resulting in haemorrhage control (decreased or stopped bleeding) in 98% of patients. Nearly half of the women required uterine balloon volumes greater than 500 mL to achieve haemostasis. The device was acquired by Clinical Innovations LLC from Glenveigh Medical in 2014.
Key challenges include limited large-scale comparative effectiveness data against other balloon tamponade systems, reliance on observational and post-marketing data, and the need for trained personnel for appropriate placement and monitoring. Further randomized controlled trials would strengthen evidence regarding its relative efficacy and cost-effectiveness in diverse PPH settings.

Name: sFlt-1/PlGF ratio based testing - PE
Developers: Roche Diagnostics; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc; Medical University Vienna; Charité University Medicine Berlin
Indication: Early detection of PE
Target: Serum or urine levels of sflt-1 and PlGF
Mechanism of action: Using immunoassay methods to identify and quantify sFlt-1/PlGF ratio in patient samples
Key features and challenges:
Soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1) and placental growth factor (PlGF) are angiogenic biomarkers implicated in the pathogenesis of preeclampsia (PE). In 2003, Maynard et al. demonstrated that excess placental production of sFlt-1, an antagonist of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and PlGF, contributes to endothelial dysfunction and clinical features of PE. Subsequent research has established that elevated sFlt-1, reduced PlGF, and an increased sFlt-1/PlGF ratio are strongly associated with PE and other placenta-related disorders, including intrauterine growth restriction and stillbirth. These alterations are more pronounced in early-onset disease and may be detectable prior to clinical symptom onset.
Gestational age–specific cut-offs have been proposed. A study published in 2013 identified sFlt-1/PlGF ratio thresholds of >85 (20 + 0 to 33 + 6 weeks) and >110 (≥34 + 0 weeks) as highly suggestive of PE, with a cut-off of 33 demonstrating high sensitivity (95%) and specificity (94%) for exclusion of disease (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24166751/). The PROGNOSIS study (2016) validated a single cut-off of <38 to reliably rule out PE within one week (negative predictive value >96%) and ≥38 to rule in PE within four weeks (positive predictive value >25%) (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27399996/). Ongoing research continues to assess the predictive performance of the ratio across gestational ages and in combination with other clinical or ultrasound parameters (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4369131/#b8).
Commercial automated assays have been developed, including Roche’s Elecsys sFlt-1 and PlGF immunoassays, enabling rapid laboratory-based assessment in clinical settings (https://diagnostics.roche.com/be/en/products/params/elecsys-sflt-1-plgf-preeclampsia.html
; https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0009912010000731). 
As of 2022, use of these biomarkers had been incorporated into German national guidelines for hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, though broader international guideline adoption remains variable (https://register.awmf.org/assets/guidelines/015-018l_S2k_Diagnostik_Therapie_hypertensiver_Schwangerschaftserkrankungen_2019-07.pdf).
Emerging research has explored non-invasive urine-based testing. A 2024 study evaluated soluble proteins and urine-derived exosomes using a biologically intact exosome separation technology (BEST) platform (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-024-75080-2). The urinary sFlt-1/PlGF ratio demonstrated higher sensitivity compared with commercial blood-based assays, suggesting potential for non-invasive early risk stratification. Additional studies have similarly reported promising results for urinary sFlt-1/PlGF testing (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11033-023-09053-5).
Key challenges include variability in gestational age–specific cut-offs, differences in assay platforms, cost and laboratory infrastructure requirements, and limited global harmonization of guideline recommendations. While the sFlt-1/PlGF ratio is well validated for short-term prediction and rule-out of PE, further research is needed to standardize implementation pathways, evaluate cost-effectiveness across health systems, and assess integration with other predictive tools.
Recent updates:
Roche Diagnostics test is CE approved since 2009 (https://www.nsmedicaldevices.com/news/roche_diagnostics_launches_first_diagnostic_preeclampsia_test_in_europe_090106/)
Thermo Fisher Scientific test is FDA approved as of 2023 (https://ir.thermofisher.com/investors/news-events/news/news-details/2023/Thermo-Fisher-Scientific-Announces-FDA-Clearance-of-Breakthrough-Immunoassays-to-Aid-in-the-Risk-Assessment-of-Preeclampsia/default.aspx)

Name: sFlt-1/PlGF ratio-based testing - PTL
Developers: Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development; Washington University
Indication: Detection and prediction of PTL
Target:
Serum levels of soluble Fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFLT-1) and
placental growth factor (PlGF)
Mechanism of action: Soluble Fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFLT-1) and placental growth factor (PlGF), which is one of the vascular endothelial growth factors (VEGFs), play a key role in angiogenesis (an important process in vascularization of the placenta) and their ratio may have an effect on preterm birth.
Key features and challenges:
Soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1) and placental growth factor (PlGF) are key regulators of placental angiogenesis. The sFlt-1/PlGF ratio is well established in the evaluation of preeclampsia and has been shown to rise approximately 4–5 weeks before clinical onset of disease. Because preterm birth (PTB) is increasingly considered a placental disorder in certain phenotypes, this angiogenic biomarker ratio has been investigated as a potential indicator of placental dysfunction and spontaneous PTB (sPTB). In 2023, evidence suggested that sFlt-1 and PlGF may be detected in extracellular vesicles, including exosomes, in maternal plasma, supporting their potential role in placental disease prediction.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36619545/)
In 2019, the PREPARE (Prematurity REduction by Pre-eclampsia cARE) study proposed an integrated care model incorporating risk stratification tools, including the sFlt-1/PlGF ratio, to reduce preterm birth among women with preeclampsia. Published outcome data from this initiative remain limited.
(https://bmcpregnancychildbirth.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12884-019-2445-x)
In 2020, a study assessing women with early-onset (<34 weeks) preeclampsia found that an sFlt-1/PlGF ratio >655 at diagnosis was associated with a five-fold increased risk of delivery within 48 hours, highlighting its utility in predicting imminent preterm delivery in the context of severe placental disease.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32707515/)
In 2023, research conducted at the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development reported that abnormal sFlt-1/PlGF ratios at 28–32 weeks’ gestation were associated with subsequent preterm delivery due to preterm labour with intact membranes or preterm premature rupture of membranes, but only in cases with placental lesions of maternal vascular malperfusion. No significant association was observed in cases without such placental pathology, suggesting that predictive value may be limited to specific placental-mediated phenotypes of PTB.
(https://reporter.nih.gov/search/2Qv3svS9-EmT030NkiIPzw/project-details/10915313)
Overall, sFlt-1/PlGF ratio testing is well validated in preeclampsia and shows emerging potential as a predictive biomarker for preterm birth in cases associated with placental malperfusion. However, its predictive utility for spontaneous PTL without underlying placental pathology remains uncertain.
